News.title: Desperate hunt for boy, 3, who vanished from village playground as cops ask locals to search their gardens and sheds
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

FIND HIM Desperate hunt for boy, 3, who vanished from village playground as cops ask locals to search their gardens and sheds

A DESPERATE hunt has been launched for a missing three-year-old boy who vanished from a village playground.

Noah was last seen at 3pm on Tuesday in Brantham, Suffolk, as officers urge locals to search their gardens and sheds.



The child became separated from a relative after visiting the playground in Merriam Close.

Noah is reported to have run off down the alleyway beside the playground towards the new build housing estate, police said.



The three-year-old is white with curly ginger hair and was wearing a white t-shirt with the TV character Bluey on, shorts and white trainers.

The BBC reported that more than 100 people had joined the searches on Tuesday evening.

A Coastguard helicopter was seen circling the village, which is near the estuary of the River Stour.

Suffolk Constabulary has issued an urgent appeal for help to locate the missing three-year-old.

A spokesperson for the force said: “Emergency services are currently in Brantham conducting searches.

“Residents in the area are asked to check their gardens, sheds and outbuildings.”



A spokesperson for HM Coastguard said: “We are assisting Suffolk Constabulary with an incident at Brantham by sending an HM Coastguard helicopter and Coastguard Rescue Teams from Felixstowe and Holbrook.”

Anyone who thinks they have seen Noah is asked to contact Suffolk Police, quoting CAD 203 of 15 September.

News.title: Dramatic moment fashion boss grabs protester on runway, holds her down and covers her mouth as he’s placed on leave
News.content:
THIS is the shocking moment a top fashion boss reportedly tackles a protester to the ground in the middle of a major runway show.

Dramatic footage shows the CEO wrapping one leg around the screaming woman while clamping a hand over her face at New York Fashion week.



The bizarre brawl unfolded on Sunday after activists from the People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA) stormed onto the catwalk.

Shouting and waving signs, the pair screamed “get wool off the runway now” as top models sashayed past them at Swedish brand COS’s Fall-Winter 2026 show.





But their efforts were thwarted by Steven Kolb, the CEO of the Council of Fashion Designers of America (CFDA), who allegedly jumped in and manhandled the pair.

Wrapping both arms around one protestor, he dragged her to the floor while a second clip shows him grabbing a male protestors face to stop him shouting.

READ MORE FAN FURY Wild moment mass brawl erupts in stands as fan stomps on man & punches thrown

In a statement following the runway ruckus, PETA accused Kolb of “assaulting” their members.

Top fashion honcho Kolb later apologised for his “inappropriate” actions.



He has agreed to meet and apologise to the PETA protestors who did not “deserve that treatment”.

“I am deeply sorry and hold myself accountable,” the fashion chief wrote on Instagram shortly after the catwalk chaos.

He insisted that the extraordinary outburst was “out of character” and admitted there was “no justification for physically restraining another person”.



The top boss has taken leave, effective immediately, and will reportedly be seeking professional help.

PETA founder Ingrid Newkirk said: “Today’s actions show how top people in fashion use violence to silence people who expose how sheep are… killed for scarfs and sweaters.

“PETA is calling on H&M and COS to ban wool from its collections and is urging everyone to shop elsewhere until they do.”

Animal rights prptestor Mason Melito, 22, told CNN that the “violence the CEO of the CFDA showed toward us… completely mirrors the violence inherent in the wool industry”.

PETA claimed the pair were filing for criminal charges against Kolb – but Melito said they are “just considering our options right now.”



He added: “What we really want to do is talk to Mr. Kolb.”

CFDA organises New York Fashion Week and hosts the awards ceremony dubbed the “Oscars of Fashion”.

News.title: Harry and Meg school-run fiasco shows they’ll NEVER stop bleating until they get their security – paid for by YOU
News.content:
TWO days. That is how long Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet lasted at their English prep school before their parents pulled them out.

Archie is seven, his sister five. They arrived in pristine uniforms on the Monday and were gone by the Wednesday, which is not even long enough to lose a jumper.



“Security” was the first word out — leaked by a not-so-mysterious figure close to Team Sussex.

It made the television news.



Then the story developed. By the time it reached glossy mag Hello!, the villain had become the traffic, the distance, the impossible school run.

What actually happened, we later learnt, was that the convoy carrying the kids had simply become separated in busy traffic.



The exclusives were handed out — by Team Sussex or a source close to them — like Meg’s sprinkles to a few sympathetic outlets, mostly not on the record.

We have been here before.

In May 2023, the couple’s spokesman announced a near-catastrophic car chase through Manhattan — a relentless pursuit lasting over two hours, at the hands of highly aggressive paparazzi.

It led to bulletins on both sides of the Atlantic and invited the Diana/Paris comparison, which was the point.



The tale fell apart within a day.

The NYPD logged no collisions, no ­injuries, no arrests.

The then-Mayor of New York, Eric Adams, said he found claims of a two-hour, high-speed chase in his city hard to believe.



The cab driver who had them in the back, Sukhcharn Singh, would not call it a chase at all — ten minutes, and he was never in danger.

Two hours thus became ten minutes, and nobody “close to Team Sussex” who had spun this nonsense ever explained the gap.

That is why the school story matters.

This is the Meghan and Harry tale repackaged.

We all worry about our kids and nobody minds this family being protected.



But it is equally clear Harry and Meghan will not stop bleating about their security until they get what they want out of the royal protection service, Ravec.

Cute pictures one day, the same children revealed to have been pulled from school the next. Both can be true. The Sussexes are worried parents and, at the same time, a cynical pair with a firm eye on the outcome.

Media lawyers sent a letter insisting the children were private and must never be photographed. Those same children then appear on a social media account with millions of followers.



Notices go out about their privacy, from Press regulator IPSO, and days later the media is briefed that the kids are no longer at their school.

Revealed by a newspaper, it is intrusion.

Revealed by the family and set to a pop soundtrack, it is a moment.

You don’t need Einstein to see the play, from a prince who has spent years taking on the newspaper groups over all this.

Let’s be clear about one thing. Nobody wishes these children any harm. Not this trade, not the readers, not anyone.



They are seven and five and they didn’t choose this life.

But they have been used, and not by the photographers. They have been used by the two people whose job it was to keep them out of all this.

We should take the fear seriously, though.

Harry’s mother died in a car that was chased into a tunnel 29 years ago last month, driven by a man over the drink-drive limit — and the Prince has said ever since that the photographers killed her.

The world has moved on. Harry hasn’t, and it is hard to blame him.



For years, photographs of his children were arranged so we never quite saw their appearance — hoods adjusted, faces turned.

Then comes footage of them running through long grass in the sun. And the next moment, their school has lost them.

At the other end of the family, the Wales children have gone to school for years without a single bulletin once term started. No convoy. No pictures.

Strip it back and this is about armed officers, paid for by the public, being permanently assigned. Protection is not something you decide you are owed. It is provided when the danger warrants it.

There is an obvious answer — and it isn’t new. Hire retired royalty protection officers. They retire in their mid-fifties, fit, word-perfect on the drills, fluent in the radios and the rhythm of a school gate.



Harry’s own father did exactly that for Camilla before they married — two full-time men, privately funded and not a penny of public money spent.

Ravec has written to Harry. A board has been convened and a review is under way, now that he and his family are living here.

The ground has shifted and it is right that officials look again, weighing the threat and nothing else.

Experts put private cover at around £2.3million a year. That is 30-odd constables who could be on the beat instead.

If it gets the nod, there will be a backlash, and by then it will be too late to walk it back.



The Palace won’t comment. Neither will the Home Office. Ravec has never publicly discussed anything ever.

Meanwhile, the rest of us cope.

Every school day, millions of parents must find their young kids’ shoes in the morning, get the breakfast cereal down them and still get to work.

If a household with its own protection team cannot foresee traffic in the first week of term, who can?

Here’s an idea. Set the alarm three-quarters of an hour earlier.



Unless there is a shortage of alarm clocks in their local shops — in which case, Harry, I will send one free of charge.

News.title: Seriously injured bell ringer rescued by crane after horror 20ft fall inside church tower
News.content:
A BELL ringer had to be rescued by crane after he plunged almost 20ft inside a church tower.

Fire crews had to smash through a leaded window to get to the badly injured man.



He received life-saving aid from specialist medics in the 142ft tower before being lowered down during a two-hour rescue.

It happened on Sunday just before the 10.30am service at St Luke’s and Christ Church in Chelsea, West London, when the bells are usually rung for 20 minutes beforehand.



A source said the victim was craned because the tower was “such a confined space”.

London Fire Brigade said it had been called “to reports of a man who had fallen around five to six metres in the church bell tower”.

Emergency services, including an air ambulance and a medical hazardous area response team, also attended the scene.

The man was transported to a major trauma centre at hospital that specialises in treating life-changing injuries.

The church said the “whole community is in deep shock”.

It added: “The injured party was stabilised at the scene and subsequently transferred to hospital where he is currently being treated for his injuries.”



St Luke’s has ten bells that were cast 200 years ago.

They are rung by a team of volunteers.

The church, where author Charles Dickens married in 1836, is known for hosting big charity fundraisers, with Prince William and Prince Harry both attending events in the past.

News.title: Cruel dementia leaves relatives feeling relief at death – their loved one has already been mourned as they slowly vanish
News.content:
MY deepest sympathy to Andy ­Burnham following the death of his father Roy, who had Alzheimer’s.

Consequently, he didn’t know that his son had become Prime Minister.





That’s perhaps the cruellest part of this terrible disease.

It not only robs people of their memories, but often stops them enjoying the special moments of the present day.

My 95-year-old mother has Alzheimer’s too, so I know all too well how soul-destroying it is to watch someone ­disappear by degrees.

It’s a prolonged form of grief because there are so many moments of loss before the final one.

Nearly one million people in the UK are currently ­living with some form of dementia and, as our population ages, the number is ­projected to rise to 1.4million by 2040.

It’s fair to say that dementia is one of the great health and social care ­challenges of our age, so it’s good to have a PM who clearly understands that.

On rare occasions, my mum shows a flicker of ­recognition towards me, but mostly not.

So my regular visits to her care home are taken up with me explaining who I am, then ­listening to imaginary worries that are escalated by the disease.





It’s exhausting and that’s just in short bursts.

For anyone who’s doing the day-to-day caring themselves, I don’t know how they cope.

Recent research from the Alzheimer’s Society found that 43 per cent of those caring for someone with dementia reach breaking point.

More than half said ­caring had damaged their mental health.

I’m only surprised it’s not higher, ­particularly if you’re dealing with the frightened confusion of someone who no longer knows who you are, or constant anger or, in many cases, physical ­aggression.

In her late eighties, my mother was ­living independently and a keen volunteer guide at Westminster Abbey.

She adored that job, but when she fell and shattered her hip at home, she had to take time out after a replacement and went rapidly downhill from there.

“I hate not being able to do things for myself,” she said shortly after the op.



“If I ever go doolally, just take me out to sea in a boat and push me overboard.”

And she wasn’t joking.

So when I look at her now, three years after her move to a care home, I know full well that if she was still compos mentis, she’d be hissing at me to put her out of her misery.

I can’t and, of course, I wouldn’t. But it’s also important to say at this juncture that, when it finally comes, her death will be a release.

If you’re someone whose loved one lives with dementia but you still experience those small pockets of happiness, then it’s understandable you will want to keep them with you for as long as possible. But it’s not always like that.

People of a certain age will remember Judith Chalmers, the spirited, adventurous globe-trotter who presented travel shows such as Wish You Were Here.

She died in May this year, aged 90, from complications relating to Alzheimer’s disease.

The day after her death, her son Mark Durden-Smith, also a TV presenter, was interviewed live from her garden.

When the news presenter expressed sympathy for his loss, Mark had the courage to say: “It’s a relief, to be honest.”

I say courage, because society has ­constructed a rather singular approach to grief in which, to many, the only ­permissible emotion following a death is devastation.



But dementia doesn’t work like that, and by the time death comes, families have already mourned the loss of memories, chats, personality and recognition one painful piece at a time.

Until eventually, they see you as a stranger and retreat within themselves to such an extent that they’re having no life at all.

She’s no Madge for Teri

DESPERATE Housewives star Teri Hatcher is taking over the Miranda Priestly role in the stage version of The Devil Wears Prada.

Apparently, they wanted Madonna but she turned it down.

Good. In 2002, I saw her make her West End theatre debut in the play Up For Grabs, in which she played a ruthless art dealer.

Not only was she painfully awkward, but the audience was packed with her music fans who rose to their feet and shouted, “Go, girl!” with gusto when she appeared on stage.

As the mighty Miranda might say, please bore someone else with your enthusiasm.



SORRY, PARK IS CLOSED

IS there anyone left in the park with George?

First, Ariana Grande pulled out of the forthcoming theatre production of Sunday In The Park With George after saying she needs a mental health break from being under public scrutiny. Fair enough.

But now her co-star Jonathan Bailey, of Bridgerton fame, has issued a long-winded and vague statement about how it’s his “passion project” and how lucky he feels to have “shared in its journey with the team” but that he’s also dropping out. Go figure.

Producers are now scrabbling around for replacements but the show could be delayed for a year or more.

Which, in a mostly freelance-based industry where jobs are hard to come by, will be bad news for the dedicated backstage team who have bills to pay.

MANY kids are missing out on school trips because the cost is so high.

Research ­suggests that one in four parents who paid for a foreign trip last year spent more than £1,000.

Eek. The only school trip I ever went on was a day trip to Calais in 1977 that cost £55.

The idea was to improve our French, and I was encouraged to ask a passer-by where the nearest market was. He replied: “I dunno, love. I’m from Birmingham.”



ESCORT JESTER

ANOTHER day, another Sussex drama.

This time, their security team has decided that Archie and Lilibet’s school run isn’t “operationally secure” because of distance and heavy traffic.

Hmmm.

The distance was known from the second they signed up to the school, and heavy morning traffic at the start of the autumn term is hardly a new phenomenon.

Could this and the fact that the Home Office is currently reviewing their security arrangements by any chance be related?

VOTE FOR COMMON SENSE . .

THE PM’s fondness for devolution is being sorely tested by the small Oxfordshire village of Piddington, which was expected yesterday to vote to formally withdraw itself from the UK and become a principality like Monaco.

Unfortunately for them, it’s not legal. But what it has achieved is plenty of publicity for their major grievance.

Namely the plans for 1,250 undocumented, male asylum seekers to be accommodated on an old Ministry of Defence site next door.

The women of Piddington (population 358) made a video expressing their concerns that has now been viewed millions of times, and also wrote to every female MP for support.

“They would outnumber us ten to one. As fellow women, you will understand the serious risks,” they said.



Meanwhile, their own MP – Lib Dem Calum Miller – has signed a letter in support of the asylum seekers.

No doubt the people of Piddington will remember this when he next appears on their doorstep asking for votes.

Meanwhile, it remains to be seen if this wholly peaceful, yet devastatingly effective protest will spark enough common sense from the Home Office to rethink the plan.

Whatever the outcome, I look forward to the TV series of Mrs Bates (or whoever) vs The Home Office.

THE rescue team that responds to serious call-outs on Snowdon has said it needs a “serious conversation about what is happening in our mountains”.

They’re talking about climbers who are “unprepared for what they are facing”.

Otherwise known as, sigh, social media influencers.

Yes, just like the “adventure junkies” who get into trouble in the world’s “no-go” areas, we’re now seeing a trend for photos taken in hard-to-reach terrain with no warning of the preparation it takes to get there.

Consequently, the rescue teams say they dealt with 59 emergencies in August alone.



“There has to be greater focus on prevention and responsibility,” says one of the rescuers.

Or better still, just stick to taking photos in cute bakeries.

News.title: Secret Brit plans to fight enemies in space revealed after US confirms it already has weapons in orbit
News.content:
BRITAIN is gearing up to fight enemies in space with secret weapons as a global arms race heats up.

Defence chiefs are developing “offensive capabilities” to counter threats from Russia and China – but exactly what they involve is a closely guarded secret.



The push is revealed in Britain’s new Space Strategy, which says the UK must be able to “deny adversaries” freedom of action in space.

Experts say such technology could include jamming enemy satellites, launching cyber attacks or even using lasers to temporarily blind their sensors.



It comes as the US revealed for the first time it already has “space control weapons” stationed in orbit.

US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink refused to reveal what the weapons can do amid growing fears over Russia and China’s activities in space.



Former Armed Forces minister Al Carns told The Sun: “Space is the next frontier of war fighting. China is a superpower. America is the same.

“We have got to accept that the UK is a middle power.”

Russia and China have both tested weapons capable of physically destroying satellites, while Moscow has already used jamming and cyber attacks during its invasion of Ukraine.

Dr Mark Hilborne, of King’s College London’s Defence Studies Department, said: “The kind of capabilities the UK could use would be things like electronic warfare and jamming… things like cyber attacks, offensive cyber attacks.”



He said directed-energy weapons could also be used to “dazzle” satellite sensors and temporarily blind them, with jamming, cyber attacks and directed energy all “achievable” for Britain.

And Dr Hilborne warned the impact of an attack on vital satellite services could quickly be felt by ordinary Brits.

He said: “Banking, power grids, many many military functions, your Uber driver and the pizza delivery guy – all of them would be undermined by GPS going down.”

Space warfare expert Juliana Suess, an Associate Fellow at defence think tank RUSI, said there was “quite a lot to be worried about” from Russian and Chinese activity in space.



She said disruption to satellite navigation was already an “everyday occurrence” in Ukraine, the Baltics and Eastern Europe, adding: “Especially in the initial stages of a conflict, I think the attempt to deny satellite services is almost guaranteed because it’s something that we’ve already seen.”

Luke de Pulford, executive director of the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China, warned: “Beijing isn’t investing billions in counter-space capabilities for pure research purposes; they are preparing to cripple their adversaries at the push of a button.

“The UK is playing catch up and still refuses to recognise the threat.”

Britain’s new Space Strategy, published earlier this month, says the UK must be able to “deny adversaries” freedom of action in space, with operations “both defensive and offensive in nature”.



By 2035, defence chiefs want a “significantly expanded set of military capabilities in space” – but officials are refusing to reveal what those future capabilities will involve because of security sensitivities.

Some £880million is being invested over four years in intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance and Space Control.

An MoD spokesperson said: “From communications, to retail, to banking, Space is vital to our security and prosperity.

“We’re working closely with allies to counter growing threats in an increasingly important environment.

“Our new space strategy, backed by £7.8 billion, will help strengthen Britain’s defences, protecting the critical space capabilities we rely on every day.”

News.title: Moment exhausted 15st ram Rambo gets stuck in pipe after fleeing flock of nine randy ewes
News.content:
A KNACKERED ram got wedged in a concrete pipe after taking ­refuge from a flock of nine “amorous” ewes.

Bulky Rambo, who weighs 15st 10lbs, headed into the culvert to take a rest from his duties but ended up having to be freed by firefighters.



The crews used chimney rods and ropes to winkle him out after managing to slip a sheet beneath his bulk.

Owner Bex Maynard said Rambo emerged completely unharmed on Sunday from the pipe at Western Farm in Kingsdon, Somerset.



She joked: “Rambo maintains that he was simply ­taking a well-earned break from his romantic duties.

“To be fair, there are nine rather amorous ewes all competing for his undivided attention and a chap is entitled to a little peace and quiet occasionally.”



She added: “Judging by Rambo’s expression, he emerged considerably less concerned by the whole episode than everyone else involved.

“We cannot thank the crews enough for coming out, taking such care of the daft bugger and getting him safely out.”



Bex has put in a gate and mesh across the culvert’s entrance to avoid a repeat.

You can donate here: https://www.justgiving.com/team/rambos-pipe-dream

News.title: Lucy Letby inquiry - latest: Nurse's 'boyfriend' doctor 'put her before patients'
News.content:
Serial killer Letby, now 36, was convicted of killing seven babies - a scathing report has criticised the hospital where she worked and her 'boyfriend' doctor

An inquiry into the crimes of Lucy Letby, who was convicted of killing seven babies and attempting to murder seven more, has found three deaths could have been avoided if hospital staff had acted differently - and criticised her doctor "boyfriend".

A scathing report said there was a "complete failure to protect babies" at the Countess of Chester Hospital, where Letby, now 36, worked between 2015 and 2016.

The report found safeguarding action should have been taken after a doctor, named in the report as Dr ZA, disregarded an insulin test result for Baby F in August 2015. Had action been taken, the death of Baby I, a two-month-old girl who died in October 2015, would have been prevented.

It also found that, if Letby been moved off the ward following Baby I's death, the deaths of two of three triplet brothers who suffered unexplained collapses in June 2016 - Baby O and Baby P - would have been prevented. It would also have prevented attacks on babies G, H, J, K, L, M and N.

The inquiry found that Letby's doctor "boyfriend", consultant paediatrician Dr Mark Deakin, a colleague of the killer nurse at the hospital, had "blurred boundaries" and put his desire to help her above his duties to his patients.

Other findings included that senior nurses never accepted concerns from consultants about Letby were - or might be - justified, and there was a delay in senior management calling the police. Lady Justice Thirlwall, who chaired the inquiry, said the "lack of consideration shown to parents" by hospital management was "reprehensible".

Letby was found to have killed and harmed babies by injecting air into their blood, poisoning them with insulin and overfeeding them with milk.

News.title: 'Pain endured by the families of victims of Lucy Letby must now force change'
News.content:
'Pain endured by the families of victims of Lucy Letby must now force change'

The deaths of three babies at the hands of Lucy Letby could have been prevented if police were called in sooner, an inquiry prompted by the child serial killer’s crimes has found

View Image Voice of the Mirror has its say...

Every parent who places a desperately ill newborn into the hands of a hospital does so with absolute trust. The Thirlwall Inquiry has laid bare how catastrophically that trust was betrayed at the Countess of Chester Hospital. Babies who should have been protected were left exposed by a system that failed at every level. Warnings were missed, suspicions were ignored, and parents were kept in the dark for years. Lady Justice Thirlwall’s verdict of a “complete failure to protect babies” should haunt the NHS. Nothing can undo the suffering of those families, or answer the unbearable question of how many lives might have been saved. But their pain must now force change. Safeguarding cannot be treated as paperwork, guidance or someone else’s responsibility. It must be the first duty of every hospital, every manager and every clinician. When concerns are raised, action must be immediate, independent and unavoidable. No hierarchy, reputation or fear of embarrassment can come before a child’s safety.

‌



Pensions reform must be fair

A £500-a-year rise in the state pension will be welcome to millions of retirees still struggling with food, energy and council tax bills. The Government has promised that pensioners whose sole income is the state pension will not be dragged into paying income tax simply because their income exceeds the £12,570 threshold. That reassurance matters. But the picture is less clear for those with modest workplace pensions, deferred payments or additional state pension entitlements, who could still face an unexpected tax bill. Ministers must spell out exactly who is protected and who is not. There is also a bigger debate coming. The triple lock has protected pensioners well, but its cost is climbing sharply. Any future reform must be fair, sustainable and, above all, protect the poorest pensioners first.

Fox gives those with Parkinson’s hope

Michael J Fox has spent decades turning a cruel diagnosis into hope for millions. His Emmy speech, and the tears it brought, showed the courage behind that fight. By refusing to surrender to Parkinson’s and raising £1.58 billion for research, he has given sufferers something precious - hope.

News.title: Met Office names 29 areas facing heavy rain on Wednesday - see full list
News.content:
Met Office names 29 areas facing heavy rain on Wednesday - see full list

Weather maps issued by the Met Office have turned blue as a band of low pressure will sweep eastwards throughout Wednesday, leading to downpours for many regions

View 3 Images Rain is forecast on Wednesday (Image: Met Office)

These striking weather maps show large swathes of the country will face heavy rain on Wednesday.

‌



The downpours will sweep eastwards throuhout the day, with western Scotland likely to experience the worst of the weather. The Met Office, which has issued the maps, says the cloud will thicken and temperatures will be below average for the time of year.

‌



It will be a stark contrast to the sunny start to the week, during which the mercury hit 27C in Exeter, Devon, on Monday. It was also a sunny start to the week for most, with 6.7 hours of sunshine recorded in part of Flintshire, north Wales.

‌



View 3 Images Northern Ireland and Scotland look set to receive the brunt of the miserable weather (Image: Met Office)

But nearly 30 areas will see rainfall on Wednesday, forecasters believe. By 7pm, the rainfall appears to be focused over Scotland, with Perth and Kinross, the Highlands, Stirling and Lanarkshire all braced to bear the worst of the miserable conditions. In Northern Ireland, Down and Antrim will also see patches of rain, the maps indicate.

The most severely affected areas could experience 4mm of rain per hour, while 2mm is anticipated more broadly, according to the weather maps.

‌



By 8pm, the heavy band of rain will have shifted to drench Moray, Aberdeenshire and Fife in Scotland, with up to 4mm of rainfall possible, reports the Express.

The rain will also have extended to cover Dumfries and Galloway, as well as Cumbria. The latest weather maps suggest conditions will have deteriorated further in Northern Ireland, with Tyrone and Armagh in particular forecast to experience heavy showers. Conwy and Gwynedd in north Wales are also predicted to see rain showers.

By 11pm, Met Office weather maps turn yellow in places, indicating extremely heavy rainfall. Dumfries and Galloway, South Ayrshire, Stirling and large parts of the Highlands could all see up to 8mm of rain per hour.

‌



View 3 Images Take care on the roads during morning rush-hour as they may be wet (Image: Joe Giddens/PA Wire)

Thursday also appears unsettled too, though the worst-hit areas then will be across the south of England. The Met Office says it will also be breezy then, with strong westerly gusts on the cards.

The fiercest of the gales will be across the western coast of Scotland, including North Ayrshire and Argyll and Bute. Using the weather maps, we have listed below the areas likely to see rain on Wednesday.

News.title: School bus tyre bursts during morning journey in Germany leaving 16 children in hospital
News.content:
School bus tyre bursts during morning journey in Germany leaving 16 children in hospital

Sixteen children were taken to hospital after a school bus tyre burst in the eastern German state of Saxony on Tuesday

View 3 Images Sixteen children were taken to hospital after a school bus tyre burst in a wooded area in the German state of Saxony. (Image: Bild)

Sixteen children have been taken to hospital after a school bus tyre burst in a wooded area in the German state of Saxony.

‌



The bus was carrying 40 schoolchildren to Bärenstein primary school when one of its tyres burst near Bärenstein, in the Erzgebirgskreis district, on Tuesday morning, the German news agency dpa reports.

‌



The bus was travelling along a diversion route for the B95 federal road, which is currently closed for roadworks, when the incident happened, according to dpa.

‌



A Chemnitz police spokesperson said the 16 children taken to hospital are believed to have suffered acoustic trauma. None sustained serious injuries.

View 3 Images The bus was travelling on a diversion route when one of its tyres burst (Image: Bild)

The accident triggered a major emergency response, with paramedics, police and firefighters attending the scene. Fire crews from Sehmatal and the neighbouring areas of Kretscham-Rotensehma, Neudorf, Cranzahl and Sehma were deployed, according to reports.

‌



Emergency services reportedly remained at the scene until the early afternoon.

A replacement bus was arranged for the remaining 24 children. Police said an expert would examine the bus as part of an investigation into what caused the tyre to burst.

View 3 Images Authorities will investigate what caused the tyre to burst (Image: Bild)

Article continues below

It comes after 16 people were injured when a school bus carrying high-school students from Germany crashed in the east of the Netherlands on August 24.

Eight of those injured were seriously hurt, while the others suffered minor injuries, the police department of Gelderland province said at the time.

The bus, which was carrying more than 50 people and was registered in Austria, crashed near the town of Wezep, about 62 miles east of Amsterdam, at around 3am BST after colliding with a delivery van. The van's driver was among those injured.

News.title: Delta flight from Dublin to New York forced to divert after emergency at 35,000ft
News.content:
Delta flight from Dublin to New York forced to divert after emergency at 35,000ft

The Delta Air Lines flight left Dublin and began flying towards New York before declaring an emergency over the Atlantic and making a U-turn just 90 minutes in

View 2 Images A flight from Dublin to New York was forced to make a U-turn over the Atlantic Ocean (Image: PA)

A flight from Dublin to New York was forced to make a U-turn over the Atlantic Ocean after declaring an in-flight emergency shortly into its journey.

‌



Delta Air Lines flight DL45 departed Dublin Airport at 1:15pm on Tuesday before heading towards its scheduled destination at John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK).

‌



The plane climbed to an altitude of 35,000 feet, but just 90 minutes into its more than seven-hour journey, it issued a squawk 7700 code - the general emergency signal used by air traffic controllers and pilots.

‌



View 2 Images A flight from Dublin to New York was forced to make a U-turn over the Atlantic (Image: Graham Hughes/NurPhoto/Shutterstock)

Flight tracking data showed the wide-body Boeing 767-300ER jet making a sharp U-turn back towards Ireland.

Article continues below

Air traffic control prioritised the returning jet for an immediate diversion back to Dublin Airport, where emergency ground crews were placed on standby ahead of its landing at around 4:15pm.

A Delta Air Lines spokesperson told the Mirror that the flight returned to Dublin following a medical situation involving a passenger.

The spokesperson said: "Delta Flight 45 from Dublin to New York-JFK returned to Dublin due to a customer medical situation onboard. We thank our crew for their professionalism and our customers for their understanding".

News.title: Immigration shake-up will scupper Andy Burnham's national care service goal, nursing chiefs warn
News.content:
Immigration shake-up will scupper Andy Burnham's national care service goal, nursing chiefs warn

EXCLUSIVE: The Royal College of Nursing (RCN) has claimed plans to change indefinite leave to remain (ILR) rules amount to a 'betrayal' of migrant care workers, with the UK already one of the most restrictive places to move to

View 3 Images Shabana Mahmood is set to announce a final decision later this year (Image: Dan Kitwood/PA Wire)

Shabana Mahmood's sweeping immigration shake-up will scupper Andy Burnham's plans for a new National Care Service, nursing chiefs have warned.

‌



In a scathing report, the Royal College of Nursing (RCN) says proposals being weighed up by ministers amount to a "betrayal" of migrant nursing staff. Analysis carried out for the RCN found the UK already has one of the most restrictive sets of rules for settling nurses in the world - and this would get worse if the Home Secretary's reforms are passed.

‌



Ms Mahmood is weighing up measures that would see care workers from overseas forced to wait 15 years before qualifying for indefinite leave to remain (ILR) - up from its current level of five.

‌



This change would be applied retrospectively - meaning thousands of people already in the UK would be affected. Ms Mahmood, who argues settlement must be earned, told MPs on Tuesday that a final decision will come later this year.

Face scanning phone apps can now be used for age checks in pubs and clubs READ MORE :

View 3 Images Professor Nicola Ranger has called for the planned changes to be torn up (Image: Adam Gerrard / Daily Mirror)

Professor Nicola Ranger, the RCN's general secretary, told The Mirror: "The Home Secretary must scrap these proposals and recognise they are entirely incompatible with building a thriving and stable National Care Service.

‌



"If she doesn't, our brilliant migrant colleagues will choose to leave for where they feel more welcome and supported. At a time when domestic nursing workforce growth has stalled, these proposals would be a disaster for any hope to successfully reform social care”.

Shortly after becoming PM, Andy Burnham pledged to finally fix the social care system after decades of failure. But the RCN has warned tens of thousands of care workers and nurses in the care sector will leave if settlement rules change.

New analysis carried out for the RCN found the UK would be an outlier if the settlement delay is brought in for care workers. In the US and Australia, skilled professionals like registered nurses are offered immediate permanent residency.

‌



In Canada, care workers can settle after 16 months, while New Zealand and Ireland have a two year wait. The UK is also the most expensive place to apply for permanent residency, with a cost of £3,029 per person.

The RCN has called on migrant health and social workers to be offered immediate ILR - with the processing cost reduced to £523. Prof Ranger said: "Migrant nursing staff hold our health and care system together and have built lives in our country and become part of our communities. The Home Secretary's proposals would amount to a betrayal by reneging on our commitment to them because it’s politically convenient and would make the UK a significant outlier internationally.

"The Home Secretary must scrap these proposals and recognise they are entirely incompatible with building a thriving and stable National Care Service. If she doesn't, our brilliant migrant colleagues will choose to leave for where they feel more welcome and supported. At a time when domestic nursing workforce growth has stalled, these proposals would be a disaster for any hope to successfully reform social care."

‌



View 3 Images Andy Burnham has pledged to finally fix Britain's broken social care system (Image: DOMINIQUE JACOVIDES-POOL/SIPA/Shutterstock)

It is estimated by Skills for Care that 38% of care workers and senior care workers, and 43% of registered nurses in adult social care are not British nationals.

Earlier this year an RCN survey found 60% of migrant care workers who do not have ILR said it is very likely extending the qualifying period would affect their decision to remain in the UK. This could mean up to 46,000 nursing staff are at risk of leaving, it said.

‌



Under current rules, those in the UK on health and care worker visas have no recourse to public funds - meaning they cannot claim benefits or council housing. Ms Mahmood said the changes are necessary because of years of high net migration, with 1.6million people forecast to qualify for ILR by 2030.

Other nations allow migrant nurses to claim benefits sooner - including Canada, which permits them to claim benefits immediately after being granted permanent residence. New Zealand and Ireland allow full access after two years, while in Australia this wait is between two and four years.

In the US access to means-tested benefits is permitted after five years. The RCN report said: "Nursing staff working on a visa in the UK already face an increased risk of financial distress due to their inability to access public funds. In cases of long-term sick leave, these staff may have no income at all as they have no recourse to means-tested ill-health benefits."

‌



It continues: "Whilst many comparable countries are moving to simplify and accelerate pathways to settlement for health and care workers, the UK is moving in the opposite direction. Instead of recognising their long-term contribution and valuing internationally educated nurses, the UK government’s proposals create additional barriers to staying in the UK, increase cost and uncertainty, and risk positioning the UK as an international outlier."

The Home Secretary faces calls to tear up plans to apply changes retrospectively, including for care workers. Earlier this year Angela Rayner - who returned to the Cabinet when Andy Burnham became PM - branded the move "un-British".

Addressing the cross-party Home Affairs Committee on Tuesday, Ms Mahmood said: "We're trying to do a proper piece of work where we have the right arrangement that strikes the right balance between our responsibilities to people who have come here to work, our recognition of the failures that we inherited as a government and also our need to do right by the people who are already here who pay for the systems we already rely on."

Article continues below

She said it is a long-standing principle that the rules migrants would have to abide by would be those in place when they apply for ILR. The Home Secretary stated: "The rules that apply to you are the rules that are in force at the point of your application, not when you arrived in the country."

A Home Office spokesman said: "Last November, we set out reforms to double the standard qualifying period for settlement to 10 years for most migrants, with shorter routes for those who contribute the most to the UK.

“Under the proposals, key public service workers, including doctors and nurses, may settle after five years. A consultation on elements of those reforms has now closed, and we will set out our response in due course."

News.title: Girl, 11, remembers RNLI's crucial advice after getting in trouble in the sea at popular beach
News.content:
Girl, 11, remembers RNLI's crucial advice after getting in trouble in the sea at popular beach

Billie and her friend got into difficulty at Avon Beach in Mudeford, Dorset with the pair ending up about 20 metres away from shore before an RNLI volunteer rushed out to save them

Brave 11-year-old recalls how RNLI’s ‘Float to Live’ advice helped save her life

An 11-year-old girl remembered to "float to live" when she got into trouble in the sea at a popular beach.

‌



Billie recalled the important advice from the RNLI, which helped her dodge death in the ordeal at Avon Beach in Mudeford, Dorset. She and her friend had been swimming in the shallow water, but quickly became unable to touch the ground when the waves got bigger.

‌



Billie said: "I was thinking, oh no, this isn't going to be very good. I might get taken away by the sea. I felt very scared and I tried to swim back. I was able to swim a little bit back, but then I was out of breath and really tired."

‌



But the brave youngster acted swiftly, in line with RNLI guidance which the Mirror highlighted in its campaign this summer called Save Lives for Sam. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has backed our movement, designed to call on authorities to make it a legal requirement for safety equipment to be installed around high risk large bodies of water, to push for drowning to be treated as a national emergency and for other demands.

View 3 Images Andy and Billie were at Avon Beach in Dorset when she got into trouble (Image: RNLI/Charis Jefferson)

While Billie and her friend started to get into danger in September last year, RNLI volunteer helm Andy Reed was also at the beach with his family. He saw Billie and her friend were about 20 metres out before he picked out that she was moving into a position that could save her life.

‌



Recalling the rescue today, Andy said: "The adult that was with them was obviously concerned about how far they'd gone out. At that point I noticed Billie rolling onto her back into the 'float to live' position. She was doing exactly the right thing."

View 3 Images Andy was able to bring Billie back to the beach safely (Image: RNLI/Charis Jefferson)

The float to live position is a water safety technique promoted by the RNLI to help people survive if they get into trouble. The position is carried out by tilting your head back, relaxing, moving your hands and legs to stay up, allowing your legs to sink, floating until you can breathe easily and calling for help.

‌



It is a tested technique that saves energy and buys time until help arrives. Billie had been taught about the technique in her swimming lessons and recalled it at that crucial moment.

Billie said: "I was scared. But I felt like I knew what to do, and I made a starfish on my back."

View 3 Images The 'float to live' position can save lives of people who get into difficulty in the water (Image: RNLI/Nathan Williams)

‌



At the same time, Andy asked his partner to call 999 before he entered the water and swam toward Billie. Fully clothed, he entered the water and swam toward Billie.

He reached her and reassured her. They then made their way to her friend who was helped by another person and all made their way back to the beach.

"They were floating to live, and that undoubtedly bought them those extra few minutes before I was able to reach them," said Andy. "They should be really proud of their actions, and this just brings home the importance of the lifesaving technique and why we try to reach as many people as possible with our messaging."

Article continues below

The Mirror has launched the Save Lives For Sam water safety campaign to tackle the UK's growing drowning crisis. Backed by MPs, Olympic champions, national water safety organisations and bereaved families, the campaign is calling for urgent action to make our waters safer.

That includes compulsory water safety lessons in schools, a nationwide public awareness campaign, better lifesaving equipment at high-risk waterways, the introduction of Sam's Law, and a dedicated Minister for Water Safety. Find out more about the campaign and how you can support it here.

News.title: Baby 'cot cams' plan after inquiry finds Lucy Letby crimes could have been prevented
News.content:
Health Secretary Yvette Cooper has said officials will "urgently develop plans" to introduce live-streaming cameras on England's baby wards after an inquiry into Lucy Letby's murders and attempted murders.

Inquiry chair Lady Justice Thirlwall called for a series of urgent reforms to neonatal units, including CCTV for all cots and incubators, and restricting access to insulin.

Thirlwall said some of the babies Letby killed could have been saved if managers at the Countess of Chester Hospital had taken action earlier.

Her report criticises a "complete failure to protect babies" and a "profound failure of management, governance and safeguarding" at the hospital.

Thirlwall said this was because "no one seems to have understood that safeguarding action is required when a member of staff is suspected of causing deliberate harm and does not require colleagues to be sure of guilt."

She said it would never be possible to know exactly how many lives could have been saved if safeguarding procedures had been properly followed.

One of the senior doctors who tried to raise concerns about Letby with hospital managers, consultant paediatrician Dr John Gibbs, now retired, told the BBC the Thirlwall Inquiry report was "grim reading".

In a rare interview he said he accepted that consultants must bear "collective" responsibility for some of the failings identified in the report, and said he wished they had been "brave enough to follow our suspicions and escalate things to the police earlier".

Chief executive and registrar at the Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC), Paul Rees, said he was "truly sorry for the NMC's failings" in the Letby case and that "we also did not act quickly enough to suspend Lucy Letby".

News.title: Dan Thomas resigns as Reform Wales leader after arrest on suspicion of assault
News.content:
Reform UK's Dan Thomas has quit as the party's Welsh leader, after he was arrested on Sunday on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour.

Gwent Police confirmed that a 45-year-old man from Aberbargoed, in Caerphilly, was bailed pending further enquiries.

In a statement issued by his party, the Member of the Senedd for Casnewydd Islwyn said he was "standing down" from his position due to personal reasons.

He said he had been "released without charge" and had "done nothing wrong".

Thomas was appointed Welsh party leader by Nigel Farage in February.

Plaid Cymru, which runs the Welsh government, said: "Reform UK is descending into chaos."

Thomas did not take part in First Minister's Questions earlier today.

He was first elected to the Senedd in the elections in May, where his party went from having two politicians in Cardiff Bay to 34.

Reform came second behind Plaid Cymru in the vote, with Thomas becoming leader of the opposition in the Senedd.

Thomas said: "It has been the honour of my life to have been the leader of Reform Wales and see this party go from zero to 34 elected members and become the largest opposition group in Welsh history.

"With deep regret, I am now standing down from this position due to personal reasons.

"Over the weekend, I was reported to the police and was released without charge."

He added: "I will continue to serve my constituents in Casnewydd Islwyn and will fully back whoever the group selects as its next leader."

The news came on the same day that Reform MS Sarah Cooper-Lesadd defected to Plaid Cymru.

News.title: Ed Sheeran says it was 'not my decision' to drop Macklemore from tour
News.content:
Ed Sheeran has posted a long statement on Instagram, saying it was not his decision to drop Macklemore from his current US tour.

The US rapper - whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty - was ejected from the line-up after making pro-Palestinian statements at two dates in New Jersey.

His comments drew criticism from Jewish groups, after which some venues put pressure on the tour promoters to have him removed from the line-up.

In his statement, external, Sheeran said he had spoken with the venues "at length all week to try and build a bridge" - but the promoters, Messina Touring Group, had ultimately decided to remove Macklemore from the bill.

"Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine," he wrote. "Macklemore's contract for the tour was with the promoter, not me.

"I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living."

While the star said he was âappalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine" and that the "suffering and pain caused on both sides is a human tragedy", he also attempted to explain his decision to keep political issues at armâs length.

"I am not complicit," he wrote. "I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care.

"Nor does it mean I don't support causes in my own, personal way."

He continued: "There is a reason I do not use my professional platform for politics - my audience includes young people, often children, of all backgrounds.

"Those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum. I respect Macklemore's strength of purpose to stand up and shout for what he believes.

"However, there is room for multiple approaches to the same end: Peace.

"I choose to use my fame and platform to be a place of safety and sanctuary, to maintain diplomacy and keep conversations open, not closed. If we only focus on shouting the loudest, nothing will ever change. There are different approaches to being an advocate for change."

Sheeran added that, âas with all my support acts", Macklemore had been allowed to choose his own setlist.

News.title: Former England footballer Raheem Sterling admits dangerous driving on motorway before crash
News.content:
Former England footballer Raheem Sterling has admitted dangerous driving on a motorway before he crashed a Lamborghini in May.

The 31-year-old, from Berkshire, also admitted possessing nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation, and failing to provide a specimen for analysis.

Sterling, who appeared at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court, was arrested after crashing near the M3 in Hampshire on the morning of 28 May.

Sterling has 82 England caps, the last of which was won at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar.

News.title: Warning of space arms race as US confirms weapons in Earth's orbit
News.content:
The US has confirmed it deployed a space weapon in Earth's orbit, the first time it has acknowledged such offensive capabilities.

Russia and China responded by warning of an arms race in space.

However, according to the BBC's Defence correspondent Jonathan Beale, this is already happening.

Details of how the weapon operates have not been disclosed by US officials.

News.title: Thirteenth Met Police officer sacked after Charing Cross Panorama film
News.content:
Another Metropolitan Police officer has been dismissed following BBC Panorama's undercover investigation into the force's Charing Cross station.

PC Mason O'Connor was sacked after a hearing found he had breached standards of professional behaviour, relating to a comment he made to a female colleague, the Met said.

O'Connor was reported to a "proactive wider investigation" following the broadcast of the programme in October 2025 and he has become the 13th officer to be sacked since then, the force added.

Other officers who were covertly filmed for the documentary were seen calling for immigrants to be shot, boasting about excessive use of force and joking about rape and sexual assault.

Met Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley said at the time that this behaviour was "totally unacceptable".

A disciplinary panel on Tuesday heard that O'Connor had, while off-duty at a pub, told a female colleague that he hoped she would be raped on her way home.

He was found to have breached standards of professional behaviour for authority, respect and courtesy, equality and diversity, and discreditable conduct, the Met said.

As well as the 13 officers the Met has sacked, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said another two men, both former officers, had also been found to have committed gross misconduct.

The policing watchdog added it was still investigating the conduct of a further 15 officers or police staff in the wake of the Panorama film.

"This is one of our largest ever investigations in terms of the number of officers investigated," said the IOPC's Amanda Rowe.

"The sheer number of fast-tracked disciplinary proceedings show how seriously the IOPC and the Met, who held the misconduct hearings, are treating this matter," she added.

News.title: State pension likely to top £13,000 a year as UK wage growth slows to 3.9%
News.content:
The state pension is expected to top Â£13,000 a year, reigniting the debate about its long-term affordability and generational fairness.

The full, flat-rate state pension is expected to rise by Â£488 a year in April, based on the latest official earnings figure released on Tuesday.

The so-called triple lock pension policy guarantees that the state pension will increase by either average wage growth, inflation or 2.5% - whichever is highest.

Labour made a manifesto pledge to keep the triple lock until 2029, however economists have warned about the cost of the policy ahead of the Budget although pensioner groups say many people still face poverty in old age.

News.title: Two dead after car hits group of pedestrians
News.content:
Two people have died and four have been seriously injured after a car crashed into a group of people in Doncaster.

South Yorkshire Police said officers were called to White Rose Way when a black Mitsubishi L200 hit a group of pedestrians at 11:00 BST on Sunday, before hitting a black Audi and silver BMW on the opposite carriageway.

The force said two of the pedestrians had died at the scene while four other people were taken to hospital with serious injuries.

The driver of the Mitsubishi, a 30-year-old man, was arrested on suspicion of two counts of causing death by dangerous driving, two counts of causing serious injury by dangerous driving and driving while unfit and later released on bail.

News.title: Letby hospital consultant says inquiry makes for grim reading
News.content:
One of the senior doctors who tried to raise concerns about Lucy Letby with hospital managers has told the BBC the final inquiry report makes for "grim reading".

Consultant paediatrician Dr John Gibbs worked at the Countess of Chester Hospital throughout the period in 2015 to 2016 when Letby murdered seven babies, and attempted to murder seven more, on the neonatal unit.

He said that he accepted that consultants must bear "collective" responsibility for some of the failings identified in the report.

"I wish we consultants had been brave enough to follow our suspicions and escalate things to the police earlier," he told the BBC.

"When I say, 'we consultants', I am responsible as well and if my other consultant colleagues didn't go to the police, I should have."

The Thirlwall Inquiry was launched after former nurse Letby was convicted in 2023, and the final report was published on Tuesday.

In the 822-page document, Lady Justice Thirlwall described "a complete failure to protect babies on the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester Hospital".

The report found that the police "should have been notified earlier than they were" and that hospital managers had repeatedly dismissed consultants' concerns.

Reflecting on the findings for the first time, Gibbs said: "I wasn't expecting it to be an easy read and it certainly isn't. I'd imagine it's an extremely difficult read for the parents of the babies concerned.

"As I admitted when I appeared before the inquiry to give evidence, I feel we failed the babies and I apologise to the families for that."

Gibbs, who began working in Chester in 1994 and is now retired, agreed with the report's finding that hospital executives had multiple opportunities to act and potentially save babies' lives while the deaths were happening.

"But it was during that 11 months after Lucy Letby was moved off the unit, before the police got involved, that it was a very difficult atmosphere, very tense, very stressful dealing with the managers," he added.

Managers "were determined to ensure that we accepted Lucy Letby had been wrongly suspected of doing any harm," the senior doctor explained.

He also spoke of the failures of his and his wider team, specifically referencing a doctor who disregarded blood test results that suggested a baby had been poisoned with insulin in August 2015.

While one of his colleagues had missed the relevance of the results when they came back from the lab, it had been a collective team failure, Dr Gibbs concluded.

"Others of us were on call and covering the neonatal unit over the next week or two before the baby moved out of the unit. We all had the opportunity to review the notes."

News.title: Political donors could face tougher residency rules
News.content:
MPs have supported the government's proposals by approving amendments to the Representation of the People Bill. The bill is currently being scrutinised in the House of Lords.

Speaking as the bill was debated by peers, Communities Minister Baroness Taylor of Stevenage said: "We are considering how we will strengthen the residency requirements, including ensuring that the length of time spent in the UK aligns with broader government policy."

Baroness Taylor said this was "in addition to introducing a robust regime that ensures that donors contributing above the Â£100,000 annual cap must demonstrate a genuine and ongoing connection" to the UK.

Tax is one area that already has residency requirements. The criteria includes someone being declared resident for tax purposes if they have lived in the UK for at least 183 days in the tax year.

Challenged on whether the government was targeting Reform donors, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said policy on donations is "never about one political party or one particular set of issues".

He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "Fundamentally we need to make sure that people who want to influence British politics, who want a say in British politics have a stake in Britain.

"That should apply to everyone and will apply to everyone, so I wouldn't make it about any particular donations or anything that's been in the public domain."

When the government set out its plans to cap foreign donations in March and July, it did not mention the idea of an enhanced residency test for political donors.

Asked repeatedly by reporters whether the idea of tightening residency rules had only been discussed after Delo and Harborne's most recent donations to Reform, the prime minister's official spokesman would not give a timeframe.

Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokeswoman Lisa Smart accused the government of "playing whack-a-mole", as she said Labour's residency requirements "aren't good enough".

She said: "We must urgently go further and introduce a universal donation cap to stop Trump's America becoming Farage's Britain."

On Monday, Farage criticised the government's attempts to retrospectively declare some donations illegal.

He told the BBC: "If the government was allowed to do this, you know what would happen? There would be a response the other way.

"We or the Conservatives would say 'if you're going to stop legitimate donors like this, we would say to the trade unions, you can't give money'."

Farage argued such a move would "collapse" the system of political funding and lead to taxpayers having to fund political parties, a system he said would be opposed by the British public.

Since 2020, Labour has received almost Â£43m from trade unions, who raise their money through individual workers' membership fees.

News.title: Harry and Meghan change children's school over security concerns due to traffic
News.content:
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have changed their children's school only days after they first started over security concerns about traffic during the school run.

The schools' names have not been disclosed, but it is understood that the Sussexes' private security team had been concerned that the distance and the heavy traffic on the original school run route had made it difficult to make secure.

It's understood that the security for the children meant travelling with another car, and that driving in convoy proved difficult in the busy school run traffic.

The checks on the route are believed to have initially taken place before term time, but with the school traffic it was deemed not safe enough.

A source close to the couple said: "The decision for the children to move school was taken following a discussion with the family's security team about the practicalities of their current arrangements."

They added: "The parents remain extremely grateful to all the teachers and staff for the love, care and effort they have shown their family.

"This decision should in no way be interpreted as a reflection on the school or the exceptional care the children have received there."

It has also emerged that the Sussexes are going to be given a review of their publicly funded security, following their return to live in the UK.

It is understood that the committee which oversees royal and VIP security, known as Ravec, is to reconsider Prince Harry and Meghan's level of police protection now that they and their two children are full-time residents rather than visitors.

It will assess any risks they face in their new home and the type of trips taken by the couple and their family, such as regular travel routes and school runs.

News.title: Southport attack victims, survivors and families hit by data breach
News.content:
An investigation is under way after a data breach involving court files relating to victims, survivors and families of the Southport attack, the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) has said.

The unauthorised access by courts staff was identified during a review of the department's digital systems. For a limited number of people, the information accessed included sensitive and personal data, but the MOJ did not state how many people were affected.

An spokesperson said the MOJ was "appalled", but there was no evidence personal data had been shared with third parties and the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) had been told.

The prime minister has asked the Lord Chancellor to oversee the matter.

An MOJ source said its independent Data Protection Officer had assessed the matter and found that, for a limited number of people, the information accessed included sensitive and personal data likely to result in a high risk to their rights and freedoms.

Those affected are being notified directly, the department said.

News.title: Fall in small boat Channel crossings down to law enforcement, agency says
News.content:
Law enforcement activity has been a "key factor" in reducing the number of small boat Channel crossings, the National Crime Agency (NCA) says.

The number of people arriving in the UK in the first half of 2026 was down 41% on the year before, government figures show.

The NCA said the drop followed a "significant increase in arrests and seizures", although added "fluctuating demand" for crossings, and the French authorities preventing boat launches had also played a role.

However, Mihnea Cuibus, a senior researcher at the University of Oxford University's Migration Observatory, says it is "impossible" to disentangle the effects of government policy and other factors on small boat arrivals.

While recent policy changes appear to have led smugglers and migrants to alter their behaviour, Cuibus says fewer unauthorised arrivals into the EU and developments in key origin countries - such as improved security in Syria - may be partially behind the decline.

"It is hard to know how much restrictive measures contributed to reducing [arrivals] in 2026," he continues.

He said limitations on refugee family reunion and a reduction in the asylum grant rate could also have had an impact.

The Conservatives have previously said the weather played a huge role in the fluctuating numbers of crossings from France and Belgium.

NCA director general of operations Rob Jones said the agency was "devoting more resources to tackling organised immigration crime than ever before".

"That is bringing results.

"However, we are not complacent, and the job is by no means done," he continued.

"We must continue to keep up the pressure on these criminal gangs, as they continue to put lives at risk in the Channel."

News.title: Search launched for boy, 3, missing at playground
News.content:
Emergency services are looking for a three-year-old boy who went missing at a playground.

The boy, named only as Noah, was with a relative at the small park at Merriam Close in Brantham, but "became separated" from them as they left at about 15:00 BST, Suffolk Police said.

The toddler, described as white, with curly ginger hair, was reported to have run down a nearby alleyway towards a newbuild housing estate.

Residents have been asked to check their gardens, sheds and outbuildings by the police.

A helicopter has been pictured flying over the scene, which is near the estuary of the River Stour and close to the Essex border.

News.title: AI poses huge risks to national security without guardrails, minister says
News.content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) poses "huge risks" to the UK's national security and society without the right protections, a senior minister has warned.

First Secretary of State Louise Haigh - Prime Minister Andy Burnham's de facto deputy - told the TUC congress on Tuesday that the government needed to "heed the warnings" of those "at the forefront" of developing the technology.

She added the government was "ready to work with international partners" to prioritise public safety and national security.

Fears about the potential dangers of AI have ramped up in recent days after executives and current and former staff in the field warned the tech could endanger humanity.

On Monday, a spokesman for UK Prime Minister Burnham welcomed the open discussion among those developing the technology of the risks and rewards.

Speaking at the TUC congress on Tuesday afternoon, Haigh acknowledged the "enormous potential" of AI for public services, businesses and science.

While she said the UK needed to make the most of this, she added: "There are clearly huge risks to our national security and society if the right guardrails are not put in place...

"We have a solemn duty to mitigate the risks and ensure that it is for the benefit - not the detriment - of our society."

In an interview with BBC Radio 4's Today programme earlier on Tuesday, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said people should not be complacent about the risks of AI - but also not "hyperbolic".

It comes as MPs in the UK are seeking new laws on AI after a report found the technology was responsible for numerous abuses of human rights.

"Nowhere in the world, including the UK, has a current legislative and regulatory approach to AI that is fit for purpose," Labour MP and committee chair Alex Sobel said.

News.title: Number of people claiming key disability benefit hits record high
News.content:
The number of people claiming Personal Independence Payments (Pip) in England and Wales has hit a record high, according to new government figures.

As of July, just over four million people were entitled to claim the benefit, compared to 3.83 million the previous year, an increase of 7%, data from the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) showed.

Pip is designed to support people with the extra costs of being disabled or living with long-term physical or mental health conditions, and eligibility is not affected by a person's income or savings.

In July, Sir Stephen Timms, who is leading a review on Pip, said in his interim report that the system was "not fit for purpose".

Of the 4.1 million claimants, those aged 50 and above accounted for more than half.

Just under three in ten were aged 30 to 49, while 17% of claimants were aged 16 to 29.

Pip seeks to offset the extra costs that can occur for those living with certain long-term health conditions.

According to the charity Scope, the extra cost of being disabled â known as the disability price tag â has reached more than Â£1,100 a month.

The DWP said the increase in the Pip caseload had actually "slowed", falling from a rise of 400,000 in the 12 months to July 2024, to 260,000 in the 12 months to July 2026.

But they agreed the system was "no longer fit for purpose", adding that the Timms review's recommendations would "lay the foundation for sustainable reform".

But Helen Whatly, shadow work and pensions secretary, said Labour was "too quick to write people off and too slow to help them into work" - adding that it was "costing us a fortune".

Pip has been in the spotlight since the summer of 2025 when the government, led by former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer, proposed reforming and tightening eligibility criteria for the benefit as the cost of running the system increased.

Spending on Pip stood at Â£16.3bn in 2019-20, when adjusted for inflation to today's prices, and had increased to Â£27.3bn by 2024-25, government figures showed.

It is currently forecast to rise to Â£41.5bn by 2030-31.

News.title: Liverpool vs Tottenham LIVE: Szoboszlai thunderbolt knocks Spurs out of Carabao Cup
News.content:
Liverpool's Dominik Szoboszlai celebrates ( Reuters )

Dominik Szoboszlai’s thunderbolt sealed Liverpool’s win against Tottenham to knock Spurs out of the Carabao Cup as Roberto De Zerbi’s winless start to the season continued.

De Zerbi named a strong team at Anfield for the third-round clash and Spurs enjoyed a bright start, with Lucas Bergvall denied by a superb stop from Giorgi Mamardashvili.

But Andoni Iraola’s much-changed hosts struck through Alexis Mac Allister and Cody Gakpo either side of half-time and had appeared to be coasting into the fourth-round until Conor Gallagher pulled one back late on.

Tottenham's first goal of the season, after four winless outings in the Premier League, did not lead to a comeback, with defeat instead continuing their frustrating start to the season after a summer of heavy spending.

Mamardashvili had to make another excellent save to deny a deflected effort from Omar Marmoush at the death, before a rasping striker from Szoboszlai from distance sent Liverpool into the fourth round.

Follow all the action from Anfield in our live blog below

Starbucks fans have been let down by the coffee chain’s latest merchandise release.

The company announced a new collaboration with the Peanuts, including 10 collectible items available for purchase. Select items were meant to be available to Starbucks rewards members through the app as well. A secret drink menu was also unveiled as part of the lineup.

Among the coveted items available to the public were a 16oz tumbler, a mini tote bag, and a charm. But the one fans seemed most eager to grab was the $39.95 20oz Snoopy cold cup, similar to the viral “Bearista” cup that sent the internet into a frenzy last year.

However, fans who had their hopes of securing the merch dashed have voiced their dismay over long early morning lines and a lack of inventory.

“I’ve gone to multiple Starbucks and instead of a rock I’ve just come away empty handed. Snoopy cups are gone,” one customer wrote on X accompanied by the iconic Charlie Brown “I got a rock” gif.

open image in gallery Starbucks launched a limited edition collaboration with the Peanuts ( Starbucks )

“I thought about going super early to try and get the #Snoopy cup from @Starbucks today... But having to get up before 4am just to go line up is ridiculous,” another wrote. “Starbucks REALLY NEEDS to find a better way of doing things with their exclusives. Make more for us to buy, but also don't force people to do wild things to get them.”

“@Starbucks congratulations. You're a joke. I stood in line for 45 minutes this morning for the @Snoopy glass. I was 3 people away from the counter. 11 people walked in hugged a barista. Then she gave out merch from behind the counter and told the store was they were sold out,” someone else wrote.

One customer who saw a long line before her local Starbucks even opened wrote on X: “I feel like an alien watching a human greed social experiment.” Another said their local store was a “f***ing warzone at 5am for this Snoopy stuff.”

“We were in line this morning. I got my 16oz tumbler yet the glass Snoopy were sold out(only 10 available). We had a reseller in front of us,” someone else wrote on X. “Currently waiting for the mall to open. 3 Starbucks here, 1 in Macy's. Hopefully we will get a Snoopy cup. I've been up for 24hrs now.”

open image in gallery Snoopy cold cups were among the coveted items in Starbucks's newest merch drop ( Starbucks )

Some customers who are Reserve members — the highest tier of Starbucks’s rewards program — also had trouble shopping for exclusive Peanuts merch. One person wrote on X, “As a Reserve member, still can't order any special collection stuff. My wife LOVES Snoopy and one of these tumblers would be loved (alongside our regular ones). But again, can't get anything because the website is down, and stores are already out at 3:00 AM.”

The Independent has contacted Starbucks for comment.

This isn’t the first time fans have voiced their disappointment over limited edition Starbucks merch.

The coffee giant was forced to issue an apology over the “Bearista” cups, telling The Independent at the time: “The excitement for our merchandise exceeded even our biggest expectations and despite shipping more Bearista cups to coffeehouses than almost any other merchandise item this holiday season, the Bearista cup and some other items sold out fast. We understand many customers were excited about the Bearista cup and apologize for the disappointment this may have caused.”
