Sports.title: Moment Raheem Sterling is arrested with balloons and canisters in his £270,000 Lamborghini as he pleads GUILTY to dangerous driving and drug possession after crash while on 'hippy crack'
Sports.content:
Raheem Sterling told police he had 'a problem' with laughing gas after submitting rush hour motorists to a terrifying 90-minutes of dangerous driving in his Lamborghini while high on the chemical.

The former England international, 31, zigzagged across the M25 and M3 motorways in his car, forcing other motorists to get out of his way, before swerving onto a slip road and crashing into a metal gate.

He was arrested by police who claim he tried to hide nitrous oxide, or laughing gas, from them by moving it to the back seat of his black Lamborghini Urus SUV, which is worth around £270,000.

Police bodycam footage shows the moment that Sterling was arrested with canisters and a deflated balloon on his lap. An officer can be heard saying 'you can put that down' to the footballer after opening his car door.

He can then be seen taking the items from his lap and putting them behind his seat.

Sterling is asked 'can you jump out for me' and who was at the wheel at the time of the crash, but does not reply.

Police bodycam footage shows the moment Raheem Sterling is arrested with canisters and a deflated balloon on his lap

Image issued by the Crown Prosecution Service shows the damage to the Lamborghini Urus being driven by Sterling

The former England international was pictured arriving in court today to face charges following a car crash in May

Sterling, 31, crashed his £270,000 Lamborghini Urus and was charged with dangerous driving and possession of laughing gas

The officer adds: 'So you refuse to answer, okay.'

Sterling is told to get out of the car, asked his name and age at the roadside and to 'put the phone down, stop playing games. Stop tensing up.'

The former Manchester City and Chelsea star is then read his rights as he is arrested after being asked to put his arms behind his back.

His arrest, near the Minley interchange on the M3 in Hampshire, happened four weeks after he had returned to the UK following the end of an abortive attempt to revive his football career at Dutch club Feyenoord.

Sterling, from Berkshire, pleaded guilty on Tuesday to dangerous driving, possession of nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation and failing to provide a specimen after a single vehicle collision at 8.45am on May 28. Police found six cannisters of nitrous oxide in his car.

Basingstoke Magistrates' Court heard that Sterling was so impaired by the laughing gas that he was unable to perform basic police station tests like placing his finger on his nose or placing one foot in front of another.

Barrister Simon Jones, prosecuting, said of Sterling: 'He appeared to be quiet, withdrawn and lethargic and actively fidgeting. Eye lids drooping consistent with fatigue or drug impairment. He said he was feeling very cold, despite this being in the middle of a heatwave with 33-degree temperatures.'

Motorist Fiona Jennings told police she had looked across to witness the driver of the Lamborghini with a balloon in front of his face which was so big she thought it was an air bag.

Nitrous oxide cannisters were found in the car after it was stopped by police

Sterling, from Berkshire, pleaded guilty on Tuesday to dangerous driving, possession of nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation and failing to provide a specimen

Image shows the damage to the Lamborghini Urus which was being driven by Sterling when he was detained by police officers

It was so big that 'she had no idea how the driver would have been able to see the road ahead,' Mr Jones said. Ms Jennings described Sterling's driving as 'absolutely horrendous' and expressed 'genuine concern that the driver may kill someone.'

Evidence presented to court suggested Sterling was also inhaling laughing gas while at wheel of the Lamborghini a full seven hours before his arrest.

A concerned witness called police after seeing the driver of the same car entering a McDonalds car park alarmingly fast at 1.10am the same morning and seeing the driver holding up 'a pink, inflated balloon.'

By 7.45am that morning, another motorist concerned by the Lamborghini erratically changing lanes, saw the driver placing a white balloon to his mouth and inhaling its contents. For 30 minutes, that motorist watched the vehicle weave from inside to outside lane and back and come close to smashing into the central reservation.

It was after Sterling had left the M3 near Farnborough, Hampshire, hit the gate and come to halt with the tyres of his wheels ripped up, that police found him sitting in T-shirt and shirts in the passenger seat of the car.

One officer told him to 'stop tensing up' after he had stepped out of the car. Sterling replied: 'I'm not tensing up.' Sterling provided breath tests, which established he was not under the influence of cannabis, cocaine or alcohol. But he later refused requests for a blood test, insisting that a lawyer of his choosing must be present, having rejected the offer of a duty solicitor. He also refused to answer any police questions.

Mr Jones said of Sterling's conduct: 'He was attempting to impose a condition on provision of a specimen. He was told the investigation could not be delayed for that reason. At the roadside, there was cooperation without the need for legal advice. When the search for the presence of drugs started, the cooperation ended.'

Sterling's barrister, Jason Bartfeld QC, told the court that there was 'extensive personal mitigation' his case and that the footballer had taken 'voluntary steps to mitigate his difficulties.'

Mr Bartfeld agreed that this was a 'top category case' because it was a prolonged period of dangerous driving and Sterling was suffering 'serious impairment'. But he said the nitrous oxide would only have caused impairment in 'short periods' and that the chemical did not pose the same risks as cannabis or alcohol.

He claimed police had left Sterling confused about the blood sample. Sterling later told police in a statement: 'I asked for a solicitor. I did not fully understand I had not slept all night and was tired and confused.'

Sterling could face a maximum two years' imprisonment. The case was adjourned until November for pre-sentencing reports.

Sports.title: Howard Webb blames 'tunnel vision' for major VAR blunder that cost Man United in derby clash with City: Refs chief 'really disappointed' as full audio is passed on to Old Trafford bosses
Sports.content:
Refs' boss Howard Webb says that those involved in the Manchester Derby blunder were 'really disappointed' with the 'highly unfortunate' error - and has revealed that a furious United have been provided with the full transcript behind the botched VAR call which cost them the game.

Despite being flagged for offside on the field, City forward Erling Haaland's 60th minute strike was called in for review, with ref Michael Oliver subsequently ordered to overturn the original decision and incorrectly allow what would turn out to be the only goal of the game.

Replays showed that while Haaland was onside, City team-mate Enzo Fernandez - who was clearly interfering with play - was not.

Webb, who previously apologised to United just hours after the final whistle, admitted that Oliver should have been told to review the decision on the screen but, bizarrely, was not thanks to an outbreak of 'tunnel vision' in the review booth.

The decision left United boss Michael Carrick seething, and added to calls for the Premier League to scrap the controversial system.

Speaking for the first time on Match Officials Mic'd Up, Webb - who stood down VAR Matt Donohue and assistant Blake Antrobus until after the international break - was quick to address the matter.

Enzo Fernandez (right) was incorrectly adjudged to not have been offside for Manchester City's winning goal scored by Erling Haaland during their 1-0 win at rivals Manchester United

Pro Ref's boss Howard Webb has said he is 'really disappointed' with how the error came about

'We felt it was important that we acknowledged an error in this situation,' he said. 'We know that Erling Haaland, who was penalised on field for offside, wasn't in an offside position. But we also know that Enzo Fernandez, who was in an offside position, almost certainly interfered with the Manchester United defence and probably the goalkeeper as well.'

Daily Mail Sport previously revealed that Webb, head of Pro Ref, was 'mortified' at what transpired. And he added that he was not the only one.

'I was really disappointed with this outcome,' he told the show, which is broadcast on Sky Sports and TNT Sports.

'We all are. None more so than the officials themselves. They take a lot of personal pride in what they do and they're obviously hurting now, having fallen short in this situation. They'll not be officiating again until after the international break.'

Webb added that Pro Ref had held its hands up and shared audio of the blunder with United.

'We've reached out to Manchester United and acknowledged the error, as we do when these things happen,' he said.

'They don't happen that often, but we want to ensure that we are transparent and open, and we've played the audio and the footage to the football club to let them know what happened, and we're going to review this situation to understand what elements of process fell down in this situation which meant we didn't get to the right outcome.'

When explaining what had happened, Webb seemed to suggest that Donohue and Antrobus had focused only on Haaland, rather than Fernandez, whom he acknowledged was interfering with play despite not touching the ball.

Haaland's (right) goal was given after a VAR review, with it having originally been ruled offside

However, Fernandez was in an offside position and attempted to go for the ball, meaning it should have been disallowed, with Pro Ref later apologising to Man United for the error

'The on-field decision is not against Fernandez, it's against Haaland,' he said.

'You'll hear that clearly on the comms. And when the VAR starts their check, they see through the use of the semi-automated offside technology, that Haaland, when he's played, is actually onside by three centimetres, played on by (United defender Patrick) Dorgu on the far side, and the VAR gets super focused on Haaland. He establishes he's onside, he thinks that's a good goal, Haaland's not offside, as was thought initially.

'But of course, when he then runs it back through the full APP, he doesn't truly evaluate the full impact of Fernandez's position. He has a look to see if he touches the ball, because then that relates to potentially knocking it to Haaland, who goes on to score. He doesn't touch the ball, but he doesn't truly evaluate other elements of offside. In that moment, he gets tunnel vision. He gets focused on Haaland, and it's down to the rest of his team to pull him out of that tunnel, and unfortunately, that didn't happen on this occasion.'

Webb, who himself refereed a World Cup Final, admitted a clear error. 'Haaland is onside,' he said, 'and we use the technology, but that's only part of the story and the VAR gets super focused on that particular element and, in that moment, misses the evaluation of Fernandez's position, and this goal should've been disallowed.

'Highly unfortunately, it wasn't, and we'll review it, reflect upon it, and try to take the learning forward to prevent this unusual type of error from happening again.'

Matt Donohue (left) was on VAR for the game alongside his assistant Blake Antrobus (right)

In the first half, City's Phil Foden was sent off for kicking out at Bruno Fernandes. The United skipper escaped punishment despite appearing to start the confrontation by kicking his opponent on the backside while he was on the floor.

Webb said he agreed with the red for Foden because he 'kicks out with force into the upper body'. He described Fernandes' kick as 'more petulant than violent'.

'To be violent conduct, it has to have excessive force or brutality, and when you look at that, particularly in full speed, it doesn't have those elements,' Webb added.

'So therefore, this would be a yellow card offence. And the VAR can't step in to recommend the referee looks at the screen to give a yellow card.'

Sports.title: West Ham honour club legend Ludek Miklosko ahead of Carabao Cup tie following his death aged 64 after a long battle with cancer
Sports.content:
West Ham honour club legend Ludek Miklosko ahead of Carabao Cup tie following his death aged 64 after a long battle with cancer

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

West Ham United paid their respects once again to club legend Ludek Miklosko, following his death on Monday, ahead of their Carabao Cup third-round tie with Fulham on Tuesday night.

Miklosko's death at the age of 64 was announced on Monday morning after a long battle with cancer.

And in the lead-up to kick-off at an emotional London Stadium on Tuesday, the Championship club came as one to honour their former goalkeeper.

The players, as well as Fulham's starting XI, observed a minute's applause in the centre-circle as a picture of the ex-Czechia international adorned the screens inside the ground.

Injured midfielder Tomas Soucek also held a West Ham goalkeeper shirt with Miklosko's name and No 1 on the back.

Soucek, who hails from Czechia too, held the shirt in one of the goals before laying it to rest behind it and in front of the home supporters.

West Ham and Fulham players observed a minute's applause in honour of Ludek Miklosko - who died on Monday after a lengthy battle with cancer - ahead of their Carabao Cup tie

Miklosko's face was adorned across the big screens inside an emotional London Stadium

The former Czechia goalkeeper (pictured in December 2024) died on Monday morning aged 64

Hammers icon Sir Trevor Booking could also been seen clapping in the stands ahead of the London derby.

Miklosko kept 126 clean sheets in eight years with the Hammers and is perhaps best remembered for an inspirational series of saves to deny Manchester United the title in 1995.

The popular Czech, signed from Banik Ostrava for £300,000, later returned to the club as goalkeeper coach and fans have continued to sing his name for many years.

West Ham's players held a moment of silence before training on Monday before repeating the feat ahead of facing Fulham at the London Stadium.

There are also plans for a tribute at next month's Championship fixture against Queens Park Rangers, where Miklosko spent the final three years of his playing career.

Miklosko, who won 42 international caps and represented Czechoslovakia at the World Cup in 1990, was diagnosed with cancer in 2021 and announced three years later his decision to withdraw from further treatment.

His son Martin said: 'We are heartbroken to announce the passing of my Dad Ludek, following a brave and courageous battle with cancer.

'On behalf of my Mum and my family, I would like to sincerely thank the fans and everyone at West Ham United Football Club for the kind wishes, thoughts and prayers that were sent to my Dad during his illness.

Tomas Soucek, who is from Czechia, laid down a goalkeeper shirt with Miklosko's name and No

Sir Trevor Booking (centre right) was in the stands paying his respects to the ex-goalkeeper

'We know that the many messages and wishes from his former team-mates and fans alike were a huge sense of comfort to him in his battle with cancer and gave him the strength to not give up and keep fighting for as long as he could.

'We are heartbroken at his loss but take huge comfort from the immense support he received from all of you, along with the knowledge that he is now at peace and no longer suffering.

'Dad simply loved West Ham United, and especially hearing his name sung loud and proud at every game. The club, and its fans, were and always will be a part of our family, so thank you all from the bottom of our hearts.'

Sports.title: Dean Henderson signs new Crystal Palace contract until 2030 making him highest-paid player after summer interest from Nottingham Forest
Sports.content:
Crystal Palace goalkeeper Dean Henderson has agreed a new contract through to 2030.

Daily Mail Sport understands that his new terms make the Palace captain their highest-paid player and add three-and-a-half years to his deal.

Former Palace manager Oliver Glasner was keen on bringing Henderson to Nottingham Forest in the summer transfer window, lodging an enquiry three days before the deadline.

But Henderson has now committed his prime years to Palace.

The 29-year-old became club captain last season, leading Palace to the UEFA Conference League title. He made 52 appearances last term and kept 18 clean sheets.

He also played a crucial role in their FA Cup triumph, keeping clean sheets in the quarter-final, semi-final, and final.

Dean Henderson has played a critical role in Palace's recent success, winning the UEFA Conference League, FA Cup and Community Shield

Henderson joined Palace from Manchester United in 2023 for an initial £15million and has become a fan favourite at Selhurst Park.

The shot-stopper is currently sidelined with a foot injury, having played the first three games of the campaign while injured, but is expected to return after the international break.

Henderson won bronze with England at the FIFA World Cup, starting the third-place play-off match.

Sports.title: 'He went into oblivion mode': Inside Raheem Sterling's terrifying fall from grace as he admits dangerous driving - the controversy he never recovered from, his 'huge mistake' in joining Chelsea and why friends fear he is 'completely lost'
Sports.content:
'He went into oblivion mode': Inside Raheem Sterling's terrifying fall from grace as he admits dangerous driving - the controversy he never recovered from, his 'huge mistake' in joining Chelsea and why friends fear he is 'completely lost'

The look of bleak resignation on Raheem Sterling's face said everything as he walked through the little court building here in Basingstoke, just before stepping into the dock to answer for 90 minutes of terrifying driving.

It was the cold, bleak solemnity of a 31-year-old who was about to admit driving dangerously while in possession of nitrous oxide and who has truly reached rock bottom.

The police video of his arrest, played to magistrate Kirsty Allman, showed the same apparent fatalism. As officers approach him on that brilliant May morning, he sits motionless in the passenger seat of his sports car in a T-shirt and shorts.

'I have a problem with nitrous oxide,' he would later tell police. Evidence suggests he had been inhaling the chemical seven hours before multiple motorists, stunned by his vehicle careering across lanes in the rush-hour, see its driver sucking on laughing gas balloons.

When he reached Basingstoke police station, Sterling was disorientated, cold and exhausted by what evidence suggests was a solitary all-nighter. He could barely keep his eyes open.

The wall of silence that some of those closest to him encountered when contacting him in the hours after that arrest pointed to him seeking escape from any vestige of the game which is all he has known; turning his face to the wall and wanting no reminder of football. For days, he flatly refused to respond to some who have kept him going in his bleak past few years. 'He went into oblivion mode,' says one friend.

Raheem Sterling arrives at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court, where he admitted to dangerous driving in his Lamborghini Urus

'I have a problem with nitrous oxide,' Sterling would later tell police in the wake of his arrest in May of this year

The sport's capacity to build players up and spit them out cannot mitigate for Sterling's terrifying pattern of behaviour at the wheel of his black Lamborghini Urus V8 on that brilliant spring morning. Zig-zagging across all three lanes. Forcing motorists to get out of his way. It was a miracle that no other motorist was injured or killed.

Yet his descent to this chaos has been frighteningly steep and provides significant context. Few beyond Sterling's own family were privy to his thoughts in the hours before he trashed his reputation, but sources point to the madness occurring just four weeks after his attempt to relaunch his career at Feyenoord had ended ignominiously.

His criminal conduct was not the result of a wild night out. The worst of it occurred in the cold light of a Thursday morning.

He had rejected the financial security of a three-year deal which the Rotterdam club offered him, signing up to only 12 months instead, because he feared being marooned without game-time as he had been in his wretched last years at Chelsea.

'Everyone who knows him knows that he needs to feel part of a club,' says one source. But that detail somehow didn't cohere to an obstinate narrative about Sterling and money which has seen many take immense delight in his latest football failure.

Sterling had not played for nine months preceding his first Feyenoord game, in February, yet his poor first 30-minute run out from the bench became a European-wide sensation. 'He thought he could escape the scrutiny over there and start again,' says one source. 'There was no escape.'

The Sterling who returned from Holland was, one source says, at 'an all-time low psychologically', feeling a sense of 'worthlessness', having descended from the ranks of England's best players to a reject in the course of four years. 'He is lost. Completely lost,' says the source.

A few days ago he posted a photo on Instagram wearing a dark balaclava obscuring part of his face. 'You're too old for this,' read one of the most-liked comments.

Sterling, pictured alongside his partner Paige Milian, posted a photo of himself wearing a black balaclava last week

The 31-year-old has privately admitted his 2022 move to Chelsea was a 'huge mistake'

The public ridicule has evidently been fundamental to his sense of despair. In most walks of professional life, there would be a wish to relent, though that does not seem to apply to young footballers. Sterling has sought help to cope with the psychological impact of his decline but this kind of onslaught is not normal.

The collective delight in his struggles has its roots in the actions of the agent Sterling chose right back in his Liverpool days – Aidy Ward, who conducted ugly, public contract negotiations for his client.

Ward, who said he 'didn't care' about Liverpool and branded Sky Sports pundit Jamie Carragher 'a k**b', declared that Sterling wouldn't be staying at Anfield even if he were offered nearly £1million a week.

It was a scarring look for a teenage player, who has never recovered from it. He took the heaviest criticism when England were eliminated from Euro 2016 by Iceland a year later. At that stage, he had yet to surround himself with the wise influences who might have prevented his hangers-on from posting video of his lavishly furnished home, soon after the Iceland defeat. He was castigated for that.

Sterling dispensed with Ward and grew up at Manchester City, who brought out the best from him. With stronger, wiser influences around, he spoke out against the racial abuse England encountered in Montenegro in 2019 and found the voice to argue against football resuming before it was safe in 2021.

The headline of a Financial Times profile in 2021 described him as 'The England football star who took on the racists'. How distant that all seems now.

When Pep Guardiola and City director of football Txiki Begiristain candidly told Sterling his game time would be limited if he extended his contract and stayed for what would be City's Treble-winning season in 2022-23, he took a career-ending decision which will haunt him for all his days.

New Chelsea owner Todd Boehly was giddy about signing him and desperate to sell him the long-term vision with the offer of £325,000 a week. Thomas Tuchel, always a big fan of Sterling's, was also part of the appeal.

The collective delight in Sterling's struggles has its roots in the actions of the agent he chose right back in his Liverpool days - Aidy Ward, pictured, who conducted ugly, public contract negotiations for his client

Sterling was dumped into the 'bomb squad' at Chelsea by then boss Enzo Maresca

But then BlueCo's big football experiment at The Bridge played out and he was binned. Graham Potter played him at wing back before Enzo Maresca arrived to do Behdad Eghbali's dirty work, ditching him two days before the 2024-25 season because the American co-owner didn't share Boehly's enthusiasm.

One minute Chelsea's website was proclaiming him 'a positive influence and setting standards'. The next, it was expunging all mention of him. One minute, Maresca was proclaiming his 'importance'. The next, he was dumping him into the 'bomb squad'.

Everything unravelled after that. A professional life in the 'bomb squad' of unwanted Chelsea players left him training alone at 8pm. By the time he secured a season's escape to Arsenal, it was quite clear that his power, pace and confidence had gone.

Chelsea have moved on, enjoying better PR under Xabi Alonso but Sterling is the collateral damage. That decision he took to join them weighs heavy on him. 'It's the feeling that he made such a huge mistake,' says the source.

Had money been Sterling's main motivating factor, he would have taken the Saudi Arabia deal that Chelsea cooked up with one of the Gulf state's clubs, to force him out in 2024. All who know him well say he would play for a fraction of his old salaries if he could just revive what he had.

He's by no means the only one. The modern pattern of players combusting and their careers going pop prematurely has seen Dele Alli and Kalvin Phillips reduced to the shadows by the age of 30. Aaron Ramsdale is the latest.

In part, it is because they have too many people telling them how wonderful they are and throwing disproportionate sums of money at them.

Sterling's attempt to relaunch his career at Feyenoord ended ignominiously. 'He thought he could escape the scrutiny over there and start again,' says one source. 'There was no escape'

There was the usual morbid fascination with Sterling's decline here in Basingstoke, on Tuesday.

When he arrived in a chauffeur-driven Mercedes van at midday, members of the public gathered near the photographers to get a view and motorists caused a commotion by slowing in a busy road to rubberneck. Those who didn't care hammered on their horns. Even at a bland town centre court, there were scenes.

His friends don't know where he goes from here in a sport which has devoured him and expelled him, and neither, one assumes, does he.

'He needs to get a foundation and get settled,' says one friend. 'He needs to determine whether he loves the game enough to continue within it.'

Sports.title: Silverstone set to avoid clash with Wimbledon final next year - with Bahrain to host 2027 curtain-raiser as F1 makes changes to calendar
Sports.content:
Silverstone set to avoid clash with Wimbledon final next year - with Bahrain to host 2027 curtain-raiser as F1 makes changes to calendar

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Silverstone will host the 2027 British Grand Prix on July 4, the Sunday that coincides with the middle weekend of Wimbledon, in a highlight of next year's Formula One calendar that is due to be released on Wednesday morning.

According to multiple sources, the schedule is also due to name Bahrain as the opening round of the season, which will contain 10 sprints, up from six this year.

Bahrain is pencilled in for March 14 with Saudi Arabia coming the following weekend before the travelling circus decamps to Australia as part of a 24-race programme.

Daily Mail Sport understands that Silverstone bosses have willingly agreed to the early July date and that the circuit's chief executive Stuart Pringle is content the overlap with Wimbledon is not a concern.

This collision of two iconic British sporting events has been the case in several recent years.

Despite the crossover this July, a crowd of 564,000 attended the Northamptonshire track over the weekend. It was the biggest attendance ever recorded at a Formula One event, eclipsing Adelaide in 1995.

The British Grand Prix won't clash with the Wimbledon's men's final next year as the Silverstone-based race will be held during the middle weekend of the SW19 action

Jannik Sinner won the men's Wimbledon final this year - with that showpiece and the British GP having collided in recent years

It is understood that the firm intention among F1 executives is that the first round will actually be staged in Bahrain, if world affairs allow, rather than be moved to Malaysia as is happening this year ('the Bahrain GP in Kuala Lumpur' on October 4) as the American/Israeli-Iranian war splutters on.

Monaco is expected to stay in its new June slot, back a week from its traditional May date.

Sports.title: How London lost out on the World Championships to NAIROBI: Inside shock decision that ignores Kenya's doping scandals and left bidders embarrassed
Sports.content:
The buzzword was ‘disappointment’ but shock was the undertone. That London has failed to land the 2029 World Athletics Championships was of less surprise upon the unveiling on Tuesday than the identity of the winner – Nairobi.

The allure of the event going to Africa for the first time is obvious. It is also indisputable that Kenya has contributed as many doping scandals as great athletic performances in recent years.

But internally, the threat was perceived from elsewhere. According to sources involved in London’s doomed bid, the past fortnight had seen a growing fear that their main competition would come from Munich.

When they received an email a little after 10am on Tuesday with the verdict, it dawned that their suspicions had been misplaced – Nairobi had been chosen to host in 2029, Munich in 2031, and London was left red-faced and empty handed.

As frontrunners and slight favourites for 2029, those behind London’s bid were devastated by the stunning twist at the end of a troubled process.

The initial difficulties can be traced to rows with West Ham United over the use of the London Stadium, which staged a highly-successful World Championships in August 2017 but has long been the reserve of footballing operations during non-summer months.

The London Stadium won't play host to the 2029 World Athletics Championship after bidders lost out to Nairobi, Kenya

The stadium was the backdrop for magical moments at the London 2012 Olympics, such as Mo Farah's win in the 5,000m (pictured)

Instead the Championships will head for the Kasarani Stadium in Kenya, where Everton played a friendly against Kariobangi Sharks in 2019

Daily Mail Sport reported in April that West Ham were trenchantly opposed to signing off on any plans to vacate their home ground during a sizeable chunk of September 2029, and that hurdle existed well beyond the April 3 deadline for provisional bid submissions to World Athletics.

A source close to the stand-off claims that two days prior to the deadline for final submissions, on August 5, there was still uncertainty if the bid would proceed. But London’s bid had influential support, including £45million of backing from the government and mayor’s office, and West Ham did compromise. The bid was submitted on time.

The mystery in the wake of failure is whether the high-profile row, which included public digs from 800m Olympic champion Keely Hodgkinson, had any bearing on the voting among the 26-member World Athletics Council in Budapest.

Senior figures within Athletic Ventures, which spearheaded the London bid and combines UK Athletics, The Great Run Company and London Marathon Events, are adamant the West Ham issue was not to blame for losing the vote. But it is also clear that the uneasy mood will not have helped to inspire confidence among those voters who were torn.

Similar would be said of the low crowds in the early stages of the European Championships staged in Birmingham this summer. They were cited by two sources following the announcement of Nairobi’s victory on Tuesday.

World Athletics president Sebastian Coe has previously played down those fears, citing that major events in London always deliver strong crowds. However, it is perhaps noteworthy that Coe did not have a vote in the staging decision and will conclude his final term in office next September.

Jack Buckner, CEO of UK Athletics and co-founder of Athletic Ventures, said: ‘We are deeply disappointed that the 2029 World Athletics Championships will not be held in London. We believed we had an outstanding bid which would genuinely take the sport to new levels.

‘Athletic Ventures has the ambition to bring those events here and, although today’s announcement hasn’t gone our way, we will review and regroup. We know the world’s athletes love competing here and we’ll continue to explore further opportunities to make that happen.’

The initial difficulties of London's bid can be traced to rows with West Ham United over the use of the London Stadium

World Athletics president Lord Coe did not have a vote in the staging decision and will conclude his final term in office next September

In announcing Nairobi’s win, Lord Coe said: ‘Nairobi presented a compelling and emotional bid, and taking the World Athletics Championships to Africa for the first time will be historic. Kenya is one of the great athletics nations.

‘It was important that the World Athletics Championships should come to Africa when we had the right host, the right bid and the right circumstances. Nairobi has demonstrated emphatically that this is their moment.’

Irrespective of the above, there is some awkwardness around a host better known lately for its doping scandals - more than 300 Kenyan athletes have been sanctioned for doping offences since 2017. It was only in March that Kenya was removed from the World Anti-Doping Agency compliance watch list. To receive this level of validation so soon has raised eyebrows within the sport.

For London mayor Sadiq Khan the news was a blow that could soon be compounded, if a fight between Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury materialises in Cardiff over Wembley Stadium.

A spokesperson for the mayor said: ‘The mayor is disappointed that London will not host the 2029 World Athletics Championships. London put forward an outstanding bid, and he thanks all the partners who supported it.

‘Sadiq congratulates Nairobi. Their selection means that the World Athletics Championships will be held in Africa for the first time ever in what is a landmark moment for athletics. He wishes them every success in 2029.

‘London remains the sporting capital of the world, and the mayor will continue working to bring more of the world’s biggest events to our city.’

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."

Collins: Ireland must build on World Cup near miss

Ireland captain Nathan Collins is confident his side have laid the foundations to qualify for future tournaments having seen hopes of reaching this summer's World Cup finals come to an end.

Collins and his team-mates were agonisingly close to the play-off final when they led the Czech Republic 2-1 in Prague on Thursday evening with just four minutes of normal time remaining.

Image: A dejected Nathan Collins and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson

However, Czech skipper Ladislav Krejci's late equaliser took the tie to extra-time and ultimately to penalties, where the hosts prevailed 4-3 to extend Ireland's wait for a first return to the big stage since 2002.

Asked about their progression to the play-offs, which was secured by back-to-back wins over Armenia, Portugal and Hungary, Brentford defender Collins said: "I'm not seeing many positives right now because we're in the gutter.

"But what we've created, the environment created with the fans and country, has been special. That's something we need to keep growing, to get even better at.

"That can help us get better on the pitch. We can push that and get fans to more tournaments."

Ireland had hoped to return to the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday for a showdown with either Denmark or North Macedonia for a place in the finals, but the Czechs will now host the Danes, who were 4-0 winners in Copenhagen.

Instead, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side face a friendly against the Macedonians.

Collins said: "The motivation has to be the same. We've to win to keep improving as a team and country. Any game we play at home is a big game."

Sports.title: 'Pain' - Irish heartbreak as Czech Republic win on penalties
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland's World Cup hopes were cruelly and heartbreakingly dashed as Czech Republic came from 2-0 down - to then beat them on penalties.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, who went two goals up after 23 minutes in Prague, were four minutes plus stoppage-time away from victory - before Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci headed in a corner to force extra-time.

Ireland were also a handful of penalties away from going through, as penalty saving expert Caomhin Kelleher saved from Mojmír Chytil in the shoot-out to give them a momentary advantage.

But Finn Azaz and Alan Browne both missed their spot kicks, allowing Patrick Schick and then Jan Kliment to win it for the hosts.

As a result, Czech Republic will go on to face Denmark on Tuesday for a spot at the World Cup - as Ireland's wait for a first World Cup appearance since 2002 goes on.

After Wales and Northern Ireland's semi-final exits, it also means England and Scotland will be the only teams from Great Britain and Ireland at the World Cup this summer.

Image: Ireland's players walk off the pitch after defeat

World Cup play-off finals - Europe Bosnia & Herzegovina vs Italy

Sweden vs Poland

Kosovo vs Turkey

Czech Republic vs Denmark

How Ireland threw away their lead

Ireland came flying out the blocks flying in Prague. Four shots in the opening ten minutes, including Nathan Collins crashing a shot off the bar from range, set the tone for a brilliant display - and they got their rewards.

A long throw caused chaos and Nathan Collins was deemed to have been caught slightly late by Vladimir Darida by VAR, who sent referee Glenn Byberg to the monitor for a review.

Troy Parrott, who else, crashed in the penalty for his sixth goal in the last three Ireland matches. And it got better for Ireland four minutes later.

Ryan Manning's corner found Dara O'Shea at the back post and his header across was cleared off the line by Vladimir Coufal - but off goalkeeper Matej Kovar and over the line.

Image: Czech Republic goalkeeper Matej Kovar scores an own goal to give Ireland a 2-0 lead

Ireland were in dreamland but a moment of Manning madness brought the Czech Republic back into it. The defender's needless tug back on Krekci - when the ball was heading out of play - was penalised by referee Byberg, with Patrick Schick pulling one back from the spot.

Ireland did, however, manage to settle the nerves down - right throughout the second half. Despite sustained Czech pressure in the second half, they barely threatened.

It was Ireland who had the better chances after the break, with Jayson Molumby striking the post and Parrott denied by a solid Kovar save at a corner. But then heartbreak struck with four minutes of normal time remaining, as Krejci bundled the ball in at the near post from a set piece.

Krejci could have even won it with the last kick of the game but scuffed his finish, as extra-time came.

Substitute Tomas Soucek missed a glorious chance for the hosts, with Adam Idah was denied a one-on-one chance by a goal-saving challenge from Stepan Chaloupek. Penalties came and the lottery fell in the hosts' favour.

Image: Jan Kliment scored the winning goal in the penalty shoot-out

Hallgrimsson confident in Ireland future despite 'pain'

Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"One word is pain. I feel pain. I feel pride for the performance of the players. They gave it all. I feel gratitude for all the supporters who supported us through the whole game, even after the loss. I feel pride being a part of that group. Personally, I know all the players will feel pain now. Only pain.

"We take with us that we can play teams higher in the FIFA ranking and can punch above our weight: Portugal, Hungary and here. We can compete with these teams. We came here with three wins in a row, a long time since that happened for this national team.

"So there's growth in this squad. It's maturing. These are been the biggest game most of these players have played. That's encouraging to know we're growing. It's strange to say that after we lost today.

"I know I'm biased in this, all the statistics and metrics of the team have improved. Big games, being on the line, crunch times all the time, we've managed to go through this. It showed the resilience, character of these players, that's why I feel confident going on."

Sports.title: Wilson key for Wales, NI aim for big upset while history beckons for ROI
Sports.content:
Sky Sports assesses Thursday's 2026 World Cup play-off semi-finals as Wales host Bosnia-Herzegovina, Northern Ireland go to four-time winners Italy and the Republic of Ireland face Czech Republic in Prague.

Thursday 7.45pm: Wales vs Bosnia-Herzegovina (winner will play Italy or Northern Ireland)

Harry Wilson is not the new Gareth Bale, but he's doing the job of Bale at his best, especially for Wales.

Fans have long been excited about Wilson's natural talent, but are now seeing his influence in the Premier League on a weekly basis for Fulham. This season, he has 10 goals and six assists for club, while for country, his stats are even better with five goals and two assists in his last five games.

If Wilson starts running the show, his confidence will feed to the other players and to the home crowd, and Wales will be very difficult to stop on their own patch.

Which World Cup group would Wales be in? If Wales qualify for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Craig Bellamy wanted to create an identity for Wales when he took over as head coach. It's now clear: he wants front-foot football coupled with intensity and energy.

Bellamy doesn't always see that in international football as he finds it slower at times compared with club football, but his Wales side will not be ponderous. You could see during the qualification campaign that Wales' intensity in winning the ball back very quickly and holding possession grew. Now it's about consistently doing it.

Apart from consistency in play, there needs to be consistency in selection. Much is always made about the 'spine' of a good team, from the goalkeeper to the glory hunter! Leeds United provide a fair chunk of Wales' spine with 'keeper Karl Darlow on form and in receipt of the No.1 keeper's jersey. Joe Rodon is the rock at centre-back that success relies upon, while team-mate Ethan Ampadu's versatility means he can link anywhere between defence and midfield. Throw in one of the in-form Premier League stars, Harry Wilson, and a strong spine can take a team a long way.

Ask Bellamy if he has thought about preparing for the play-off final against either Italy or Northern Ireland and you'll get glared at. It's Bosnia, Bosnia and Bosnia. He won't entertain anything beyond Bosnia until the game is over. It's a danger, a banana skin he wants to avoid. Thinking too far ahead isn't good on this occasion.

Geraint Hughes

Thursday 7.45pm: Italy vs Northern Ireland (winner will play Wales or Bosnia-Herzegovina)

On paper, perhaps in reality, it's David vs Goliath.

Northern Ireland enjoy David vs Goliath. Once upon a time it was David (Healy) vs England and David (Healy) vs Spain.

For smaller nations there is comfort in being the underdog. A loss would be met without a major backlash, a win makes you a hero. That's how Michael O'Neill's side will approach Thursday's assignment in Bergamo against Italy.

Which World Cup group would Northern Ireland be in? If Northern Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Conor Bradley and Daniel Ballard are out. Between them they represent 50 per cent of the Northern Ireland players currently plying their trade in the Premier League.

The pair's absence is as much a blow to Northern Ireland's attacking prospects as it is defensively. Ballard represents their best aerial threat from set-pieces, Bradley their most dynamic player on the ball.

And yet for some reason that only football can explain, hope remains. The four-time World Cup winners are heavy favourites but far from the Azzurri powerhouse of old.

If Northern Ireland have it their way, it's unlikely to be a pretty spectacle. But can they frustrate their hosts? 0-0 at half-time? Pounce on the sense of angst that will exist among the home support?

To call it a free hit would be to downplay the importance of the game. But Northern Ireland are free from the weight of expectation.

Daring to dream of a result that becomes instant folklore.

Michael Morrow

Thursday 7.45pm: Czech Republic vs Republic of Ireland (winner will play Denmark or North Macedonia)

Image: Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson and captain Seamus Coleman spoke to the media in Prague

History beckons for the Republic of Ireland here in Prague.

Make no mistake, this will be the biggest game to date for a lot of these Irish players as they attempt to take another step to this summer's World Cup but they must get past Czech Republic to do so.

Which World Cup group would Republic of Ireland be in? If the Republic of Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group A with co-hosts Mexico, South Africa and South Korea.

Still coming off the euphoria of the incredible back-to-back wins against Portugal and Hungary last November, this is an Irish team full of confidence.

Having spoken to a few people around the Czech Republic team, those results have been noted and they are particularly worried about Irish striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in those two games in November - including the 96th-minute winner against Hungary.

Head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson spoke ahead of this game about one of the key aspects is visually and mentally being ready for the challenge ahead of them, he seemed as calm and confident as usual.

However his key selection dilemma is does he bring back the experienced, tried and tested players such as Seamus Coleman, Robbie Brady and Chiedoze Ogbene - all three have had limited game-time this season for a variety of injuries.

Coleman and Brady especially are the only two players in the squad who were part of Ireland's last team in a major tournament which was in 2016 - their experience could prove vital.

Image: Can Troy Parrott recreate his Irish heroics in Prague on Thursday?

Their opponents are in a state of flux.

Czech Republic have a new head coach who takes charge of his first game on Thursday, with West Ham's Tomas Soucek also being stripped of the captaincy after November's internationals having caused shockwaves in the local media - Wolves' Ladislav Krejci has replaced him.

The pressure feels like it's all on the home side which could play into Ireland's advantage as they look to take another step to qualify for this summer's World Cup - their first since 2002.

Danyal Khan
