World.title: Seven noncitizens charged in North Texas election-integrity investigation
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Seven noncitizens have been charged in North Texas as part of a sweeping federal election-integrity operation, as the Trump administration ramps up its push to investigate and prosecute election-related crimes ahead of the midterms.

Fox News exclusively joined Homeland Security Investigations as federal agents carried out arrests in the Dallas–Fort Worth area, getting a firsthand look at how investigators are identifying and pursuing suspected cases of noncitizen voting.

U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Texas, Ryan Raybould, announced that six defendants were indicted on Sept. 10, while a seventh was charged with a criminal complaint the following day.

Federal agents arrested six of the defendants over the following several days, while a seventh, who had been considered a fugitive, surrendered to federal authorities.

"One of the individuals, an illegal alien from Mexico, actually was a 2023 convicted felon for lying on a passport application," Raybould said. "So this person has already interacted with our office, the Department of Justice, and chose to then again commit a serious federal violation."

In an exclusive one-on-one with Fox News, Raybould said the seven cases are only the beginning of his office’s efforts.

Earlier this month, the DOJ charged five people in Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Wisconsin in cases involving alleged illegal voting or fraudulent registration during the 2022 or 2024 elections.

"It’s important to clean up our elections and make sure that they’re free and fair," Raybould told Fox News.

"And my job as U.S. attorney is to prosecute cases and controversies. And so if fraud happens, whether it’s our elections, our health care fraud system, stealing from the American taxpayer, I’m going to go after it."

Raybould said prosecutors are focused on whether federal law was broken, not which candidate received an allegedly illegal vote.

FBI ARRESTS SUSPECT ACCUSED OF PAYING LA HOMELESS TO FORGE SIGNATURE USING REGISTERED VOTERS' IDENTITIES

"We don’t even know who they voted for, frankly, like we don’t care," Raybould said. "You can vote for whoever. That is not what we are focused on, it's the act. You're not allowed to vote if you're an illegal alien."

The federal effort to identify potential noncitizen voters has drawn scrutiny from Democrats over how investigators are accessing and analyzing voter information.

Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, (D-N.Y.), and Sen. Alex Padilla, (D-Calif.), on Monday made public a complaint from an anonymous DHS whistleblower alleging that personnel working on the department’s "Unlawful Voter Initiative" were directed to access state voter records in ways that may violate state laws.

DHS has pushed back on those allegations.

"The Department accessed publicly available data from states’ voter rolls and cross-referenced them with known aliens in our systems. It’s not rocket science; it’s an easy step to secure our elections," a DHS spokesperson told Fox News.

Asked about the allegations, U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould defended investigators’ use of federal databases and publicly available information.

"HSI has access to databases, and they have a right to access that database," Raybould told Fox News.

"They also can cross-reference that database with publicly available information."

Raybould compared the investigative approach to health care fraud cases, in which federal authorities analyze government data to identify potential outliers for further investigation.

WHITE HOUSE UNLOADS ON VIOLENT ‘CRIMINAL ALIEN’ NABBED AFTER INVESTIGATORS UNCOVER ELECTION OFFENSE

"We look at Medicaid data to identify outliers all the time, to pick targets," Raybould said. "Everybody should be in favor of making sure that illegals do not vote in our elections.

Raybould said prosecuting election fraud should have bipartisan support.

"If someone is illegal, and they vote in an election, that draws down the value of the vote of American citizens, and so it also undermines our democracy, and the vote is absolutely critical," Raybould said. "It's how we elect our leaders. It's an important voice for American citizens when they get to cast the ballot."

The seven non-citizens are charged with the following offenses:

Helen Sayen Adams, is a 67-year-old citizen of Nigeria and lawful permanent resident (Green Card holder) since May 2024, is charged with voting by an alien in a federal election and false statement of citizenship in order to register to vote. Adams allegedly falsely claimed U.S. citizenship on a Texas voter-registration application in June 2024 and voted in the November 2024 general election in Tarrant County. She later admitted she was not a U.S. citizen.

Joshua Nmelichukwu Akpom, is a 27-year-old citizen of Nigeria and lawful permanent resident since 2016, charged with false statements in relation to naturalization. As alleged, Akpom falsely denied on his 2026 naturalization application that he had ever claimed U.S. citizenship, registered to vote, or voted, despite registering in 2017 and voting in the 2018 general election. Due to the five-year statute of limitations, prosecutors relied on the naturalization offense rather than the voting conduct.

Carlos Salas Barrios, is a 41-year-old Mexican citizen and lawful permanent resident since 2018, charged by complaint with allegedly voting by an alien in a Federal Election. Barrios unlawfully cast a provisional ballot in Tarrant County in the November 2024 general election despite not being a U.S. citizen and not being registered. Although the ballot was ultimately rejected, casting it was still unlawful under Texas and federal law.

Khalwinder Singh Bhengura, is a 69-year-old citizen of India and lawful permanent resident since 2022, charged with voting by an alien in a federal election and false statement of citizenship in order to register to vote. Bhengura falsely claimed U.S. citizenship when registering to vote in January 2024 and again when applying for a Texas driver's license later that year in August. He voted in the November 2024 general election and later admitted he knew he was not a citizen. He was arrested on Sept. 11.

Celestin Katubadi, is a 20-year-old citizen of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and lawful permanent resident, charged with voting by an alien in a federal election and false statement of citizenship in order to vote. Katubadi cast a provisional ballot in Tarrant County during the November 2024 general election after falsely claiming U.S. citizenship on an affidavit of provisional-voter. Although his ballot was rejected, casting it was still unlawful by Texas and federal law.

Rocio Thrasher, is a 38-year-old Mexican citizen and lawful permanent resident since 2017, charged with voting by an alien in a federal election and false statement of citizenship in order to register to vote. According to the indictment, Thrasher allegedly falsely declared U.S. citizenship when registering in June 2024 and voted in the November 2024 general election. She later admitted knowing she was not a citizen.

Moises Anwar Arellano Alba, is a 36-year-old illegal alien from Mexico ordered deported in July, charged with voting by an alien in a federal election and false statement of citizenship in order to register to vote. He allegedly falsely claimed U.S. citizenship when applying for a Texas driver's license in 2023 and voted early in the 2024 general election in Dallas County despite being a noncitizen and convicted felon. He admitted in immigration proceedings that he had voted. Arellano Alba was a fugitive until this morning when he surrendered himself to federal agents.

World.title: Pentagon reveals secret space weapons are already in orbit — but won't say what they do
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The U.S. has weapons orbiting Earth that can be used to defend American forces from attacks in space, the Air Force secretary revealed this week in a rare public acknowledgment of capabilities the Pentagon has largely kept secret.

Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said Monday that the Space Force now has "on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action," but declined to say what the weapons are, how they work or when they were deployed.

The carefully worded disclosure marks a shift in how openly the U.S. military talks about weapons in orbit as China and Russia develop their own capabilities to disrupt, disable or destroy satellites.

TRUMP TO TRANSFORM SPACEFLIGHT FROM SPECTACLE TO STATUS QUO TARGETING 3 LAUNCHES PER DAY

"Is there any question in the room, by anybody, about whether or not the Chinese or Russians have been developing these sorts of weapons?" Meink told reporters after his remarks at the Air & Space Forces Association’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference in National Harbor, Maryland — right outside of Washington, D.C.

"For over a decade, we’ve been talking about the fact, and we have expressed concern, that the Chinese and Russians were developing weapons for space," he continued. "We need to focus on making sure we can protect ourselves operating in that environment."

Exactly what the U.S. has put into orbit remains a mystery.

The U.S. has previously discussed placing weapons in space, including plans to deploy space-based interceptors capable of destroying incoming missiles as part of President Donald Trump’s Golden Dome missile defense system.

But Meink’s disclosure goes a step further: The Space Force already has weapons in orbit for "space control," a mission aimed at protecting U.S. access to space and, if necessary, denying an adversary the ability to use it.

The Pentagon has historically revealed little about the weapons developed for that mission, with publicly known U.S. counter-space capabilities largely based on the ground.

"What the U.S. is going for is a wow factor here," Clayton Swope, deputy director of the Aerospace Security Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told Fox News Digital. "Wow. The U.S. has never talked about space weapons like this before."

"That's really what is exceptional and newsworthy about this revelation," Swope said. "The U.S. is saying we're putting weapons in space to make sure that our adversaries can't use space, or to make sure that we can continue to use space."

Meink appeared to make clear that the ambiguity surrounding the weapons is intentional. He told reporters his language was "very well thought out" and declined to say whether the systems are kinetic or non-kinetic. Kinetic weapons physically strike or destroy a target — think bombs, bullets and missile — while non-kinetic systems can disrupt or disable it without blowing it up — like cyber attacks or radio jams.

"There are a lot of factors that roll into how we talk about these things," Meink said, explaining that publicly revealing a capability can contribute to deterrence while disclosing too much about it can undermine that advantage.

"We’re not going to talk about the specifics of what we’re doing, whether we’ve tested it, not tested it, or anything else," he said. That leaves a wide range of possibilities.

Fox News Digital did not hear back from the Space Force when reached for details of the weapon.

INSIDE AMERICA'S LASER REVOLUTION AS THE MILITARY NEARS BIG BATTLEFIELD BREAKTHROUGH

Swope said "space control weapons" could encompass everything from kinetic systems capable of firing missiles or projectiles at another satellite to jammers that interfere with satellite communications or lasers designed to temporarily overwhelm imaging sensors.

"We really don't have enough information to know precisely which one of these types of capabilities we're talking about," Swope said. "It's really anybody's guess what type of weapon we're talking about."

FATAL AIR AMBULANCE CRASH EXPOSES GROWING GPS DANGER FACING US FLIGHTS

But whatever the Pentagon has deployed, putting a weapon in orbit rather than launching it from Earth could offer one potentially significant advantage: speed and surprise.

A weapon launched from Earth toward a satellite could potentially give an adversary warning that an attack was underway. A capability already positioned in orbit could dramatically shorten that window.

"Maybe something measured at dozens of minutes could be compressed into just mere minutes," Swope said.

"And you wouldn't have any indication that maybe a jammer was turned on, on the satellite, other than all of a sudden your signal is being interfered with," he added.

"If you can act fast without your adversary knowing, if you can have surprise, that gives you a strategic or an asymmetric advantage in combat," Swope said. "And having systems in orbit do just that."

Even observing the spacecraft itself may offer few clues about what it can do.

"Space is a very transparent place," Swope said, noting that governments and civilian observers can track where satellites are, how fast they are moving and what orbits they occupy.

"But what you'll see often is, oh, it's a satellite," he said. "It's a lot of technology with solar panels and antenna on it. And you don't really know much beyond that."

A satellite equipped to jam another spacecraft’s signals, for example, might look much like an ordinary communications satellite.

"Any signal can be a jamming signal," Swope said. "It just depends on if it's the one you want to receive, or the one that someone's trying to use to jam you."

The concept of weapons operating in orbit is not new. Swope pointed to the Soviet Union’s work on co-orbital anti-satellite weapons dating to the 1960s. Russia has continued developing counterspace capabilities, including systems designed to operate in orbit near other satellites.

China has also developed and tested technologies that could threaten spacecraft, including satellite-servicing and debris-removal systems that have legitimate civilian uses but could potentially be repurposed to interfere with another satellite.

Other forms of interference are already widespread.

"When we talk about jamming and spoofing and cyberattacks against space systems, these happen all the time, both from Russia and China and other countries like North Korea and Iran," Swope said. "There is so much jamming and spoofing happening around the world right now, it's almost ubiquitous."

Those attacks can target systems such as GPS and satellite communications without physically destroying a spacecraft.

That distinction could become critical during a conflict. Jamming, spoofing or cyberattacks may remain below the threshold that prompts a major military response, while physically destroying a satellite could represent a significant escalation.

"If you drop a bomb on a satellite ground station or you shoot a missile at a satellite in space, that's a big difference," Swope said. "That's a huge escalation."

The stakes are particularly high because modern U.S. warfare is deeply dependent on space-based systems for communications, navigation, intelligence, missile warning and targeting.

"Space is an enabler of joint operations," Swope said. "We can't do military operations the way that we do them today without satellites, without systems in space."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

China increasingly faces the same dependency, making control of space potentially decisive in a conflict between the two powers.

"Whoever has space and can deny that to their adversary has a huge asymmetric advantage in a conflict," Swope said.

"China depends on space as well, and their use of space for joint operations looks very much like the United States," he added. "Both countries, I would go so far as to say, depend on space to conduct military operations on Earth."

World.title: German tennis star takes a jab at Trinity Rodman & losers try to cancel Ella Langley over old hunting photos
World.content:
'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday-Friday on OutKick.com.

Wow, the Dolphins are really bad.

We're not talking the usual levels of Miami Dolphins bad. We're talking about 1–15 bad, à la 2007. Except it'll be 1-16 now. If they're lucky to squeak out that one W at all.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

But you know what? I'm at peace with it.

As a lifelong Dolphins fan, I'm accustomed to sadness, disappointment and misery. That's because every year when Week 1 rolls around — despite knowing better — I delude myself into thinking "this season will be better!"

I'm like Amy Klobuchar wearing the same dumb shirt and the same goofy grin.

This year, I have no such delusions. Every week, I fully understand the team will s---- itself worse than that HYROX chick. Only this time, instead of a quarterback who gets concussed every other week, we have one who runs fast and wears rhinestone cleats.

Ah, the serenity of low expectations. I'm as carefree as Bo Nix.

So with that, let's get to our Tuesday Nightcaps — featuring Trinity Rodman, Ella Langley and Aryna Sabalenka.

And there will be nothing about Sydney Sweeney, Holly Rowe or Arch Manning. Because I'm tired of hearing about all of them.

Let's roll.

The mob tries to cancel Ella Langley over hunting photos

Some people really don't like Ella Langley.

I've heard a multitude of reasons for this: She cut a song with Morgan Wallen. She followed Charlie Kirk on TikTok. She got some lip filler. She's allegedly MAGA.

The real reason is probably because "Choosin' Texas" has spent a bazillion weeks at No. 1, and a good chunk of our population just likes to hate on people who are successful.

But now, the miserable souls of the interweb have found a new reason to smear the good name of Ella Langley — she's a hunter!

Some folks with too much time on their hands dug up some old photos of Ella showing off bucks she harvested in her home state of Alabama.

I love how that second post said she'd been "caught" hunting animals. As if Ella didn't pose for that photo and post it on her own social media account.

Damn, you really busted her!

Let's see what the comments are saying.

Very sane people over there on the Twitter machine.

As the founding mother of OutKick OutDoors, I'm obviously pro (legal and humane) hunting and fishing. And I won't bore you with all the reasons why hunting — particularly whitetail deer hunting — is crucial for conservation, preventing the spread of disease, and funding for the protection of wildlife and their habitats. I encourage you to do your own research if you're interested in learning more.

JORDAN DAVIS FACES FAN BACKLASH OVER HAWAII AXIS DEER HUNT DESPITE STRONG CONSERVATION BACKING

I also have no problem with people who choose not to hunt or choose not to eat meat. That's absolutely your prerogative.

But I guarantee at least 99% of the people screeching at Ella right now have no problem stopping by the Taco Bell drive-thru or picking up a pack of chicken at the grocery store. But harvesting your own fresh venison apparently makes you evil.

Spare me the outrage, losers.

Alexander Zverev throws shade at Trinity Rodman

Trinity Rodman is a world-class soccer player for the USWNT. But she's also a tennis WAG.

So while her boyfriend, Ben Shelton, competed in the US Open the past couple of weeks, Trinity was in the stands supporting him.

Unfortunately for Trinity (and America), Shelton lost to Germany's Alexander Zverev in the men's final. That's after she played a soccer game in Washington, D.C. on the same day and then rushed 200 miles to NYC to catch the end of the match.

When he won, Zverev gave Trinity a shoutout.

"Trinity, I thought you have a game today," Zverev joked. "Well done to you as well. You’re the lucky charm ... not today, but usually."

The crowd laughed. Trinity laughed. Ben laughed.

And then Iman Shumpert wanted to see Ben defend his lady's honor.

"I ain't gonna lie, Ben, get up in there, you gotta say something. I ain't gonna lie, he just shot..." Shumpert said. "You need a rematch. Yeah, you gotta treat it like boxing. Hey, Ben, go get your get back, buddy."

Zverev might have stolen the Grand Slam title. But I don't think she's stealing Shelton's girl. She seems pretty into him.

Let's open the mailbag.

No one cares about women's basketball

...at least according to Keith H.

Keith writes: No one watches Women’s basketball and no one cares about whatever "tournament" is going on. The only things more boring are Women’s hockey, Women’s soccer, and watching paint dry.

Amber:

Folks, Keith cares so little about women's basketball that he clicked on a story about the USA women's basketball team's semifinal game against Spain. Then, he found the writer (me) and typed out an email about how much he doesn't care. On a Saturday night. While college football was on.

Going to such lengths suggests to me that Keith actually cares a lot about women's basketball.

Listen, folks, the reason we cover so much WNBA is because our women's basketball coverage consistently performs spectacularly well in metrics like page views, search and engagement. If it didn't, we wouldn't spend so much time and energy writing about it. All of our show hosts wouldn't be talking about it. And we certainly wouldn't send a reporter all the way to Europe to cover it.

We give the people what they want. And even the "hate reads" count as page views, baby.

More love for Upstate New York

A couple of weeks ago, I wrote about making my first trip to the St. Lawrence River in Upstate New York. But it certainly won't be my last.

Brian S. writes: It’s not a very manly phrase, I realize, but I was tickled pink reading your reaction to the St. Lawrence River. I was born - 1969 - and raised in Upstate New York. The River and 1,000 Islands have been a destination for my family since the 40’s. We grew up trailer camping in the state parks there, before renting cottages once we outgrew the camper, and eventually my folks purchased a summer home in Cape Vincent, a short drive from Clayton, where you were.

My now adult children looked forward to every summer stay, even though the drive from New Jersey is about 5-1/2 hours. Whenever I bring friends to the area for the first time, they all have the same reaction as you had. We may have even crossed paths last weekend, as my wife and I were there visiting for a few days, and we even checked out the Bassmasters tourney.

I’m glad you were able to experience the beauty of the region, and hope you’re able to visit again in the future.

Amber:

Every summer, my husband and I like to retreat to Lake Superior, and the St. Lawrence area area reminded me a lot of the Northwoods.

There's just something so serene about the small towns around the Great Lakes. Everything's just slower there — in the best way possible.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Who cares what Aryna Sabalenka is wearing?

Lucia writes: May I ask why the uproar over Sabalenka’s choice of tennis attire, but I hear nothing about Osaka’s abysmal fashion choices. First, let’s ask why she needs an entrance ‘outfit’? They definitely say ‘look at me’, but I don’t see them as making much of a statement about her tennis skills. Secondly, Osaka’s court wear yesterday could have very easily been made out of the Hefty Bags you referenced in your article. With that said, I’m not a fan of Sabalenka’s attire either. Nike should be embarrassed they put their ‘swoosh’ on the fishnet. While she may have a contractual obligation, she and her management should have put their respective foot down.

Lastly, I don’t understand why the urge to make a ‘fashion’ statement has become a thing. Used to be the serve, the smash, the volley said it all.

Amber:

To be fair, I have seen plenty of people poke fun at Osaka's wild get-ups.

I think the entrance outfit and the non-traditional kits are just part of tennis culture right now. It's like NFL and NBA players playing dress-up just to walk from their cars into the stadium on game day.

Sabalenka's mesh kit wasn't my favorite, either. But it got us talking. And that was probably Nike's goal.

One more thing: 'South Park' is back tomorrow

My fellow "South Park" super fans will likely agree that last season was the worst one yet.

No, not because they made fun of Trump. They made fun of Trump for five whole seasons when they had an orange-faced Mr. Garrison acting as President of the United States.

The difference is that those seasons were original, funny and clever. This past season was none of those things.

It was just Trump having a "butt baby" with Satan and the same "small d—" joke over and over and over. We get it. Even my liberal friends were like, "Can we please go back to the actual characters of 'South Park?'"

But, naturally, Hollywood loved it. So Trey Parker and Matt Stone were awarded their first Emmy.

Well, "South Park" is back tomorrow. Except they're calling it "South America" to make fun of Trump's renaming of the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario.



And you know what? Cool. That's the kind of satire they should be doing. And judging by the trailer, it's actually going to be about the boys this time.

So, fingers crossed, this season won't just be another giant turd sandwich.

You sold out and got your Emmy, Matt and Trey. Now please go back to being funny.

That's because Simmons stepped on something of an online landmine Monday night while he was watching his former Denver Broncos team play the Kansas City Chiefs.

During the broadcast, ESPN's Joe Buck noted that Broncos' linebacker Jonathan Cooper was not in the lineup because he's currently suspended on the NFL exempt list while he awaits a Nov. 10 trial on four charges, including felony second-degree assault by strangulation of his former girlfriend.

3 NFL STARS HIT COMMISSIONER'S EXEMPT LIST AFTER OFFSEASON FILLED WITH LEGAL TROUBLE

The former NFL great complained that ESPN was mentioning his former teammate during the broadcast but the situation between New England Patriots coach Mike Vrabel and former reporter Dianna Russini wasn't discussed on TV.

NBC REMINDS PREGAME VIEWERS ABOUT MIKE VRABEL-DIANNA RUSSINI SCANDAL COACH AND PATRIOTS WANT TO FORGET

Vrabel has been put before the court of public opinion for the relationship, but there are no allegations of abuse that will be heard in a court of law. The analogy between Cooper and Vrabel is flawed at best.

World.title: Finneas, Aaron Rowe exit Ed Sheeran tour in protest of Macklemore being dropped
World.content:
Finneas and other musical artists have withdrawn as supporting acts for Ed Sheeran on Tuesday in protest of Macklemore being dropped from the tour after the rapper says New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft organized a boycott against him.

Macklemore, whose real name is Ben Haggerty, joined Sheeran’s “Loop” tour in New Jersey earlier this month. He made remarks to the Metlife Stadium crowd that included the phrase “Free Palestine” before performing his protest anthem “Hind’s Hall.”

He announced Monday that he was no longer on the tour after Kraft called Sheeran and threatened to cancel Sheeran’s planned tour if Macklemore was still performing.

All of the opening acts listed for Sheeran’s upcoming tour dates have now announced their departures.

Finneas put out a statement the next day saying he decided to withdraw from his upcoming tour dates with Sheeran. He wrote on Instagram that he stands “with Palestine and its people.”

“Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed,” Finneas wrote.

This is not the singer’s first public display of support for Palestinians amid the Israel-Hamas war. He and his younger sister, Billie Eilish, joined fellow celebrities last year to promote a benefit concert to support relief efforts called “Together for Palestine.”

Finneas’ statement came roughly an hour after one of Sheeran’s other openers, Irish singer Aaron Rowe, announced he was dropping out.

Rowe posted his statement to Instagram as well, saying in part that he could not stand by while billionaires silenced voices speaking up against “Israeli genocide” and those who highlight the “savage murder of children.”

“Ed has been a friend to me and has changed my life, I could never thank him enough for this,” Rowe wrote. “But as Irish people we know all too well about genocide, forced famine, and violent occupation.”

A United Nations commission said that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza in findings from an independent inquiry published last year. Israeli government officials have denied the allegations, calling them “distorted and false.”

Beoga, Sheeran’s house band, also said the group was departing the tour. The Irish band described itself as being friends with Sheeran for over 10 years who “never saw ourselves playing in stadiums of that size and that opportunity is not lost on us.”

“It’s important that everyone knows that the real enemy is the zionist lobby,” the band’s statement said. “They have worked tirelessly to silence artists who want to speak freely about a genocide happening before our eyes, for fear of retribution.”

The band’s statement went on to criticize Kraft and express support for Macklemore and his message. It added that the real issue is that Palestinians have been killed.

Beoga’s Instagram post was captioned “Saoirse don Phailistín,” which translates from Irish to “Freedom for Palestine.”

Danish band Lukas Graham issued a statement apologizing to fans but confirming that the group was departing Sheeran’s tour. The statement called on the band’s roots as a small community in Denmark where “speaking your mind was part of everyday life.”

“We should be able to speak about war, about civilians being killed, about children who deserve to group up,” the band said. “Wherever they live. Whatever flag flies over them.”

Sheeran put out a statement Tuesday morning as backlash against him grew clarifying that it was not his decision to remove Macklemore from the tour. The “Shape of You” singer said he spent a week trying to build bridges after venues began to reach out to him to say they would pull his shows if Macklemore was still a supporting act.

“I was informed that this stance was based on how Macklemore conveyed part of his message during his performance, rather than everything that was said,” Sheeran said. “I spoke with venues at length all week to try and build a bridge. One of those people was Robert Kraft.”

But Sheeran says it was his concert promoter who held the contract with Macklemore and the promoter who chose to drop the rapper. He expressed his respect for Macklemore’s “strength of purpose to stand up and shout for what he believes.”

Messina Touring Group, the promoter for Sheeran’s tour, told Rolling Stone Monday that it was informed that multiple venues “will not allow a concert to take place with Macklemore on the lineup.” The statement said cancellations would “impact hundreds of thousands of fans,” confirming that Macklemore would no longer perform on his previously scheduled dates.

The company did not respond to multiple requests for comment from NBC News regarding Macklemore’s removal from the tour.

In his own statement on Monday, Kraft did not deny Macklemore’s accusations.

He said the decision to bar the artist from Gillette Stadium was based on Macklemore’s “recent actions” on stage and “a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community.” Kraft added that the decision was not about trying to stifle Palestinian advocacy or diminishing the suffering of Palestinians.

“I would welcome the opportunity to sit down with Macklemore and discuss the facts, because ultimately our goal is the same — peace for all people, an end to suffering, and an end to all hate,” Kraft said.

World.title: Trump’s handpicked Kennedy Center board again votes to close venue, calling it ‘unsafe’
World.content:
President Donald Trump’s handpicked Kennedy Center board voted Tuesday to immediately shutter the performing arts center citing the institution’s “dire” financial and structural shape.

The vote came shortly after a federal judge in Washington, D.C., rejected the board’s latest effort to add Trump’s name to the building’s facade — a move the board says is necessary to save the memorial to John F. Kennedy from bankruptcy.

In a social media post after the vote, Trump said renovations wouldn’t happen unless his name was added to the building.

“The closing will take place immediately, however, the Renovation and Reconstruction, which is a very large and complex job, cannot begin until such time as the D.C. Circuit rules on the Board’s approved name,” Trump wrote in the Truth Social post. “If the ruling is a negative one, which it should not be, and is not overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court, the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place.”

“In the meantime, 17 Million Dollars, raised by President Trump, has been put into The Kennedy Center account to keep it afloat,” he added. Congress appropriated $250 million for the project last year.

The board had cited a partial ceiling collapse in the center’s Grand Foyer earlier this month as evidence the center needed to be immediately closed for repairs.

A construction consultant and the center’s director “consider the main building to be unsafe for continued occupancy, and anticipate further risk to the public and employees if the building is not immediately closed and renovations begun,” the board said in a draft resolution to close the center for two years.

It was the third time since February that the board voted to close the center for renovations for a two-year period. Ex-officio board member Rep. Joyce Beatty, D-Ohio, has challenged those efforts in court, saying the board had not done its due diligence before deciding it needed to close the venue.

The center was initially scheduled to close on July 5.

A tarp remains in place on the facade of the Kennedy Center on Sept. 2. Finn Gomez / Getty Images

Attorneys for the board have said the legal action has kept them from doing necessary repairs, but the judge presiding over the case noted at a hearing Tuesday — as he had previously — that his earlier order preventing full closure allowed for emergency repairs.

Trump, who was elected chairman last year by the board he appointed, joined the closed-door meeting virtually and spent several minutes criticizing both Beatty and the judge who blocked his name from being added to the façade, according to a source familiar with the meeting.

Attorneys for the center are expected to ask the judge to lift his block on the center’s closure this week. A source familiar with Beatty’s legal strategy said her attorneys will oppose that move and argue that the repairs can be done without shutting down the center.

In a separate resolution that was originally scheduled to be taken up Tuesday as well, the Kennedy Center said it “is in a dire financial position” and facing potential bankruptcy after it “exhausted its fiscal resources” — and that only Trump can rescue it.

In order to do so, the board had said he would have to be recognized for his efforts on the exterior of the building.

“The Kennedy Center is in such a precarious fiscal position that it will not be able to support its payroll obligations, nor routine maintenance contracts within a matter of weeks,” the draft resolution that was made public in a court filing said. “While actively considering alternative means of fiscal survival, President Trump has offered to step in and raise the necessary funds to keep the Center from bankruptcy during its much needed renovation.”

“With certain fiscal collapse within weeks, the board seeks to determine what recognition and acknowledgement will comply” with the judge’s earlier order banning the center from being renamed the Donald J. Trump and John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.

The board did not vote on the resolution at the meeting because members said they needed to focus on the closure issue.

The trustees had voted last month to instead add the words “renovated and restored by President Donald J. Trump” to the building and to rename the center’s grounds “President Donald J. Trump Plaza” by Sept. 8. The new draft resolution offered numerous similar suggestions.

In a ruling issued just ahead of the board vote, U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper found the latest attempt to add Trump’s name to the facade was also illegal.

“Simply put, Defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress’s blessing. The board resolution bucks a federal court order and a statute Congress enacted.”

He also noted the board’s threat about fundraising — and its claim that the center may need to be razed if Trump’s repair plan isn’t followed — with skepticism.

The “government offered ‘no proof that current or future donations hinge on President Trump’s name being on the building’ and ‘no competent evidence that removing the Trump name would prevent the Center from fulfilling its artistic mission, as it has done for the last sixty years,’” he wrote.

Instead, Cooper suggested, the opposite could be true.

“The renaming of the Center coincided with declines in revenue and contributions, as artists cancelled performances, the Washington National Opera ended its 50-year residency, and ticket sales and viewership of the Kennedy Center Honors broadcast dropped precipitously. The Board also has access to the $257 million that Congress appropriated for necessary capital improvements,” he wrote, but that’s “beside the point for present purposes.”

And while cultural institutions often honor big donors by naming buildings or features after them, Cooper said, “Congress had other ideas for the Kennedy Center.”

“It limited such memorials and donor recognitions to discrete (and discreet) areas, so as not to detract from the Center’s function as an ongoing memorial to President Kennedy. The current Board’s apparent disagreement with that approach does not change the law,” he wrote.

Cooper said he could “not license a violation of those authorities under threat that some unidentified donors will withhold their largesse if the Board is not allowed to have its way. It can even less reward a decision by Board members, including the Chair, to curb the Center’s fundraising efforts because they cannot abide statutory restrictions on displaying his name.”

Beatty praised Cooper’s ruling in a statement, saying “The law is extremely clear: The John F. Kennedy Center is named for President Kennedy — and no one else. But President Trump is holding the Kennedy Center hostage unless he can put his name on this sacred memorial.”

“This unlawfulness is as breathtaking as it is wrong, and it needs to stop,” she said.

“Legal sanity has once again prevailed over Trump’s vanity,” her attorneys, Norm Eisen of Democracy Defenders Action and Nathaniel Zelinsky of Washington Litigation Group, said in a joint statement.

World.title: Iran war driving up inflation for Americans, CBO report says
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The war with Iran is driving up inflation and borrowing costs may increase for Americans, according to a new report released Tuesday by the Congressional Budget Office.

The report found the war was responsible for more than one-third of the increase in inflation this year, and inflation will likely continue to grow in the first quarter of next year. The CBO specifically blames the war for more than 40% of inflation during the second quarter of 2026 and an estimated half a percentage point of higher inflation during the first quarter of 2027. Interest rates are likely to rise as a result, making borrowing more costly the report found.

Interest rates are likely to keep rising as a result, making borrowing more costly, the report found. The rate on the typical 30-year mortgage was under 6% before the war started; it’s at 7.22% as of Tuesday, according to Mortgage News Daily. Wall Street, likewise, expects the Federal Reserve to raise its key interest rate Wednesday in a bid to tamp down inflation.

The main driver of increased inflation is fewer oil and natural gas shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, the CBO report says. The average price of a gallon of gasoline in the U.S. is up 45% since the beginning of the war, hitting $4.32 as of Tuesday. Diesel, which is essential to the economy as it fuels farm equipment and other commercial vehicles, has increased 66% to a record $6.26.

The Congressional Budget Office is a nonpartisan federal agency controlled by Congress that conducts analysis related to the federal budget and the economy.

The estimate comes a day after the Pentagon’s watchdog found the Iran war resulted in a shortfall of U.S. munitions and “bottlenecks” in supply chains.

The CBO report estimates it will be five years before the Pentagon is able to replace munitions expended during the war, which it estimates has cost roughly $38 billion as of Aug. 1. That cost estimate does not include the price tag for repairing damage Iran inflicted on “hundreds of buildings and structures at U.S. bases” in the Middle East.

The Pentagon didn’t cooperate with requests from CBO, according to the agency. The White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

One of the reasons the CBO says it could not estimate the cost of damage to U.S. military bases and other facilities in the region is because the Defense Department hasn’t shared with the office “information about the value of damaged or destroyed equipment and property” or what repairs the Pentagon plans to make, the funding for which could in part be picked up by the countries where the facilities are located.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., in a written statement called for an end to the war and described it as “a one-two punch that’s burning a hole in Americans’ pockets and burning a hole in our munitions supply, hurting our military readiness.”

The report estimated it would cost $13.1 billion to replace missile defense interceptors alone, and the overall cost to replace munitions expended through Aug. 1 would be $21.7 billion. It will take roughly $2 billion to $3 billion per month to maintain the war’s status quo, and more if the conflict escalates, the report found.

World.title: U.S. and China face grave AI risks but mutual distrust stalls cooperation
World.content:
BEIJING — The United States and China are both gripped by safety fears as they reckon with their rapid advances in AI, but intensifying competition and deep mutual distrust could derail the kind of cooperation experts say is vital to head off the strategically vital technology’s greatest dangers.

Artificial intelligence is increasingly at the center of the rivalry between Washington and Beijing, and is expected to be a major topic of discussion at a summit in Washington next week between President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

The summit comes as AI leaders and researchers in the U.S. warn that companies should “slow the pace” of AI development, citing recent incidents involving autonomous agents. Trump has dismissed such concerns as a “hoax” while agreeing with executives such as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei that the U.S. must maintain AI dominance over China through export controls and other measures.

00:00 00:00 How exactly could AI cause widespread danger? 02:35

China, which tightly regulates AI and largely avoids the existential worries the technology provokes in the U.S., has interpreted calls to slow its development as targeted squarely at its own progress. U.S. companies say the Chinese AI sector is being driven in part by large-scale “illicit distillation” of their most advanced models.

Chinese officials, who say distillation is a conventional practice that U.S. companies also use on Chinese models, in turn accuse America’s AI executives of trying to stave off competition.

Senior Col. Zhu Qichao, a noted voice on Chinese military AI and national security, called for “cooperation” with the U.S. while warning against “vicious competition.”

“Because with the development of emerging technologies, it definitely comes with many possibilities,” said Zhu, the director of the Institute for Defense Technology and Strategic Studies at the People’s Liberation Army National University of Defense Technology.

“On one hand, it benefits humanity, but on the other hand, there are also considerations regarding risks,” he told NBC News on Tuesday at the Xiangshan Forum in Beijing.

AI and the worries around it were a major focus at the annual defense forum, where rooms were packed with scholars, military officials and commentators from the U.S. and other countries, many of which are being pressured to pick sides in the U.S.-China AI race.

Wu Xinbo, left, at the Beijing Xiangshan Forum on Tuesday. Johannes Neudecker / dpa/picture alliance via Getty Images

Though Trump and Xi agreed at their May summit in Beijing to hold high-level AI talks, no such talks have been publicly confirmed ahead of Xi’s visit next week.

Wu Xinbo, dean of the Institute of International Studies at Fudan University in Shanghai, said China was wary that the talks could be used to further slow its progress.

“On the other hand, I think both sides need to sit down to talk about the risks posed by AI development,” he said at the forum, adding that “it will take a long way before the two sides can really forge some important consensus on this issue.”

For U.S.-China cooperation to work, the U.S. needs to be open to both sides benefiting, said Francesca Giovannini, executive director of the Harvard Belfer Center’s Initiative on Managing the Atom.

“The United States operates on a very specific type of theory. And the theory is, whoever wins the AI race wins everything,” she said in an interview at the forum. “So if this is your zero-sum game idea, you won’t be conceding anything.”

China is unlikely to agree to a slowdown at the behest of U.S. AI companies, said George Chen, a partner and chair of digital practice at the Asia Group, an American strategic advisory firm based in Washington.

“I don’t think what happens in the U.S. really matters to China,” he said Tuesday in a phone interview from Hong Kong. “They want to do AI at their own pace, and to a very large degree a lot of people in the industry, in the government, they have a very proud sense that this is finally the chance for China.”

China, which sees its “open-weight” AI models as a tool for diplomacy, has promoted the technology as a global “public good” that should be managed by the international community. At a summit in India on Sunday, Xi offered the 11-member BRICS group of nations help developing open-source AI and urged them to join China’s global AI governance initiative.

But China is also keenly aware of the risks it faces from its own AI success, with Xi telling a Shanghai conference in July that authorities must “ensure that AI is always under human control.”

The industry must make mandatory filings and submit security assessments to officials, with many of the companies having to submit technical filings to an algorithm registry. The government has also imposed rules requiring watermarking and safety requirements.

Foremost among the risks are potential threats to China’s ruling Communist Party, which worries the technology could be weaponized against it and has imposed ideological controls to ensure products fall in line with socialist values, for example.

“Hostile forces and individuals with ulterior motives misuse generative AI technologies — such as deepfake audio-video, AI-generated graphics and text, and intelligent bot farms — to manufacture political rumors, spread harmful information, and incite confrontation at low cost and on a massive scale,” Chen Yixin, the Chinese minister of state security, said in an article Sunday in the state-backed China Cybersecurity Magazine that called for greater party control and government oversight of AI.

Anthropic said last week that Chinese AI labs had secretly routed requests to its Claude models. Don Feria / AP Content Services for Anthropic

Chen said AI could enable misinformation campaigns and cyberattacks on China’s critical infrastructure and, in an apparent reference to the U.S., warned that countries with “advantages” in AI could restrict other nations’ access to their technologies.

He also warned of espionage and data leaks, days after Anthropic released a report that found Chinese AI labs had secretly routed requests to its Claude models, some of which contained sensitive information from individuals, major companies and state-affiliated actors.

Like the U.S., China increasingly views AI as a national security issue, down to the individual researchers working on it. On Tuesday, China tightened travel curbs on its citizens, barring some whose work has implications for national technology security from leaving the country.

The new rules add to an extensive AI regulatory regime that includes restrictions on AI companions over mental health concerns, mandated labeling of AI-generated content and a requirement that trained models must use data conforming to Chinese values.

Experts say it could take a major crisis for the U.S. and China to finally work together on AI, much like the 1962 Cuban missile crisis pushed the U.S. and the then-Soviet Union to start negotiating on nuclear weapons.

AI is expected to be a major topic of discussion at the U.S.-China summit in Washington next week. Alex Wong / Getty Images

AI has already had profound military implications, including for targeting, and could be integrated into systems supporting the nuclear chain of command, said David Finkelstein, vice president of the Center for Naval Analyses.

“This is scary stuff, and I think that this is an area where the two sides ought to be sitting down and talking to each other,” he said at the forum.

U.S.-China competition is inevitable, but there is still room for the two sides to negotiate because their respective positions “are not necessarily very much entrenched,” said David Santoro, president and chief executive of Pacific Forum International, a Honolulu-based think tank.

“There are still ways that we can better understand each other and hopefully come up with mechanisms so we can better control this emerging technology,” he said in an interview at the forum.

Santoro said he was “not very optimistic,” however, about the prospect for a major agreement in the near term.

“I don’t know that we will be able to get to a position where we agree on something substantive,” he said. “But at least the first step has got to be talking to each other.”

Eric Baculinao and Erin Tan reported from Beijing, and Mithil Aggarwal from Hong Kong.

World.title: FBI Director Kash Patel clashes with Democrats at oversight hearing
World.content:
WASHINGTON — Lawmakers pressed FBI Director Kash Patel during a contentious oversight hearing on Tuesday about his leadership of a bureau that has seen massive changes since the start of President Donald Trump’s second term.

Patel faced scrutiny from Democrats about changes to the FBI’s hiring process amid firings and departures from the bureau since Trump retook office in January 2025. He also faced questions about his use of government aircraft.

As he lashed out at Democrats in the room, an FBI X account launched attacks on several members of the Senate Judiciary Committee.

Following several heated exchanges with Senate Democrats, Patel told Sen. Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, that he “would appreciate it if you concluded this hearing.”

Sen. Dick Durbin, the Illinois Democrat who is not seeking re-election this year, noted this will likely be his last FBI oversight hearing until retirement and said he was “disappointed” the Senate Judiciary Committee “has stood by” since Trump retook office in January 2025. “I look forward to a day, hopefully in the very near future, when this committee will fulfill its duty to hold Director Patel accountable for his leadership,” Durbin said.

Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., compared Patel to a “thug” and said he was using the FBI “to go after reporters” and stonewalling members of Congress who had questions about his oversight of the FBI.

Democrats also questioned Patel over reports of an investigation into leaks that resulted in a story in The Atlantic focusing on concerns about his personal behavior. In April, Patel filed a $250 million lawsuit against the magazine over the story that made allegations about his drinking, with Patel’s team saying the FBI director “does not drink to excess.”

Republican Senate Judiciary members largely praised the FBI director. They discussed with Patel how the FBI was handling what they claimed was “weaponization” of law enforcement during the prior administrations. Republicans have complained former special counsel Jack Smith obtained records of legislators’ phone calls and accused him of spying, though Smith had obtained records of legislators’ communications with members of the executive branch because they turned up during the investigation into Jan. 6 and Trump’s efforts to overturn the 2020 election.

Patel’s FBI has overseen the firing of numerous FBI employees who were involved in prior investigations into Trump, including individuals involved in the 2022 search of Mar-a-Lago that has been a particular focus for Trump.

Joe diGenova, the 81-year-old Trump loyalist who had been heading a “grand conspiracy” probe targeting former law enforcement officials involved in Trump investigations, told NBC News that Patel had been “absolutely superb in supporting our investigation.” DiGenova resigned last week after a conflict with Justice Department leadership about the direction of the investigation.

If Democrats take control of the House or Senate, Patel’s FBI is expected to face increased scrutiny and investigations.

World.title: Board votes to close Kennedy Center immediately for renovations, source says
World.content:
The Trump-aligned Kennedy Center board voted to immediately close the institution for renovations, a source familiar with the vote said, after President Trump and his allies on the board repeatedly warned of financial and physical ruin for the center if no action is taken.

For more than a year, the president has pushed for the center to be overhauled and for its performing arts programming to be shaken up — and his administration has pushed to add his name to the building.

Mr. Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick — whose wife, Allison, sits on the Kennedy Center board — called into the board's meeting Tuesday, a source familiar with the matter told CBS News. One Democratic member of the board who has sued over the changes to the center, Rep. Joyce Beatty of Ohio, alleged in a statement that the president "verbally berated" her ahead of Tuesday's vote.

Earlier Tuesday, a federal judge again blocked the board — which is chaired by Mr. Trump and composed of his Cabinet members and political allies — from adding Mr. Trump's name to the building after he had previously ordered it to be removed.

"Defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress's blessing," U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper said in his ruling.

Cooper's ruling came in response to the board's vote in August to add the inscription "Renovated and Restored by President Donald J. Trump" beneath the Kennedy Center's name on the building.

Last December, the board had voted to rename the center "The Donald J. Trump and The John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts," and added Mr. Trump's name to the facade. Judge Cooper ruled in May that Mr. Trump's name had been added illegally and ordered its removal. At the time, he also blocked the administration from closing the venue for renovations.

Since Mr. Trump's name was removed, the exterior wall displaying the Kennedy Center's name has been obscured by a tarp-covered scaffold.

Lawyers for the Justice Department argued in court filings in the lawsuit that the center's "dangerously dilapidated, outdated, and decrepit" conditions and recent financial losses put the living memorial to President John F. Kennedy in a "financial and structural death spiral" that requires it to be closed for renovations.

Last year, Congress approved $250 million for the renovation project.

In a Truth Social post shortly after the board voted Tuesday, Mr. Trump said that construction would not begin on the center until after the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit rules on a Justice Department appeal of Cooper's earlier order barring the first renaming, with Mr. Trump's name on the building.

"If the ruling is a negative one, which it should not be, and is not overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court, the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place," Mr. Trump said, adding that he has raised $17 million so far in donations to send to the center to "keep it afloat."

The source of the donations mentioned by Mr. Trump was not disclosed, and it's unclear where the donations are going.

World.title: FBI investigation thwarts "mass casualty attack" from man accused of ISIS allegiance
World.content:
A Pennsylvania man planned to carry out an ISIS-inspired "mass casualty attack" against the American people before an FBI investigation thwarted him, according to federal law enforcement officials.

Speaking at a press conference Tuesday, federal officials said Jonathan Kramer, 21, of Valencia, had pledged allegiance to the Islamic State of Syria. He was arrested Saturday outside of a hotel in Cranberry Township, around 25 miles north of Pittsburgh, with a rifle, ammunition and dozens of knives in his possession.

Richard Evanchec, special agent in charge for the FBI's Pittsburgh field office, called the planned attack an "imminent threat of violence inspired by ISIS."

Officials didn't elaborate on any specifics surrounding the alleged planned attack, including when or where it might have occurred.

"This defendant made repeated attempts to encourage and coordinate violence through encrypted platforms such as advising others on attack methods, discussing chemical poisons, vehicle attacks, drone delivery explosives and firearms-based assaults," Evanchec said.

Federal charges have been filed against a Pittsburgh-area man accused of plotting an attack in support of ISIS. KDKA Photojournalist Fred Williams

Investigators said a search of Kramer's hotel room and home led to the discovery of a semi-automatic rifle, loaded rifle magazines, a rifle scope and boxes of ammunition, along with 30 knives and a note. The note told people not to look for him, saying "I cant live In constant Fear," according to court paperwork.

The FBI said it also found social media correspondence that led investigators to believe an attack was being planned.

United States Attorney Troy Rivetti referred to the FBI investigation that led to Kramer's arrest as being "covert."

"We want to thank the individual who first reported this defendant's dangerous and troubling behavior, as well as the other individuals who agreed to speak to law enforcement this weekend," Rivetti said.

Rivetti said that the cooperation of the public in investigations is key for law enforcement to be able to "prevent horrific crimes from being committed in our community."

"We hope this prosecution serves as a stark reminder to everyone of the importance of vigilance," Rivetti said.

U.S. Congressman Mike Kelly (R-PA), whose district includes Butler County, said in a statement that he commends the diligent work of the FBI and law enforcement for apprehending Kramer before he could potentially follow through with an alleged attack.

"This disgusting, hate-filled extremism has no place in our nation," Rep. Kelly said.

Kramer has been charged with one count of receipt or transfer of a firearm or ammunition knowing or having reasonable cause to believe such firearm or ammunition will be used to commit a felony or a federal crime of terrorism.

Officials said that Kramer waived his right to a detention hearing, but requested a preliminary examination hearing that is scheduled for Wednesday.

World.title: Americans' incomes hit a record high in 2025. Now for the bad news.
World.content:
American households earned a record median income of $87,460 last year, according to new Census Bureau data. The catch? That figure is only slightly above the previous peak set in 2019.

Adjusting for inflation, that means the typical household has gained little economic ground in six years marked by pandemic upheaval and surging consumer prices. In 2019, households had a median income of $85,320, a level that wasn't surpassed until 2025, the Census said on Tuesday.

While the new data indicates that Americans' incomes have continued to climb, it also shows that the typical household in 2025 earned only about 2.5% more than in 2019. By comparison, median household income climbed 19% during the six years before the pandemic, from 2013 to 2019.

The Census report also showed that women's paychecks rose 3.2% last year, while men's declined slightly. The solid gain for women narrowed the gender wage gap, though it remains large, with women earning nearly 84 cents for every dollar earned by men, up from less than 81 cents in 2024.

Declining poverty rate

The Census figures also may reflect some tax changes implemented under the "One Big Beautiful Bill" act, or OBBBA, which President Trump signed into law in July 2025. High-income households and corporations were among those that received the biggest benefits from its tax cuts, according to tax experts.

The top 10% of earners reported income growth of 1.7% last year to $261,300, while the poorest one-tenth reported a slight decline to just over $20,000, according to the Census Bureau.

"It's notable that the median income for the top earners is increasing, while income for the lowest earners is stagnant," said Kristin Seefeldt, associate professor of social work and public policy at the University of Michigan, in an email. "The tax code has been revised to lower marginal tax rates for everybody, and we see the top earners benefiting from that."

Last year, the official U.S. poverty rate fell 0.5 percentage points to 10.2%. Some public policy experts cautioned that the impact from OBBBA's cuts to social safety net programs may not appear until the Census reports on 2026 income and poverty rates, which will be released in 2027.

OBBBA instituted new restrictions to Medicaid and food stamps, with the latter program reporting a sharp decline in enrollment in 2026.

"The poverty numbers look pretty good — especially child poverty — but these numbers do not reflect cuts in benefits that started to take effect at the start of 2026," said Amanda Nothaft, director of data and analysis at the University of Michigan's Poverty Solutions.

World.title: Iran war could cost $2 billion per month, Congressional Budget Office estimates
World.content:
The war with Iran could cost approximately $2 billion to $3 billion per month for as long as it continues, according to a report released by the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office on Tuesday. The report estimates those costs could rise when there are tit-for-tat exchanges of fire with Iran.

The office estimated the war between Feb. 28 and Aug. 1 has directly cost the U.S. about $38 billion, a figure that does not include repairing U.S. bases in the region damaged during the conflict. In addition, the office estimates inflation during the first quarter of 2027 could be 0.5% higher than what was projected before the war because of rising energy prices.

The CBO noted that replacing munitions accounts for the majority of the costs incurred during the war. In particular, the CBO said the large expenditure of interceptor missiles used to defend against incoming missiles leaves behind a "reduced inventory of interceptors for several years."

"The shortfall would become especially problematic if a conflict arose with an opponent whose arsenal included large numbers of ballistic and cruise missiles," according to the report, which pointed out that China maintains such an arsenal and could employ it if there were a conflict over Taiwan.

The report said a comparison of the reported use of interceptors with the number the Pentagon has purchased indicates the U.S. has "probably used between one-half and two-thirds of its inventory of those munitions since June 2025." Those munitions include Patriot and THAAD interceptors as well as the Navy's Standard Missiles 3 and 6.

The White House and the Pentagon have downplayed concerns about depleted weapons inventories. President Trump on Truth Social said, "We have virtually unlimited amounts of mid- to high-grade ammunition, far more than we can ever use." Admiral Brad Cooper, the head of forces in the Middle East, recently told "60 Minutes," "I'm not concerned at all. We're well-armed and ready for any contingency."

The CBO said the Defense Department did not respond to requests for information.

The CBO analysis was released a day after the Pentagon inspector general published a report that said the Pentagon's Office for Acquisition and Sustainment concluded the use of munitions in the conflict has led to "strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply."

The CBO estimates it will cost $21.7 billion to replace the munitions used in the conflict through Aug. 1: $7.3 billion for the land-attack cruise missiles, $13.1 billion for the missile-defense interceptors and $1.2 billion for other munitions.

It will also cost about $1.9 billion to replace lost equipment, according to the report, including a THAAD air defense radar destroyed by Iran. The CBO noted the radar can cost roughly $500 million and is essential for the battery to take down missiles. If the Pentagon decides to request supplemental appropriations to replace lost aircraft with newer versions, the total cost could rise from $1.9 billion to $3.3 billion.

If the war continues at a relatively low intensity, it could cost roughly $2 billion to $3 billion each additional month, according to the report. Monthly costs could rise if there is an escalation similar to the one in July, which saw repeated tit-for-tat strikes. The CBO said the war in July cost about $3 billion.

In June, the Trump administration sent Congress an $87.6 billion supplemental funding request that included $67 billion for the Department of Defense for needs related to the Iran war.

Republicans are trying to provide up to $73 billion in new funding for the war through the party-line reconciliation process, but the House-adopted budget blueprint to initiate the process has been stalled in the Senate.

The CBO released its estimate in response to a request from Democratic Rep. Brendan Boyle of Pennsylvania, who is the ranking member on the House Budget Committee.

"Donald Trump's disastrous war in Iran has already taken the lives of brave American servicemembers and left others wounded. Beyond that human toll, this nonpartisan CBO report makes clear that the war has also cost American taxpayers tens of billions of dollars and counting, while continuing to drive up costs," Boyle said in a statement to CBS News.

World.title: Patel defends lowering hiring standards related to prostitution, bestiality
World.content:
FBI Director Kash Patel on Tuesday defended his agency's decision to lower its hiring standards, after he faced a barrage of questions from incredulous lawmakers who demanded to know why engaging in acts of bestiality is no longer an automatic disqualifier for employment.

In a series of extraordinary exchanges with both Democratic and Republican members of the Senate Judiciary Committee, Patel insisted that several changes were made to ensure that victims of sexual assault or trafficking involving animals were not precluded from employment at the FBI.

"We did not want to punish victims of bestiality, victims who were trafficked," Patel told Democratic Sen. Dick Durbin during an oversight hearing before the Senate Judiciary Committee.

"We did not want to make it an automatic disqualification for the FBI to consider you if you are a victim of these awful, heinous acts. They still have to go through the same rigorous standards and application process," Patel added.

Tuesday's hearing marked the first time that Patel has publicly addressed the new hiring standards related to prostitution, employment theft and bestiality, after CBS News first reported about them in August.

Previously, anyone who engaged in such conduct was automatically precluded from working at the bureau.

Now, a person can still be considered eligible in certain circumstances.

For prostitution, job candidates can still be hired as long as they have not hired sex workers or engaged in acts of prostitution three or more times and the conduct took place more than 10 years ago.

For employment theft, a person can be considered if the theft took place more than three years ago, and for bestiality, a job candidate can still be eligible as long as the acts occurred before the age of 18, multiple sources familiar with the changes previously told CBS News.

Sources previously told CBS News that the new eligibility requirements do not distinguish between candidates who were coerced into sexual activity with animals, as opposed to those who engaged in such acts willingly.

On the eve of the hearing, Democrats from the Senate Judiciary Committee sent a letter to Patel demanding a "full accounting" for why such changes were made and asked the bureau to provide "the number of applicants hired, extended conditional offers, or placed under case-by-case review since June 16, 2026, whose files would previously have been automatically disqualified, broken out by category of conduct."

Lawmakers on Tuesday from both sides of the aisle repeatedly grilled Patel over the decision, with most of them primarily focusing their questions on the changes related to acts of bestiality.

"Tell me what it said before," Republican Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana asked, referring to the automatic disqualification for acts of bestiality.

"It automatically disqualified any individual who participated on either side of it. Obviously, we are never going to hire the criminal side," Patel said.

"Either side of what, the bestiality?" Kennedy asked.

"Yes," Patel responded.

"So you disqualified the animal?" Kennedy responded.

"Well, we have great canines," Patel said.

"I'm trying to understand why you did this," Kennedy continued. "Why would you even get into bestiality?"

Patel told lawmakers that some FBI applicants were trafficked and forced to engage in "degrading acts" such as those involving animals, and the changes were meant to assist people in that category.

"Some of these individuals would go on to be law enforcement officers, who qualified to be law enforcement officers and later applied to the FBI," Patel said.

Patel also told Kennedy that the changes related to prostitution were meant to ensure that victims who were forced into the act were not precluded from employment.

"It's not if you frequented a prostitute. It's if you were a prostitute?" Kennedy asked.

"If you were, yes, the victim forced into it," Patel responded.

The internal changes to the automatic disqualification, however, relate to both the solicitation and engagement of prostitution, sources previously told CBS News, and an FBI spokesperson also previously acknowledged that the changes might also apply to an applicant who admits to hiring a sex worker in a place where it is lawful.

Current and former FBI agents and legal experts familiar with the bureau's hiring practices previously told CBS News they were deeply troubled by the changes, saying it is indicative of challenges the FBI may be having with recruiting new talent.

Several also said they were baffled by how the bureau was justifying the changes, noting that all applicants have an opportunity to disclose personal issues that could impact the results of their polygraph prior to taking the test, such as a history of sexual abuse.

Patel did not explain during the hearing why the bureau has lowered the standards for candidates who may have stolen in the past from their employers.

World.title: Here's why a high-yield savings account is worth opening this week
World.content:
