World.title: Polls show Argentine distrust of Milei's shift on the Falklands
World.content:
Polls show Argentine distrust of Milei's shift on the Falklands

14th Monday, September 2026 - 22:06 UTC Full article

Photo: Nicolás Aguilera/AFP

Two private Argentine pollsters released findings this week pointing to an adverse reception of President Javier Milei's shift on the Falklands, even though the sovereignty claim commands broad consensus in Argentine society.

The consultancy Analogías, which surveyed views of the national government between September 5 and 8, reported that 61% of respondents expressed distrust of the president's new position: 49.8% said they did not believe him at all and 11.2% believed him little. The firm did not publish technical details such as sample size or margin of error.

Monitor Digital, which analyzed 89,900 mentions of the government on social media, ranked the Islands as the second axis of the official digital conversation, clustered around terms such as sovereignty, measures, the United Kingdom and the United States. Its director, Diego Corbalán, told Perfil the volume did not translate into support: “In some way the government managed to place the issue, but it is not clear that all of it works to its benefit.”

The same study played down the reach of the matter beyond political circles. Across nearly a thousand Google trends recorded in the week after the September 3 televised address, the cluster associated with the Islands appeared only at 27th place, with some 50,000 searches, and the foreign policy category accounted for 0.8% of the total, far below sports and entertainment.

The sequence began with that address, in which Milei asserted sovereignty over the archipelago and announced measures against oil development. The following day the government confirmed sanctions against individuals and companies linked to that activity, and this week it is preparing to send Congress a National Sovereignty Defense bill.

The announcements followed the World Cup episode in July, when National Security Minister Alejandra Monteoliva endorsed a ban on flags and shirts referring to the Islands during the semifinal between Argentina and England. The players themselves defied the measure by displaying a banner at the end of the match, and the episode led to the suspension of debate on the land ownership bill in the Senate.

On Sunday the government distributed to the press an institutional video by Santiago Oria, director of audiovisual production at the Presidency, combining statements by Milei, remarks by U.S. President Donald Trump on a possible review of Washington's neutral position, and footage of the match against England, set to terrace music. Milei and La Libertad Avanza figures shared the piece.

Corbalán criticized the strategy in political terms: in adopting it, he said, the libertarians “embrace the whole Kirchnerist populist mode,” which he described as chauvinism.

Islanders confirmed their status as a British Overseas Territory in the 2013 referendum, with 99.8% of the vote.

World.title: Falklands donate £40,000 to Red Cross appeal for Nepal flood victims
World.content:
Falklands donate £40,000 to Red Cross appeal for Nepal flood victims

14th Monday, September 2026 - 21:52 UTC Full article

The flash flood tore through the north of the country on August 26, destroying homes, roads and bridges and cutting off entire communities

The Falklands Legislative Assembly has approved a donation of £40,000 to the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) in support of its emergency response to the floods that devastated northern Nepal.

The flash flood tore through the north of the country on August 26, destroying homes, roads and bridges and cutting off entire communities. The worst-hit districts were Rasuwa and Nuwakot. The IFRC estimates that around 93,000 people have been affected. The Legislative Assembly put the death toll at more than 1,300; Nepali police confirmed 469 in the days following the disaster, and humanitarian agencies maintain that thousands remain missing, among them more than 500 foreign nationals.

The cause is still under investigation, though early indications point to the collapse of a glacier near the Langtang Lirung peak upstream, which is believed to have sent a sudden surge of water into the Bhote Koshi river.

The donation will support the work of the IFRC and the Nepal Red Cross Society, whose teams are on the ground providing clean water, shelter, first aid and emergency supplies. The IFRC released nearly one million Swiss francs from its disaster response fund on the day of the disaster and launched a 25 million Swiss franc emergency appeal the following day.

The Falklands hold a long-standing connection with Nepal. Gurkha soldiers took part in the liberation of the Islands in 1982 and two died as a result of the conflict: Lance Corporal Budhaprasad Limbu, of the 1st Battalion, 7th Duke of Edinburgh's Own Gurkha Rifles, was killed on June 24 at Goose Green when his spade struck a grenade during battlefield clearance work, and Corporal Krishnakumar Rai, of the Queen's Gurkha Engineers, died months later in an ordnance explosion while engaged in similar work. Memorials to both were unveiled in the Islands in 2019. Gurkha units have continued to serve in the archipelago since.

MLA Jack Ford, Chair of the Legislative Assembly, said: “Our thoughts are with everyone affected by this terrible disaster. The Falkland Islands know what it means to depend on the courage and kindness of others in our own hour of need, and the people of Nepal hold a special place in our history. This donation is a heartfelt expression of the solidarity and gratitude our community feels towards them.”

World.title: Milei sets out the sovereignty bill he will send to Congress over the Falklands
World.content:
Milei sets out the sovereignty bill he will send to Congress over the Falklands

14th Monday, September 2026 - 10:55 UTC Full article

The government wants to toughen that framework, after filing a criminal complaint last week against five companies linked to the Sea Lion project

Argentina's government was finalizing on Monday the content of the sovereignty bill on the Falklands it will send to Congress, at a meeting with its own lawmakers chaired by President Javier Milei. The executive has yet to decide whether it will submit one bill or two.

The core of the package is a reform of Law 26,659, passed in 2011 at the initiative of then deputy Fernando Solanas, which bans and penalizes hydrocarbon activity without Argentine authorization on the disputed continental shelf. The government wants to toughen that framework, after filing a criminal complaint last week against five companies linked to the Sea Lion project and raising to 60 the number of individuals and companies facing administrative proceedings, which remain open with no penalty applied.

The bill also envisages creating a National Security Council bringing together the foreign, defense and economy ministries and the State Intelligence Secretariat, with the stated aim of flagging threats to national security. Peronist lawmakers have raised the hypothesis that the body would serve as an additional route to draw on reserved intelligence funds.

That objection rests on recent budget increases. Emergency decree 867/2026, issued after the president's September 3 address, allocated 30.519 billion pesos to the SIDE, of which some 10.905 billion covers current spending and 19.614 billion capital investment for infrastructure and technology. Unlike July's expansion, this one did not increase reserved expenses, according to the fact-checking organization Chequeado. Legislative sources cited by the Argentine press argue, however, that the capital allocation could end up feeding discretionary funds. With both expansions, the agency received some 79.780 billion pesos in under fifty days, taking its current budget to around 176 billion, 82% above the year's original allocation. In 2024, both chambers of Congress repealed a SIDE increase directed entirely to reserved expenses. The opposition is preparing a formal request for information.

The same decree allocated some 217.954 billion pesos to Defense, distributed among the Army, Air Force, Navy and Joint Staff, and 119.290 billion to the National Space Activities Commission. The Integrated Naval Base in Tierra del Fuego falls under the decree, though it is not itemized separately. Defense Minister Carlos Presti and Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno traveled to the province to get the project back on track. Deputy Jorge Taiana, a former defense minister, said work began in 2021, reached barely 9% completion — a figure he attributed partly to the fact that construction in Tierra del Fuego is only possible some seven months a year — and that the current administration halted it entirely.

Separately, socialist deputy Esteban Paulón formally demanded that the executive reactivate the National Council on Matters Relating to the Malvinas Islands, created by Law 27,558 in 2020, which was to meet every 120 days and has convened only once, in August 2024. He gave the government ten business days to produce a timetable.

The package reaches a hostile Congress. La Libertad Avanza lost votes in the lower house last week and failed to secure the support needed to convene a Senate session. On Tuesday, the executive presents the 2027 budget. Opposition figures argue that, before toughening sanctions, the government should enforce existing law.

World.title: New US-Mexico water agreement means reduced allotments but a heathier Colorado River
World.content:
A long-running dispute between Mexico and the United States over Colorado River water-sharing has been resolved — at least for the next two years — with Mexico getting significantly less water as a result.

The U.S. is also receiving less water as part of a joint effort to mitigate ongoing drought conditions and low reservoir levels in the Colorado River basin.

In fact, under the new agreement, formally called Minute 334 and finalized by the International Boundary and Water Commission (IBWC) on Sept. 2, Mexico’s 16.7% (250,000 acre-feet) annual reduction of its previous typical water allocation is equivalent to water-use reductions imposed on U.S. Lower Basin states (Arizona, California and Nevada).

The agreement also implements a strategy to manage the salinity of Colorado River water as it reaches Mexico. Consultations regarding possible further cuts are contemplated for 2028 if conditions worsen.

Minute 334 was signed by Mexican IBWC Commissioner Adriana Reséndez and her U.S. counterpart, Chad McIntosh, with the participation of Mexican IBWC Secretary Manuel Morales. The U.S. Department of the Interior confirmed the approval of both governments.

“This Minute makes sure water is shared fairly among our users and protects the health of the Colorado River during these difficult times,” McIntosh said in a news release. “Both countries deserve a lot of credit for agreeing to these water reductions and other measures.”

Reséndez insisted on proportionality between the two countries, defending Mexico’s position even as it has struggled to meet its obligations in the original 1944 treaty.

When the most recent five-year cycle of that treaty came to an end on Oct. 24 last year, Mexico still owed 865,136 acre-feet of water, though the terms of the treaty grant Mexico five years to catch up.

The reduction agreed to in Minute 334 is equivalent to one-sixth of Mexico’s annual allocation established in the treaty, about 1.85 billion cubic meters.

The two nations also agreed to cooperate on managing the Colorado River Delta in Mexico, which has been transformed from a lush 2-million-acre wetland into a mostly dry salt flat due to decades of intensive upstream dam construction and water diversions.

With reports from El Universal, WaterWorld and The Colorado Sun

World.title: MND Local: WTA Tennis, an international film fest and more events in Guadalajara
World.content:
Late September in Guadalajara brings an action-packed calendar. Upcoming events include a World Migrant Day celebration benefiting a local nonprofit organization, an international film festival and the 2026 Guadalajara Open, an important stop on the Women’s Tennis Association (WTA) professional tour.

Top female tennis players to compete at the Guadalajara Open this week

Following hard on the heels of the U.S. Open in New York City, Zapopan welcomes a select group of the WTA’s brightest stars to the Guadalajara Open this week.

The annual event, played at the Panamerican Tennis Center in Parque Metropolitano, attracts a diverse group of top female tennis players from around the globe. The field will compete in singles and doubles for a US $1.2 million purse and a top singles prize of US $185,500.

Confirmed players for this year’s event include world number 11 Marta Kostyuk of Ukraine and world number 14 and defending champion Iva Jovic of the United States.

Kostyuk returns to Mexico as one of the hottest players on the WTA tour during the 2026 season, having reached the semifinals of Wimbledon and Roland Garros, in addition to claiming two titles on clay last spring. She last competed at the Guadalajara Open in 2023, where she reached the second round.

Latin American tennis will also be well represented, with Colombian veteran Camila Osorio and Mexican No. 1 Renata Zarazúa scheduled to compete.

For details, visit the tournament website.

Dates: Sept. 13-19, 2026.

Sept. 13-19, 2026. Location: Centro Panamericano de Tenis, Zapopan, Jalisco.

Centro Panamericano de Tenis, Zapopan, Jalisco. Cost: Individual tickets start at 866 pesos, not including fees. Tournament packages are available on Boletomovil.

Aeroméxico to launch nonstop service from Guadalajara to Paris in 2027

Savoring the perfect pain au chocolat is about to get a little easier for Francophile Tapatíos. Starting April 13, 2027, the city will have its second direct European flight route, as Aeroméxico launches nonstop service between Guadalajara’s Miguel Hidalgo International Airport (GDL) and Paris-Charles de Gaulle (CDG).

The route will run three times per week on Tuesdays, Fridays and Sundays, departing Guadalajara at 1:55 p.m. and arriving in Paris at 9:25 a.m. the following day. Return flights will operate on Mondays, Wednesdays and Saturdays, departing Paris at 11:40 a.m. and arriving in Guadalajara at 4:10 p.m. the same day.

“Adding Guadalajara–Paris … strengthens our network, offers customers more travel options and further consolidates our position as the leading airline between Mexico and Europe,” Giancarlo Mulinelli, senior vice president of global sales at Aeroméxico, told Aviacionline last week.

Celebrate World Migrant Day with the Rhizome Center

Later this month, Guadalajara residents will have the opportunity to celebrate World Migrant Day at a community celebration featuring local food, culture and a social cause.

Hosted by The Rhizome Center, this year’s festival, “Many Journeys. One Community,” is both a fundraiser and an opportunity to raise awareness about the organization’s work. During the event, guests can sample food from 15 migrant kitchens, enjoy live French, Cuban and Syrian music, listen to storytelling, and meet artists sharing their craft and culture.

The Rhizome Center was founded in 2018 during President Donald Trump’s first term, with a mission to provide direct support to deportees and refugees sent to Mexico.

Since his return to office, the need has grown. Many deportees arrive with no resources or documentation to regularize their status in Mexico. Filling that void, the organization provides legal aid, crisis assistance, counseling and other services.

Run by executive director and founder Tran Dang, The Rhizome Center derived its name from plant rhizomes — the underground roots that provide essential nutrients — symbolizing humanity’s resilience and interconnectedness across borders.

For more information about The Rhizome Center for Migrants and details on how to support the cause, visit the group’s Instagram account. Donations are accepted via PayPal and Zelle.

Date: Saturday, Sept. 27, from 3 p.m. to 7 p.m.

Saturday, Sept. 27, from 3 p.m. to 7 p.m. Location: Casa Zuno, Avenida Unión 2226, Colonia Americana, Guadalajara.

Casa Zuno, Avenida Unión 2226, Colonia Americana, Guadalajara. Cost: General admission is 375 pesos. VIP tickets are 500 pesos per person and guarantee a seat.

The MUBI film fest lands in Guadalajara next weekend

View this post on Instagram A post shared by MUBI México (@mubimexico)

Global distributor, producer and streaming service MUBI recently added film festivals to its portfolio and announced a Guadalajara edition from Sept. 18-20. The festival will screen independent feature films and shorts, alongside filmmaker Q&As, workshops, installations and DJ sets.

Anticipated films on the schedule include:

“Her Private Hell” by Nicolas Winding Refn

“Pulp: What Do You Do for an Encore?” by Garth Jennings

“Hope: The First Impact” by Na Hong-jin

“Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” by Jane Schoenbrun

“Rose” by Markus Schleinzer

For moviegoers seeking nostalgia, Ridley Scott’s 1991 feminist classic “Thelma & Louise,” starring Susan Sarandon, Geena Davis and Brad Pitt, is also on the schedule.

For full program details, visit Mubi Mexico’s website. In addition to Guadalajara, MUBI Fest 2026 made stops in Mexico City, São Paulo, Bogotá and Buenos Aires this year.

Dates: Sept. 18-20.

Sept. 18-20. Location: FICG Cineteca, Av. Perif. Pte. Manuel Gómez Morin 1695, Rinconada de la Azalea, Belenes Norte, Zapopan.

FICG Cineteca, Av. Perif. Pte. Manuel Gómez Morin 1695, Rinconada de la Azalea, Belenes Norte, Zapopan. Cost: Tickets available on the MUBI website.

MND writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

World.title: Mexico City-area airports to halt takeoffs and landings for 4 hours tomorrow
World.content:
Takeoffs and landings at the Mexico City International Airport (AICM) will be suspended for four hours on Wednesday, Sept. 16, to ensure that military aircraft can operate safely in the capital’s airspace while the annual Independence Day parade takes place below.

The Mexican Navy, which operates the AICM, announced the suspension in a statement.

El AICM suspenderá operaciones aéreas por desfile del 16 de septiembre. ➡️ https://t.co/T6iEPTFtOa @aeropuertos_GAM pic.twitter.com/wJK8Khf3YB — Aeropuerto Internacional Benito Juárez CDMX (@AICM_mx) September 14, 2026

“To ensure the safety of the military air maneuvers that will be carried out to commemorate the 216th anniversary of the start of Mexico’s independence, and as directed by the aviation authority, the Mexico City Benito Juárez International Airport (AICM) will suspend aircraft takeoffs and landings on September 16 from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.,” the navy said.

“According to NOTAMs [Notices to Airmen] A8260/26 and B1724/26, … issued by the Federal Civil Aviation Agency (AFAC) and disseminated through the Mexican Airspace Navigation Services (SENEAM), the airport will be closed to all types of flights during the specified hours.”

The Felipe Ángeles International Airport (AIFA) in México state will also suspend takeoffs and landings between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m. Wednesday. Military aircraft that will conduct flyovers as part of the Independence Day festivities will take off from the Santa Lucía Air Force Base, which adjoins AIFA.

The navy advised air passengers who have a flight scheduled for Wednesday to ask their airlines about the status of their flights as “this event will result in some adjustments to scheduled times.”

The Independence Day parade is scheduled to begin at 10 a.m. Wednesday with a flyover of nearly 100 Air Force and National Guard airplanes and helicopters above the Zócalo, Mexico City’s central square — including F-5 fighters performing a fleur-de-lis maneuver.

The ground procession will start near the Zócalo, pass the Palacio de Bellas Artes (Palace of Fine Arts), continue along Juárez Avenue and Paseo de la Reforma, and end at the Campo Marte military complex near Chapultepec Park.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Following a higher soda tax, is a salty foods tax coming next?
World.content:
Lawmakers from Mexico’s ruling party Morena, the Workers’ Party (PT) and the Green Party (PVEM) have submitted a congressional proposal to apply a Special Tax on Production and Services (IEPS) to certain processed foods with excessive sodium content, such as cured meats, instant soups, sauces and dressings.

The initiative seeks to expand a tax strategy that has been applied since the 1980s to products considered harmful to health, such as sugary drinks, tobacco and high-calorie foods.

The bill’s proponents estimate that a tax on products with high sodium levels could generate approximately 12 billion pesos (US $116.6 million) in additional federal revenue, while helping reduce the prevalence of diseases associated with excessive salt consumption.

The focus would be on processed products exceeding technical criteria for sodium content, particularly front-of-package warning labels under NOM-051, which indicate “Excess Sodium.” This means that the potential measure would not penalize the domestic use of salt, nor would it, in principle, indiscriminately cover all salty foods.

The initiative follows growing concerns regarding average sodium intake in Mexico.

According to the NGO El Poder del Consumidor (The Power of the Consumer), the Mexican adult population consumes an average of 3.3 grams of sodium per day, far exceeding the World Health Organization (WHO) recommendation, which advises against exceeding 2 grams daily. Excess sodium consumption is related to cardiovascular diseases – the leading cause of death in Mexico – and hypertension.

Meeting the WHO’s target of a 30% reduction in sodium intake by 2030 could save an estimated 7 million lives globally and annually prevent approximately 5% of deaths in Mexico from cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease and stomach cancer.

Dr. Jorge Vargas, a researcher at El Poder del Consumidor, told the news outlet Infobae that “the fact that Mexico is finally considering a sodium tax is positive news,” but cautioned that the technical design would be a decisive factor in determining whether the tax alters consumption habits and drives companies to reduce the salt content of their products. He also urged lawmakers to review the results observed in other countries before voting on the initiative.

The proposal follows a recent IEPS increase targeting domestic sugar consumption, which, according to the government’s 2027 budget proposal, is forecast to bring in over 76.92 billion pesos ($4.5 billion) next year from soft drinks alone.

With reports from El Universal and El Financiero

World.title: In latest national survey, Coahuila is ranked the safest state in Mexico
World.content:
Almost three-quarters of Mexicans believe their state is an unsafe place to live due to crime, according to the results of the 2026 National Survey of Victimization and Perception of Public Safety (ENVIPE).

The National Institute of Statistics and Geography (INEGI) conducted the survey at more than 102,000 homes across Mexico between Feb. 16 and April 10. The results were published last Thursday.

The survey found that 74% of adults believe their state is an unsafe place to live due to crime. That figure declined 1.6 percentage points compared to a year earlier.

However, it remains very high at a time when the federal government is touting sharp reductions in homicides and high-impact crimes such as kidnappings, extortion and violent robberies.

Among Mexico’s 32 federal entities, the northern border state of Coahuila stands out as a success story in terms of reducing violence and strengthening residents’ sense that it is a safe place to live.

Where are perceptions of insecurity highest?

According to the ENVIPE 2026 results, 90% of México state residents consider their state an unsafe place to live due to crime. That figure rose 2.2 percentage points compared to 2025.

México state, which includes many municipalities that are part of the greater Mexico City metropolitan area, thus replaced Morelos as the state with the highest percentage of residents who have security concerns. In the first eight months of 2026, México state was the country’s fifth most violent state in terms of total homicides, behind Guanajuato, Baja California, Chihuahua and Sinaloa.

The states with the next highest percentages of residents with security concerns were:

Morelos: 88.7% (down 1.4 percentage points compared to 2025)

Tabasco: 87.6% (down 2.2 percentage points)

Guanajuato: 85.9% (down 2.6 percentage points)

Zacatecas: 83.3% (down 4 percentage points)

Where are perceptions of insecurity lowest?

According to the ENVIPE 2026 results, the state with the lowest percentage of residents with security concerns is Coahuila. Just over one quarter of Coahuila residents — 27.8% — consider their state unsafe due to crime.

That figure declined 9.9 percentage points in the space of a year, allowing Coahuila to replace Baja California Sur as the state with the lowest proportion of residents with security concerns.

The states with the next lowest percentages of residents with security concerns were:

Yucatán: 35.5% (down 4.1 percentage points compared to 2025)

Aguascalientes: 41% (down 8 percentage points)

Querétaro: 44.6% (down 12.5 percentage points)

Baja California Sur: 49.2% (up 11.8 percentage points)

In a report about the latest ENVIPE results, Televisa’s news division N+ said that 15 years ago, Coahuila was one of Mexico’s most violent states due to the presence of organized crime groups such as Los Zetas and the Gulf Cartel.

N+ reported that after the security “crisis” in Coahuila — epitomized by events such as the 2011 Allende massacre — the presence of federal security forces was beefed up and a “joint strategy” for the state was drawn up.

“Mega military barracks were built … and there were purges of local police forces,” N+ reported, referring to the dismissal of officers in cahoots with organized crime.

Eduardo Guerrero, a security consultant, told N+ that “the case of Coahuila is exceptional.”

What has been achieved in the past 15 years is a “great feat,” he said, referring to the reduction in violence in the northern state.

N+ noted that there were more than 1,100 homicides in Coahuila in 2012 before highlighting that the state registered just 100 murders in 2025, the lowest annual figure on record.

Javier Oliva Posada, a professor and researcher at the National Autonomous University, told N+ that the reduction in violence in Coahuila is not just due to government “force and the show of force.”

He mentioned crime “prevention and deterrence programs” and the “training” of local police forces as factors that have contributed to the reduction in violence.

Coahuila has obtained the enviable designation of “safest state in Mexico” under the leadership of Governor Manolo Jiménez Salinas, who has been in office since December 2023. Coahuila is one of just two states currently governed by the Institutional Revolutionary Party, or PRI, which for most of the 20th century was Mexico’s predominant political force.

Jiménez said last week that he and his fellow coahuilenses felt “very proud” to be able to say that “Coahuila is the safest state in Mexico.”

He attributed the achievement to “great teamwork” and pledged to continue “protecting” the state.

“We’re going to keep working on security every day with more prevention, proximity, intelligence and force,” said Jiménez, who acknowledged close coordination between his administration and the federal government and its security forces.

The governor also said that “more police cars, more barracks, … more weapons, more cameras and more training” are coming to Coahuila.

“In this way, we’re going to continue strengthening the greatness of this beautiful state of Coahuila de Zaragoza,” he said.

Additional ENVIPE data

Among the other data points derived from the 2026 ENVIPE were the following:

At least one member of 11.7 million households was a victim of a crime in 2025. That number is equivalent to 28.5% of all households across Mexico.

A total of 23 million adults were victims of crimes in Mexico last year. There were 23,473 victims per 100,000 adult residents, a slight reduction compared to 2024.

Mexico City recorded the highest crime victimization rate last year (34,930 victims per 100,000 adult residents). Chiapas recorded the lowest rate (13,462 victims per 100,000 adult residents).

Fraud was the most common crime committed in Mexico last year (8,290 cases per 100,000 adult residents) followed by extortion and muggings.

INEGI estimates that a total of 33.8 million crimes were committed in Mexico in 2025. Just 9% of those crimes were reported to authorities. Authorities opened investigations into 73.5% of reported crimes. All told, 93.4% of crimes committed in Mexico last year were either not reported or not investigated.

INEGI said that the total estimated insecurity and crime-related cost for Mexican households in 2025 was 267.3 billion pesos (US $15.57 billion). That amount — equivalent to 1.06% of GDP, according to INEGI — includes economic losses due to crime, expenditure on measures aimed at preventing crime and medical costs associated with being a victim of a crime.

The Mexican Navy is considered Mexico’s most trustworthy security authority, with 89.5% of ENVIPE respondents saying they had confidence in it. The Mexican Air Force ranked second (88.9%), followed by the Mexican Army (87%), the National Guard (79.4%) and the Federal Attorney General’s Office (64.6%).

Traffic police are considered Mexico’s least trustworthy security authority, with just 45.8% of ENVIPE respondents saying that they had confidence in them. Municipal police forces are seen as the second least trustworthy security authority, with 57.1% of respondents saying that they had confidence in them.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: MND Local: Fishing, celebrations and storms in Baja California Sur
World.content:
In Baja California Sur, September is a month of celebrations and storms. The former, like those in towns and cities across Mexico, are largely Independence-themed, with parades on Sept. 16 after regional politicians have delivered the iconic grito on Sept. 15, a symbolic reenactment of Miguel Hidalgo’s call to arms in Dolores, Guanajuato, in 1810.

In addition to the civic celebrations, there are also many parties … particularly in Los Cabos, which can turn any civic holiday into an excuse for fine dining or revelry. Hilton Los Cabos, for example, is hosting a “Viva Mexico” dinner at onsite restaurant Talavera on Sept. 15; Grand Fiesta Americana is spotlighting dinner and live music at its Independence celebration on the same day; and at El Squid Roe, “tequila and margaritas flow” as DJs and live entertainment are featured across all three levels of the signature Cabo San Lucas nightclub on the eve of Independence Day.

Epic Viva México Celebration at El Squid Roe Cabo! 🎉🌮

Watch this video on YouTube

September storms and rainfall

September is traditionally the month when Baja California Sur residents take their vacations. Not only because it’s a slow month for tourism, but also because it’s a good month to be somewhere else.

It’s the month when hurricanes are most likely to hit and to be most potent. Of the 10 strongest hurricanes ever to hit Baja California Sur (measured by sustained wind speed), seven of them struck in September. But even if it’s one of the fortunate years without damaging tropical storms, there’s no dodging the rain.

Baja California Sur gets less rain than any state in Mexico each year (176 millimeters, or about 6.9 inches). But you wouldn’t know it in September. That’s because the state gets nearly 40% of its annual rainfall (71.6 millimeters) during this single month, per data from Mexico’s national weather service. In Los Cabos, the percentages are even higher, with almost half of annual precipitation falling in September.

That’s on average. During strong storms, the amount of rain can dwarf the average annual rainfall. The best example of this comes from Hurricane Juliette in 2001, when Caduaño and Santiago — small communities in Los Cabos — were deluged with more than three feet of rain (39.8 inches), the most intense downpour ever measured in the state.

Nothing so dramatic has happened so far this year, although the maximum rainfall from Hurricane Marie in Los Cabos (66.3 millimeters in El Tezal) was equivalent to about 32% of the municipality’s average annual rainfall.

The rainbow that follows

September can be a challenging month due to storms and the attendant fallout — from flooding to power outages — but it’s also transformative, as rains turn the brown landscape a vibrant green.

The speed of this color change is amazing. Palo blanco, palo verde and other trees, which have dropped their leaves to conserve water during the long, hot summer, flush with new leaves within a matter of days following September rains. A mass flowering likewise occurs as many native species of wildflowers, grasses and vines burst into bloom simultaneously.

Resurrection shrubs like palo Adán, ocotillo and the Baja fairy duster (Calliandra californica) also spring back to life, sprouting not only leaves but vivid pink and red blossoms, while stately cardón and organ pipe cacti swell in size as they absorb and store precious water, giving the landscape a new dimension.

This transformation is a kind of foreshadowing of that of the tourism high season, which begins in October.

High tourism season draws near

October is now only a few weeks away, promising some of Los Cabos’ biggest annual events. Sammy Hagar’s annual birthday bashes at Cabo Wabo Cantina, a local tradition since 1990, return … along with the attendant lines, as Redheads line up around the block for a chance to purchase limited dinner show tickets, sold on a first-come, first-served basis. This year’s shows, as usual, are scheduled for Oct. 9, 11 and 13.

The biggest events in October, however, are the two Bisbee-sponsored fishing tournaments: The Los Cabos Offshore and Black and Blue (aka “The Super Bowl of Fishing”). These are scheduled for Oct. 12-17 and Oct. 19-24, respectively, and offer a chance for fishing glory for those who hook enormous black and blue marlin or other approved billfish and game fish species, but also enormous amounts of prize money.

The Bisbee’s East Cape Offshore, which kicked off Bisbee’s annual trio of tournaments in Los Cabos in August, boasted a prize pool of US $1.6 million this year … and that was the warm-up event. The Black and Blue, in particular, has topped eight figures before, with a world-record in excess of US $11 million in 2022, while the Los Cabos Offshore reached more than US $2.7 million last year.

Fishing tournament returns in La Paz

Those are the headliners, but not the only fishing tournament on the October calendar. In the state capital of La Paz, the La Paz Fishing Tournament returns for its second edition on Oct. 18, with a prize pool of 200,000 pesos for those who boat the biggest marlin.

Chris Sands is a writer and editor for Mexico News Daily, and the former Cabo San Lucas local expert for the USA Today travel website 10 Best and writer of Fodor’s Los Cabos travel guidebook. He has also contributed to numerous other websites and publications, including The San Diego Union-Tribune, Marriott Bonvoy Traveler, Forbes Travel Guide, Porthole Cruise and Travel, and Cabo Living.

World.title: El Grito de Independencia: Common myths and misconceptions
World.content:
If you have been anywhere in Mexico during the month of September, you’ve noticed that something in the air begins to shift. Not only has the rain called a truce, especially in the city, but you see every corner covered in green, white and red as the middle of the month approaches. Every city and every town is getting ready for El Grito de Independencia, also known as El Grito de Dolores.

There are many myths around this holiday — one of the biggest, if not the greatest, celebrations for Mexicans. People dress up, host dinners with pozole and tequila, and gather to scream “¡Viva México!” at the same time as the current president, just like people did with Miguel Hidalgo in 1810 … right?

When did Mexico actually become independent?

Before unveiling the truth behind some of the most common misconceptions, a disclaimer needs to be addressed. Although it is not exactly a myth, the date on which Mexicans celebrate their independence commemorates not when the conflict ended, but when it began. In other countries, the commemoration often happens on the day the document declaring the nation’s sovereignty was signed.

Nevertheless, in Mexico, both dates are close together, as they are both in September. The Declaration of Independence was signed Sept. 28, 1821, ending the 11-year armed conflict that had been ongoing since Sept. 15, 1810 … or was it the 16th?

Did El Grito happen on Sept. 15 or Sept. 16?

It is often a challenge to know whether to celebrate Mexican independence on Sept. 15 or Sept. 16. There is even an urban myth suggesting President Porfirio Díaz changed the official date of El Grito de Independencia from Sept. 16 to Sept. 15 to align with his birthday. Although Díaz’s birthday was indeed Sept. 15, historical evidence shows the tradition predates his presidency.

Regarding practical matters, the tradition of celebrating on the evening of Sept. 15 began much earlier — around 1840 — partly because it made more sense to stage fireworks, music and civic speeches in the evening rather than at 2 a.m. or 5 a.m. on Sept. 16.

This confusion is logical since the event happened unexpectedly. During the evening of Sept. 15, Miguel Hidalgo and the other members of the conspiracy received news that they had been caught and were forced to launch the uprising immediately. So, in the early morning of Sunday, Sept. 16, Hidalgo called on all inhabitants of Dolores Hidalgo, Guanajuato, to take up arms and initiate the war that would go on for 11 years. This version fits the context, as Sunday Mass was perhaps the most important gathering moment for a Catholic community.

What did Miguel Hidalgo really shout that night?

To explain what Miguel Hidalgo shouted that night, more context is needed. The Spanish crown had been stripping privileges from the Spanish population born in Mexican territory, also known as criollos. This meant that people who had Spanish parents did not receive equal treatment, including being restricted from accessing positions of power. Naturally, the situation made criollos angry enough to organize a conspiracy, though they were not initially seeking a complete break from the Spanish monarchy.

While there is no single consensus on what Hidalgo said, primary sources and early historical accounts suggest he praised not only the Virgin of Guadalupe and the Catholic Church, but also the then-imprisoned King Fernando VII. According to accounts documented by historians, Hidalgo’s call sounded much closer to:

“¡Viva la religión! ¡Viva nuestra madre santísima de Guadalupe! ¡Viva Fernando VII! ¡Viva la América y muera el mal gobierno!” (“Long live religion! Long live our most holy mother of Guadalupe! Long live Fernando VII! Long live America and death to bad government!”)

To which the gathered crowd responded: “¡Viva la Virgen de Guadalupe y mueran los gachupines!” (“Long live the Virgin of Guadalupe and death to the gachupines!”)

The real spirit of El Grito

Although debunking myths can feel a bit like unveiling a magic trick, El Grito continues to be an epic start for an epic battle. Whether the cry rang out at midnight or dawn, or whether Porfirio Díaz moved the party to coincide with his birthday, Sept. 15 remains the heart of Mexico’s collective identity. The historical moment brings people together in gatherings where food, music and community are enjoyed at their finest. So, pour the tequila, dish out the pozole, and get ready to shout.

Lydia Leija is a linguist, journalist and visual storyteller. She has directed three feature films, and her audiovisual work has been featured in national and international media. She’s been part of National Geographic, Muy Interesante and Cosmopolitan.

World.title: The National Palace’s new resident has four legs and one role: to support emotional well-being
World.content:
The Mexican government has just introduced a new resident of the National Palace. And no, it’s not a politician or public official. It’s a puppy, and his name is Rollo.

In a video posted on the government’s official social media accounts, Rollo is seen running playfully through the corridors and gardens of the National Palace. In another scene, he’s behind a desk, wearing a tie.

Él es Rollo, trabaja en Palacio Nacional. Es un cachorro mestizo adoptado que hoy se divierte en jardines y oficinas bajo el resguardo de la Dirección General de Comunicación Digital de la Presidencia. Tiene un papel muy importante: el apoyo y bienestar emocional de todas y… pic.twitter.com/aoRmKbXHlT — Gobierno de México (@GobiernoMX) September 10, 2026

“This is Rollo. He works at the National Palace,” the post says, adding that the adopted pet, a mixed-breed, has a “very important role: the support and emotional well-being of everyone.”

The video also indicates that Rollo has a brother named Theo, who is still looking for an adoptive family. However, details of where and how to adopt him have not been shared.

Rollo joins other animals living at the National Palace, including the cats that inhabit its gardens and other areas of the palace. President Claudia Sheinbaum herself has shown off these pets during tours of the presidential headquarters.

In May 2026, during the visit of the K-pop group BTS to the National Palace, Sheinbaum said that 16 cats lived there. However, the number of these animals has varied over the years.

In 2024, it was reported that 19 cats inhabiting the National Palace were designated as “living fixed assets” — a legal measure to guarantee resources for their food, medical attention and care for the rest of their lives.

The gatos that have been publicly identified include Coco, Zeus, Roja, Ollie and Balam — two of whom have made a debut on the internet. During the 2026 FIFA World Cup, Coco appeared in posts on official government accounts wearing Mexico’s jersey. Meanwhile, Zeus once wandered into a morning press conference during Andrés Manuel López Obrador’s term (2018-2024).

Unlike Rollo, these cats were not adopted. According to information from the presidential office, they have been there for years, and there is no precise record of how each one arrived.

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

Key Facts —

What happened. Bank of America (BofA) reaffirmed its sell rating on Banco do Brasil (BBAS3), cutting the price target to R$20 (US$3.88).

—

How big. Non-performing loans overdue more than 90 days hit 5.61% in the second quarter of 2026.

—

What it means. BofA expects 2026 net profit of R$17.6 billion (US$3.42 billion), below the bank’s own guidance range.

—

The catch. Most of Banco do Brasil’s employee strike ended on September 11, but about eighteen union chapters kept striking.

—

Who it affects. Shareholders face renewed selling pressure, while 71,500 employees received a signing bonus of R$3,000 (US$582) each.

—

What comes next. BofA forecasts a 2027 profit rebound to R$23.6 billion (US$4.58 billion), but sees returns still below its cost of capital.

The Banco do Brasil headquarters building in Brasília. Photo: Agência Senado, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

Banco do Brasil, Brazil’s largest state-controlled bank, is facing a rough stretch on the stock market. Bank of America (BofA) reaffirmed its sell rating this month, and fresh earnings data show credit quality getting worse.

Non-performing loans climbed to 5.61% of the loan book in the second quarter. That ratio was 3.96% a year earlier, and 5.05% just three months before.

A labor strike briefly added to the turmoil, shutting some Banco do Brasil branches from September 10. Most of that strike ended within a day, but a handful of union chapters are still walking out.

Banco do Brasil trades on Brazil’s B3 exchange under the ticker BBAS3. The stock has drawn increasingly cautious commentary from multiple analyst desks this earnings season.

Why BofA Turned More Bearish

Bank of America reaffirmed its sell rating on Banco do Brasil (BBAS3) in a report dated Tuesday, September 8, 2026. Analysts cut the price target to R$20 (US$3.88) per share, down from R$21 (US$4.08).

That target implies the stock could fall about 11% from its last close, the bank said. BofA now forecasts 2026 net profit of R$17.6 billion (US$3.42 billion).

That figure sits below the bank’s own guidance range of R$18 billion to R$22 billion (US$3.49 billion to US$4.27 billion). BofA blamed higher provisioning needs tied to worsening asset quality.

Asset-quality problems are no longer limited to farm loans, BofA noted. Credit-card delinquency alone doubled from 7% to 14% in a single quarter.

Bad Loans Keep Climbing

Banco do Brasil’s overall non-performing loan ratio, loans overdue more than 90 days, reached 5.61% at the end of June. That is up from 5.05% in the first quarter and 3.96% a year earlier.

The bank’s expanded credit portfolio totaled R$1.31 trillion (US$254.3 billion) at the end of the quarter. That was up just 0.6% from three months earlier, near the low end of management’s own growth guidance.

The cost of credit rose 16.1% year-on-year, to nearly R$18.5 billion (US$3.59 billion). It still fell 2.1% from the first quarter, easing slightly.

Despite the deterioration, Banco do Brasil posted a net profit of R$3.9 billion (US$757 million) for the quarter. That was up 3.3% from a year earlier, and return on equity rose to 8.3%.

Itaú BBA, a separate Brazilian investment bank, projected a similarly elevated cost of risk near 6.4% for the quarter. JPMorgan and Itaú BBA both described Banco do Brasil as entering a genuinely difficult stretch.

A Rural Debt Wildcard

Part of BofA’s caution centers on a new government program for rural debt. Medida Provisória 1.376, a provisional measure in effect since late August, lets farmers restructure overdue loans.

BofA estimates Banco do Brasil could renegotiate about R$30 billion (US$5.82 billion) of loans. That is out of roughly R$100 billion (US$19.41 billion) in farm debt the program covers.

The effect on the bank’s provisions and interest income is hard to predict, BofA said. Management has suggested each R$1 billion (US$194.1 million) renegotiated could add up to R$200 million (US$38.8 million) to net profit.

BofA cautioned that the benefit likely applies to only a small share of restructured loans. A severe El Niño weather pattern could also delay any recovery in farm credit quality.

The Strike That Mostly Ended

Labor unrest briefly compounded the pressure on Banco do Brasil this month. Workers walked out on September 10 as part of a broader campaign across Brazil’s public banks.

The union side wanted better funding for Cassi, Banco do Brasil’s employee health plan, plus pay and career gains. Banco do Brasil reached a settlement just one day later, on September 11.

The deal included a real pay increase of 0.6% above inflation, plus profit-sharing paid within 72 hours. It also included a R$3,000 (US$582) bonus for roughly 71,500 employees.

Other terms extended paternity leave from 20 to 35 days for staff. The bank also advanced R$360 million (US$69.9 million) to shore up the Cassi fund.

A total of 116 union bases approved the agreement, but about 18 rejected it. As of Monday, those holdout chapters, including Angra dos Reis and parts of Bahia, were still on strike.

Caixa Econômica Federal, a separate state bank, remains on a full nationwide strike. Its dispute centers on Saúde Caixa, its own employee health plan, not on Banco do Brasil’s terms.

What Comes Next

BofA does expect some recovery, projecting 2027 net profit of R$23.6 billion (US$4.58 billion). But it still sees return on equity at just 12.2%, below the bank’s cost of capital.

That gap between returns and the cost of capital is the core of BofA’s sell call. Until asset quality stabilizes, the bank said, higher profit alone will not be enough to change its view.

Investors are now watching the remaining strike holdouts and the pace of rural debt renegotiation. Both could shape Banco do Brasil’s results well into 2027.

World.content:

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

Key Facts —

What happened. Analysts say Mexico’s newly delivered 2027 Paquete Económico (economic budget package) leaves little room before a possible investment-grade downgrade.

—

How big. The plan sets spending at MXN$10.6 trillion (US$619.1 billion) against MXN$9.16 trillion (US$535.0 billion) in revenue.

—

What it means. Public debt (SHRFSP) is projected to keep climbing, from 54% of GDP in 2026 to 56.4% by 2030.

—

The catch. Fitch and Moody’s already rate Mexico at their lowest investment-grade rung, one step above junk status.

—

Who it affects. Holders of Mexican government bonds, since a downgrade would raise the country’s borrowing costs.

—

What comes next. Rating agencies will judge Mexico on whether it actually hits these targets through 2027, not on the plan itself.

The Bolsa Mexicana de Valores, Mexico’s stock exchange, in Mexico City. Analysts say the newly delivered 2027 budget leaves Mexico with little margin before a possible ratings downgrade. Photo: Wotancito, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

The Numbers Are Finally Public

Mexico delivered its 2027 economic package to Congress on 8 September, but its detailed figures were not published right away. This week, financial press finished parsing them, and the reaction was uneasy.

Bloomberg Línea, among other outlets, now frames Mexico as closer to losing its investment-grade credit rating. The reason is not a new crisis, but the actual math inside the plan itself.

What the Budget Actually Shows

The package sets total spending at MXN$10.6 trillion, equivalent to roughly US$619.1 billion at this week’s exchange rate. Projected revenue comes in lower, at MXN$9.16 trillion, or about US$535.0 billion.

That gap of nearly MXN$1.7 trillion, around US$99.3 billion, must be covered through new borrowing. Mexico’s public sector borrowing requirement, known as the RFSP, is set at 4.1% of GDP for 2026.

It is projected to ease only slightly, to 3.9% of GDP, in 2027. That is a smaller improvement than earlier government guidance had suggested before the full package became public.

Public debt under the broader SHRFSP measure tells a less reassuring story. It is projected to rise from 54% of GDP in 2026 to 55% in 2027, then to 56.4% by 2030.

Why Analysts Are Uneasy

The core concern is simple. Mexico is promising fiscal consolidation, yet its own budget projects debt continuing to climb for years, not stabilizing.

Héctor Villarreal, of the fiscal think tank ITED, put it carefully. Hacienda’s messaging is more credible than before, he said, but the government may still be “kicking the can down the road.”

Adriana Hernández, a former Treasury consultant, framed it as a watch-and-wait situation. Rating agencies, she said, will track this closely, and markets need to stay alert alongside them.

José Luis Clavellina, of the fiscal research group CIEP, said compliance depends on factors beyond the document itself. Actual execution, real growth, and investor confidence will decide whether the targets hold.

A Second Warning From Closer to Home

Days before the Bloomberg Línea analysis, the Mexican rating agency HR Ratings issued its own alert. On 11 September, it warned the debt trajectory in the 2027 package could pressure Mexico’s sovereign rating.

HR Ratings currently holds Mexico at BBB+ with a stable outlook. That is three notches above losing investment grade on the agency’s own scale, a cushion the international agencies do not share.

HR Ratings also projects weaker 2026 growth than Hacienda’s own numbers, at 1.1% to 1.3%. Slower growth would make the government’s debt ratios harder to hit than currently projected.

Where the Big Three Already Stand

Mexico has less room to absorb bad news than it once did. Moody’s downgraded the country to Baa3 in May, citing weakened fiscal strength.

Fitch rates Mexico at BBB-minus, one single notch above sub-investment-grade status. The agency has said explicitly that Mexico would lose its investment grade if it fails to consolidate its fiscal strategy.

S&P has not cut its rating, but it moved its outlook to negative earlier this year. A negative outlook typically signals a downgrade is under active consideration, not imminent but plausible.

Why This Differs From Earlier Warnings

Mexico has faced investment-grade warnings for weeks, tied to Pemex debt and a widening first-half deficit. Those were forward-looking concerns about a budget nobody had fully seen yet.

This week’s reaction is different because the numbers are now real. Analysts are responding to Mexico’s own stated targets, not to speculation about what the targets might say.

That distinction matters for credibility. A government can dismiss speculation, but its own published figures are harder to argue with.

What Foreign Investors Should Watch

None of this means a downgrade is certain, or even likely in the near term. Mexico still holds investment-grade ratings at all three major agencies, plus HR Ratings domestically.

The real test runs through 2027 itself. If revenue underperforms or Pemex needs support again, little fiscal space remains to absorb the surprise.

Bondholders will likely watch each quarterly fiscal report closely from here. A single weak print could shift the conversation from cautious concern to active downgrade risk.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Mexico’s 2027 Paquete Económico? The government’s 2027 budget package, delivered to Congress on 8 September, covering revenue, spending and fiscal targets.

How big is the 2027 deficit target? The RFSP is projected at 3.9% of GDP in 2027, down only slightly from 4.1% in 2026.

What is HR Ratings? A Mexican domestic credit rating agency, which currently rates Mexico BBB+ with a stable outlook.

Where do Fitch, Moody’s and S&P stand? Fitch and Moody’s hold Mexico at their lowest investment-grade level; S&P has a negative outlook.

Is a downgrade imminent? No, but analysts say the risk has grown because the budget confirms debt will keep rising through 2030.

World.title: Chile: IMF Backs Kast Agenda, Sees 3% Growth Path
World.content:
Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Get the brief

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

Key Facts —

What happened. The IMF (International Monetary Fund) publicly backed the economic agenda of Chilean President José Antonio Kast.

—

How big. The Fund sees Chile’s economy growing near 3% a year over the medium term, versus under 1% in 2026.

—

What it means. IMF mission chief Bikas Joshi called this year’s slowdown temporary, tied to falling copper production.

—

The catch. The 3% path depends on two conditions holding: copper prices staying elevated, and Kast’s reforms actually passing Congress.

—

Who it affects. Investors pricing Chilean assets, and Chilean workers waiting for the growth the reform push promises.

—

What comes next. The IMF wants Chile to bank high copper revenue into reserves instead of funding permanent new spending.

La Moneda, Chile’s presidential palace in Santiago. The IMF this week endorsed President José Antonio Kast’s economic program. Photo: Draceane, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

An Unusually Warm IMF Verdict

The International Monetary Fund does not often sound enthusiastic about a government’s economic plan. This week, on Chile, it came close.

Bikas Joshi, the Fund’s new Chile mission chief, said growth could near 3% a year over the medium term. That forecast hinges on two things going right at once.

A Very Slow 2026

The immediate picture is far less impressive. The IMF now projects Chile’s economy will grow only between 0.25% and 0.75% this year.

That is a sharp deceleration from earlier in President Kast’s term. The Fund raised its 2026 forecast to 2.4% in April, only to cut it again in May.

Joshi described the current slowdown as temporary rather than structural. He tied it directly to a transitional decline in copper production, not to weakening demand or policy missteps.

Why the IMF Isn’t Worried Yet

Copper prices help explain the Fund’s patience. The metal hit a record above US$14,500 per tonne in early September, up roughly 18% this year alone.

Joshi said Chile should use this favorable stretch to strengthen both fiscal and external reserves. He wants the exchange rate, not new spending, to keep absorbing the shock.

His warning ran alongside the praise. High commodity dependence leaves Chile exposed to price swings, and to rising costs as ore quality declines at older mines.

Cuts, Deregulation and Spending Restraint at Once

Kast’s program combines tax cuts, deregulation and reduced public spending simultaneously. Critics have argued that mixing stimulus with austerity sends contradictory signals to the economy.

The IMF disagreed directly with that criticism. Joshi called the measures “complementary, not opposed,” each aimed at a different part of the economy.

Tax cuts and deregulation, he said, target medium-term competitiveness and private investment. Spending restraint, meanwhile, protects short-term fiscal sustainability while those slower-moving reforms take hold.

Regulatory reform drew the Fund’s clearest praise. Joshi singled out permit-streamlining efforts as the most promising piece of the government’s agenda so far.

The Copper Catch

Nothing here is guaranteed. The 3% medium-term path assumes copper prices hold near current highs, not just for months but for years.

It also assumes Kast’s reform package clears Chile’s Congress largely intact. Neither condition is fully within the government’s control.

Joshi’s own language reflected that uncertainty. He described the 3% figure as achievable “if” both conditions hold, not as a baseline forecast.

What Kast Actually Proposed

The government calls its package the National Reconstruction Plan. It would cut Chile’s corporate tax rate from 27% to 23%, phased in gradually.

It also adds an employment tax credit and strips back permitting procedures for new investment. In May, the IMF called parts of this “somewhat optimistic” and urged cheaper alternatives instead.

This week’s statement reads as a softer tone on the same plan, four months later. The Fund still wants fiscal consolidation, but now frames the package’s pieces as working together.

A Third Data Point in Six Months

This week’s statement is the IMF’s third distinct read on Chile since Kast took office on 11 March. April brought an upgrade, May brought a cut, and September brought qualified encouragement.

Taken together, the sequence shows an institution still calibrating its view of an untested government. It also shows a government whose numbers keep moving with commodity prices beyond its control.

What It Means for Chileans

For ordinary Chileans, the immediate reality is a near-stalled economy. Growth below 1% this year limits new hiring and wage gains regardless of what happens with copper next year.

For investors, the IMF’s endorsement of the policy mix reduces one source of uncertainty. It does not remove the risk that copper prices retreat before the reforms fully take effect.

Foreign residents holding Chilean-peso assets face the same conditional outlook. A favorable currency and rate environment now rests partly on a metal price outside anyone’s direct control.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the IMF say about Chile’s economy? It projected medium-term growth near 3% a year, while backing President Kast’s tax, spending and deregulation agenda.

Who is Bikas Joshi? The IMF’s newly assigned mission chief for Chile, who delivered this week’s assessment.

Why is 2026 growth so weak? The IMF projects only 0.25% to 0.75% growth this year, which it attributes to a temporary drop in copper output.

What conditions does the 3% forecast depend on? Copper prices staying elevated, and Kast’s reform agenda passing largely as proposed.

What does the IMF want Chile to do with copper revenue? Build up fiscal and external reserves rather than fund permanent new spending.

World.content:

Get the brief

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

Key Facts —

What happened. Argentina’s government formally named Alfredo Mario Soto as the new director of the Casa Argentina in Paris.

—

How it was done. Human Capital Minister Sandra Pettovello signed Resolution 341/2026, published in the Official Bulletin on 15 September.

—

Who he is. Soto is a Rosario-based law professor, a former resident of the house, and a fluent French speaker.

—

The catch. The resolution accepted predecessor Santiago Muzio’s resignation effective 7 September, days before the appointment became public paperwork.

—

Who it affects. Argentine students and researchers housed at the Cité Internationale Universitaire de Paris, and the campus’s other national residences.

—

What comes next. Soto’s three-year term begins as petitioners wait to see if a removed memorial plaque is restored.

The Casa Argentina, formally the Fondation Argentine, at the Cité Internationale Universitaire de Paris. Argentina has now formally named a new director for the residence. Photo: Cité internationale universitaire de Paris (CIUP), via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Appointment Is Now Official

Argentina has made it official. A government resolution has formally named Alfredo Mario Soto as the new director of the Casa Argentina in Paris.

Human Capital Minister Sandra Pettovello signed Resolution 341/2026. It appeared in Argentina’s Official Bulletin on 15 September, converting weeks of reported speculation into paperwork.

What the Resolution Actually Says

The text designates “el abogado Alfredo Mario Soto” as director of the Fundación Argentina, the residence’s formal legal name. It also accepts the resignation of his predecessor, Santiago Muzio.

That resignation is dated as effective 7 September, a detail that had not been formally confirmed until this filing. Soto’s own term begins the following day, 8 September.

His appointment runs three years, under bylaws the foundation approved by a 1982 government decree. That structure predates the current controversy by more than four decades.

The resolution is administrative housekeeping on its face. But it closes a chapter that had dragged on publicly since Muzio’s resignation became widely reported on 13 September.

Who Alfredo Soto Is

Soto is not an outsider to the institution he now runs. He is a doctor of legal and social sciences and heads the graduate school at the National University of Rosario’s law faculty.

He was previously a resident of the Casa Argentina himself, and he speaks French fluently. Both details matter after a tenure marked by conflict with French-speaking neighbors on campus.

His predecessor, a lawyer and dual French-Argentine national, was accused of running the house with the opposite instincts. Soto’s academic background reads as a deliberate contrast.

Why Muzio Left

Santiago Muzio was appointed to the post in 2024 by the Milei government. His two years there were the most contentious in the residence’s recent history.

A memorial plaque honoring victims of Argentina’s military dictatorship disappeared from the building in February. Its removal, on a date tied to the dictatorship’s anniversary, drew immediate outrage.

More than a thousand academics, writers and diplomats signed a June letter demanding a full financial and administrative audit. No results from that audit have been published.

Muzio also refused to sign the campus’s charter of values, which bars discrimination based on gender and sexual orientation. He said he was following the Argentine government’s own position on sex.

Other national houses at the Cité Internationale distanced themselves publicly from the Argentine residence. Paris’s mayor asked France’s foreign minister to open an investigation in July.

A Presidential Visit in the Background

One Argentine outlet reported that the government pushed Muzio out ahead of a presidential trip. President Javier Milei is due in France around a Paris Week event scheduled for 30 October.

Other coverage frames the pressure as coming mainly from French academic and municipal circles instead. Both explanations can be true at once, and neither has been fully confirmed independently.

What is now confirmed, through this week’s resolution, is the government’s own paper trail. It accepted the resignation and named a successor within a single administrative act.

What Happens to the Plaque

The missing memorial plaque remains the clearest test of Soto’s tenure. It was installed in 2022 on 24 March, the anniversary of the 1976 coup, and vanished this February without explanation.

Petitioners who organized last spring’s letter say its return is the single clearest signal a new director could send. Soto has not yet made a public statement about it.

The investigation Paris municipal officials requested has also not been reported as concluded. Whether it produces findings before Soto settles into the role remains an open question.

Why This Matters Beyond One Building

The Casa Argentina sits inside a campus of more than forty national residences. How Argentina runs its house is visible to diplomats and students from dozens of countries at once.

A formal, published resolution signals the government wants the episode closed administratively. Whether it is closed politically depends on what Soto does with the plaque and the pending audit.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Argentina’s new Casa Argentina director? Alfredo Mario Soto, a law professor from Rosario and a former resident of the house.

Who signed his appointment? Human Capital Minister Sandra Pettovello, via Resolution 341/2026, published 15 September 2026.

When does his term start? His three-year term is effective from 8 September 2026, the day after Muzio’s resignation took effect.

Why did Santiago Muzio resign? Amid accusations over a removed dictatorship memorial plaque, student expulsions, and refusal to sign the campus charter of values.

Has the missing plaque been restored? Not as of this report, and it remains the measure petitioners plan to judge the new director by.

World.title: Colombia: Promigás Warns Gas Deficit Is Now Structural
World.content:

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

Key Facts —

What happened. Promigás, Colombia’s largest gas transporter, says the country’s natural-gas shortfall has stopped being temporary and is now structural.

—

How big. National gas production fell 12% in 2025 alone, and 31% cumulatively since 2021.

—

What it means. Imported, regasified gas covered 34% of Colombia’s total supply in August 2026, up from almost nothing in 2021.

—

The catch. Proven reserves have nearly halved, falling from 3.16 trillion cubic feet in 2021 to 1.72 trillion now.

—

Who it affects. Factories, natural-gas vehicle owners and households whose bills already track import-linked gas prices.

—

What comes next. Promigás wants faster import terminals, revived exploration, and targeted subsidies for vulnerable consumers.

Colombia’s hydrocarbon hub at Barrancabermeja. Promigás says the country’s natural-gas output has fallen so far that the deficit is now structural. Photo: Ymc16, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

From Coyuntural to Structural

Colombia’s gas pipeline operator has changed its language on the country’s energy shortfall. Promigás says the deficit has stopped being “coyuntural,” the Spanish word for temporary or cyclical.

In a report released this week, the company called it a structural gas deficit instead. That single word shift signals a much harder problem for the next government to fix.

Production in Free Fall

The numbers behind that shift are stark. National gas production dropped 12% in 2025 compared with the year before, according to Promigás data reported by Colombian outlets this week.

Measured against 2021, the decline reaches 31%. Colombia is now producing roughly a third less gas than it did just four years ago.

Proven reserves tell the same story. They have fallen from 3.16 trillion cubic feet in 2021 to 1.72 trillion cubic feet by the end of 2025.

That is a drop of nearly half in under five years. Reserves measure how many years of supply Colombia has left at current extraction rates.

Imports Take Over

Colombia has plugged the gap with imported liquefied gas, regasified at coastal terminals. Average regasified volumes rose from just 5 million cubic feet per day in 2021 to 174 million in 2025.

Through August 2026, imports made up 28% of the country’s total gas supply. In August alone, that share climbed to 34%, Promigás said.

An expansion of import infrastructure once planned for September 2027 has now been moved up to October 2026. Colombia is racing to build capacity it did not expect to need this soon.

Demand Is Already Shrinking

Higher import-linked prices appear to be pushing consumption down. Non-thermal gas demand fell 7% between January and August 2026, compared with the same period the previous year.

Industrial gas demand alone contracted 23% over that stretch. Colombia’s natural-gas vehicle fleet and its petroleum sector also used measurably less gas.

Promigás president Juan Manuel Rojas warned the risk is not only about averages. A single unexpected drop at one field, he said, can now ripple through entire market segments.

Five Fixes Promigás Wants

The company laid out five priorities for policymakers. First, secure and diversify imports, including clearer rules for sharing infrastructure costs among users.

Second, revive domestic production through new exploration, faster reserve conversion, and unconventional resources. The long-delayed Sirius offshore project was named specifically as a priority to accelerate.

Third, expand transport capacity toward consumption centers. A planned VIM-Interior pipeline connection could add up to 400 million cubic feet of daily capacity, Promigás estimates.

Fourth, restore regulatory stability so infrastructure projects get approved on a predictable timeline. Fifth, protect vulnerable households and competitive industries with targeted subsidies rather than blanket price increases.

Rojas summed up the dilemma in blunt terms. Colombia, he said, must work on securing imports now and rebuilding domestic supply for later, at the very same time.

A Warning Foretold

This is not the first alarm on Colombian gas. Industry group Andesco warned in January that monthly deficit risk could hit 39% in 2026 and 58% in 2027.

Promigás’s new report suggests those warnings are no longer theoretical. The country crossed real thresholds this year, not just risk-model projections.

What changed is the framing, not just the numbers. Regulators previously treated shortfalls as temporary supply hiccups tied to weather or single-field outages.

Calling the deficit structural means something different. It means the underlying reserve base itself can no longer support Colombia’s current demand without permanent, large-scale imports.

Why Foreign Residents Should Care

Colombia prices much of its regulated gas off a formula tied partly to imported costs. As imports grow from a third of supply toward more, household and business gas bills are more exposed to global price swings.

Industrial users, already down 23% in consumption this year, face a similar exposure. Businesses that depend on cheap domestic gas for manufacturing now compete for a shrinking, import-heavy pool.

The timeline Promigás sketched runs through the rest of this decade. Whether Colombia’s next government funds the fixes it proposed will shape gas prices for years to come.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does “structural” gas deficit mean? Promigás says the shortfall no longer stems from temporary conditions, but from a reserve base too small for current demand.

How much has production fallen? National gas output dropped 12% in 2025 and 31% cumulatively since 2021, according to Promigás.

How much of Colombia’s gas is now imported? Imported, regasified gas reached 34% of total supply in August 2026, up from almost none in 2021.

What does Promigás want done? Faster import infrastructure, revived exploration, better pipeline capacity, regulatory stability, and targeted subsidies for vulnerable consumers.

Has this been warned about before? Yes, industry group Andesco flagged rising deficit risk in January, though this week’s report treats the shortfall as now structural.

World.title: Colombia: Fired DANE Chief Ricardo Valencia Defends His Numbers
World.content:

Get the brief

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

Key Facts —

What happened. Ricardo Valencia, fired as director of DANE (Colombia’s national statistics agency) on 14 September, is now publicly defending the data that got him removed.

—

What he said. Valencia told local media DANE’s technical independence “is sacred,” and that he stands by his reading of the July unemployment data.

—

No warning. He says he never received any communication from the presidency objecting to his conduct before he was dismissed.

—

The catch. The government that fired him is the same one that had appointed him only 26 days earlier, under President Abelardo De la Espriella.

—

Who it affects. Anyone relying on DANE numbers: bondholders pricing Colombian debt, renters with CPI-linked leases, and pensioners on indexed benefits.

—

What comes next. Congress can summon Valencia’s successor, economist Juan Manuel Alvarado Nivia, to explain the dispute.

Casa de Nariño, Colombia’s presidential palace in Bogotá. President Abelardo De la Espriella’s government dismissed statistics chief Ricardo Valencia 26 days after appointing him. Photo: Mriobomorales, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.
