World.title: French police take to streets in mass protest over pay, staffing and resources
World.content:
Thousands of French police officers took to the streets of Paris to protest against their working conditions on Tuesday. The protest — led by the Alliance Police Nationale union — began at the Champs-Élysées and culminated at the National Assembly.

 

After the march, union representatives headed to the Interior Ministry to share their grievances — they subsequently told reporters that the meeting showed positive signs authorities were taking their grievances into account.

Mounting anger among police officers has been fuelled by a range of issues: including discontent around the special police duty allowance (ISSP), their "risk bonus", which has not gone up since 2019.

Alongside side this, the Alliance Police Nationale union is also calling for an increase in resources for administrative, technical and scientific staff, as well as action on career progression and staffing levels. The union estimates it requires an additional 300 to 500 million euros a year to meet its needs.

Police officers demonstrate outside the National Assembly in Paris on 15 September 2026 Photo Estelle Nilsson, Euronews

Ahead of the protest, one officer working in Rennes described a situation, which he qualified as "alarming". He condemned staff shortages, equipment problems and the lack of decent pay: "we need equipment, we need manpower, we need recognition in our pay," he said, arguing that working conditions "are getting worse and worse".

Longterm discussions

On 4 September, major police unions — Alliance, Unité and UNSA Police unions — were received by Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez. After the meeting, the unions complained that there had been no meaningful progress on their budget demands.

But on Tuesday, they appeared to reach a turning point.

After his meeting with France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez, Fabien Vanhemelryck, secretary-general of the Alliance union said authorities had been open-minded and took note of the gravity of the situation for officers.

“The only thing we can be satisfied with is that there is an open-mindedness and an awareness of the situation", he said.

Vanhemelryck told reporters that Nuñez asked officers for a "few days", as he was working on a "plan."

At the start of the summer, Alliance launched a "zero initiative" campaign, soon joined by Un1té. The union set 15 September as the next step in its mobilisation, speaking at the time of a possible large-scale "social rentrée" for police officers.

Tuesday's mobilisation comes just a few months before professional elections within the national police, scheduled for December, which is adding to the pressure from the unions.

World.title: Carney bound for Europe as Ottawa seeks closer ties with EU
World.content:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to travel to Europe on Tuesday as Ottawa pushes for deeper ties with Europe amid frosty relations with Washington.

 

Carney is scheduled to visit Strasbourg in eastern France and Liverpool in the UK's northwest during his trip to the continent.

In Strasbourg, the Canadian leader will give a speech at the European Parliament (EP) and meet with EP members to "strengthen Canada’s ties with the EU in trade, investment, and security." He will also attend European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s State of the European Union address on Wednesday.

Carney is expected to use the trip to seek a new arrangement with the EU that could allow Canadians to live and work across the bloc without visa restrictions, a senior Canadian official familiar with the talks told the Associated Press.

According to the official, the Canadian government is not looking for a Norway or Switzerland-style deal with the EU and has not proposed "associate membership" of the bloc.

Ottawa is instead looking for a bespoke arrangement aligned with its priorities and centring on investment, per the report.

Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Carney clarified that Canada was not looking to become a member of the EU but that the country had its sights on forming what he called a "unique alliance" with the bloc.

Canada Prime Minister Mark Carney and President Donald Trump hold a press conference at the White House in Washington, D.C., Oct. 7, 2025. AP Photo

Canada has been increasingly looking to Europe amid an ongoing trade spat with Washington that reignited last month after talks over a deal to avoid hefty duties on some Canadian goods fell apart.

Following the breakdown in negotiations, 50% US duties impacting around C$28 billion worth of Canadian goods came into effect in late August, prompting Ottawa to announce counter-tariffs of up to 15, 25 or 50% on roughly C$27.6 billion in imports from the US.

Carney nevertheless told an audience at the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto on Tuesday that Canada "will continue to be the US's most important partner in many key areas."

"Even at times of disagreement over our long-shared history, we have always maintained deep ties," Carney said at the event, which saw global investors come together with Canadian executives and representatives from the public sector amid a push to attract more investment into Canada.

In the UK leg of his trip, Carney is due to meet his British counterpart Andy Burnham for the first time, with the pair lined up to go over issues including defence and security, artificial intelligence, energy and critical minerals.

World.title: Canada still a crucial partner for US in 'many key areas,' PM Carney says
World.content:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has reassured the US that Canada will remain a key partner despite an ongoing trade war that has seen relations between Ottawa and Washington unravel.

 

Speaking at the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto on Tuesday, Carney said: "To our American friends, let me say this. We will always be neighbors, and Canada will continue to be the US's most important partner in many key areas."

"Even at times of disagreement over our long-shared history, we have always maintained deep ties," Carney went on, while pledging that Canada would be an "even better partner" when future "opportunities return."

"Stronger, more resilient, more independent, ready to advance our mutual, economic, and security interests," he told the audience.

The two-day Investment Summit, billed as a "first-of-its-kind gathering" in Canada, brought together global investors, Canadian executives and representatives from the public sector as Ottawa seeks to diversify and bring new investment into the country.

The goal, the government says, is to attract C$1 trillion in investment over the next five years.

In a statement later on Tuesday, Carney's office said the summit had resulted in nearly C$500 billion in new investment commitments, including almost C$100 billion in new capital for Canadian assets from pension funds, insurers, and institutional investors, C$325 billion in new financing for Canadian businesses and infrastructure from banks, and over C$14 billion in capital to grow Canadian businesses, infrastructure, and "strategic sectors" from investment funds.

The flags of Canada and the United States fly over a stadium in Ottawa, Saturday, Sept. 12, 2026. AP Photo

It comes amid a growing trade dispute between the US and Canada that came to a head last month after negotiations over a deal to avoid hefty duties on some Canadian goods fell apart.

Following the breakdown in talks, 50% US duties impacting around C$28 billion worth of Canadian goods came into effect in late August, prompting Ottawa to announce counter-tariffs of up to 15, 25 or 50% on roughly C$27.6 billion in imports from the US.

World.title: ECB staff raise stability concerns about rumours of Lagarde's early departure
World.content:
In a letter seen by Euronews, European Central Bank staff members have questioned the institution’s stability in the face of rumours of the early departures of its president, Christine Lagarde, and board member Isabel Schnabel.

 

The staff calls the board to provide "appropriate clarity regarding potential leadership transitions", as discussions of major departures can affect both monetary policy and ECB internal reforms.

"We do not take a position on the accuracy of these reports, nor do we question the right of any individual to consider future professional or public responsibilities," the staff members write, referring to press coverage of the rumours. "However, when such possibilities concern members of the Executive Board, and specifically the ECB President, they inevitably raise institutional questions."

In early February, the Financial Times, which also first reported on the letter, spread the news about a possible early departure by Lagarde before the end of her mandate in October 2027.

What she would like to do next is not certain, but she has floated some options herself, telling Euronews that she would like to play a role in French presidential election campaign – albeit not by standing as a candidate.

Another possibility is her taking the helm of the World Economic Forum, which the Wall Street Journal first reported in February.

Another board member, Isabel Schnabel, might depart before the end of her term, as she is in negotiation to take a senior role at the International Monetary Fund, the German outlet Handelsblatt reported in early September.

These rumours are circulating just as other ECB leaders prepare to depart on schedule. Among them is Chief Economist Philip Lane, whose mandate ends in May 2027.

"Prolonged uncertainty regarding the future of the institution's senior leadership can therefore affect trust in the ECB's communications, create concern among staff and stakeholders, and complicate the orderly planning of leadership succession and strategic priorities," the letter says.

The potential reshuffle also comes in a moment of high uncertainty for the eurozone.

The volatility of energy prices due to the ongoing wars in the Middle East and Ukraine are making the job hard for the ECB to keep inflation low. Last week, Lagarde announced an interest rate hike to keep inflation low, that the ECB's 2% inflation target will not be met by the end of 2027.

World.title: Spain's Supreme Court refuses to apply amnesty to Catalan leader Puigdemont
World.content:
Spain's Supreme Court has refused to apply amnesty to Puigdemont for the alleged offence of embezzlement in the "procés" case — Catalonia's independence movement, which peaked in the 2017 referendum and unilateral declaration of independence. The court is also keeping in force the national arrest warrant for Catalonia's former president.

 

Investigating judge Pablo Llarena, who is leading the case, has dismissed the request filed by Carles Puigdemont following the ruling by the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) on 16 July.

The court agreed with the Socialist-led government's argument that the 2024 amnesty law for Catalan separatists complies with EU legislation.

But Puigdemont, who headed Catalonia's regional government when it held a banned independence referendum and attempted to secede from Spain, was excluded on two grounds: that Puigdemont had intended to obtain personal financial gain, and that the events had harmed the EU's financial interests.

The EU court said granting amnesty for the misuse of funds did not undermine the bloc's financial interests.

However, Llarena maintains that the European ruling doesn't affect his other ground for excluding the amnesty: the alleged intent to obtain personal financial gain.

The ruling stresses that the new request isn't being rejected because the CJEU's interpretation is irrelevant, but because that interpretation doesn't reach the second argument underpinning his refusal to apply the amnesty.

Llarena also notes that Spain's Constitutional Court has not yet ruled on how the Amnesty Law should apply specifically in this case. Those rulings, he says, have neither overturned nor specifically endorsed his finding of personal financial gain — and he adds that he cannot predict the outcome of the appeals still pending before that court.

Puigdemont's arrest warrant remains in force

The defence had asked for the national arrest warrant to be withdrawn on the grounds that the case might be closed, that the amnesty should apply, or that pursuing the men twice for the same acts would be unlawful.

Having rejected all three grounds, Llarena finds no basis to lift the warrant either. He notes, though, that this doesn't rule out reviewing the measure in future if circumstances change, nor does refusing the amnesty by itself justify any tighter restriction.

Because the warrant is national in scope, Puigdemont and Comín can be arrested only if they enter Spanish territory.

Supreme Court refuses to transfer the case

Llarena also rejects requests to transfer the case to the High Court of Justice of Catalonia (Catalonia's own regional high court) or to courts in Barcelona.

He likewise dismisses the request to close the case on grounds of "non bis in idem" — the legal principle barring double punishment for the same act — which the defence argued applied because an accounting-liability case is already underway at Spain's Court of Audit.

As a result, Llarena maintains that the CJEU's ruling doesn't touch the argument he says still blocks the Amnesty Law from covering the embezzlement charges against them.

World.title: Two years after COP29, Azerbaijan turns climate commitments into investment
World.content:
Azerbaijan has committed up to 1 billion manat (€540 million) to climate-resilient irrigation infrastructure under its 2026-2030 state programme, as the country hosted a regional climate week two years after staging COP29 in Baku.

 

The figure, announced by Agriculture Minister Majnun Mammadov at Baku Climate Action Week, represents nearly 40% of the state agricultural budget earmarked for climate adaptation.

The funding will support modern irrigation systems across the South Caucasus, where water shortages, shifting growing seasons and soil degradation are accelerating.

Discussions held at the Baku Convention Centre within the framework of BCAW 2026 Euronews Baku Bureau, September 2026

The government also launched an AI-based farmer scoring system this year, developed in partnership with the UN Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO).

First piloted in 2024 and tested in 2025, the digital platform distributes advance subsidy payments to smallholder farmers managing between five and 100 hectares.

Mammadov said eligibility is assessed across three criteria: adoption of modern farming practices, the economic value of the chosen crop, and whether the farmer uses water-saving or soil-regenerating techniques.

"The scoring system evaluates three fundamental pillars," Mammadov told Euronews. "First, the adoption of modern agricultural practices, second, the economic value and profitability of the crop for the farmer and the wider economy."

"And third, ecological impact. How the selected crop interacts with soil health and whether the farmer utilises climate-supporting subsidies like soil-regenerating or water-saving techniques."

Smallholder farmers are the most exposed to climate volatility across the Caucasus, where minor shifts in temperature or water availability can destroy yields.

Mammadov said international investors in local farming infrastructure would receive the same subsidy access as domestic operators.

Majnun Mammadov, Minister of Agriculture of Azerbaijan and Mukhtar Babayev, Representative of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan for Climate Issues, COP29 President Euronews Baku Bureau, September 2026

"Agriculture is in a very unique position, it is causing climate change, and it is being affected by climate change," FAO Representative in Azerbaijan Nasar Hayat said.

'Opportunity to build'

Separately, the UN Industrial Development Organisation urged Azerbaijan to prioritise domestic industrial use of green hydrogen before pursuing European export ambitions.

Petra Schwager, chief of UNIDO's climate and technology partnership division, said pipeline exports to Europe would take years because the infrastructure does not yet exist.

In the short term, she said, green hydrogen derivatives such as green ammonia could be used in domestic fertiliser manufacturing and shipping fuels.

"The true benchmark of success for industrial decarbonisation is not policy pledges or technology partnerships, but verifiable CO2 emission reductions," Schwager said.

Ms Petra Schwager, Chief of Climate and Technology Partnership Division, United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO) Euronews Baku Bureau, September 2026

On financing, Turkey announced two new mechanisms ahead of COP31 in Antalya: BRIDGE, a technical support platform for developing countries to structure investment-ready projects, built alongside the UN Development Programme, and SURF, which adapts a Turkish municipal lending model to scale low-cost credit lines to cities across developing nations.

Fatma Varank, CEO of COP31 and Deputy Minister of Turkey's Ministry of Environment, Urbanisation and Climate Change, pointed to the long-term cooperation between host nations.

"Along our shared journey from Baku to Antalya, we have an opportunity to build on this foundation and achieve stronger outcomes by sharing experiences, deepening partnerships and channelling climate finance towards tangible implementation," Varank said.

Azerbaijan's Deputy Foreign Minister Yalchin Rafiyev confirmed that a Black Sea subsea cable project to carry renewable electricity from Azerbaijan and Central Asia to European markets remains a priority.

"Continuity between the COPs is extremely important in order to keep the legacy for the host country, but at the same time, globally it is very important," Rafiyev told Euronews.

Mr Yalchin Rafiyev, Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs, Republic of Azerbaijan, BCAW 2026 Azertag, September 2026

He said COP29's legacy had brought Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan forward with specific green grid proposals.

At COP29 in 2024, wealthier nations agreed to provide at least $300 billion (€258 billion) per year by 2035 to help developing countries cut emissions and manage climate impacts.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres said at the time the deal provided "a base on which to build" but fell short of what the crisis required.

According to Jens Nielsen, Founder and CEO of the World Climate Foundation, global climate diplomacy is undergoing a structural evolution, which is “changing from the politics of climate change to the economics of climate change."

"We need to move beyond commitments and action straight into bankable financial transactions," Nielsen told Euronews.

Baku Climate Action Week was held in parallel with the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change regional climate week for Eastern Europe, the Caucasus and Central Asia.

World.title: Erdogan hints at larger nuclear partnership with Russia, unsettling Turkey's allies
World.content:
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan is signalling a move to expand nuclear power cooperation with Russia, just as his country’s first Russian-built nuclear station prepares to go live later this year. The deepening partnership is likely to unsettle Turkey’s western allies.

Advertising

On the sidelines of a recent gathering of regional leaders in Kyrgyzstan, Erdogan told his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, that Russia and Turkey “will take steps together to open some new power plants, along with the opening of the Akkuyu nuclear power plant”.

The Akkuyu nuclear power plant, built by Russia’s state nuclear company Rosatom on Turkey's Mediterranean coast, is due to go online later this year.

Erdogan’s announcement comes amid strained ties with Russia, as the Turkish leader has deepened relations with United States President Donald Trump.

Ozgur Unluhisarcikli, head of the Ankara office of US think tank the German Marshall Fund, describes Erdogan’s move as a “gesture” to Putin.

“Although Turkey is competing with Russia geopolitically, and although Turkey is firmly anchored in NATO and is improving its relationship with the United States, it does not intend to sever all ties with Russia,” Unluhisarcikli explained.

“Indeed, Turkey sees the Turkey-Russia relationship as a long-term strategic one. And this is, by the way, consistent with Turkey's balancing act.”

Trump tests Turkey's energy dependence on Russia with lure of US power

Nuclear lifeline

For Ankara, nuclear energy promises to help it break free from its heavy reliance on imported power. Once operational, the Akkuyu plant in southern Turkey will supply as much as 10 percent of the country’s electricity.

Rosatom owns the Akkuyu power plant and will recoup the estimated €21.5 billion construction costs by selling electricity to Turkey, generating annual income of around €2-3 billion.

Such income could be a vital tool for Moscow to mitigate tightening sanctions by both the European Union and the United States.

“The Akkuyu nuclear power plant allows Russia to build itself various state-to-state payment channels to store liquidity in Turkish banks without necessarily interfering with any sanctions regulations,” according to George Voloshin of Acams, a global organisation dedicated to anti-financial crime, training and education.

Voloshin believes that, given the project's 60- to 80-year lifespan, Turkey’s commitment to Russian nuclear power will shape bilateral ties for the long term, with consequences.

“It will be a source of scrutiny from western partners of Turkey. At the same time, nuclear energy has been so far shielded from any sanctions, so for Russia it is clearly a kind of lifeline,” he said.

The Akkuyu plant, currently under construction, will be Turkey's first nuclear power station. © AFP/Dogan News Agency/Ibrahim Mese

Turkey seeks Black Sea shipping deal as attacks threaten grain trade

Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Ankara has maintained that it is not bound by EU or US sanctions on Moscow. Yet behind the scenes, it has quietly followed many restrictions and secured crucial waivers, especially for Russian gas.

By leveraging its pivotal location near Syria and Iran, Ankara has walked a diplomatic tightrope between its western partners and Moscow.

However, deepening nuclear cooperation with Russia threatens to complicate the already difficult balancing act.

“It would reinforce the already existing distrust between Turkey and Europe and Turkey and the United States,” warned Unluhisarcikli.

“But at the same time, Turkey is in talks with other countries, the United States and South Korea. These are the main two competitors for Russia.”

Mutual dependency

Turkey’s dependence on Russian fossil fuels has stirred unease at home, and the idea of doubling down with Russian nuclear energy only heightens the sense of anxiety. “It is a dilemma,” Unluhisarcikli conceded.

Yet with Russia willing to shoulder the hefty construction costs, cash-strapped Ankara has a strong incentive to continue the partnership.

Russia expert Zaur Gasimov of Istanbul’s Turkish-German University points out that more than a decade of joint investment makes it tough for Turkey to turn to alternative suppliers.

"It's quite a profound project,” said Gasimov, “Russia conducts the training of Turkish specialists in the field of nuclear energy, which started 15 years ago. We now have three or four waves of Turkish engineers who stayed for longer periods in Russia; they learn the Russian language for two years, and you have an infrastructure of specialists.”

However, Gasimov stresses that, given the scale of investment by both sides, it has created an important mutual dependency. “Its importance makes the two sides, somehow, at the end, interested in preserving a certain level of the relationship,” he said.

This shared reliance might help keep Turkish-Russian rivalries in check, from North Africa to the Middle East, the Caucasus and the Black Sea.

Yet any step toward deeper nuclear cooperation is bound to invite sharper scrutiny and rising suspicion from Ankara’s western allies.

World.title: Criticism of LGBTQ+ raids in Turkey is growing
World.content:
Several raids and arrests of LGBTQ+ persons in Turkey have triggered sharp criticism from numerous Turkish organizations — and also from Brussels.

Raids targeting LGBTQ+ activists and organizations took place in Turkey over the weekend. Several people were arrested by the Turkish authorities and many social media accounts were blocked. The Turkish government's actions have drawn sharp criticism from across the country and also from Brussels.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan had announced the operation as part of the "Decade of Family and Population” scheme, a national strategy proclaimed in May 2025 that was to counter the drastic decline in the country's birthrate and strengthen the traditional, conservative family view in Turkey.

On Tuesday, Istanbul saw demonstrations again. Turkish LGBTQ+ associations emphasized in a joint declaration that it wasn't a crime to set up an association and advocate for rights.

"Freedom of assembly, freedom of opinion, protection of privacy and presumption of innocence apply to LGBTQ+ people as well," the declaration stated.

The LGBTQ+ community also received support from the women's movement. 120 women's rights organizations signed a joint declaration in which they criticized authoritarianism in Turkey.

"As women, we stand against the operations carried out in the name of 'keeping the family safe.' We know that the repression of our bodies, our lives, our identities, and our right to organize is part of the same authoritarian politics. Being [LGBTQ+] is not a crime! Organizing as [LGBTQ+] people is not a crime!", the organizations stated.

'The aim is criminalization'

The government is trying to criminalize the LGBTQ+ community, says Yildiz Taghizade of Women for Women's Human Rights (WWHR), an organization that co-signed the declaration. This criminalization did not just start with the operations of the past few days, but had already been going on for a few years, according to Taghizade.

"The aim is not only to target LGBTQ+ people, but to practically ban the LGBTQ+ community from engaging in politics, getting organized, claiming rights and showing presence in the public sphere," Taghizade said.

It was no coincidence that the operation came with the slogan "My family is safe."

"The government is trying to justify its actions by invoking the protection of families and children, but this narrative doesn't work. Because when we look at Turkey today and what is actually a factor of uncertainty for families, we come across very concrete issues such as poverty, the housing crisis, unemployment, care work [caring for and tending to relatives, the ed.] passed on to women, and male violence against women," Taghizade said.

Criticism from medical community, trade associations, politicians

Other organizations also criticized the government's actions. The Turkish Medical Association (TTB) described them as a violation of human rights, demanding an end to the politics of discrimination. It was unacceptable, it said, to treat gender identity and sexual orientation as a crime, take people out of their homes at night and block digital channels — all in the name of family protection and security.

The chairman of the Workers' Party of Turkey (TIP), Erkan Bas, called for the immediate release of those arrested, arguing that the mere existence of LGBTQ+ persons was no crime.

But all those who did not share the government's views were "'called to order' by judiciary, truncheon and censorship. If they had their way, they'd love nothing more than to enshrine the criminal offense of 'being an opponent of the government' by law and sit back," Bas said.

According to human rights activists, the criminalization of the LGBTQ+ community in Turkey is nothing new Image: Murat Kocabas/Middle East Images/picture alliance

In the name of 'national security'

The raids took place on Sunday in Istanbul, Ankara and Izmir. Over the weekend, numerous websites and social media accounts belonging to LGBTQ+ groups, various organizations and activists were blocked. On the day of the raids, another 32 accounts were suspended. On the following day, the number of blocked accounts reached a total of more than 100.

Among those affected were Amnesty International Turkey, the left-leaning Evrensel newspaper, the Academics for Peace initiative, the Lawyers for Justice association, the women's rights organization Mor Dayanisma, the LGBTQ+ rights group Kaos GL and the Media and Law Studies Association (MLSA).

The legal basis was a ruling by an Istanbul court announced on September 13. The Public Prosecutor's Office in Bakirkoy justified the suspensions by citing investigations into accounts that had spread "obscene content and LGBTQ+ propaganda."

According to several media outlets, the accounts were also blocked on grounds of "national security."

Critics called the move digital censorship.

Homosexuality not a criminal offense

Homosexual relationships are not a criminal offense in Turkey. However, the Turkish government had repeatedly referred to the LGBTQ+ community as a movement of "perverts."

Justice Minister Akin Gurlek had previously accused LGBTQ+ organizations of "promoting immorality." He declared in a social media post that "no criminal organization, abuse network or illegal activity which targets children, youths or families will be tolerated."

EU: stigmatization incompatible with our values

The EU expressed concern as well.

Commission Spokesperson Christian Wigand pointed out that Turkey, as an EU accession candidate, "should promote and ensure respect for the human rights and dignity of all individuals, irrespective of their gender identity or sexual orientation." He added that "stigmatization and discrimination are contrary to the values of the union."

Emma Sinclair-Webb, Turkey director at Human Rights Watch, interpreted the arrests as proof of the government's intention to criminalize LGBTQ+ persons without enacting new laws.

This article was translated from German.

World.title: High fuel prices challenge the German government
World.content:
Chancellor Friedrich Merz wants to provide relief to motorists. But exactly how this is to happen remains unclear.

Gas stations in Germany are only allowed to raise their fuel prices once a day, at 12 noon. In Berlin, on the morning of September 15, E10 gasoline cost about €2.25 ($2.60) per liter and diesel about €2.37. At noon, prices rose by about €0.20 per liter. The highest prices were recorded at a highway gas station in southern Berlin, where Super Plus cost €3.03 per liter.

Drivers are angry. While it's possible to use public transportation in large cities, residents of rural areas have hardly any realistic alternative to driving. Those living in regions near national borders have an advantage. On September 7, filling up a 60-liter tank with E10 gasoline cost about €31 less in the Czech Republic and Poland than in Germany. In Luxembourg, the difference was €28, and in Austria, €25. These figures were calculated by the Federal Statistical Office.

Germany has nine neighboring countries. Gasoline is significantly cheaper in seven of them, and diesel is cheaper in six. Only in the Netherlands and Denmark do drivers have to pay more for fuel than in Germany.

German government expresses 'great and growing' concern

But relief is in sight. That's what Chancellor Friedrich Merz(CDU) has promised.

"Many people who need their cars every day have reached their breaking point," Merz said Tuesday at an event hosted by the German Foreign Trade Association (BGA) in Berlin. "I believe we must take action."

However, the chancellor added that the "exact measures" have not yet been determined.

"We are therefore in close dialogue within the federal government and with the German states." A proposal will be announced "very soon," Merz said.

But what might that look like? On Monday (Sept. 14) in Berlin, deputy government spokesperson Steffen Meyer rejected any government responsibility for the high prices.

"It's not the actions of the federal government or anything like that causing prices to rise so sharply. Rather, it's largely due to the escalating situation in the Middle East, attacks on oil pipelines and the blockade of shipping lanes," Meyer said.

The fact is, however, that Germany imposes higher taxes and levies on fuels. The ADAC automobile club has pointed out that while the oil price remains below previous peaks, E10 gasoline is more expensive than ever before.

"From the ADAC's perspective, there is therefore a need to provide greater clarity, especially regarding refinery and wholesale markets," said an ADAC spokeswoman.

Donald Trump blames Ukraine for record US diesel prices To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Price gouging at the pumps

Herbert Rabl of the Gas Station Interest Group (TIV) puts it more bluntly.

"They're raking it in. The oil companies aren't cutting into their profit margins at all," Rabl told the Rheinische Post newspaper.

He said that this is an issue that has long been the subject of political debate, but that the federal government remains divided on what, if anything, can be done about it.

However, the problem that the conservative bloc of Christian Democratic Union/Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) face as coalition partners is that the state coffers are empty, and the federal government cannot cover its budget shortfall without taking on a historically high level of new debt.

"Ultimately, the only way to bring these prices down is to end the hostilities and ensure the freedom of navigation," said spokesperson Meyer.

A new fuel rebate or tax relief?

Faced with rising oil prices that followed the outbreak of the war on Iran, the German government introduced a fuel rebate in the spring. From May 1 through June 30, 2026, the energy tax on gasoline and diesel was temporarily reduced. Factoring in value-added tax, this was expected to lower fuel prices by about €0.17 per liter.

"We had a fuel rebate; we subsidized prices," Federal Economy Minister Katherina Reiche (CDU) told the n-tv network.

But she says that won't be possible again: "Together, we in the coalition have decided that we don't have the financial scope for that at the moment."

As an alternative, the conservatives are exploring the possibility of at least providing tax relief for commuters or supporting low-income earners with direct payments.

But that's not enough for the SPD. It is proposing a completely different approach and, as it did shortly after the outbreak of the Iran war, is advocating for a government-imposed cap on fuel prices. One of the ways they plan to finance this relief is through an excess profit tax on energy companies. In addition, the SPD supports a temporary reduction in energy taxes to deal with crisis situations. Their goal is an immediate price reduction at the gas pump.

Saudi oil pipeline attack could raise global gas prices To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

AfD standing to profit from bickering

But while the federal government continues to debate and weigh its options amid internal disagreements, other parties feel time is running out. Regional elections will be held in two states on September 20.

In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, SPD Premier Manuela Schwesig is fighting to stave off a win for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD). In the latest polls, the AfD was in the lead with 38%, while the SPD has recently gained ground, and is now polling at 34%.

The AfD wants to drastically lower fuel prices by abolishing the CO₂ tax on fossil fuels and reducing the energy tax to the European minimum. It also proposes lowering the German value-added tax on gasoline and diesel from 19% to 7%.

"There is the option of introducing a fuel cap and, at the same time, an excess profit tax, as in Luxembourg," Schwesig said on Monday (Sept. 14) in Schwerin.

She criticized the federal government's inaction: "The chancellor is just allowing this to drag on, and that is causing frustration."

A solution from the EU?

According to the SPD-led Federal Finance Ministry, Minister Lars Klingbeil will "strongly push" for the introduction of an excess profits tax at a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin this coming Friday.

Officials in Berlin point out that an excess profits tax is currently being discussed at the European level.

"Large member states such as Spain and Poland are on our side," said a spokesperson for the finance ministry on Monday (Sept. 14) in Berlin.

"Such an excess profits tax would be one way to use the excessive profits that oil companies are reaping during this crisis — by fleecing consumers and imposing excessive price hikes — to provide targeted relief for the people who are particularly affected by these high gas prices," he added.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Knobloch: 'It is a very dangerous situation at the moment'
World.content:
Charlotte Knobloch survived the Holocaust by passing as the daughter of non-Jewish farmers. She recently spoke with DW to express her shock following the AfD victory in Saxony-Anhalt's state election.

Charlotte Knobloch, president of the Jewish Community of Munich and Upper Bavaria, is dismayed by the electoral victory of the nationalist Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in the Saxony-Anhalt state election. Knobloch told DW that there were now once again a number of Jewish people who, in the wake of such events, were considering leaving Germany.

It took decades, Knobloch said, for Jews in Germany to regain trust in the country after the Holocaust. That had ultimately been achieved.

But now, there were great fears again: "That is, in sum, the biggest problem for me, because we successfully tried to rebuild the Jewish communities after 1945, to give the Jewish people a home again, which they hadn't had for a long time..."

AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund's (center) party received nearly 44% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt Image: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

Standing up against the far-right 'requires some courage'

In Saxony-Anhalt's September 6 state election, the AfD, classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" by the state's Office for the Protection of the Constitution, had received almost 44% of the vote. Although AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund fell short of an absolute majority, he still has a good chance of becoming the next premier in the state parliament, meaning he'd become the first head of a state government from a right-wing extremist party after World War II.

Charlotte Knobloch issues a stark warning: "We can't allow any of those people to become state premier. It is a very dangerous situation at the moment, in my view. I hope the other parties realize that and stand up against it. They can do it. It requires some courage of course."

The nonagenarian, seen here with Chancellor Friedrich Merz, is still present in Germany's public life Image: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

Charlotte Knobloch, who is almost 94 years old, is one of the most prominent and well-known representatives of Jewish life in Germany and one of the last surviving witnesses of Nazi dictatorship between 1933 and 1945. Born in 1932, she was initially raised by her grandmother, who was deported to the Theresienstadt concentration camp in 1942 and died there. A family acquaintance saved the girl by accommodating her on her farm in Middle Franconia and passing her off as her own child.

Knobloch: 'danger looming' today did not exist like this 10 years ago

Asked by DW when and how she still thinks about that horrible era, she said: "There were times when this happened only rarely. When it was mentioned by the media from time to time, but not permanently. These days, I wake up thinking about it, and I also go to bed thinking about it."

Knobloch spoke to DW correspondent Tina Gerhäusser in Munich Image: DW

Knobloch served as vice president of the World Jewish Congress between 2005 and 2013, and as president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany from 2006 to 2010. For a long time, she has been warning against growing antisemitism in Germany. However, she herself did not foresee the rise of far-right extremist parties like the AfD.

"There's a danger looming that did not exist in this form ten years ago," Knobloch said. "There have always been Nazis, there have always been Jew haters, but not in the way as it's the case today."

In Knobloch's view, the established parties have up to now failed to speak out decisively against the AfD: "Today's political parties must jointly, not alone, address the issue. I still see a chance here, that people will at least be willing to listen and discuss it. And that's very, very important."

Young people need to be included in the conversation

Politicians have to speak to young people in particular more intensively and address their fears, which isn't happening enough, Knobloch says.

"There's talk about it, but there is no real discussion, because young people are naturally afraid that what they say will become public. What I want to say is, we'll have to find ways to bring young people back into the fold."

Last week, Knobloch received death threats. On Thursday, a witness discovered the scrawled threats on a park bench and a rubbish bin in the English Garden in Munich and informed the police, according to a police headquarters statement. Knobloch subsequently canceled her attendance at an event. The threats were directly linked to the AfD's election victory in Saxony-Anhalt, a spokeswoman said in response to a query from the dpa news agency.

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: South Africa now probing deaths of 8 women near Johannesburg
World.content:
Police have warned women to take extra care in parts of Johannesburg as similarities between at least eight deaths fuel fears that the cases could be connected.

South African police are now investigating the deaths of eight women found east of Johannesburg over the past two months, after another body was discovered on Tuesday and an earlier case was added to the widening investigation.

The deaths have raised fears that a serial killer or group of killers could be operating in the area. Several of the victims were found naked or partially clothed, with some showing signs of sexual violence.

"The challenge is ahead of us and the deaths of these young women must not be in vain," acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia told reporters following a meeting to discuss the killings.

What have South African police said?

The South African Police Service (SAPS) has issued a public warning urging women to exercise caution when jogging or carrying out similar activities in the area.

"While investigations are still underway and SAPS has not, at this stage, confirmed that the deaths are linked to a serial killer, the similarities are sufficiently concerning for the police to issue a public warning and intensify investigations," police spokesperson Athlenda Mathe said.

President Cyril Ramaphosa on Tuesday ordered police to prioritize the investigations, saying the deaths were causing "fear and uncertainty" and promising that "no stone will be left unturned."

What do we know about the victims?

The bodies have been discovered at several locations across the Ekurhuleni municipality, east of Johannesburg.

Police said the first victim, a 37-year-old woman, was found naked and bound with cable ties on July 15. A suspect was arrested two days later.

A 32-year-old woman was found partially clothed on August 24. Another woman's body, found in a river near the Tembisa township on September 7, has now been included in the wider investigation.

One of the victims, aged 38, disappeared after leaving her eight-year-old daughter at home to go jogging. Her partially clothed body was found behind a hotel on September 12.

Another woman's body was discovered in the Kwa-Thema township on Tuesday.

Why are women still unsafe in South Africa? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Are South African police investigating a serial killer?

Police have not confirmed that the deaths are the work of a serial killer.

"We are still investigating whether we are dealing with one perpetrator or a group of men that are behind the murders of these women," police spokesperson Athlenda Mathe said.

Police said similarities between the cases were sufficiently concerning to issue a public warning, including advising women to exercise caution while jogging in the area.

How serious is violence against women in South Africa?

Violence against women is a longstanding problem in South Africa. UN Women says the country has some of the world's highest rates of violence against women and children.

Around one in three South African women experience physical or sexual violence during their lifetime, according to the United Nations.

The killings come as violent crime remains a major source of public concern ahead of municipal elections in November.

Edited by: Kieran Burke

World.title: Why do authoritarian regimes target the LGBTQ+ community?
World.content:
A recent crackdown on the LGBTQ+ community in Turkey is symptomatic of a wider rights regression, according to experts. It's worse under authoritarian regimes, but why is it such a popular policy for these states?

Raids on gay bars and homes, hundreds of arrests and rhetoric about state responsibility to "protect families and children." Turkey's latest crackdown on LGBTQ+ communities is not such an outlier.

"It's not uncommon, we've seen it before," Dr Koen Slootmaeckers, from the international politics department at City St George's, University of London, told DW.

"Turkey's been doing this for a while, but it seems like a much higher intensity," Slootmaeckers said. "We've seen it in different places too. I think what we are seeing with the rise of the far right is a crackdown on anything that looks different. It's really about an us versus them narrative and a reinforcing of 'traditional family values.'"

Those values were cited by Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek after the weekend's crackdown: "As per the duty to protect families and children given to the state by the constitution, no criminal organization, abuse network or illegal activity which targets children, youths or families will be tolerated!"

Attack on LGBTQ+ rights accelerating

The reference to protecting children from harm is also typical of authoritarian government actions against LGBTQ+ communities on a wider scale, added Slootmaeckers, whose work often focuses on gender and sexuality policy.

Slovakia debates marriage equality To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"They're trying to bring back discourses around paedophilia and homosexuality being intertwined. It's not always direct but there is a definite tendency."

Sentiments such as those expressed by Gurlek have become increasingly normalized of late, according to a 2026 report from South Africa-based civil rights nonprofit, Civicus.

"Women's and LGBTQI+ people's rights are under the most coordinated and wide-ranging attack in decades," the report reads.

It adds that "The USA has set the global narrative" under President Donald Trump and points to the recent criminalizing of same sex relationships in Burkina Faso and Trinidad and Tobago among its evidence of rights regressions.

While the methods of oppression vary, Slootmaeckers said the underlying reasons are often, at least partly, opportunistic rather than ideological.

Scapegoating a common strategy

"In authoritarian regimes, as we've seen in Hungary and Poland in the past, there is often a tendency when political power becomes threatened to use these issues as an easy way to scapegoat and distract — by claiming that LGBT people are a threat to the social fabric because they challenge family and the future of the nation, so to speak. It's an easy way of creating a scapegoat and often distracting from other crises," he said.

Turkey was ranked 47 of 49 countries in the annual Rainbow Map compiled by the International Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trans and Intersex Association. Countries ranking lower means laws and polcies there aren't LGBTQ+ friendly.

But, for many observers it is countries that are dropping in such rankings that are troubling. One of those is Serbia. It has gradually slipped to 29th spot, below the European average.

Groups associated with President Aleksandar Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, have been linked to a wave of violence against an LGBTQ+ community which feels increasingly marginalized. A recent survey from the European Union Agency for Fundamental Rights found that 80% of respondents said they avoided holding the hand of their partner in public, for example.

EU hopes put up 'guardrails' amid violence in Serbia

While Serbia is not one of the 64 countries around the world which have laws that criminalize homosexuality, some of which carry the death penalty, there is a definite sense of unease.

"In the Balkans, most countries still want to join the EU, so there ar some kind of guardrails on how far they can go. But we see things like [Vucic] trying to cancel [pan-European LGBTQ+ event] EuroPride in 2022 in Belgrade when he felt threatened surrounding Kosovo," said Slootmaeckers, who wrote a book called "Coming in: Sexual politics and EU accession in Serbia" in 2025.

Will Hungary's new govt. bring real change on LGBTQ+ rights? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"We can see this tactic of pandering to family values and then positioning LGBT rights as an expensive frivolity, as a means of redirecting the attention of people from the actual political problem," Slootmaeckers said.

"I think across Europe, not just in the Balkans or Eastern Europe, we see the return of homophobia and transphobia. We see a culture where anything considered 'out there' is threatened and it becomes normalized that we can exclude people again."

Exclusion appears to be the word for many in the Turkish LGBTQ+ community, with rights group Kaos GL, whose offices were raided, calling the latest crackdown "state-led discrimination, politics of fear and the dismantling of civil society."

For those living under authoritarian regimes elsewhere, the threat of similar scenes continues to loom.

Edited by: Carla Bleiker

World.title: Russia: Trump's Ukraine ceasefire proposal is 'good idea'
World.content:
The Kremlin has hailed an "energy ceasefire" proposed by US President Trump, but has criticized a French initiative to share its nuclear deterrent. Meanwhile, hostilities have continued on the ground and in the air.

The Russian government has welcomed United States President Donald Trump's suggestion that Russia and Ukraine should cease mutual attacks on each other's energy infrastructure.

"We consider this to be a very good idea overall," said Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov on Tuesday, describing the proposal as an "energy ceasefire."

Peskov did not say whether the Kremlin would agree to such a proposal, insisting only that, in addition to no more Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, Russia must also be allowed to export its oil unhindered.

"It is necessary to ensure safe commercial shipping and navigation here, including for oil tankers," he said adding that Russia would stay in touch with Washington.

Ukraine 'energy ceasefire': What has Trump claimed?

US President Trump claimed on social media on Monday evening that both Ukraine and Russia had "agreed" not to strike "energy targets" – although Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy spoke only of a "strong US proposal" for a "mutual halt" to strikes on critical infrastructure.

"If this can become the first de-escalatory step — a step toward ending Russian strikes on our critical infrastructure and our strikes in response — then Ukraine is ready to support de-escalation," he said in his daily evening address.

"If our American partners can ensure that Russia is genuinely ready to stop this war aimed at destroying life — and to do so for real and for the long term Ukraine will take its own de-escalatory steps."

Russia, Ukraine exchange drone strikes

Meanwhile, Russia launched 200 more drones Ukrainian cities overnight, killing two people – one in the capital, Kyiv, and another in the southern city of Zaporizhzhia.

In addition to petrol stations in the capital, energy and port infrastructure in other regions were also hit, Ukrainian officials said.

In response, President Zelenskyy said Ukraine had struck an oil refinery in Syzran in Russia's Samara region on the Volga River, as well as drone production ​facilities in the Taganrog and Oryol regions.

"Russia continues to attack our energy sector, regular logistics ​and critical infrastructure," Zelenskyy said on social media. "our responses to them for this are tangible."

Ukraine claims successful ground offensive

Meanwhile, on the frontline in eastern Ukraine, Ukrainian forces have reportedly liberated more than 10 square kilometers of occupied territory and "cleaned up" a further 75 square kilometers which had been infiltrated by Russian troops north of the town of Lyman in the Donetsk region.

The offensive, which has reportedly been underway for several days, is aimed at relieving pressure on the nearby cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk — key fortified locations in Ukraine's so-called "fortress belt."

Russia slams French nuclear initiative

Also on Tuesday, Russia criticized a French security initiative to bring European countries under its nuclear umbrella.

"Of course, this is creating risks for us," foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told reporters. "And of course, we must control it."

France, the only nuclear power in the European Union, has proposed allowing participating allies to temporarily host nuclear-armed French aircraft in an effort to boost Europe's nuclear deterrent.

Paris would retain national control over its nuclear arsenal, with the final decision on its use remaining with the French president.

Finland this week became the tenth country to join the plan, which already included Belgium, Denmark, Germany, Greece, the Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Sweden and the United Kingdom – with the latter's own nuclear arsenal dependent to a large degree on US technical support.

Estonia is also "in discussions" about joining, Prime Minister Kristen Michal told the AFP news agency earlier this week.

"We would describe this French initiative, to put it mildly and in very diplomatic terms, as reckless," said Zakharova.

World.title: Ovechkin still backing Putin party in parliamentary vote
World.content:
Ice hockey legend Alexander Ovechkin has lent Vladimir Putin's party a helping hand in its parliamentary election campaign. That's in keeping with a pattern of support by an athlete who claims not to be political.

When Russia's parliamentary elections are held from September 18 to 20, Alexander Ovechkin won't be there to cast his ballot in person. On Monday he took his first few strides back on the ice in the United States as he starts gearing up for a new National Hockey League (NHL) season with the Washington Capitals, his 22nd in the world's best league.

Before leaving his homeland, where he spent his summer break, he did make his contribution to the election campaign, however, appearing in a video promoting the ruling United Russia party, which steadfastly supports President Vladimir Putin.

In the video, which has been widely shared on social media, Ovechkin doesn't speak but can be clearly seen in the third row of a group of supporters behind Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, who is heading the United Russia list for the parliamentary vote.

Ovechkin's appearance has faced criticism, including from Ukrainian skeleton pilot Vladyslav Heraskevych, who was disqualified from the 2026 Olympic Games for insisting on wearing a helmet depicting athletes killed in Russia's war in Ukraine.

Ovechkin a long-standing Putin supporter

This is certainly not the first time that Ovechkin has expressed his support for Putin, with whom he shares his profile photo on his Instagram account.

Ovechkin's Instagram account features a profile photo of him with Putin Image: @aleksandrovechkinofficial/instagram

And, at times, Ovechkin's public support has appeared even more active than in the current United Russia video. Back in 2017, Ovechkin used his Instagram account to announce the creation of "PutinTeam" a group to help support Putin in the 2018 presidential campaign.

"I have never hidden my feelings about our president; I have always openly supported him. I am certain there are many of us who support Vladimir Putin! So let's unite and show the world a strong, united Russia!" he wrote.

"Being part of such a team is a source of pride for me; it feels just like pulling on the Russian national team jersey, knowing the whole country is rooting for you."

The creation of PutinTeam came three years after Russia had invaded and seized the Ukrainian territory Crimea in 2014, a move that was met with widespread condemnation in the international community. Later that year, Ovechkin appeared to express support for the operation, posting a photo of himself on Instagram holding up a sign with the message: "#savechildrenfromfascism."

"Our grandfathers and grandmothers witnessed all the horrors of fascism! We will not let it happen in our time," he wrote.

Putin has painted the Ukrainian authorities as "neo-Nazi" or fascist, in particular when justifying Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, launched in February 2022. What Putin calls a "special military operation" raised questions in the minds of many about how this might affect Ovechkin's view of the man he had always so publicly supported.

On February 25, 2022, a day after Russia launched the invasion, a reporter covering the Washington Capitals asked Ovechkin if he still supported Putin.

"Well, he's my president," Ovechkin replied. "But how I said, I'm not in politics, I'm an athlete."

He did issue a vague appeal for peace but declined to criticize Moscow's military action.

"Please, no more war. It doesn't matter who's in the war — Russia, Ukraine, different countries," he said.

Back on the ice with the Capitals

Whatever you may think of his political views, Ovechkin is without a doubt one of the best players to ever lace on a pair of skates.

Now, back on the ice in Arlington, Virginia, ahead of the Washington Capitals' training camp, "Great8" is focused on getting his aging body (he turns 41 on Thursday) ready to compete for what would be a second Stanley Cup for both him and the Caps.

For much of the offseason, Ovechkin had left open whether he would return for another year. After all, he has achieved just about everything you can in the NHL, having broken Wayne Gretzky's career goal-scoring record two seasons ago. Going into the 2025-26 campaign he has 929 goals in 1,573 regular season games. In July though, after a conversation with his wife, he decided to come back for one more year in Washington – and he hasn't ruled out extending his career beyond that.

Over 40 and still going strong

"I'm going to be 41. I've had a lot of pressure on my shoulders over the years," he said. "I'm going to focus on the game and helping my team to win," he told reporters after his first skate. "I'm still a good player and can still help the team to win."

His numbers support that last assertion, having scored 32 goals in 2025-26. Only two other players have ever scored more over the age of 40.

"I can't wait for the season," he said. "On paper, you can see our team is one of the best teams but now we have to work for the Stanley Cup."

The bookies disagree, however, with some putting the Capitals way down at 18 (of 32) on their list of Stanley Cup candidates for 2027.

On the other hand, the prospect of United Russia's winning this weekend's parliamentary elections, the first since the launch of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, appears a safe bet.

Edited by: Jonathan Harding

World.title: Spanish scientists find first evidence of Diplodocus dinosaur in Europe
World.content:
Paleontologists in Spain say they have found the first evidence of the long-necked Diplodocus genus of dinosaur outside of North America. They found bones at the rich La Tejeria fossil site in Teruel in eastern Spain.

Researchers writing in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology this week said they found the first skeletal evidence of the Diplodocus dinosaur outside of North America, uncovering various vertebrae and chevron bones dating back around 150 million years at a site in eastern Spain.

The team from the Dinopolis Foundation in Teruel, studying the rich La Tejeria fossil site in the El Castellar municipality, said the dinosaur joined a growing list of giant sauropods found in the area.

Although the long-necked herbivore with its vast tail is one of the world's most recognizable dinosaurs, fossilized remains had until this point only been recovered in North America.

Dinosaurs like the Diplodocus and Stegosaurus were once thought to have lived exclusively on the North American continent but more and more evidence to the contrary is now being unearthed Image: Andia.fr/imageBROKER/picture alliance

What did the researchers say about the find?

The paper published on Monday concluded that the find was "one of the most complete diplodocid skeletons from Europe."

It said that systematic study and analysis of 14 caudal vertebrae and several chevron bones "reveals that it can be confidently referred to as Diplodocus," one of several genuses in the diplodocid family of sauropod dinosaurs.

"This discovery consists of the first evidence of Diplodocus outside North America (Morrison Formation) and is one of the strongest piece of evidence that supports the exchange of continental faunas between North America and Europe during the Late Jurassic," the authors wrote.

Although the diplodocus is well known worldwide, not least thanks to the famous skeletal cast nicknamed "Dippy" that for years greeted visitors entering the British Natural History Museum, the researchers said that the "European diplodocid fossil record is scarce and fragmentary."

How could dinosaurs cross an ocean?

During the time of the dinosaurs the continents were only just starting to drift apart. In recent decades scientists have begun to theorize that the proto-Atlantic Ocean still had ephemeral land bridges or episodic sea regressions or some other temporary means of crossing that occasionally enabled land-based dinosaurs to move vast distances between the separating continents.

Recent fossil finds, not least in Spain and Portugal near the Atlantic coast, have been further reinforcing this notion. This is part of a land bridge thought to have connected Iberia to what's now Canada.

The authors said the find "constitutes one of the strongest pieces of evidence of episodic dispersal events and faunal exchanges across the proto-North Atlantic Ocean during the late Kimmeridgian–early Tithonian" period, approximated 150 million years ago.

Another route linked North America with Scandinavia, and one much further south connected what's now Brazil to Cameroon.
