One explains what to do when an evacuation order is issued, while the other covers what should be included in an emergency kit. A moose wandered onto the tracks at Warsaw Central Station on Sunday evening, disrupting rail services in the Polish capital for more than 80 minutes before it was safely removed. The animal first appeared on a platform before moving onto the tracks, forcing Polish Railway Lines (PLK), the company responsible for Poland’s rail infrastructure, to suspend, cancel and divert several train services. View this post on Instagram A post shared by TVP3 Warszawa (@tvp3warszawa) Videos and photographs shared online showed the moose lying on the tracks and running along the railway line at Warsaw Central, the capital’s busiest station, which is mainly underground and therefore not easy for such a large animal to access. Police do not know how the moose ended up at the station, reports broadcaster TVN24. Officers were first alerted at 7:10 pm on Sunday and cordoned off the platform where the animal was located. When emergency services arrived, the moose was tranquilised. It was then placed on a large sheet and carried out of the station by police officers and emergency workers before being loaded onto a specialist vehicle to be returned to a forested area. PLK, which named the moose Emil, later confirmed that the animal had been safely removed and that normal train services were being restored. The company added that the disruptions lasted just over 80 minutes, using a pun combining the Polish words for moose (łoś) and 80 (osiemdziesiąt) to produce the word “łosiemdziesiąt”. ❗Aktualizacja❗Zwierze zostało bezpiecznie zabrane z torów. Przywracana jest rozkładowa organizacja ruchu pociągów. Utrudnienia trwały przeszło łosiemdziesiąt minut. https://t.co/Xui2B6SxyU — PLK SA (@PKP_PLK_SA) September 13, 2026 The Eurasian moose (also known as the Eurasian elk) has long been native to Poland, but by the mid-20th century hunting and habitat loss had brought the species close to extinction in the country. Its population subsequently recovered, reaching an estimated 6,000 animals by the 1980s and around 30,000 by 2019, helped by a moratorium on moose hunting introduced in 2001. Several hundred live in the Kampinos national park on the northwestern outskirts of Warsaw. They are therefore relatively frequent visitors to the capital, according to the Interia news website, although venturing onto train lines in the centre is unusual. The growth in the moose population, combined with urban expansion and changes to its habitat, has led to other high-profile encounters in areas inhabited by humans. In 2022, a moose was spotted on the roof of a shopping centre in the northern Polish city of Elbląg. A moose was this morning spotted on the roof of a shopping centre in Poland. World.title: Poland issued EU’s third most residence permits to immigrants in 2025
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland issued first residence permits to almost half a million immigrants in 2025, which was the third-highest figure in the European Union, behind Spain and Germany but ahead of Italy and France. However, the number of permits issued by Poland fell for the fourth year running, as the country continued to tighten its migration rules. Previously, between 2017 and 2022, Poland had led the EU figures for six years running, reaching a peak of almost one million permits in 2021. The new data, released on Friday by Eurostat, the EU’s statistical agency, show that Poland issued 467,314 first residence permits to immigrants from outside the EU in 2025. As was the case last year, Spain (635,438) issued the most, followed by Germany (605,292). Poland was then followed by Italy (433,099) and France (377,462). However, whereas in those four other countries the number of permits rose in 2025 (by 13.1% in Spain, 11.1% in Germany, 25.0% in Italy and 9.2% in France), in Poland the figure fell by 4.4%. That decline has come amid a tougher new migration strategy by the current government, a coalition that ranges from left to centre right, led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk. Ahead of elections in 2023, Tusk, then in opposition, accused the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which had ruled Poland since 2015, of allowing “uncontrolled” migration, including through widespread abuses of the visa system. Shortly after coming to power in those elections, Tusk, a former president of the European Council, declared that the “survival of Western civilisation” depends upon preventing mass migration. His government has since introduced tougher entry requirements for foreign workers and students, suspended asylum rights for migrants who irregularly cross the border from Belarus, and stepped up deportations of immigrants who have committed crimes or entered the country unlawfully. Poland has introduced tougher new rules regulating the entry of foreign students and immigrant workers. “This is another step towards regaining control over migration and increasing the safety of Poles," says the government https://t.co/gYdikpc6pL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 2, 2025 The new 2025 data show that, in relative terms (the number of permits issued in relation to countries’ populations), Poland was only ninth in the EU (12.8 permits per 1,000 people), behind Malta (56.9), Cyprus (46.7), Portugal (27.3), Lithuania (18.5), Ireland (13.4), Croatia (13.2), Luxembourg (13.1) and Spain (12.9). That marks a significant decline since 2021, when Poland issued 967,345 permits, which was the highest in the EU in absolute terms but also second-highest in relation to population. In 2025, as in previous years, Poland issued the most first residence permits to Ukrainians (241,126, 51.6% of the total), who are by far the country’s largest immigrant group. They were followed by Belarusians (128,468, 27.5%), Georgians (10,249, 2.2%), Indians (9,230, 2%) and Turks (7,533, 1.6%) – the same top five nationalities as in 2024. Indians are now the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, followed by Colombians, according to new data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Ukrainians remain by far the largest immigrant group, followed by Belarusians https://t.co/hNiOqmeUfX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2026 Following a decade of unprecedented mass migration, the number of foreigners with residence permits in Poland this year passed two million for the first time, making up just over 5% of the country’s population. Around 1.5 million of those are Ukrainians. In June, the number of foreigners working in Poland reached 1.14 million, making up almost 7% of the workforce. While Ukrainians constitute two thirds of the total, the fastest-growing nationalities are Colombians and Indians, who are now the third- and fourth-largest groups of foreign workers. The rise in migration has come as Poland’s economy has boomed but the country has also faced a demographic crisis, with a shrinking, ageing population and one of the lowest birth rates in the world. In 2023, the state Social Insurance Institution (ZUS) calculated that, in order to maintain its ratio of working-age population to retirees, Poland would need to attract almost two million immigrant workers over the following decade. However, it admitted that that target was “unrealistic”. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has warned that the Central European Visegrád Group (V4) would seek to block any European Union climate policies that push up energy prices. Speaking after a meeting with the leaders of the other V4 countries, Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic, Tusk said that they could not accept policies that further weakened competitiveness at a time when they were already facing high electricity costs. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk w #Bratysława ⤵️ Polska i grupa #V4 nie pozwoli na żadne zmiany i na żadne propozycje instytucji europejskich, czy innych państw, które mogłyby wpłynąć na pogorszenie sytuacji energetycznej w naszych państwach. Ceny energii w tym regionie muszą spaść. pic.twitter.com/BFnRx8Clse — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) September 10, 2026 In recent months, Poland and some other member states have been pushing for a softening of the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS), a cap-and-trade scheme launched in 2005 that makes polluters pay for carbon emissions in sectors such as power generation and heavy industry. They have also secured a postponement of the introduction of ETS2, which will cover emissions from road transport and buildings. “Whether we are talking about ETS1, ETS2, or other proposals, anything that brings a risk of more expensive energy for us will be blocked by us,” said Tusk on Thursday at a press conference alongside the other V4 prime ministers, as well as Ireland’s Micheál Martin. “Poland and the V4 will not allow any changes or any proposals from European institutions or other countries that could worsen the energy situation in our countries,” he added. “Energy prices in this region, including in Poland, must fall.” Poland has recorded the EU's third-fastest rise in household electricity prices this year. The country now also has the bloc’s second-most-expensive electricity, when taking cost of living into account https://t.co/WNLdCfOP16 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 30, 2025 Tusk argued that high energy prices pose a threat not only to Central European economies but also to the competitiveness of the EU as a whole. “We can forget about any dreams of competing with China or the United States if our energy prices remain as they are right now,” warned Tusk. Slovakian Prime Minister Robert Fico likewise said the V4 countries were united in their approach to the emissions trading system. “We will be very active, and we will also engage in discussions outside the meetings of the European Council and the Council of Europe to discuss what steps to take to bring down these energy prices,” he said. Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš also expressed frustration with rising energy costs. “All of us in our industrial region pay a lot of money for emissions allowances. And what did the commission tell us in 2020? That the price of this allowance in 2030 will be €26.50. Right now, it’s €80,” he said. According to the Eurostat data, households in Poland paid €27.09 per 100 kilowatt-hours (kWh), including taxes and levies, for electricity in the second half of 2025. That was the 11th highest figure in the EU and below the figure of €28.96 across the bloc as a whole. However, when adjusted for purchasing power standards (PPS), which account for differences in costs of living, Polish households faced the second-highest electricity prices in the EU, at 37.15 PPS per 100 kWh, behind only Romania (49.52 PPS) and the Czech Republic (39.16 PPS). The effects of ETS on electricity bills has moved to the centre of political debate this year after the main opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), called for Poland to unilaterally withdraw from the system, saying it makes “Poles a cash machine for the EU’s absurd leftist climate policy”. The opposition-aligned conservative president, Karol Nawrocki, has also twice sought to call national referendums on rejecting EU climate policies, including ETS, arguing they are too expensive. Both his efforts were rejected by the government’s majority in parliament. While the government has rejected the idea of withdrawing from ETS – which it says would result in large, ongoing fines being levied against Poland – it has pushed for reforms to the system. In July, the European Commission outlined proposals to soften ETS in response to pressure from countries such as Poland, allowing industries to continue emitting CO2 for longer while providing more financial support for investment in clean technologies. Yet there are also a number of other EU member states that argue against weakening ETS, saying it would penalise those who moved early to cut emissions. Poland's right-wing opposition wants to withdraw from the EU Emissions Trading System, saying it makes Poles "a cash machine for absurd leftist climate policies"@PStrzalkowski explains what costs ETS really brings, and what prospects there are for reform https://t.co/UxpMWpG1pE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 4, 2026 Just before the European Commission unveiled its proposal in July, Poland’s climate minister, Paulina Hennig-Kloska, said she had assembled a coalition of 10 countries calling for ETS reform and a more realistic emissions-reduction path. They also want ETS funding mechanisms to account for national differences, including energy mixes and GDP per capita, to ensure a fairer transition for lower-income countries starting from a more challenging position. Poland, for example, has a historical reliance on coal, which it still uses to produce around half of its electricity, helping make it one of the EU’s biggest emitters. Renewables generated 29.4% of Poland's electricity in 2025, almost exactly the same figure as in 2024, ending a period of strong growth since 2021. Coal (52.2%) remained the dominant source, though its share declined. For more, read our full report: https://t.co/XjD9hfhabo pic.twitter.com/WklP7dYL78 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 2, 2026 However, the country has made significant progress in expanding renewables in recent years, particularly solar and onshore wind. In 2025, renewables accounted for just over 29% of Poland’s electricity generation, almost three times the share recorded a decade earlier. Further progress is expected this year, after Poland began to generate electricity from offshore wind farms for the first time. Under a national energy and climate plan approved by the current government in June, it plans by 2040 for Poland to generate 18-21% of power from offshore wind and 22-27% from onshore wind. A further 15-16% will come from nuclear, 14-18% from solar, 7-8% from gas and 0-5% from coal. Poland’s first offshore wind farm has begun to deliver electricity, with Prime Minister @donaldtusk celebrating the development as a "key element of our energy security and sovereignty". World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun has published a video of himself using a hammer to attack a monument in Poland dedicated to soldiers from the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a World War Two partisan formation that fought against the Soviet Union but was also responsible for massacring Poles. Braun declared that the monument, which was also recently vandalised by other unknown perpetrators, should be removed as it “insults the memory of victims of the Ukrainian genocide against Poles” and “glorifies Nazism”. The incident comes amid recent tensions between Warsaw and Kyiv over World War Two history, and in particular the fact that the UPA continues to be honoured in Ukraine. Pomnik UPA w gminie Dołhobyczów w powiecie hrubieszowskim do likwidacji❗️ Obelisk obrażający pamięć ofiar ukraińskiego Ludobójstwa na Polakach powinien zostać usunięty profesjonalnymi narzędziami natychmiast po udokumentowaniu przestępstwa banderyzmu!#StopBanderyzacjiPolski… pic.twitter.com/8Q4QZ2z5vJ — Grzegorz Braun (@GrzegorzBraun_) September 10, 2026 The monument in question is located in the village of Liski, a few kilometres from the border with Ukraine, and marks the burial site of 41 UPA soldiers killed while fighting against the NKVD, the Soviet secret police, in 1946, in the aftermath of World War Two. The area previously had a large ethnic-Ukrainian population. The memorial was vandalised last month, when it was sprayed with black paint and its arch was damaged. On Monday this week, further damage was discovered to the inscription on the monument. Police announced that they had launched an investigation into vandalism, property damage and ethnic hatred, but had not yet identified the perpetrators, reported the Polish Press Agency (PAP). On Wednesday evening, Braun published a video showing himself and another man using a hammer to repeatedly strike the front of the monument, causing visible damage to the stone, which contains the names of the killed UPA soldiers. They also appear to attempt to remove a separate plaque. During the video, Braun, who is a member of the European Parliament and finished fourth in last year’s Polish presidential election, claimed that local residents are “afraid they would be set on fire” if they attempted to remove the memorial themselves. It is not clear when the video was recorded. Shortly after Braun published it, local police in Hrubieszów county, where the monument is located, issued a statement saying that officers were investigating damage to the monument. Interior ministry spokeswoman Karolina Gałecka shared their statement and declared that “the perpetrators will not go unpunished”. Sprawcy zniszczenia pomnika w Białymstoku nie pozostaną bezkarni. Policjanci zabezpieczają dowody i przesłuchują świadków. https://t.co/7HCApuhPZ1 — Karolina Gałecka (@K_Galecka) September 10, 2026 Braun, who regularly carries out stunts intended to demonstrate his anti-Ukrainian, antisemitic and anti-LGBT views, and is already facing multiple legal cases over such incidents. He is currently on trial for attacking a celebration of the Jewish festival of Hanukkah in parliament using a fire extinguisher. Last month, he was charged with the crime of denying Nazi crimes for claiming that the gas chambers at Auschwitz are “fake”. He was also charged with theft over incidents in which he tore down Ukrainian and European Union flags, and with vandalism of an LGBT+ exhibition. If convicted, some of the crimes Braun is charged with carry potential years-long prison sentences. Braun’s Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) party, which recently called for a “normalisation of relations with Russia”, enjoys support of around 8-9%, according to polling averages. That could make it a key player in deciding who can form a government after next year’s parliamentary elections. Figures from Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun's party celebrated Russia Day at the Russian embassy and presented a letter hailing Russia's development, blaming "globalists" for the Ukraine war and calling for normalisation of Polish-Russian relations https://t.co/SU3gEdVod0 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 13, 2026 At the time of writing, there had been no response from Ukrainian authorities to Braun’s latest stunt. However, when the same monument was vandalised last month, the Ukrainian embassy in Warsaw issued a statement expressing its “deep indignation”. “Regardless of the difficult and tragic chapters of our shared history, burial and memorial sites should remain outside the realm of political disputes and be treated with respect,” they wrote. The embassy also expressed “particular concern that this incident occurs against the backdrop of a rising number of hostile acts toward Ukrainians in Poland, including reports of aggression and attacks on Ukrainian citizens” “Any attempts to shift historical disputes into the realm of vandalism, intimidation or hostility toward modern Ukraine and Ukrainians are dangerous and must be met with an appropriate legal response,” they added. Poland and Ukraine have been embroiled in a diplomatic dispute since May, when President Volodymyr Zelensky named a military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. His Polish counterpart, Karol Nawrocki, responded by stripping Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour. Tensions have since cooled, and Ukraine has made moves to defuse the crisis. However, significant differences remain, in particular over memory of the so-called Volhynia massacres, in which the UPA led the killing of around 100,000 Polish civilians. Poland regards the episode as a genocide. Ukraine strongly rejects that label, and also continues to honour the UPA for its role in fighting against Moscow-imposed Soviet rule. Recent months have also seen a rise in anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Poland, including a series of cases of verbal or physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are by far Poland’s largest immigrant group. Reported anti-Ukrainian hate crimes were up 30% in the first half of this year. Demonstrations took place in 25 Polish cities on Sunday against the “growing wave of hate and violence” against Ukrainians, who are Poland’s largest immigrant group. Reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland are up 30% this year https://t.co/gGAEc6QZWT — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 10, 2026 In 2017, Ukraine responded to the dismantling of a UPA monument in Poland by introducing a ban on exhumations of Polish victims of the Volhynia massacres on its territory. It is believed that tens of thousands still remain buried in unmarked mass graves. However, last year, in a diplomatic breakthrough, Kyiv allowed such exhumations to resume, and since then the remains of dozens of victims have been found, researched and reburied. Earlier this month, Poland also granted Ukraine permission to conduct a search for the remains of Ukrainian civilians killed by Polish resistance fighters during World War Two. World.title: Prague Run Day to Bring Six Races to Riegrovy Sady on September 19
World.content:
On September 19, runners of all levels can take part in a new running event combining track and park races in one of Prague’s best-known green spaces.

There are six different races to choose from, so whether you’re looking for a serious challenge or just want to get out and run, there’s an option for you.



Six races to choose from

The programme includes six races, ranging from a short family run to a one-hour challenge.

The day will begin with the 800m Family Run, designed for young runners and their accompanying adults. There will also be an 800m race on the athletic track, offering participants the opportunity to compete over a short distance in a traditional track setting.

For those looking for a longer challenge, the 1 Mile race will take place on the athletic oval. The organisers describe it as a special opportunity to race over the classic distance, with participation limited to a maximum of 30 runners.

The 5km Solo Run will offer a more familiar challenge for runners of different experience levels. It is followed by the 4x3km Relay, a team race in which four runners each complete two 1.5km laps.

The final event of the day will be the Golden Hour Race, a one-hour running challenge taking place during the golden hour.

The event will be based at the Sokol Vinohrady athletic oval, which will serve as the main hub for the day.

Find all race distances, times and registration details at praguerunday.cz

📍 Riegrovy Sady Athletic Oval

📅 Saturday, September 19

🏃 6 races for different levels

🏅 Medal for every participant

World.title: Prague Is Turning a Historic Factory Chimney Into an Observation Deck
World.content:
A glass elevator will carry visitors through the preserved chimney of a former distillery before emerging above its rim to reveal views of the city.

Inside the developing Lihovar district in Smíchov, a historic factory chimney is being transformed into a viewing platform, with visitors set to travel through the structure in a panoramic glass elevator.



The chimney, which stands approximately 50 meters tall, is part of the former Zlíchov distillery. Rather than demolishing the industrial landmark, developers have incorporated it into the redevelopment of the site.

The project is being developed by Trigema, which is building the new Lihovar district on the former distillery grounds.

The elevator itself is one of the project’s most unusual features. Once it reaches the top of the chimney, the cabin will lift a special cap weighing approximately 500 kilograms, allowing it to rise above the chimney’s opening.

The glass cabin will then serve as an observation deck, offering a 360-degree view of Prague.

From industrial site to new Prague district

The Lihovar development is being built on the site of the former Zlíchov distillery in Prague 5. The redevelopment includes new buildings alongside the preservation of selected elements of the original industrial complex.

The factory chimney is among the structures being retained. Another is the historic former brewhouse, which is planned for cultural use.

The opening date for the observation deck has not been announced.

World.title: Riegrovy Sady to Host Goodbye Summer Party With Three Live Acts
World.content:
Summer may be drawing to a close, but the music season at Riegrovy Sady is not over yet.

On Thursday, 17 September, Energy Pub will host the Goodbye Summer Party, organised by Ploom in cooperation with Energy Pub.



The evening will feature a DJ set by Forgen, a performance by Jirka Drtil and a live concert by Renne Dang, following his sold-out show at Forum Karlín.

Tickets cost CZK 100 and the event is open exclusively to guests aged 18 and over.

The last long days and warm evenings of summer will get a musical send-off at Riegrovy Sady. The Goodbye Summer Party is designed for everyone who is not quite ready to say a final goodbye to summer and wants to enjoy one of the last outdoor evenings of the season.

The evening will kick off with a set by DJ Forgen, followed by a performance by musician Jirka Drtil. The main highlight of the evening will be a concert by Renne Dang, Ploom brand ambassador, whose current music blends elements of rap, pop and pop-punk.

His distinctive personal lyrics and energetic guitar-driven sound have already taken him to some of the country’s biggest stages. His recent achievements include a sold-out concert at Forum Karlín.

The Last Party of the Summer

Music will not be the only reason to head to Riegrovy Sady in September. The evening will also feature a dedicated Ploom zone, where adult guests can take a break during the programme and enjoy the atmosphere of one last summer party.

Every ticket holder will also receive a complimentary welcome drink. A food pop-up by Pavel Berky will be part of the event as well.

Where: Energy Pub, Riegrovy Sady 28, Prague 2

Line-up: DJ Forgen, Jirka Drtil, Renne Dang

Tickets: CZK 100, including a welcome drink

Entry: 18+ only

Capacity: Limited

World.title: Fresh from France: Meet Benjamin, the Founder of The French in Prague
World.content:
For the past 12 years, Benjamin has been building a life in Prague – and helping bring a taste of France to the Czech capital.

What began as a business supplying wine to hotels, restaurants and wine bars 10 years ago has gradually grown into The French, a food business focused on bringing French products directly to Prague.

The company started with an e-shop selling mainly wine, pâté, jam, honey and foie gras. But Benjamin soon realized there was something missing: fresh French produce.

“The idea, step by step, was that we were missing fresh products to be able to open a physical shop. That’s how, two years ago, we started importing fresh products.”

Today, The French operates two shops in Prague and imports a wide range of products directly from France, with a focus on freshness and quality while keeping prices accessible.

“It cannot be fresher than what we import.”

From Breakfast to Dinner

Fresh fruit and vegetables have become one of the shop’s main attractions. The products are imported weekly, with a truck leaving France every Tuesday carrying oysters, mussels, cheeses, fish, meat, fruits and vegetables.

“Two days ago it was in the sea and today it’s already in Prague, sitting in our fridge.”

The shop aims to cover the entire day, from breakfast to dinner. Customers can pick up croissants and pain au chocolat in the morning, fresh coffee, and a selection of French products for lunch and dinner.

Among the more distinctive products are French crème fraîche and salted butter. Benjamin points out that the natural colour of the dairy products can change during the year depending on what the cows eat. “If you have the same colour of butter or cream throughout the whole year, it’s because they are not eating grass.”

A New Home in Vinohrady

The company recently expanded with a larger shop in Vinohrady, giving customers access to a wider range of ultra-fresh products imported directly from France, as well as cosmetics from Provence.

The French also supplies restaurants and hotels across Prague with products including butter, cream, cheese, ham, sausages and olives. Much of the range comes directly from the Rungis International Market near Paris, one of the largest food markets in Europe.

The company also works with direct farmers, with some products clearly marked as coming from individual producers. “In Prague, you don’t have any shop that is grouping all of these categories of products.”

Customers can also order through The French’s e-shop at francouzske-speciality.cz and either have their purchases delivered or collect them from a shop.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by The French.cz (@the_french_cz)

But Benjamin says the experience is intended to be more personal than a standard supermarket. “We are not a shop where people are just behind the cash desk. We have people going into the shop to explain what we have, recommend what to cook and what to pair.”

The shops also have a weekly tasting calendar, giving customers the chance to try different products and discover new flavours.

French Food for Everyone

Although many customers are French, The French is not specifically aimed at the French community.

The Vinohrady shop attracts a large number of expats, while the company’s Prague 4 location has a much higher proportion of Czech customers. Benjamin says the goal is to serve people living in the neighborhood regardless of nationality. “We are not targeting especially expats or especially French. We are trying to target everyone living in the area who like gastronomy.”

There are, however, some differences in what Czech and French customers look for. Stronger French cheeses, for example, can take some getting used to, while certain French cuts of meat differ from traditional Czech ones.

Some types of fish are also relatively unfamiliar. Red mullet, or rouget, is widely used in French cuisine and high-end restaurants but is less common in Czech kitchens.

Growing Across Prague

The French has ambitious plans for the coming years. After opening its Vinohrady location and another shop in Prague 4, the company is preparing to open another location in Prague 9 in January.

The long-term goal is to operate five or six shops across Prague, with Holešovice, Karlín and Dejvice among the areas being considered.

World.title: Prague Has the Most Unaffordable Rents for Minimum-Wage Earners in the EU
World.content:
Prague has the highest rent-to-minimum-wage ratio among EU capitals, with the average two-bedroom apartment costing 185% of the gross minimum wage.

Prague has become the European Union’s least affordable capital for minimum-wage earners looking to rent a home, according to a new analysis by the European Trade Union Confederation (ETUC).



The average monthly rent for a two-bedroom apartment in the Czech capital reaches €1,710, compared with a gross monthly minimum wage of €924. This means rent alone amounts to 185% of the minimum wage.

Lisbon follows in second place, with rent accounting for 168% of the gross minimum wage. Budapest ranks third at 159%, followed by Bratislava at 158%.

Other capitals where average rent exceeds the gross minimum wage include Sofia (154%), Athens (153%), and Riga (151%).

The figures highlight the pressure facing minimum-wage earners in cities where housing costs have risen significantly faster than incomes.

How Prague Compares with Western Europe

Prague’s position is particularly striking when compared with several Western European capitals.

In Paris, average rent accounts for 138% of the gross minimum wage, while the figure stands at 125% in Madrid and 113% in Dublin.

At the other end of the ranking, Brussels is the most affordable capital for minimum-wage earners in the comparison. Average rent there represents 70% of the gross minimum wage. Berlin follows at 76%, while the figure is 85% in Nicosia and 87% in Luxembourg.

Housing Costs Across the EU

According to Eurostat’s latest figures cited in the analysis, housing and utility bills account for 23.6% of household spending across the European Union.

The ETUC has called for stronger collective bargaining, greater consideration of housing costs when setting minimum wages, and increased investment in social housing.

The organisation also noted that rents can be more affordable when measured against national minimum wages rather than those in capital cities. Among the 16 EU countries analysed, the share of the gross minimum wage required for rent ranged from 33% in Poland to 61% in Malta.

World.title: Prague 8 Pirates to Host English-Language Guide to Czech Local Elections
World.content:
EU citizens living in Prague 8 can learn how to vote in the upcoming municipal elections at an event on 17 September.

The Prague 8 branch of the Czech Pirate Party is inviting international residents to an English-language evening explaining how EU citizens can take part in Czech local elections.

The event, titled “Hey, You Can Vote Too!”, will take place on Thursday, 17 September, at 6 PM at Pauza Palmovka in Prague 8.



The evening will offer a practical introduction to the Czech voting system, an overview of the Prague 8 Pirates’ local programme, and an opportunity for international residents to share their views on life in the district.

Organisers say the event is intended to help EU citizens understand their voting rights and discuss what they would like to see improved in Prague 8.

Who Can Vote in Czech Local Elections?

Citizens of other EU Member States can vote in Czech municipal elections if they meet certain conditions.

Voters must:

Be at least 18 years old by the second day of the election.

Have permanent or registered temporary residence in the municipality.

Be entered in the supplement to the permanent electoral register.

EU citizens who are not already registered must apply by 7 October 2026 at 4 PM.

“Many people from other EU countries live in Prague 8, work here, raise their families here and use the same schools, parks, streets and public services as everyone else. Yet many still do not know that they can vote in local elections,” said Martin Štěrba, the Czech Pirate Party’s candidate for mayor of Prague 8.

“We want to explain how it works and hear directly from them what Prague 8 could do better.”

The Czech municipal elections will take place on 9 and 10 October 2026.

Voters in Prague 8 will elect representatives to both the Prague 8 Municipal District Council and the Prague City Assembly.

World.title: Nearly 40 Percent of Young Czechs Experience Financial Stress Every Month
World.content:
Money worries affect almost one in three Czech adults, but younger people are facing a greater burden.

A new survey found that 39 percent of people aged 18 to 26 experience financial anxiety at least once a month, with household income playing a major role in how people feel about their finances.



Financial concerns are common across the Czech Republic. According to a survey conducted by Ipsos for Home Credit, 28 percent of adults experience worries about money at least once a month. Another 35 percent report financial stress several times a year.

Young adults face the greatest pressure

People aged 18 to 26 are the most likely to experience regular financial stress. Nearly four in ten respondents in this age group said they worry about money at least once a month.

Home Credit attributed the pressure partly to the cost of housing and everyday expenses. For young adults trying to establish themselves financially, rising prices in recent years have made it harder to absorb unexpected costs.

An unplanned bill or other expense can therefore create a serious problem, particularly for those who have limited savings.

Household income makes a significant difference

The survey found a clear relationship between household income and financial anxiety.

Among households earning up to CZK 40,000 per month, 41 percent of respondents reported experiencing financial stress. The proportion decreases as household income rises.

People living in households with monthly incomes above CZK 70,000 reported the lowest levels of financial concern.

Age and education also appear to influence how people view their finances. Respondents aged 54 to 65 and university students reported lower levels of stress than some other groups. In both categories, 43 percent said they did not experience financial stress at all.

Financial stress may also affect physical health

The consequences of financial difficulties can extend beyond anxiety and everyday worries.

The material also refers to research published by the American Mayo Clinic in 2025. According to the research cited, long-term financial distress and food insecurity may be associated with poorer cardiovascular health and a higher risk of death.

The findings underline the potential connection between financial security and overall well-being. However, the Czech survey does not establish whether financial stress directly causes health problems.

The survey was conducted by Ipsos in June 2026 among 1,026 people.

World.title: A Prague Institution: Indian Jewel Celebrates 30 Years of North Indian Flavours
World.content:
The family-run restaurant has been bringing authentic North Indian flavours and warm hospitality to Prague since 1996.

For 30 years, Indian Jewel has been serving authentic Indian cuisine in the heart of Prague. Established in 1996 by Sanjeev Wadehra, the family-owned restaurant is celebrating three decades in the Czech capital in 2026 — a milestone that makes it one of the longest-standing Indian restaurants in the country.



The restaurant’s story began with Sanjeev Wadehra, who brought recipes, cooking traditions and spice blends directly from India to Prague. Today, the kitchen continues to focus on authentic North Indian cuisine, with dishes prepared according to traditional recipes rather than adapted to passing culinary trends.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Indian Jewel Prague (@indianjewelprague)

To celebrate its 30th anniversary, Indian Jewel is offering Prague Morning readers a complimentary welcome drink or dessert. Simply mention Prague Morning when you visit.

Among the highlights are tandoor specialities, prepared in the traditional clay oven, alongside lamb, chicken and shrimp curries. The menu also offers a wide selection of vegetarian dishes, as well as biryanis, freshly baked naan and other Indian classics.

Popular choices include Butter Chicken, Chicken Tikka Masala and Lamb Rogan Josh, while the tandoor menu offers another way to explore the flavours of North India.

But food is only part of the restaurant’s story. Indian Jewel has built its reputation on consistent quality and warm, personal hospitality. Many members of the team have been with the restaurant for years, creating the family atmosphere that Sanjeev and his wife, Mohini, consider an important part of its success.

The restaurant moved to its current location at Rybná 9 in 2021, after many years at its previous home in the historic Týn Courtyard. Despite the change, the philosophy has remained the same: authentic food, attentive service and a welcoming atmosphere.

World.title: PM Péter Magyar to meet Pope Leo XIV in private Vatican audience
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar is set to travel to the Vatican on 24 September, where he will be received by Pope Leo XIV in a private audience.

Péter Magyar is about to visit the Vatican very soon

Magyar announced the visit on Facebook, adding that he will subsequently hold talks with Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican’s Secretary of State and a key figure in its diplomatic and governmental affairs. The meeting will give Magyar an opportunity to discuss issues of interest with the head of the Catholic Church before his talks with one of the Vatican’s most senior officials.

The Pope had a meeting not so long ago with Viktor Orbán

Pope Leo XIV has previously received former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán at the Vatican. Orbán met the pontiff in October last year and was accompanied by his wife, Anikó Lévai, and several members of his family, writes VG.hu.

During that meeting, the two sides discussed bilateral relations and the role of the Catholic Church in Hungarian society. Family policy, the education and future of young people, and the protection of Christian communities living in war zones were also among the topics addressed. Orbán said afterwards that he had asked the Pope to continue supporting Hungary’s efforts to promote peace.

Tisza delegation previously met the Pope

The upcoming meeting will also follow an earlier Vatican encounter involving Magyar’s political movement. In April, Pope Leo XIV received representatives of the European People’s Party at the Vatican, including members of the Tisza Party. Magyar’s private audience therefore means the continuation of the relations between the Vatican and the Tisza politicians.

World.title: Talented Hungarian footballer Patrik Farkas joins Liverpool FC
World.content:
Liverpool have signed another Hungarian player, with 19-year-old midfielder Farkas Patrik securing a professional contract with the Premier League club. Farkas returns to Merseyside as a free agent from Blackburn Rovers, having previously spent time in Liverpool’s academy between 2021 and 2022.

From Szeged to Liverpool

Farkas began playing football in Szeged before moving to Kecskemét and subsequently continuing his development in England. After his first spell at the club, he joined Blackburn’s academy and became a free agent this summer, as per Liverpool FC.

The midfielder has now returned to the Reds and was already included in the U21 squad for a Premier League 2 match on Monday. Although his professional contract does not make him a member of Liverpool’s senior first team, the U21 side represents an important pathway towards the club’s senior squad.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s Telegram channel!

‘A dream come true’

Farkas described his return as a dream come true. “I’m very happy and can’t wait to get started,” he said, according to the club’s official website. “I’m happy to be back in Liverpool. There are some new faces, but it’s good to see old friends again and get to know everyone else.” The 19-year-old describes himself as a box-to-box midfielder capable of playing in several positions.

His brother as also at the club

Farkas is not the only member of his family at the club. His younger brother, Erik Farkas, plays for the U18 side. The 17-year-old has made an impressive start to the season, scoring twice and providing an assist in his first two matches. Patrik said the brothers have played together since Erik was four and continue to push each other to improve.

Another Hungarian at Merseyside

Farkas Patrik joins Dominik Szoboszlai, Milos Kerkez and Ármin Pécsi among the Hungarian players currently linked with Liverpool. Pécsi is on loan at Austrian club Hartberg. With Patrik now beginning his professional journey at the club, Liverpool’s connection with Hungarian football continues to strengthen.

World.title: One more warm day until cold front splits Hungary in two
World.content:
Hungary is set for a dramatic weather divide this week as a wavy cold front crosses the country, bringing a sharp drop in temperatures to the west while summer-like warmth lingers in the east.

Wednesday will bring us one more warm day

According to a forecast video from the meteorologists at HungaroMet, the contrast will be particularly noticeable on Thursday, before another, even stronger cold front arrives early next week.

Wednesday will begin with a southerly airflow, bringing temporary warming to the Carpathian Basin. After patches of morning fog clear, mostly sunny conditions are expected, with afternoon temperatures reaching 23–28°C. Winds will strengthen in several areas, with particularly strong gusts possible around the Kisalföld region and Lake Fertő.

Cold front will divide the country

The weather will change considerably on Thursday as a cold front reaches Hungary and becomes temporarily stalled over the country. This will create a striking contrast between the western and eastern parts of the country.

Temperatures in western and north-western Hungary are expected to reach only 19–20°C, while the eastern Great Plain could still see highs of 28–30°C. Despite the unusually large regional difference, HungaroMet says the national average temperature will remain broadly in line with the seasonal norm.

The temperature divide will persist into Friday, while conditions become increasingly favourable for precipitation across a larger part of the country. Rain, showers and thunderstorms may develop in several areas, making Friday a more unsettled day.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s Telegram channel!

Weekend offers temporary respite, but cold reclaims Hungary on Monday

By Saturday, the frontal system is expected to move eastwards away from Hungary. Some light rain may still occur across southern and eastern areas, but sunshine will dominate elsewhere. The temperature contrast will remain, with noticeably cooler conditions in Transdanubia while temperatures fall less sharply across the Great Plain.

Western areas may begin to warm gradually again during the weekend, but the improvement is unlikely to last. A new, fast-moving and more pronounced cold front is forecast to reach the region on Monday, bringing another 3–4°C drop in temperatures nationwide. The next front is not expected to produce particularly heavy precipitation, however, with only moderate rainfall effects currently anticipated.

World.title: Hungarian minority in Ukraine: Our reader writes from the scene – agreement signed, but where are the results?
World.content:
Hungary and Ukraine have recently reached an agreement in order to restore the rights of the Hungarian minority in Ukraine. The agreement defines basic rights in language, education, social and political, and cultural spheres. The Ukrainian side undertook to expand the range of rights of the Hungarian minority in settlements where ethnic Hungarians make up more than 10% of the population.

This article was written by our reader, P. M.

These are key known points from the agreement:

Names of streets, squares, and plates on buildings of local administrations must be translated into Hungarian

People may address local authorities using the Hungarian language, and local officials must speak it

Agitation for elections, voting rules, and ballot papers at local elections must be translated into Hungarian

Public events may be held in Hungarian. People are allowed to use Hungarian national symbols, but they can’t dominate Ukrainian ones

Educational facilities with Hungarian-speaking groups get the “school of national minority” status. Such schools must have a Hungarian-speaking principal and a vice principal. Students and teachers have a right to speak Hungarian in schools off-hours

Educational diplomas and certificates must be translated into Hungarian. Tasks of national exams (except Ukrainian language and History) must be translated too

The agreement was signed in June this year; however, Kyiv’s been slow to meet Budapest’s requirements, and, unfortunately, things are staying the same for the Hungarian minority in Ukraine now.

Who has the right to represent the Hungarian minority in Ukraine?

A bilateral group working on ensuring the rights of ethnic Hungarians was established after signing for rapid response to possible violations. From the Ukrainian side, we have non-governmental organisations and influencers. However, there is a nuance. There is a rising concern that Kyiv doesn’t fulfil the agreements responsibly.

Rumour has it that the group doesn’t consist of the largest organisations representing the Hungarian diaspora in Ukraine or organisations which are trusted not only by the local minority but also by Budapest, but consists of little-known regional organisations, which don’t even have any political representation in local authorities. For example, one of the participants of the group is Boris Vashkeba, a chairman of a small and rather young organisation called “Transcarpathian Society of Hungarians”.

It’s legitimate to ask about such organisations’ right to fully represent the interests of the community and about the appropriateness of their presence in important groups like this one.

Are the rights of the Hungarian minority a loophole for Ukraine’s EU accession?

There is also a certain point of view that Kyiv has agreed to this deal only in order to make Hungary stop interfering with negotiations on Ukraine’s EU accession. However, it didn’t work out. Only two (Fundamentals and External Relations) of the six negotiation clusters were opened. Budapest refused to approve screening results for the Internal Market and Competitiveness clusters on 1 September, for the third time since July.

The situation is pissing Ukrainian officials off, so they continue to blame Budapest for halting Ukraine’s EU integration. Despite this, Magyar states that Ukraine, like any other country, should have no privileges for EU accession and promises to open the other clusters only when all agreements are implemented, including the ones concerning ethnic Hungarians in Ukraine.

Fate of the Hungarian minority in Ukraine remains uncertain

After signing the agreement this summer, Minister of Foreign Affairs Anita Orban claims that Ukraine’s accession process will automatically be halted if Ukraine fails to comply with the minority agreement. It’s reported that Ukraine undertook to implement education measures by the end of 2026, and social and political measures in 2027. It’s also reported that there would be an audit soon, which would determine if there was any work being done in this field.

Meanwhile, Magyar has recently said that Hungary doesn’t see enough progress made by Ukraine in complying with the agreement and once again has confirmed that the rights of the Hungarian minority in Ukraine are a very important problem for Hungary. That’s why Budapest voted against the EU’s initiative to stop granting temporary protection to military-age Ukrainian men.

Magyar explained that many people escaping from Ukraine to Hungary belong to Ukraine’s Hungarian minority, which his government tries to protect. Nevertheless, Kyiv keeps repeating that it’s illegal to cross the border for military-age men in Ukraine now.

World.title: FM Orbán files criminal complaint over former FM Szijjártó’s countless private jet travels
World.content:
Hungary’s Foreign Minister Anita Orbán has filed a criminal complaint over the use of private and military aircraft for official trips during the tenure of her predecessor, Péter Szijjártó.

Billions in additional costs alleged

Orbán said an internal review of the Foreign Ministry had uncovered serious irregularities and alleged that the routine use of chartered aircraft from 2022 onwards may have caused significant financial damage to the state. She says the ministry increasingly replaced scheduled commercial flights with private or military aircraft even though the number and nature of diplomatic engagements had not changed significantly.

She estimated that private flights between 2022 and 2026 cost around HUF 4 billion (currently more than EUR 10.9 million) more than travelling on scheduled services. This figure, she stressed, does not include the cost of military aircraft, meaning the total could be higher.

According to FM Orbán, they haven’t even considered cheaper options

Orbán also claimed that aircraft were chartered for relatively short journeys to cities including Bratislava, Vienna and Belgrade, where travelling by car or train would have taken only a few hours. She said investigators found no evidence that cheaper travel options had been systematically considered before individual journeys, even though these private flights should have not been considered as an opportunity, according to the policies of the ministry, writes ATV.

On that basis, Orbán said she believed the circumstances raised suspicions of mismanagement causing particularly significant financial damage and potentially involved responsibility among the ministry’s former senior leadership.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s Telegram channel!

Fidesz calls complaint ‘frivolous’

The Fidesz parliamentary group rejected the allegations, calling the complaint frivolous and insisting that Szijjártó’s flights complied fully with the relevant government regulations. The party argued that the former foreign minister’s travel schedule was organised efficiently, claiming that Szijjártó frequently travelled overnight so that he could conduct meetings during the day.

It also said he returned home immediately after official programmes rather than unnecessarily extending his stays abroad. Fidesz further defended Szijjártó’s record as foreign minister, pointing to what it described as record levels of investment and job creation during the period.

Stay up-to-date: Hungarian Parliament elects five new constitutional judges

Szijjártó’s flights have long been controversial

The former foreign minister’s use of private aircraft has attracted media scrutiny for years. According to figures previously published by the Foreign Ministry, 53 private-jet journeys were made for Szijjártó over four years at a reported cost of HUF 4.87 billion (more than EUR 13.3), writes HVG.hu.

The issue has also been complicated by disputes over access to travel-cost information, with the government previously changing legislation concerning the disclosure of such data. The latest complaint is therefore likely to reignite a long-running political dispute over the cost and transparency of Szijjártó’s official travel. Any criminal responsibility, however, remains to be established.

World.title: Exotic South American animal spotted in Hungary’s mountains
World.content:
A trail runner had an extraordinary encounter in the Börzsöny hills after spotting and filming an exotic South American animal wandering through the forest.

Out-of-place exotic animal runs around in Hungary

Dániel Bárdos was running towards the Hárombarát Saddle on Sunday afternoon when he noticed an unusual animal moving through the woodland. He quickly took out his phone and recorded the creature, which appears to be a coati, also known as a red-nosed coati, a relative of the raccoon native to South America.

‘It wasn’t particularly interested in me’

Dániel said the animal was clearly aware of his presence but showed little fear. It continued sniffing and searching for food while moving in his direction, eventually prompting the runner to move away himself. He later shared the footage in the ‘Csak a Börzsöny!’ Facebook group, describing the encounter as an unexpected meeting with a South American mammal.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s Telegram channel!

Is it the same coati seen last year?

The sighting has raised questions because a similar animal was reported in the Börzsöny area on 21 November 2025. At the time, speculation suggested that the coati could have escaped from the Törökmező Tourist Centre and Small Animal Park near Nagymaros. The park did not officially confirm this, however, writes KEMMA.hu.

Following the latest sighting, the park reportedly confirmed that all of its coatis were accounted for. It said it would nevertheless work with the local municipality to try to locate the creature and would be willing to take it in if it was found to be healthy.

The park’s owner believes the animal may instead have escaped from private ownership. Although the two sightings occurred in the same region less than a year apart, there is currently no evidence that they involved the same individual.

Hungary is full of exotic creatures: Hatvanpuszta zebra scandal deepens as details of illegal keeping, escaped animals, and carcasses dumped in a pig pit emerge

Keeping coatis is prohibited in Hungary

Norbert Riezing of the Duna–Ipoly National Park Directorate said that keeping coatis is prohibited in Hungary. The species was added to the European Union’s list of invasive alien species of Union concern in 2016, bringing strict restrictions on keeping, breeding, reproducing and trading the animals.

Certain people who legally owned coatis before the rules took effect on 3 August 2016 were allowed to keep them for the remainder of their natural lives, provided they prevented the animals from escaping or reproducing. For now, the origin of the coati filmed in the Börzsöny remains a mystery.

Read also: Hungary admits “embarrassing blunder” over King Charles III’s Lipizzaner horses, but there’s another twist

World.title: Hungarian police allegedly detained the 7th richest man of the country
World.content:
Police have reportedly detained billionaire property businessman Dániel Jellinek and Norbert Szivek, the former chief executive of Hungary’s Hungarian National Asset Management Inc. (MNV), in connection with a long-running investigation into alleged corruption surrounding state-owned Volán bus companies.

The two are linked to a long-running police investigation

Multiple Hungarian media outlets reported that the two men were taken from properties linked to them on Tuesday morning. However, police had not officially confirmed the detentions at the time of publication. Dániel Jellinek is currently the 7th richest Hungarian, while Norbert Szivek was the former head of the Hungarian National Asset Management Inc. (Magyar Nemzeti Vagyonkezelő, MNV).

Prime Minister Péter Magyar also referred to the reports on Facebook, saying police investigators had detained Jellinek, whom he described as one of Hungary’s wealthiest businessmen and a former business associate of István Tiborcz, son-in-law of former prime minister Viktor Orbán.

Investigation centres on allegedly overpriced buses

According to Telex, the reported detentions come days after Hungary’s National Investigation Bureau (NNI) announced that eight former executives had been made suspects in an investigation into allegedly overpriced purchases involving Volán companies.

According to the NNI, the investigation concerns transactions carried out between 2015 and 2018, which are suspected of causing around HUF 10 billion (EUR 27.4 million) in financial damage. Investigators say more than 600 used buses were purchased at inflated prices, while the acquisition of a Volán company’s headquarters in Kecskemét allegedly caused at least HUF 550 million (EUR 1.5 million) in losses.

The NNI is investigating suspected misappropriation causing particularly significant financial damage and money laundering involving particularly large sums. Police investigators say allegedly illicit funds were channelled through intermediary companies and fictitious loan agreements before being invested in property projects in Budapest, Balatonvilágos and Törökbálint.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s Telegram channel!

Why Szivek is central to the case

Szivek headed MNV between 2015 and 2018, when the state asset manager exercised ownership rights over the Volán companies. According to police reports, the then leadership had knowledge of valuable state-owned properties that could generate significant profits if sold.

The authorities allege that money connected to the bus purchases and the Kecskemét property deal was transferred through intermediary companies and subsequently invested elsewhere. Szivek was among the eight people reportedly questioned as suspects last week. At that stage, investigators had not requested coercive measures against them.

Jellinek’s business connections

Jellinek, head of Indotek Group, is one of Hungary’s best-known property investors and has had extensive business dealings with companies linked to Tiborcz István, son-in-law of former prime minister Viktor Orbán.

Investigations by G7 cited by Hungarian media have examined financial transactions involving Jellinek-linked companies and businesses associated with Tiborcz. Jellinek has also been involved in major property deals, including the Gellért Hotel and a large Belgrade office complex. Jellinek was separately convicted of budget fraud in January 2025 in a case involving false invoices.

Stay up-to-date: Hungarian Parliament elects five new constitutional judges

Major escalation

The reported detention of Jellinek and Szivek would mark a major escalation in the Volán investigation, which has been under way for several years. The NNI has said the investigation is continuing, meaning further suspects could potentially be identified. Neither Jellinek nor Szivek has been convicted in connection with the Volán case, and the allegations against them remain subject to the ongoing criminal proceedings.

World.title: Hungarian Parliament elects five new constitutional judges
World.content:
Hungary’s parliament has elected five new members of the Constitutional Court in a secret ballot, replacing judges whose mandates have ended or are due to expire following recent constitutional changes.

New members join the court following constitutional changes and a major reshuffle

The new judges are Nóra Chronowski, a constitutional lawyer and university professor; András György Kovács, a Curia judge and administrative lawyer; Miklós Ligeti, criminal lawyer and legal director of Transparency International Hungary; Árpád Gábor Orosz, former head of the Curia’s Civil Law College; and Zsolt Szomora, a criminal law professor at the University of Szeged.

All five candidates, nominated by the Tisza majority, received 137 votes in favour and six against, with no abstentions. They subsequently took their oaths before parliament.

Why were five new judges needed?

The reshuffle followed the 17th amendment to Hungary’s Fundamental Law, which restored a compulsory retirement age of 70 for Constitutional Court judges. As a result, the mandates of Constitutional Court President Péter Polt, together with Mária Ádám Haszonicsné, Miklós Juhász and Zoltán Lomnici, ended on 1 September after all four reached the new age limit.

Parliament had 60 days to fill the vacancies. A fifth seat was also due to become vacant because Ágnes Czine, the court’s deputy president, will complete her 12-year mandate in November. Under the new rules, newly elected Constitutional Court judges will serve nine-year terms instead of 12. The reform also provides for the court’s president to be elected by the Constitutional Court judges themselves.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s Telegram channel!

What do the new judges stand for?

The nominees outlined their priorities during parliamentary hearings. Chronowski said she would see the annulment of legislation as evidence of successful constitutional review rather than failure. She highlighted the democratic rule of law, human dignity and the protection of minorities and vulnerable groups.

Kovács said the court should revive and further develop the constitutional jurisprudence established during Hungary’s democratic transition. Ligeti was particularly critical of the institution’s recent record, saying the Constitutional Court needed to be “rethought and rebuilt” and describing it as a “captured Constitutional Court”.

Orosz stressed that restoring public trust would require credible and independent judges, while Szomora advocated constitutional dialogue between the branches of government rather than treating institutional disagreements simply as conflicts.

Stay up-to-date: PM Magyar says former PM Orbán could face prison over threats against new asset recovery office staff

Fidesz-KDNP boycotts the election

Opposition Fidesz-KDNP alliance did not participate in the vote. Its MPs left the chamber beforehand, having described the procedure as illegitimate and a mockery of constitutionalism. The Mi Hazánk (Our Homeland) parliamentary group did participate and nominated five candidates of its own, but its nominees failed to receive backing from the relevant parliamentary committee.

The appointments mark a significant renewal of Hungary’s 15-member Constitutional Court, amid continuing political debate over judicial independence, the rule of law and the balance between state institutions.
