World.title: Sturt versus Norwood stirs up 1978 controversy ahead of SANFL final
World.content:
Football Park was barely four years old when Sturt and Norwood last met in a famous grand final that included a brief tussle between players and officials in the Sturt dug-out.

The Redlegs came away with a one-point win in 1978 despite Sturt being favoured, but with both teams meeting again for this weekend's SANFL Grand Final, there are several controversies that remain front of mind for some.

First and foremost, there was the winning goal.

After kicking 5:9 to Norwood's 1:5 in the first quarter, Sturt was in front and living up to expectations, having only lost one game for the entire season.

But, 29 points down in the last quarter, the Redlegs mounted a comeback, briefly taking the lead before Sturt kicked another goal.

"Then there was a rough contest in Norwood's forward pocket, and [Redleg] Phil Gallagher took it out of the ruck, quickly slammed it on his boot, and it went straight to Sturt fullback Colin Casey," said SANFL senior media producer Zac Millbank.

"He kicked it straight back out of the area and then Phil Gallagher went to mark Casey's kick, but he actually dropped it."

Field umpire Des Foster blew his whistle and gave what commentators at the time assumed to be a weak free kick to Gallagher.

Foster later said that he actually called it a mark but admitted it was the wrong call, explaining that his field of vision had been obscured by players at the key moment when the ball came down.

In front of more than 50,000 spectators and a live television audience, Gallagher went back and kicked a goal, putting Norwood in front.

Sturt's Lucas Slade and Norwood's Alex Wright will compete for the SANFL flag on Sunday. (Supplied: Matt Talbot)

There were about three minutes left, however, and Sturt made several more 50-metre entries but only managed a point.

Mr Millbank pointed out that Sturt had kicked 14 goals and 25 points that day, so the upset loss could not be blamed on "the Des Foster blunder".

"Fourteen goals and 26 points is just horrendous kicking and some of the shots were very simple ones," he said.

Regardless, the moment went down in history as one of the most contentious free kicks or marks ever played at Football Park, the former stadium that was home to SA football between 1974 and 2013.

Mr Millbank said there had been a lot of commentary on the SANFL's social media pages about the 48-year-old moment since Sunday's match-up was confirmed, proving the incident was very much "still on people's minds".

Norwood captain Jacob Kennerley and Sturt captain Tom Lewis are playing for the cup on Sunday. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

Sturt captain Tom Lewis said he was reminded about the 1978 final by a pedestrian walking past his house on Monday morning.

"He reminded me at about 7am how disappointed he was at that grand final and asked us to right a few wrongs," he said.

"Both clubs have such a history; it does bring a lot of excitement, a lot of pressure.

"I'm thoroughly looking forward to it, and the boys are. Everyone's amped up; I know Norwood are as well, so hopefully we get a good turnout."

A dug-out scuffle

Another memorable moment occurred in the third quarter in 1978 when Norwood player John Wynne overran the ball on the boundary and ended up inside the enemy's camp, much to his own apparent amusement.

A skirmish ensued, with more players and officials from the Redlegs getting involved, until umpires quelled the situation and broke the parties apart — even as strong words continued to fly.

"Legend has it that master [Sturt] coach Jack Oatey was a bit ruffled after that incident," Mr Millbank said.

"I don't know how true it is, but there's a bit of thought that Wynne did it deliberately to try and stir him up a bit, put them off their game."

Norwood took the 1978 premiership after a long period of SANFL dominance for Sturt, in which they had won five flags in a row from 1966 to 1970, and then in 1974 and 1976 as well.

The fact they had only dropped one game for the entire season — a feat Sturt repeated in 2025 before winning the premiership — had made them the "raging favourites".

For this year's grand final, however, the shoe is on the other foot, and Norwood are the warm favourites going into the game.

Norwood beat Sturt by 19 points during the second semi-final earlier this month. (Supplied: Matt Talbot)

Having won the minor premiership and winning the second semi-final against Sturt two weeks ago, the team has only played one match in three weeks.

Coach Jade Sheedy said that after the team's main training session, they had another strong session on Saturday, "which put the boys through their paces and tried to replicate as much as we can to get them ready for a grand final," he said.

"Our preparation has been good … players are fresh."

Norwood captain Jacob Kennerley said it was always a big game when Sturt and Norwood met, "so to be able to play in a grand final against them is a bigger deal".

"You can certainly feel the anticipation living in the eastern suburbs and knowing that rivalry, the history, the '78 grand final was obviously huge," he said.

"I've heard a lot about that even though it was 48 years ago now. That famous Gallagher mark, my former number 11, so I know a lot about the history."

Digging deep for a repeat

Sturt, which finished third on the ladder, has played three finals to get to the big dance, and will defend their 2025 premiership with a slightly different list to Sunday's preliminary due to injuries.

This includes midfielder Jared Dakin, who injured his hamstring in the opening quarter against Woodville-West Torrens; key defender Casey Voss, who dislocated his shoulder in the game; and ruckman Amos Doyle, who was a late withdrawal due to a neck injury.

The Superjesus will play a set before the SANFL Grand Final at Adelaide Oval on Sunday. (@they.muse)

Coach Marty Mattner said Doyle had been progressing and may still play on Sunday, depending on Wednesday's training, and there was still a window open for Voss, although his inclusion is considered unlikely.

"The positive is that everyone who hasn't been playing in the league side is fit and ready to go," he said.

"Realistically there’s probably seven or eight in that [reserves] group who have played league footy this year."

The 2026 SANFL Grand Final, which will feature Adelaide rockers The Superjesus in pre-game entertainment, will commence at Adelaide Oval from 2:30pm Sunday.

World.title: Rush to put Zverev in Alcaraz-Sinner tier premature despite twin titles
World.content:
When the latest edition of the ATP singles rankings dropped earlier this week, a 24-year streak came to an end.

After being bounced in the first round of the US Open, Novak Djokovic dropped out of the top-10 for the first time since 2018.

Djokovic's exit marks the first time since October 2002 that neither he nor Rafael Nadal nor Roger Federer is inside the top-10.

For tennis fans who wondered when the 'Big 3' era in the men's game would end, the end is now.

Novak Djokovic's first-round exit at the US Open caused him to drop outside the top-10 for the first time since 2018. (Getty Images: Mike Stobe)

With the Djokovic-Federer-Nadal triumvirate dominating the men's game for so long, the question of who their successors would be has been a popular one around tennis.

Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz have emulated Federer and Nadal's rivalry from the mid-2000s, exchanging grand slam titles while playing some spellbinding epics along the way, but would any other men's players on tour join them as Djokovic joined Federer and Nadal?

Alexander Zverev appears to be the third member of the party, having claimed two of the four available grand slam titles this year.

But questions remain as to whether Zverev's candidacy to join the very top tier of men's tennis is legitimate.

Alexander Zverev wins US Open without realising it Alexander Zverev wins his second grand slam title of the year with a dominant victory over American Ben Shelton in the men's US Open final.

Since first achieving a top-10 ranking in May 2017 as a 20-year-old, Zverev has been one of the most consistent performers on the men's tour.

Zverev has spent 414 weeks as a top-10 ranked player throughout his career, currently 15th all-time. He ranks second among active players in this metric, behind only Djokovic, with 959 weeks, just behind Federer's 968.

At the time of writing, Zverev has spent 102 consecutive weeks ranked inside the top 10 since his most recent streak began in September 2023.

Those numbers are not the problem when it comes to Zverev's bid to be considered the best player in the world.

It is this one.

Career wins against top-10 ranked opponents Wins % Novak Djokovic 69 66 Roger Federer 64 62 Rafael Nadal 55 67 Carlos Alcaraz 16 70 Jannik Sinner 14 50 Alexander Zverev 5 22

Despite being a constant presence in the top-10 rankings over the best part of the last decade, Zverev has consistently struggled to beat the other players ranked in the same vicinity.

The German owns an unenviable 5-18 (21.7 per cent) win-loss record against fellow top-10 opponents in grand slam matches. He has won 59 of his 146 matches against top-10 opponents overall, roughly a 40 per cent conversion rate.

Zverev's record pales in comparison to Alcaraz and Sinner, as well as Djokovic, Federer and Nadal.

Alcaraz has an astounding 16-7 record against top-10 opponents at grand slams, with his 69.6 per cent conversion rate by far the best among the elite cohort, while Sinner has gone 14-14 in such matches.

Zverev has been beaten by Sinner (pictured) in two of his six grand slam final appearances. (Getty Images/Frey)

Nadal, Djokovic and Federer all won over 60 per cent of their matches against top-10 opponents at grand slams, with Djokovic's 69 wins leading the way.

This record against the very best players helped make Zverev a perennial grand slam semifinalist and finalist before he broke through with his first title at Roland-Garros earlier this year.

While Zverev now has two grand slam titles to his name, the calibre of opponents he has overcome suggests he hasn't really gone up a tier.

The German claimed the French Open title without facing a single top-10-ranked opponent, with the runner-up Flavio Cobolli the top-ranked player at No.14.

US Open finalist Ben Shelton is the only top-10 ranked opponent Zverev has beaten en route to his two grand slam titles this year. (Getty Images: Simon Bruty/USTA)

Overall, the average ranking of the players Zverev beat en-route to his first grand slam title is 57.7, with his fourth-round opponent, world No.106, Jesper de Jong the lowest-ranked.

Zverev had a slightly tougher run to the US Open title, but still faced just one top-10-ranked opponent in finalist Ben Shelton (eighth).

On average, Zverev's US Open opponents ranked 45th overall, with his first-round opponent, Lorenzo Sonego, the lowest-ranked at No.89.

Zverev's victories offer hope for the rest of the non-Alcaraz and Sinner division on the men's tour, including players such as Australia's Alex de Minaur.

De Minaur, like Zverev, has struggled against top-10 opponents at grand slams, winning just two of 14 matches.

Zverev's breakthroughs offer hope for the likes of Australia's Alex de Minaur (pictured). (AP: Christinne Muschi)

Despite reaching a career-high ranking of No.5 this year, de Minaur has yet to win a grand slam quarterfinal.

The Australian has a 0-7 record in quarters, with six of those losses coming over the last three seasons.

De Minaur has looked downtrodden after his recent grand slam exits, but will hope that like Zverev, he too can capitalise on the bracket breaking just right for him at some point down the line.

For now, Zverev looks to have graduated above the class featuring the likes of Shelton, Daniil Medvedev, Felix Auger-Aliassime, de Minaur and others.

But for him to truly climb into the upper echelon of men's tennis, it is time he starts taking down the big names when it matters most.

World.title: Australian company Sharon AI buys former Visy paper mill site at Ettamogah
World.content:
Albury residents have raised concerns about a major industrial site being sold to a company specialising in artificial intelligence (AI).

Sharon AI, based in Sydney and New York, has confirmed it has bought the former Visy paper mill site at Ettamogah, north of Albury.

The Australian-owned company describes itself as a high-operating computing company "neo-cloud" that rents out its infrastructure and equipment for AI use.

The site was sold by Visy to Sharon AI. (ABC News: Philippe Perez)

"Sharon AI has purchased a paper mill in Ettamogah, with plans to return the underutilised brownfield site into a running operation that benefits the local community," a spokesperson said.

"We will say more at a later date."

The company would not disclose what it intends to develop at the site, but said it would undertake appropriate community consultation.

"Sharon AI is committed to building real-world infrastructure throughout Australia, which creates jobs and a positive impact to local communities," the spokesperson said.

Locals sceptical

Katie Lucantonio lives near the Ettamogah site and said she was concerned about the uncertainty of a potential data centre in the area.

"The way I look at it … it's like if Coca-Cola were to purchase it, I would expect there to be some sort of [soft-drink] manufacturing there," Ms Lucantonio said.

"Health is the number one [concern].

"Second to that is the environment, and the health of the flora [and] fauna.

"It's surrounded by native bushland … and further on, you've got farms nearby.

Local resident Katie Lucantonio says her top concern about the paper mill site sale is the community's health. (Supplied: Katie Lucantonio)

"What I've seen … is if you don't get on the front foot of these issues, particularly in pre-planning stages, there's no, or very little, community consultation."

NSW Liberal Albury MP Justin Clancy said the local community had a right to ask questions if a large-scale data centre development was planned.

"There are two aspects to this that we need to look at," Mr Clancy said.

"Obviously one is we know that our use of data and AI is increasing significantly at a rapid rate in this nation and right across the globe, and there's certainly a call there to make sure that we as a nation have sovereign capability.

" We need to balance that with, on the other hand, legitimate questions around energy usage, water usage and also local amenity. "

Earlier this year, the NSW government announced measures to encourage data centre builders to follow new guidelines to fast-track projects.

If builders met environmental and efficiency standards and avoided net costs to consumers, the government promised to evaluate applications within 75 days.

Proposed legislation for the program is set to be debated in parliament later this year.

Justin Clancy says it is right for the community to ask questions about data centre development in regional towns. (ABC Goulburn Murray: Sarah Krieg)

Albury Mayor Kevin Mack said he could not comment on private land ownership, but any development would be assessed through normal planning processes.

"Albury is open for business, and we welcome investment that creates jobs and supports our growing regional economy," Cr Mack said.

"Our role is to ensure the right planning and infrastructure are in place so opportunities can be realised when they arise."

Data centres are 'nothing new'

The Australian Energy Market Operator said about 3 per cent of Australia's electricity was consumed by data centres this past financial year, a figure set to increase to 13 per cent by 2035.

Johanna Lim from the University of Sydney's United States Studies Centre said the substantial resources needed to operate data centres were cause for community concern.

"While the services that these data centres are providing are usually at a national or even global level, many of these impacts tend to be felt more locally, and I think that's a key driver of this debate," she said.

Albury is already home to the Leading Edge Data Centre, near the airport. (ABC News: Philippe Perez)

"Regional areas that have lots of land can provide for these larger sites, and that can be easier to accommodate compared to more land-constrained areas like Sydney and Melbourne."

She said more community pushback will change how data centre companies conduct themselves through the planning process.

"I think the important thing here is that for these data centres, community engagement starts early, before decisions have effectively already been made, and there's a level of transparency that needs to be done, or that needs to be presented to communities," she said.

Albury is already home to one data centre, located near Albury Airport.

World.title: Trump allies and adversaries join forces in AI fight
World.content:
Political enemies have united in Washington to push for AI regulation, but US President Donald Trump continues to baulk at pressure to put controls on the technology.

Former Trump strategist Steve Bannon and left-wing senator Bernie Sanders joined Democrats, Republicans, advocates and actors at an event calling for urgent action.

"I don't think you could find any two harder partisans than Bernie Sanders on the left and Steve Bannon on the right," said Mr Bannon, who is now a popular MAGA podcaster.

"And I think that speaks to … what the threat is. We have to rise above it. This is a hinge in history."

The "Pro-Human Assembly" event reflects a growing consensus in Washington to act on AI. But chasms of disagreement on the specifics mean there is no clear path forward.

"Congress, under both Democratic and Republican control, have been asleep at the wheel," Senator Sanders told the audience.

"And we now have a president whose ignorance regarding this issue is truly embarrassing."

Calls to press pause, cut off China

Senator Sanders, an independent who caucuses with the Democrats, has proposed a range of legislative measures. Next week, he will introduce another bill that would pause the development of advanced AI until a regulatory body is set up.

But his proposals are among scores of bills introduced in recent years that have failed to advance through Congress.

Some White House officials and members of Congress oppose American regulation because they fear it will allow China to get too far ahead of the US.

Mr Bannon called on the Trump administration to cut Chinese access to American AI, including by banning Chinese nationals working in US AI labs.

"We should quarantine, now, every aspect of the ecosystem of artificial intelligence away from the Chinese Communist Party," he said.

"It's the only way you're going to get your hands around it and actually think through, with adults, what should be actually the regulatory apparatus."

'The robots will not be taking over'

But Mr Trump has been resisting calls for action, despite dire warnings from AI executives Dario Amodei (Anthropic), Sam Altman (OpenAI) and Elon Musk (xAI), who say their technology is developing at a dangerous pace and could bring catastrophic consequences.

"I know about AI. I also have common sense about AI," Mr Trump told a separate event via a speakerphone chat with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

"The robots will not be taking over. The AI will not be taking over the rest of the world. The whole thing is a hoax."

US voters revolt against data centres War veteran Loretta Thornton's home offered such tranquillity, she named it 'Serenity'. Then, Elon Musk built America's largest data centre next door.

Republican congressman Chip Roy said the president was right to doubt the industry's reasons for requesting government intervention.

"When he calls it a hoax, he's saying, 'Wait is this real? What are y'all's motives?''' Mr Roy told reporters at the Pro-Human Assembly.

"Now, is the issue of whether we can lose control of AI, is that in any way a hoax? No, of course not.

"We've all been wondering where this could go, and that's what I think we need to try to address."

World.title: Housing downturn ends record profit run for sellers
World.content:
Brisbane is still the country's most profitable capital for sellers despite the housing downturn, while one in five Melbourne units recorded a loss, according to the latest figures from data property firm Cotality.

The June quarter data marks an end of record resales, from their 21-year high in March.

Brisbane resales had a median $525,000 profit, with 99.8 per cent of sales in the quarter making a gain.

Meanwhile in Melbourne, 20.8 per cent of units were sold at a loss, and about one in 10 Sydney units went for less than their purchase price.

Houses returned a profit more reliably than units overall, with 97.8 per cent of houses making a gain compared to 90.5 per cent of units.

Nationally, sellers made a median $371,000, with 95.4 per cent of the more than 94,000 resales analysed returning a profit.

In Sydney, 11.4 per cent of units sold for less than their purchase price. (ABC: John Gunn)

Head of research at Cotality Gerard Burg said profitability was still "exceptionally high by historical standards" even as a softening housing market pushed down prices.

"Most sellers are still benefiting from the significant value growth accumulated over the past five years, which is providing considerable protection against the early stages of the downturn," he said.

"With home values falling across more markets, that buffer will become increasingly important in determining resale outcomes."

Gerard Burg says the profitability seen in Brisbane contrasted with the weaker performance in Melbourne. (ABC News: Billy Draper)

Mr Burg said there was a "real contrast" in the unit markets, with a "much weaker performance" in Melbourne, where CBD unit values peaked in 2017.

"So, it's very hard to get a profitable resale in that type of environment," he said. "In contrast, there's been a lot of demand for units in Brisbane."

'Normalising of the market'

Brisbane real estate agent Brett Andreassen said the data confirmed what he had been seeing for months — prices have come down.

"It is probably more of a normalising of the market because the last few years were anything but," he said.

"I think because this crazy growth happened over five years, everyone thought that was the normal — when it really wasn't."

Mr Andreassen said sellers whose property had been on the market for months "have still got those previous figures in their heads".

"Whereas a lot of the owners that are coming on the market now have adjusted their expectations to the current reality," he said.

Brisbane real estate agent Brett Andreassen says the drop in resale profits "definitely rings true". (Supplied)

Adelaide was the country's second most profitable capital, followed by Perth with a $472,000 and $470,000 median gain respectively.

Home prices in each city had jumped since COVID-19, when relative affordability had boosted interstate migration, Mr Burg said.

Regions make more gains

Meanwhile, regional markets had higher profitable resales than the capitals, with 97.5 per cent compared to 94.1 per cent.

Metro sellers still made a bigger gain, with a $415,000 median compared to $324,500.

Homes sold in Brisbane last quarter made a median profit of $525,000. (ABC News: Charlie Mclean)

Mr Burg said the downturn put more recent buyers at risk, with homes held for less time more likely to be resold at a loss.

Nationally, the median time between purchase and sale of a house for a profitable resale was typically 9.3 years.

The median time off the market for a loss-making house was 4.4 years.

How a housing downturn affects your city New Cotality modelling data shows what property prices could look like across the capitals if the market falls by 5, 10, 15 or 20 per cent.

"The longer that you hold the property, the less exposed you are to the fluctuations that occur in an individual housing cycle," he said.

Mr Burg said the current trend of declining values was likely to "persist for some time", which could to a profitable sale becoming "more challenging".

"There is significant uncertainty around the short-term economic outlook, particularly the direction of interest rates and increasing pressure on household budgets," he said.

"If housing values continue to fall, we would expect that to place further downward pressure on resale profitability over the coming quarters."

World.title: 'All this money … what for?' The uncomfortable question on Whyalla
World.content:
Whyalla locals have become accustomed to press packs descending on their city, entering their small businesses and asking how they feel about the latest crisis to befall their city.

Whether during the closure of the shipyards in the late 1970s, or the steelworks going into administration in 2016, the responses over the years have been similar.

The community has "gone through a lot" but it will "band together" because it is a "resilient town" looking forward to better days.

Stoicism and optimism aside, when the South Australian government revealed on Monday that the steelworks' ailing blast furnace would be permanently shut at a cost of more than 600 jobs, a new response emerged.

"All this money they've put into the plant, what for?" asked local cafe worker June Worsnop.

Whyalla steelworkers 'stubbornly determined' to keep plant going The closure of the blast furnace at the Whyalla steelworks has not come as a surprise to locals — who say it brings a mix of relief and uncertainty to the regional city's economy and residents.

It's an uncomfortable question given that nearly $3 billion in public funds have been committed to the Whyalla steelworks since February 2025.

And yet the plant is now going to be employing hundreds fewer workers and not producing its own steel, likely for years to come.

The shuttering of the 1960s-built blast furnace is a stark reminder that, 18 months on from the steelworks being tipped into administration, the fruits of the state and federal governments' billions for Whyalla are still a long way away from being realised.

The bulk of those funds — $1.9 billion — are on the table for a new owner to take over the plant and co-invest in a green future, including a new electric arc furnace.

The new steelworks owner will be chosen before the end of the year in what Premier Peter Malinauskas says will be a "significant moment".

Two bidders — Jindal Steel and M Resources — are in the running, while BlueScope Steel retains its right of last offer.

Whyalla's steelmaking gap could last years A resumption of steelmaking in Whyalla could be several years away, following the announcement that hundreds of jobs will go because of the demise of the blast furnace.

"But I won't breathe a sigh of relief, I won't take comfort nor will anyone else in my team until we start seeing that capital being invested in new equipment on the ground," the premier said on Monday.

"Because that's when we'll know that steelmaking in Whyalla in this country has genuinely got a future."

Until then, that familiar uncertainty remains.

"For the first time since steelmaking began in Whyalla," SA Opposition Leader Ashton Hurn said on Monday, "it will be without its primary steelmaking capability".

"And there is now no certainty around when steelmaking will return to the city into the future," she said.

'You can see the helplessness'

The loss of more than 600 jobs in Whyalla will be felt across the whole town, according to local gym owner Justin Fennell, who said he spent an hour on Monday night talking to one of the workers affected.

"A lot of them are only in their 30s, so they've got another 35 years of work ahead of them," he said.

Peter Malinauskas announces the closure of the Whyalla blast furnace. (ABC News: Brant Cumming)

"So, it makes it hard, it really does make it hard for those who have young families, mortgages, you can see the helplessness in them."

For others, like steelworker Steven Sharp, there was both shock and a sense of inevitability.

"We all tried our hardest, we all worked so hard to try and get it [the blast furnace] back, but just unfortunately we couldn't get it done," Mr Sharp, who is taking a redundancy, said.

"Every time something would come up, we'd feel like we were getting a step ahead and then two steps backwards.

" We knew it was a matter of time before it just couldn't go anymore. "

The state government announced on Monday that it would fund between $60 to $80 million in redundancy payments in a split with the Commonwealth.

A further $10.2 million will be made available to help workers transition, including funding for counselling, re-skilling and re-accreditation.

The impact of the job losses is significant, but it was not an unspinnable crisis for the government.

While the blast furnace closure came quicker than the government wanted, the coal-fired oven has been offline since April — giving the government ample time to prepare the public for the pain ahead.

"I think most people who work on the blast furnace, who work at the steelworks, knew that this was coming," Energy and Mining Minister Tom Koutsantonis told 891 ABC Adelaide on Tuesday.

Whyalla steelworker Steven Sharp says workers knew it was "a matter of time" before the blast furnace permanently closed. (ABC News: Brant Cumming)

On the question of what all the money has been for so far, Mr Koutsantonis said: "We haven't spent $1 billion on the blast furnace. We've spent a billion dollars keeping 1,800 people employed while we attempt to recapitalise the steelworks".

The government is also adamant that the blast furnace closure had been factored in by both companies bidding for the steelworks, meaning the sale process was not going to be impacted.

"Nothing that occurs today disrupts or undermines our ability to deliver the long-term vision of Whyalla," the premier said on Monday, "which is to have a new steelmaker with new equipment and new technology making steel that sets Whyalla up for the long term".

But if that were to change, the question about what all the money was for will get a whole lot more uncomfortable.

World.title: Why Australia's most attractive renewables state is almost $1b behind
World.content:
In 2020, the NSW Coalition government outlined a plan for a once-in-a-generation undertaking.

To power Australia's most populous state with renewable energy instead of coal, regional areas would be transformed into power stations.

Renewable energy zones (REZs) would cluster solar, wind farms and batteries around shared transmission lines.

But almost six years on, delivering the infrastructure is taking longer than planned and the state is racing to meet its own targets.

The agency responsible for the rollout, EnergyCo, has spent almost $1 billion less than budgeted over the past two years.

Ty Christopher, who spent decades delivering grid infrastructure in NSW for the previous state-owned energy corporation, Integral Energy, said there was no "single cause" for the delay.

He said it was the result of a "cumulative effect".

"I do think they are not proceeding at the pace that would be in the best interests of energy consumers in New South Wales," Professor Christopher said.

Ty Christopher spent decades delivering electricity infrastructure in NSW. (ABC News: Sissy Reyes)

In 2025-26, EnergyCo had just over $1 billion to build the zones, but spent $686 million.

The year before, in its first year as a standalone agency, it spent $885 million of a $1.44 billion budget.

Over the two years it has spent $939 million less than allocated, more than a third of its budget.

An EnergyCo spokesperson said the gap between budgeted and actual spending "reflects the timing of project milestones, procurement and construction activities, and [is] not a direct measure of REZ delivery progress".

Zones at a glance

Professor Christopher, now the director of the Energy Futures Network at the University of Wollongong, said the money could not flow until the transmission routes are settled with the communities they pass through.

"If they haven't been able to lock in the line routes with local communities, they can't spend the money to buy the easements, or start procuring equipment and building the lines," he said.

" The delays in that first stage, community engagement and consultation, are what we're seeing now in the expenditure against budget. "

NSW Energy Minister Penny Sharpe's office said the amount of large-scale wind and solar operating in NSW had risen more than 80 per cent since the 2023 election.

Its delivery agency, EnergyCo, is held up as a model for other states to follow.

But according to the independent agency tasked with monitoring whether the state is on track to meet its energy goals, NSW needs to be moving a lot faster.

NSW is 7.9 gigawatts (GW) short of its legislated target of 12GW by 2030, and the amount of renewable generation commissioned each year must nearly double to close the gap, according to the NSW Net Zero Commission's latest progress report.

Slowest in the country

Most renewable projects proposed in NSW have drawn significant opposition.

Transmission lines like this one in the Riverina have divided residents. (ABC News: Jess Davis)

Eighty per cent of wind farm proposals and 60 per cent of solar farm proposals in the state have drawn more than 50 opposing submissions, triggering a referral to NSW's independent decision-maker, according to the Net Zero Commission.

An Independent Planning Commission decision takes on average about 90 days, and objectors can then lodge an appeal, adding at least another year to the process.

This is one of the reasons approvals in NSW are among the slowest in the country.

Over the five years to March 2026, NSW had the longest average planning-approval times in the country for wind, solar and batteries, according to analysis by the Clean Energy Investor Group (CEIG).

It currently takes on average almost four years to approve a wind farm in NSW, which compares to just five months in WA and is more than five times longer than in Queensland.

However, investors still rate NSW the most attractive state for renewable investment, according to the CEIG survey.

Penny Sharpe says adjustments have been made to streamline planning approvals. (ABC News: Craig Hansen)

Speaking to reporters in August, Ms Sharpe acknowledged the process had "been way too slow".

She pointed to wind guidelines the government "inherited" that she said were "designed to make building wind farms as hard as possible".

"There's been a huge amount of work … to really try and streamline that," she said.

" We are seeing more projects being approved and coming out of the system, which is very welcome. "

In May the government introduced legislation aimed at fast-tracking approvals for priority clean energy projects.

Lines yet to be built in largest zone

Most of EnergyCo's budget was allocated to fund the early development, planning and land acquisitions required ahead of private operators building transmission lines.

New England is the biggest of the five zones, legislated to supply 8GW, two-thirds of the state's entire 12GW renewable generation target.

More than a year after shortlisting builders, none has been appointed and construction has yet to begin.

EnergyCo has failed to spend a significant amount of its budget set aside for transmission corridors. (Supplied: NSW government)

The transmission route has been redrawn multiple times.

In May it was altered to avoid landholders, challenging landscape and an environmentally sensitive cave system.

EnergyCo said such refinements were "a normal part of developing major infrastructure projects".

But each adjustment delays the start of construction.

The Sapphire wind farm sits in the footprint of the New England REZ and has been operational since 2018. (Supplied: Squadron Energy)

In 2023, the government said New England would not generate power before 2029.

By May 2025, delivery had slipped further, with an initial 6GW now split between 2.4GW by 2032 and 3.6GW by 2034.

There are five renewable energy zones at various stages of development in NSW. (ABC News)

A NSW parliamentary inquiry in July found EnergyCo had "failed to perform its central coordinating role", particularly in the sequencing of development and coordination of infrastructure.

The NSW government is currently considering the inquiry's recommendations.

EnergyCo does not expect to appoint a network operator for the New England REZ before the end of 2027.

Approved projects aren't being built

Of the projects that are approved, many are taking too long to be built or are not being built at all.

Part of the reason is the cautious approach of clean energy investors.

CEIG's survey found more than three-quarters of investors believe the renewable landscape has worsened over the past year.

And just 8 per cent of investors believed Australia was on track to achieve its target of 82 per cent of electricity coming from renewables by 2030.

As governments change their stance on clean energy projects, investors have taken a more cautious approach. (ABC Central West: Hamish Cole)

The cost of building a wind farm has risen by up to 50 per cent, making projects harder to fund.

Of the 31 wind projects awarded support under the federal Capacity Investment Scheme, only four have secured the funding to be built.

Investors also worry they won't be able to sell their power once a project is built.

An influx of wind and solar increases the risk of curtailment, being switched off when the network is full.

Ms Sharpe acknowledged the problem.

"There are projects that have been approved," she said.

"The more challenging issue is: are they getting to financial close?

We have seen real changes with costs and supply chain changes over the last few years."

To help projects reach construction, the NSW government has set up the Energy Security Corporation.

What's coming?

Getting more generation online is the key to allowing coal-fired power stations to close.

The closure of Australia's biggest power station, Eraring in the Hunter, has been delayed twice, most recently pushed back to 2029.

According to the NSW Net Zero Commission, its closure is directly linked to the completion of the Hunter Transmission Project, which connects the large inland REZs with the bulk of the state's energy consumers in Newcastle, Sydney and the Illawarra.

If that line is delayed, the aging plant may have to keep running.

Data centre power demand could help drive funding for renewable projects. (Supplied: Google)

At the same time, energy demand is set to surge.

Data centres currently account for about 4 per cent of NSW's power consumption, but that is expected to surge to about 20 per cent within a decade, according to the Australian Energy Market Operator.

The government has introduced legislation requiring data centres to build enough new renewable generation to meet their needs or sign power purchase agreements.

Ms Sharpe described it as both a risk and an opportunity, saying it could help get renewable projects "over the line" by creating new demand for their power.

Reaching the target

To meet its 12GW target by 2030, the commission says NSW must nearly double the amount of renewable generation it commissions each year.

But an accelerated rollout is likely to keep meeting community resistance.

Professor Christopher was candid about the state's chances of meeting its legislated targets.

"Do I think we'll hit it? Probably not quite," he said.

" Do I think it's in anyone's interest to rewrite the target now? Absolutely not. "

NSW needs to significantly increase renewable energy generation in order to hit its 2030 target. (ABC Central West: Hamish Cole)

Professor Christopher said the plan had been optimistic from the outset.

"The only thing that was overly naive … was people not fully countenancing the degree of community challenge," he said.

"That was underestimated."

But Professor Christopher warned against giving up on the target.

"Bold outcomes will never be achieved from setting timid targets," he said.

World.title: Friends of Australian man shocked he killed his kids in Bali
World.content:
Friends of Damien John Shaw have described their shock and horror after the Australian man apparently killed himself and his two children at their Bali home on Sunday.

WARNING: This story contains graphic descriptions some readers may find distressing.

Bali police are investigating what they say is a double murder-suicide, after the bodies of the 56-year-old and his six-year-old son and four-year-old daughter were found inside their bungalow in the popular tourist resort of Kuta.

If you or anyone you know needs help: Lifeline on 131 114

Beyond Blue on 1300 224 636

13 YARN on 13 92 76

Suicide Call Back Service on 1300 659 467

MensLine Australia on 1300 789 978

Denpasar City police have interviewed the children's mother, who was in Jakarta with family when the attack unfolded.

She had called a neighbour to perform a welfare check on her family, after she said a call to her husband disengaged and she heard one of her children crying.

'Acts of violence'

Denpasar City police said an autopsy would not be carried out on the children at the request of their mother.

"Initial external findings suggest the two children died as a result of acts of violence," the police said in a statement.

Police say the children died at their home at the hands of their father. (Supplied: Indonesian police)

Police said Mr Shaw died by suicide.

"From the CCTV there is no indication of another perpetrator," Chief Commissioner Leonard Simatupang said.

He said CCTV had recorded the children screaming.

Divorce proceedings

Mr Shaw's wife told police she had filed for a divorce in 2022.

"The reason was that the husband is temperamental, but later she revoked the case as the husband was showing improvements," Chief Commissioner Simatupang said.

"There is no medical psychiatric record about the man; it had only come from the wife's statement that the husband is temperamental and having high anxiety."

'Gaunt' appearance

Bunbury resident Tania Dagnall said she and her husband had been friends with Mr Shaw for the past 11 years.

She said they had caught up with the man they called "Damo" just three months ago in Bali and immediately noticed his "gaunt" appearance.

Damien Shaw, 56, used to work in the oil and gas industry. (LinkedIn)

"I was shocked looking at him; he didn't look like him when he walked up and joined us for coffee … he was not the buff dude I was used to seeing," she told the ABC.

"If he has done this, there's no excuse for it, never any excuse for that, ever.

" It's just horrific. "

Ms Dagnall said she was sad that Mr Shaw had not reached out to them.

"We could have been on a plane," she said.

Long-term Bali resident

The ABC understands Mr Shaw was originally from Perth but had lived in Bali for decades and had converted to Islam when he married his wife about six or seven years ago.

To comply with his adopted faith, friends say he stopped drinking alcohol and did not touch drugs.

Suspected murder-suicide in Bali Indonesian police are investigating a suspected murder-suicide after the bodies of an Australian man and his two children were found in a home in Bali.

He previously worked as an able seaman in the oil and gas industry, but retired from this fly-in, fly-out role to spend more time at home, Ms Dagnall said, often taking the children to school and swimming lessons.

"We honestly thought he was living the life, retire to a beautiful place, have a couple of kids," she said.

Mr Shaw had several properties in Perth and overseas, including a house in Japan, Ms Dagnall said, which he used as a base for snowboarding.

'I can't understand'

Despite being financially stable, Mr Shaw's marriage had become tense in recent months, friends say.

They cannot comprehend how he could have murdered his children.

"I can't understand why he would have done such a terrible thing. It just breaks our hearts," Ms Dagnall said.

Police said Mr Shaw's body was being examined at Sanglah Hospital.

Meanwhile, officers are continuing the forensic processing of the crime scene and reviewing CCTV footage from inside and outside the property.

World.title: Australia news LIVE: AI chief rejects calls for regulation, US confirms it has weapons in space
World.content:
Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has rejected calls for new artificial intelligence laws, telling the Dreamforce conference in San Francisco this morning that safety could be solved by engineers rather than regulators.

“The market forces are already there,” Huang said. “We don’t need any new laws, we don’t need any new regulations.“

Jensen Huang, chief executive officer of Nvidia Corp. Bloomberg

His comments came days after Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei called for a coordinated industry slowdown and independent auditing of safety work, a position backed in part by OpenAI, Google DeepMind and SpaceX.

Huang said safety was “job one” but described it as an engineering problem. Companies should not release products they were not confident in, he said, and could pause voluntarily without government involvement.

The chipmaker is the largest beneficiary of the AI buildout. Huang spoke a day after US President Donald Trump telephoned him mid-interview in Los Angeles to call AI safety fears “a hoax”, according to the New York Times. Some 50,000 attendees are in San Francisco for Salesforce’s annual AI conference, with around 10 million tuning in online according to the company.

David Swan travelled to San Francisco as a guest of Salesforce.

World.title: ASX eyes gains, Wall Street slips as oil prices, bond market crank up pressure; Bitcoin falls
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX eyes gains, Wall Street slips as oil prices, bond market crank up pressure; Bitcoin falls Stan Choe Updated September 16, 2026 — 6:33am ,first published 5:13am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks slipped after oil prices and the bond market cranked up the pressure on Wall Street. The S&P 500 fell 0.4 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 328 points, or 0.6 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite sank 0.8 per cent. Wall Street lost ground on Tuesday. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to rise, with futures at 6.18am AEST pointing to a gain of 31 points, or 0.4 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.9 per cent on Tuesday as it closed at its lowest level in almost three months. The Australian dollar was lower at US71.31¢. Wall Street felt pressure as the yield on the 10-year Treasury, which is the centrepiece of the US bond market, climbed to 5.00 per cent from 4.97 per cent late Monday and briefly touched 5.04 per cent overnight. It’s been jumping to its highest level in years, and Monday was the first time it breached 5 per cent since 2023.



Higher yields mean everyone from the US government to households to businesses must pay more in interest to borrow money, which slows the overall economy. They also make people less willing to pay high prices for stocks because they can earn more from sitting in bonds, which are considered safer investments. Related Article Opinion

Interest rates Trump set to explode if his man does his job Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist “The result is a market that must work harder to generate earnings growth just as investors become less willing to pay premium valuations for that growth,” according to Darrell Cronk, president of Wells Fargo Investment Institute. The last time the 10-year yield was consistently above 5 per cent was around the turn of the millennium, and it’s been a long march back since it bottomed out below 0.50 per cent in 2020. The pace has accelerated since February, after the war with Iran sent oil prices much higher. That raised worries about high inflation potentially lasting for years, which are layering atop longstanding concerns about the US government’s massive debt level and other issues.



Oil prices rose further Tuesday following several sharp swings in the morning. The price for a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, climbed 2.9 per cent to settle at $108.75. It remains well above its $US72 level from early July and from before the war with Iran began in February, as doubt continues about whether the fighting will allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf anytime soon through the Strait of Hormuz. Inflation remains high enough that the widespread expectation is that the Federal Reserve will announce on Wednesday that it will hike the federal funds rate for the first time in three years. Traders are still betting on a slight chance that the Federal Reserve could hold off on hiking interest rates, though. If it does, the market could swing because investors may see it as a sign that the Fed is less committed to getting inflation lower. Fed officials will also release forecasts for where they see interest rates heading in upcoming years, providing another opportunity to inject uncertainty into the market.



On Wall Street, stocks of companies that depend on customers having enough spare cash to spend on their products fell to some of the sharper losses. Related Article Opinion

Sydney Sweeney There’s a seriously bad industry behind Sweeney’s seriously bad ad Kishor Napier-Raman Senior Business Writer Chipotle Mexican Grill dropped 5.9 per cent. Darden Restaurants, the company behind Olive Garden and Longhorn Steakhouse, sank 4.3 per cent. Dollar Tree, whose customers may have less financial cushion than others, fell 5.4 per cent. Dave & Buster’s Entertainment tumbled 19 per cent after reporting weaker results for the latest quarter than analysts expected.



Elsewhere on Wall Street, stocks enmeshed in the cryptocurrency industry sank after the US Senate voted to block legislation creating a new regulatory framework for crypto, while demanding more limits on President Donald Trump’s investments. The price of Bitcoin slumped 4.2 per cent to $US75,920 at 6.50am AEST. Coinbase Global fell 10.1 per cent, and Robinhood Markets lost 3.4 per cent. Several artificial-intelligence stocks meanwhile held steadier following their worldwide slide the day before, after leaders of the AI industry called for a slowdown in development to address safety issues for humanity. Nvidia added 0.6 per cent a day after its 3.4 per cent drop was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500 index. Advanced Micro Devices climbed 2.2 per cent. Such stocks led the US market to records for years, but they’ve come under pressure recently on worries that their prices shot too high in the frenzy around AI.



All told, the S&P 500 fell 34.25 points to 7,585.73. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 328.09 to 52,093.11, and the Nasdaq composite fell 204.84 to 25,981.57. In stock markets abroad, indexes fell across much of Europe and Asia. But for several, the drops were not as sharp as Monday’s caused by the slide for AI stocks. South Korea’s Kospi index, for example, fell 0.9 per cent following Monday’s 3.3 per cent drop. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Wild, profane and heartbreaking: A guide to Anthony Bourdain’s best TV
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In the parlance of the business in which Anthony Bourdain made his name, the film Tony is the first course in an extended tasting menu. It’s the appetiser of a degustation menu that will run over many servings and involve many ingredients and helping hands. Related Article Cinema Before he played Anthony Bourdain, Dominic Sessa couldn’t have picked him out of a police line-up The film, which is now in cinemas, is a coming-of-age drama about a restless, angry and punch-drunk teenager (played by Dominic Sessa) on a summer-season bender of rebellion, booze, unrequited first love and soul-searching. It’s the origin story of the man who decades later would become executive chef of a feted Manhattan restaurant, a bestselling author and a frighteningly prolific TV presenter. The film foreshadows the book that propelled chef Bourdain’s meteoric second act in 2000, when Kitchen Confidential: Adventures in the Culinary Underbelly (it’s worth remembering the book’s full title) became a global bestseller. It kicks off with this memorable passage from the book’s opening chapter. “I was … a spoiled, miserable, narcissistic, self-destructive and thoughtless young lout, badly in need of a good ass-kicking”. His words. Loading It vividly pinpoints many of the qualities that would make Bourdain one of the unique, original and treasured figures TV has ever known. He was a mercurial and mouthy personality who wore his heart on his sleeve, ever inquisitive, with a yen for adventure, food, pleasure and companionship, and a well-documented taste for drugs and addictive behaviours. Bourdain died by suicide in 2018, reportedly after the breakdown of a relationship, though the toxicology report indicated he wasn’t taking drugs at the time. It’s not entirely surprising nor unexpected that Tony has also renewed interest in his TV shows.



It was here, Bourdain’s third act, as a TV presenter after quitting professional cooking following his book’s success (and revelations of the restaurant world’s unglamorous secrets), where the magic really happens. Bourdain tasting local dishes in Lima in No Reservations. First came A Cook’s Tour (SBS On Demand, Tubi). Made for the US Food Network between 2002 and 2003, it has Bourdain visiting the world’s “foodie” hotspots (Sydney and Melbourne included), eating in starred restaurants and local greasy spoons, meeting with food-scene celebrities and what would decades later be known as influencers. It’s very much in the boilerplate format of food and travel shows, and the least interesting of his TV work. The middling quality of the video has certainly not helped its longevity. Editor's pick Streaming Flawed, authentic, and uniquely ours: There’s nothing like Colin From Accounts It was in No Reservations (2005-12, Amazon Prime Video) and Parts Unknown (2013-18, Amazon Prime Video, 7Plus, 10Play) that Bourdain, his crew and creative partners took flight. They invented a format and style that transcends most if not all the norms of the food and travel genre. These shows aren’t about plugging destinations or theme parks, or even to paint a rosy picture of a place. In the Beirut episode of No Reservations, for instance, Bourdain and his crew arrive the day before war breaks out. From their luxury hotel they keep the cameras rolling, ever aware that despite their safety and boredom the rest of the population is in peril. The episode ends with this heartbreaking passage: “Maybe in the real world, the one without cameras and happy food and travel shows, everybody, the good and the bad together, are all crushed under the same terrible wheel. I really hope I’m wrong about that.” Bourdain in front of the Beirut cityscape.



Bourdain and Barack Obama sit down for a meal in Hanoi in 2016. An image from Morgan Neville’s documentary Roadrunner. Focus Features via AP These are shows that use travel and food as their starting points, but are mostly about people living in diverse parts of the globe, their cultures, habits and histories, their dreams, disappointments and hopes. Editor's pick Review What to stream this week: Patrick Brammall’s home-grown thriller, plus five more picks They are also about how Bourdain saw himself. The shows are opinionated, brash, wild and profane, as well as tender and occasionally heartbreaking – much like Tony in the film. In many episodes of No Reservations and Parts Unknown, Bourdain openly and unsentimentally discusses his depression. In Tony, the character finds salvation in the kitchen after a particularly dark and unpleasant night on the town by learning how to cook and then observing the joy that brings to diners. He also finds companionship among the fellow dirtbags toiling in the kitchen’s insufferable conditions (shout-out to Stavros Halkias as Dimitri, a character who also appears in Kitchen Confidential). Just as Kitchen Confidential lifted the lid on the dirty secrets of the hospitality trade, Bourdain’s TV shows are no less scathing of food porn and fame, not to mention his role in the dog and pony circuit of book signings and celebrity-chef talks. “Look at me now travelling the world like a Borscht Belt comedian,” he says while visiting a food festival in New Zealand in No Reservations. The willingness to make himself the butt of the joke is evident in Tony too.



Bourdain had a good eye for television. It’s hard to fathom the scale of Bourdain’s output: 104 episodes of Parts Unknown and 142 episodes of No Reservations. Bourdain died during filming of Parts Unknown, leaving a few episodes without his narration (there’s also two posthumous tribute instalments). Each episode has its own unique flavour and style, invariably shaped around a destination’s depiction in popular culture, such as a movie associated with that place. Apocalypse Now for the Congo, Mad Max for “the arse end of the world”, Australia. The final course of the Bourdain feast is arguably the most challenging. It’s the little seen 2021 feature-length documentary Roadrunner: A Film About Anthony Bourdain (Apple TV, Amazon Prime Video). It’s a difficult and painful reckoning by those who intimately knew Bourdain, focusing largely on his globetrotting, TV career after Kitchen Confidential and how his life unravelled in the months leading up to his suicide. Loading Many of the people that director Morgan Neville interviewed in Roadrunner appeared in one or more episodes of No Reservations and Parts Unknown. Bourdain’s TV family included chefs, artists, filmmakers, musicians and writers. There’s a lovely nod to that in Tony, in a pivotal scene where the charismatic French chef Eric Ripert has a blink-and-miss cameo. Ripert frequently appeared in the shows and his presence is a touching reminder of how loyal people were to Bourdain. In many ways Tony and Roadrunner are perfect bookends of Bourdain’s career and life. They shine a light on the unique talent he brought to his still luminous TV shows. If you or anyone you know needs support, call Lifeline on 13 11 14, or Beyond Blue on 1300 224 636.

World.title: Asia’s original luxury tented paradise lies just beyond Bali
World.content:
★★★★★ Reviews & adviceHotel reviews Asia’s original luxury tented paradise lies just beyond Bali Penny Watson September 16, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The resort Amanwana, Moyo Island, Indonesia Check-in Amanwana is tucked into a secluded cove on the island’s west coast, looking out to the Flores Sea. A black SUV collects me from Sumbawa’s Sultan Muhammad Kaharuddin Airport for the 20-minute drive to a private harbour where I’m offered toilet facilities and a cold towel before boarding Aman X, the resort’s two-level open-air cruiser. On the upper level it’s an exciting windswept 45-minute ride across the Flores Sea to the resort where staff wave welcomingly from the wooden pier. On shore, I’m treated to a refreshing tamarind welcome drink (and another cool towel) before being escorted to my tent for an easy-going check-in.



The look 



More like luxury suites than tents … tent interiors. The spacious en suite features a large egg-shaped soaking tub. The resort’s luxury tents are large (58 square metres), rectangular and categorised according to location – jungle, ocean view and ocean front. They’re sturdily built, with teak window and door frames, solid walls and hardy canvas rooftops. Which is to say, they feel more like luxury suites than tents except perhaps when the monkeys jump on the roof, or a gecko scurries through the bathroom. The interiors radiate luxury, with the white bed linen, mosquito nets, blinds and couches softened by dark hardwood floors, carved wood furnishings and rattan mats. I’m staying in an ocean-front tent. From the central king-sized bed I have 180-degree views across Amanwana Bay. Stepping outside, there’s a hammock swaying between the trees, umbrella-shaded recliners and two deck chairs. From any of these restful places it’s possible to see black-tipped reef sharks playing in the protected marine park shallows. Food + drink



Cocktail hours … the open-air, beachside bar at Amanwana. In my tent, little desktop glass jars are constantly topped up with cookies, cashews (which grow on the island) and yummy Indonesian kerupuk crackers. The mini-bar is generously stocked (and all-inclusive), but it’s tempting to gravitate to the breezy main pavilion for evening cocktails. Breakfast, lunch and dinner is also served in this huge space on round teak tables with white table cloths. Indonesian dishes are the specialty, the best of which is a Sumbawanese bakela meaning “sharing from one platter”. The feast is traditionally cooked on special occasions and stars a central cone of nasi kuning (yellow rice) surrounded by little dishes including spicy beef curry, grilled chicken, fish steamed in banana leaf, and urap, a delicious salad made from cooked greens, bamboo shoots and grated coconut. Out + about Mata Jitu waterfall deep in the jungle at Moyo Island. Moyo Island, neighbouring Satonda island and the surrounding waterways have been protected since 1976 and were gazetted national and marine park in 2022. Together, they form an idyllic playground where guests can chase waterfalls, hike, kayak, scuba dive and snorkel. The cascading limestone pools of Moyo’s Mata Jitu waterfall is a highlight, especially when paired with the resort’s floating sound bath experience.



The verdict Related Article Air travel Free flights on offer to spread Indonesia tourism beyond Bali Amanwana is one of Asia’s most bucket-listed luxury resort destinations. The remote location and tented approach ensure it is relaxed and comfortable (rather than fussy or pretentious) and an immersion in pristine nature. Essentials Double tents from $2991 a night, with a three-night minimum. Includes round-trip car and boat transfers from Sumbawa Airport; full board including daily breakfast, lunch and dinner; in-room refreshments and non-alcoholic beverages; laundry; and use of non-motorised watersports equipment. Amanwana, Moyo Island, West Sumbawa Regency, West Nusa Tenggara, Indonesia. See aman.com



Our score out of five ★★★★★ Highlight Marine park snorkelling straight off the beach. Lowlight



Sadly the whale shark experience is not animal-friendly. Whale sharks are hand-fed from a fishing boat, so they just stay in the one position and fish are thrown into their mouths. The writer stayed as a guest of Amanwana.

World.title: How many cups of coffee you need a day to protect your liver
World.content:
Tips & adviceCoffee How many cups of coffee you need a day to protect your liver A new study links consumption of our favourite pick-me-up to lower risk of cirrhosis. And if it’s instant, even better. David Cox September 16, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Scientists are increasingly discovering that coffee can boost multiple parts of our body, from the gut to the brain. But some of the clearest benefits of all apply to the liver, a vital yet fragile organ which we need for filtering toxins and medications from the blood and storing crucial vitamins and minerals. It’s good news for those who enjoy several coffees a day. Getty Images A new study, which tracked 355,000 adults in the UK for 13 years, has discovered that people who consumed the most coffee – five or more cups per day – had a significantly lower risk of cirrhosis (advanced liver scarring) and liver cancer. In fact, blood tests revealed that they had higher levels of proteins linked to healthy liver function. The findings have particularly intrigued scientists, because it appears that drinking coffee may offer protection against the development of fatty liver disease, one of the world’s fastest emerging chronic health conditions, which in some cases can ultimately lead to liver cancer. “To me, I think the sweet spot lies with three to five cups a day.” Hyunseok Kim, assistant professor of medicine at Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University.



Estimates suggest that as many as one in three adults in the UK may have some form of fatty liver disease, while across Europe there has been a 50 per cent rise in deaths from liver cancer since 2000. “This form of liver disease typically develops because fat starts to accumulate within the liver which perceives the fat as foreign,” says Hyunseok Kim, assistant professor of medicine at Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University, who led the latest study.who led the latest study. “So the liver attacks, causing inflammation, and if that persists, it leads to progressive scarring which can then serve as a background for liver cancer to grow.” The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up It appears that coffee could interrupt this process, as well as slow down other diseases. Instant coffee is good for you liver, studies show. Rhett Wyman Why coffee is so good for your liver



When Jonathan Dranoff, a professor of medicine at Yale University, sees patients with signs of fatty liver disease, he makes four recommendations: do more exercise, reduce intake of sugar and refined carbohydrates, limit or quit alcohol, and drink more coffee. “I actually do prescribe therapeutic coffee to people that are at risk,” says Prof Dranoff. In the late 1980s, Norwegian scientists discovered that people who consumed more coffee had lower levels of three key liver enzymes, a sign that their livers were under less stress. As well as appearing to protect people against liver scarring and cancer, coffee drinking has even been shown to slow disease progression in people living with hepatitis C, a blood-borne viral infection which causes liver inflammation. The most popular explanation relates to caffeine, a powerful stimulant which has many functions. Research has shown, for example, for people with fatty liver disease, caffeine may shield the liver by preventing the production of scar tissue. People who drank tea instead of coffee did not seem to have the same liver protection. iStock This caffeine theory is supported by studies which have shown that people who consume tea as their hot drink of choice, which has a notably lower caffeine content, do not appear to get the same amount of liver protection.



But it may not be the full story. As well as caffeine, coffee contains at least 100 different plant chemicals, which help stimulate the liver’s own innate antioxidant defences, protecting liver cells from injury. The Cedars-Sinai study showed that people who consumed multiple cups of decaffeinated coffee each day, also seemed to benefit from some degree of liver protection. Coffee is also great for the gut which supports the liver Drinking more coffee may also be helping the liver by altering the gut microbiome in various beneficial ways. Excessive amounts of alcohol, sugar and saturated fat can stimulate the growth of pathogenic bacteria within the gut, as well as triggering local inflammatory responses which make the gut more leaky. This then leads to various microbes ending up in the bloodstream and provoking a wider inflammatory response that harms the liver. It appears that coffee could have a soothing effect on the gut, promoting the growth of beneficial bacteria. The plant compounds in coffee may also improve the composition of microbes in the gut, and consequently reduce inflammation.



So how many cups is really best? A lot of this depends on your ability to tolerate caffeine, a stimulant which isn’t appropriate for everyone, as people metabolise it in different ways depending on their genetics. Pregnant and breastfeeding women shouldn’t exceed 200mg of caffeine per day. But if you can handle plenty of caffeine without noticing any ill effects, like jitteriness, insomnia, or an irregular heartbeat, then Dranoff says that it may actually benefit you to be drinking anywhere between two and four standard sized cups (around 200ml) of coffee, containing up to 90mg of caffeine. Kim believes that the maximum liver benefit may be achieved with five cups of coffee a day, based on his latest findings. “Beyond five cups, the liver benefits plateaued, while people might start getting palpitations or negative effects on other organs due to the caffeine,” he says. “To me, I think the sweet spot lies with three to five cups a day.” Filter and instant coffee are believed to have the best effect on liver function.



How best to drink coffee for your liver health? Some of the cheapest ways to consume coffee may also be some of the most effective. When Dranoff prescribes therapeutic coffee, he recommends drip coffee, for example versions made via a cafetiere, or slowly filtering hot water through ground coffee in a paper filter. He also believes that instant coffee has similar benefits. If you’re an espresso lover, Dranoff suggests boosting the benefits by choosing a long black, because this is made with a double shot of espresso and so carries more caffeine. However, right now the strongest evidence is for either filter or instant coffee. Adding a splash of milk for some extra flavour is also thought to be fine. However, scientists are highly sceptical about popular milkshake-style coffees, which are not just made by roasting beans, but also with a sizeable amount of added milk, cream and sugar, such as a Frappuccino. In such cases, they believe that the calorific nature of these drinks is definitely cancelling out any health benefits provided by the actual coffee. In his study, Kim noticed that people who consumed their coffee with sweeteners, whether sugar or artificial sweeteners, seemed to have more liver inflammation. However, this doesn’t mean that you have to stick with black coffee for the rest of your days.

World.title: My daughter’s ex-boyfriend is interning in my office. Can I tell HR he’s a creep?
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsGot a Minute? My daughter’s ex-boyfriend is interning in my office. Can I tell HR he’s a creep? Kirstin Ferguson September 16, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Each week Dr Kirstin Ferguson tackles questions about workplace, career and leadership in her advice column Got a Minute? This week: preventing a sexting scandal, burning eyes and a backfill hire with a fancy new title. Before going to HR, get all your facts together. Dionne Gain Over several years, my daughter’s ex-boyfriend sexted and sent unsolicited photos of his penis to some of her friends and acquaintances. He is very bright and has now obtained an internship at the professional firm where I work. Am I obliged to tell HR, or should I stay quiet? I am worried he may continue this behaviour with colleagues or clients. This is a genuinely difficult issue, but it is not a situation you have created; his behaviour has done that. I can’t imagine how hard this has been for your daughter and, by extension, you. Before you do anything, it is important you are clear as to your level of certainty about what actually happened. Did any of the friends or acquaintances make a complaint to the police? Did you see the images yourself or were you simply told about them? Are you confident they were unsolicited? If you have direct knowledge of what happened or credible evidence of repeated non-consensual conduct, then you might consider making a confidential disclosure to a senior person in HR. Keep your account entirely factual and explain what you know and why you have concerns. It is then for HR to decide what happens next. Your only role, if you feel you need to act, is to raise the issue – you will have no say in determining what happens after that and will need to be satisfied with the outcome whatever it might be.



Related Article Got a Minute? I was accused of intimidating my boss. How can I keep working with them? While any disclosure you make will be treated confidentially, you should also consider it likely the ex-boyfriend has probably been worried you might say something and so will likely guess it was you who made the disclosure. If he tries to retaliate in any way, you must make sure HR is aware. The cleaners at work have been spraying a carpet deodoriser every week, and it burns my eyes. I have made multiple requests to both the cleaners and to management to have this stopped, but my boss just told me to open a few windows and said no one else had complained. My doctor gave me a few days off work as my eyes were puffy, and he said I had a severe chemical irritation. When I returned to work, my boss called me in and threatened me that if I went onto workers’ compensation over this, that it would not look great for any career ambitions I had with the company and told me I was completely overreacting and making a big deal of it. I don’t know what to do. Frankly, your boss’s response is even more concerning than the spray being used. Your boss has been told about a medical injury caused by a hazard at work, and you have been threatened with a negative impact on your career if you seek workers’ compensation. That is a problem – for your boss and the organisation – on many levels. You need to keep a record of everything, including what your boss has said and when. Keep all the medical evidence you have and the earlier requests to change the deodoriser. You can then make a formal notification of a medically documented workplace injury to HR or your health and safety representative and ask for your exposure to be limited to the area while the risk is assessed. At the same time, you might like to report your concerns about the risk to your career for raising the matter. If this fails, get in touch with your workplace safety regulator or your union.



Related Article Got a Minute? What’s the best small talk for an introvert at a work event? This week, I returned to my role after spending 11 months elsewhere in the team. The person who backfilled me has now been appointed for 12 weeks to a newly created project manager role, despite having no project experience. They are also continuing to perform my role for several weeks under the guise of a handover. Management brushed off my concerns, saying the arrangement is only temporary. The inflated title implies authority and status the work does not warrant and feels like a professional slap in the face. Am I overreacting? Yes, I think you may be overreacting. It is a bruise to your ego for sure, but challenging the title itself is unlikely to get you anywhere. Try to focus only on what might be impacting you doing the job you are employed to do. A handover should have an end date so check with your manager to confirm who should be doing what over that period. I would avoid focusing on the level of experience you feel your colleague has. It could look like you only care about titles and status for yourself and not what might be best for the team. Good luck. To submit a question about work, careers or leadership, visit kirstinferguson.com/ask. You will not be asked to provide your name or any identifying information. Letters may be edited.
