World.title: As Trump’s popularity slides, his merchandise stores are closing down
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaTrump's America As Trump’s popularity slides, his merchandise stores are closing down Michael Koziol September 16, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

What in the World, a free weekly newsletter from our foreign correspondents, is sent every Thursday. Below is an excerpt. Sign up to get the whole newsletter delivered to your inbox. Knoxville, Tennessee: The sign is hard to miss as you drive along the Interstate 40 leaving Knoxville. “Trump Superstore”, it booms. “GOING OUT OF BUSINESS.” Everything store wide: 50 per cent off. I had heard about these places – great temples to Donald Trump, packed with merchandise and paraphernalia – but had never been inside one. Trump merch is usually sold by hawkers outside Republican events; this was a bricks-and-mortar shop, albeit on the barren side of a highway. A Trump superstore outside Knoxville Tennessee, which is closing down due to a lack of business. Michael Koziol The range of gear is certainly broad. Caps feature phrases such as “Trump 2028”, “Make America Charlie Kirk” and “Relax, It’s Just A Red Hat”. Several T-shirts announce their wearer is proudly voting for a convicted felon. There are Trump baby clothes, fake Trump cash, Donald and Melania bobble-head dolls, beer holders and more.



There are also some pretty spicy items condemning Democrat Joe Biden, America’s 46th president. “I could shit a better president,” one cap says. Another says, simply: “86 46″. (“86” is a slang term in restaurants for getting rid of something, and some say that in mob lingo, it means to kill someone.) Behind the cash register, I meet Sharon Huskisson, who started working here when the store opened on April 1, 2024. It’s owned by her 80-year-old neighbour, Bill Hays, who offered her the job. Sharon Huskisson, employee at the Trump Superstore in Knoxville, Tennessee, which is closing down. Michael Koziol “I said, ‘Oh, that sounds interesting’. And, of course, I love Trump, so why wouldn’t I,” Huskisson says. “It’s been a big, wonderful ride for the last 2½ years, meeting some really cool, neat people, and everybody is of the same mindset.” She pauses. “We have a few of them that are not. But we tolerate them.” Huskisson says the Trump Superstore was packed as soon as it opened, through to the 2024 election, and past Trump’s inauguration.



“It was hard to even get in here. People were lining up all the way to the parking lot. When two left, we let two more in ... It was amazing, we were like little creatures running around just trying to appease everybody.” It’s evident that’s no longer the case. Only three customers appear during my hour-long visit – including a local couple, Karyn and Bill Robbins, who are adding more T-shirts and stickers to their substantial stocks of Trump gear. Trump lovers Karyn and Bill Robbins from Tennessee at the Trump Superstore in Knoxville. Michael Koziol “We love to wear our shirts and hats out everywhere, showing our support for the president and for his cabinet,” says Karyn, 58. “I love everything he does. He is thinking about America. And they can say all the bad things they want about him, but if you look, he is doing great things for America. You just have to look at what he’s doing, and have your eyes open.” Later, a woman enters the store and quickly buys a large “Gulf of America” flag, celebrating Trump’s renaming of the Gulf of Mexico early in his second term.



This store is not the only one that’s closing down. Trump Town USA in Boones Mill, Virginia, is shutting down, with The Wall Street Journal reporting its sales were just a 10th of what they were in 2024. A store in Bucks County, Pennsylvania, closed its doors in July after six years. Another in Manchester, Tennessee, has also wound down. When I ask Huskisson why the Knoxville store is closing, she puts it diplomatically. “I think everything runs its course. It’s not anything against Trump or anybody else. It’s just all good things come to an end.” The Trump Superstore in Knoxville, Tennessee. Michael Koziol The owner, Bill Hays, was more forthright when he spoke to The Daily Beast last month: “Lack of business.” Polls indicate that Trump is an unpopular president conducting an unpopular war – resulting in higher petrol prices, which are also, obviously, unpopular.



But that sentiment is not uniform across the country. In red states such as Tennessee, Trump-backed candidates have broadly been winning their primary races. His star may be waning in swing states, but in the heartland, Trump is still a force to be reckoned with. Related Article Vale At Dollywood, I discovered the real reason she is America’s sweetheart “I think we’re all still behind him,” Huskisson says. “Something like [the Iran war] takes time. And he is a great negotiator. I hate wars, but they’re inevitable sometimes. “You know, when you elect somebody, you elect them under the faith that they’re going to do the best for the country, and you just have to let them work at it.” Before I leave, I ask Huskisson about the “86 46” caps regarding Joe Biden. She laughs and shrugs. But don’t they encourage violence against an American president?



“Kinda, sorta,” Huskisson says. It’s really just a restaurant term, she assures me. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: More sick days, help with childcare: What NZ employers are offering staff
World.content:
Could I run out of money in retirement and other questions experts wish you'd ask No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 15m

Fancy some extra sick days for when your kids pick up a daycare bug? Or an on-site nanny to let you bring your kids to work with you?

For some parents managing the juggle of early parenting, it might sound like a fever dream. But Stephanie Pow - whose business Crayon runs New Zealand's Parental Leave Register - says some New Zealand businesses are already offering these perks.

She has released updated data for 2026 showing policy details of 370 employers that employ about one in six New Zealanders.

Of those employers, 92 percent offered more than the statutory minimum leave requirement, which is 52 weeks' leave for staff who have worked for an employer at least 10 hours a week for the year before having their child.

The Government offers a payment for 26 weeks, at a rate of $811.05 a week.

What employers are doing to hold on to staff who are parents Morning Report Download MP3 2m

About half the employers on the register were topping up that Government payment and 38 percent were continuing to pay a person's full salary.

Pow said, over 12 months, 20 employers had introduced new policies and 29 had made improvements. Thirteen started offering between two and four weeks of paid partner's leave. Kiwibank became the first employer registered as offering leave for foetal abnormalities and postnatal depression.

Eight had restricted their policies in the year. "I think that's encouraging given the environment we find ourselves in…the good news is that the vast majority kept their policy the same and certainly the number of improvements outnumbered the number of rollbacks six to one," Pow said.

Pow said New Zealand was one of just three developed countries that had no provision for leave for a partner. "Having employers step up there is just as important as having them step up for primary carers.

"We are starting to see policies that encompass much more than that. Not just paid leave but how employees are supported before, during and after parental leave. That might include family formation, it can include pregnancy loss support, how annual leave is treated… noting that will change when the Employment Act comes into effect in two years... It can also include return to work support. That can be one of the trickiest transitions for people coming back from parental leave, what does that look like in terms of re-onboarding, coaching and the confidence piece… and dealing with sick kids."

She said some employers were offering additional "use it or lose it" sick leave to help parents manage children's illnesses.

Sixteen employers were helping with childcare costs, and 12 percent offered returning parents the option to work 50 percent to 80 percent of their base hours for 100 percent of their pay during a predefined ramp-up period, typically lasting one to six months.

Pow said New Zealand's 26 weeks of paid parental leave was higher than the OECD average but the relatively low wage replacement rate meant the country was in the bottom quartile of what primary carers could get from the government.

Some employers were requiring that staff committed to returning to work to access the additional payments. This was more common in the public sector.

Amelia Hooper, head of marketing at Tax Traders, said she had benefited from her employer's generous policy.

She was able to take her son with her to work two days a week because there was an on-site nanny.

"Parental policy is something I hadn't thought about until I was pregnant… I don't think you should have to choose between being a mum and having a career as well."

She said having a supportive employer meant she had come back to work sooner than she might have if she did not have flexibility and childcare support.

"I'm offered a flexible return to work, the on-site nanny and children are really welcomed at work as well which is really nice.

"It's made it more accessible for me to come back to work, which then means they don't have to fill my position. I think it's a benefit for both people and it allows me to continue in my career."

She said she had six months of full pay on leave and then if she worked 30 hours a week she was paid for 40.

World.title: Tonga Tala make it two from two at Netball World Cup qualifier
World.content:
Tonga's netballers are two from two at the 2027 Netball World Cup Oceania Qualifier in Nuku'alofa.

The Tonga Tala beat Papua New Guinea 71-47 on Tuesday, while in the day's other game, Fiji came from behind to beat the Cook Islands 65-63.

The Tala had also won their first match against the Cooks Islands, 81-55, on Monday.

Samoa had opened the tournament with a 72-56 win over PNG Pepes.

On Wednesday evening, Samoa Tifaimoana plays Fiji Pearls and PNG Pepes face the Cook Islands.

Tonga has a bye on Wednesday and will be back in action against Fiji on Thursday.

Games continue on Thursday and Friday, with the top two teams overall qualifying for next year's Netball World Cup in Sydney.

Tonga Netball Association chief executive Salote Sisifa had said before the tournament Tonga was confident of securing one of two remaining spots.

She said the Tala's Commonwealth Games campaign had offered valuable lessons.

"Tonga came out 9th place out of 12 top teams that were participating. And we take the learnings off that. Tonga was of course the only team from Pacific there."

Sisifa said Oceania Netball - of which she is also president - and Tonga need to work towards narrowing the gap between local players and the high-performance level required to compete internationally.

World.title: Two killed in crash between truck and car on State Highway 29 in Waikato
World.content:
Two people have died in a crash involving a truck and car in Karapiro around 6am.

The Serious Crash Unit and other emergency services are still working at the scene between the intersection of SH27 and SH1 Karapiro.

State Highway 29 in the Waikato is shut completely from Hinuera to Piarere.

Diversions are in place and vehicles are being turned around as the highway is expected to remain closed for most of the day.

Motorists should take alternative routes or delay travel.

World.title: Health Minister Simeon Brown denies telling hospitals to save money as flu surge bites
World.content:
Simeon Brown responds to concerns over health care system Morning Report Download MP3 13m

The health system has been under significant pressure this winter, with Auckland City Hospital saying it's been worse than expected.

On Tuesday, Tauranga Hospital emergency department (ED) staff declared a 'state of emergency', saying the ED was running up to 200 percent capacity without the staffing needed.

In July, ED staff at North Shore Hospital said they faced chronic understaffing with some patients waiting 50 hours.

Elective surgeries have also been postponed as winter illnesses surge.

In July, Christchurch Hospital ED's Dr Dominic Fleisher said a few minutes would be acceptable, but "patients are there for hours overnight". In August, St John's director of ambulance operations Doug Gallagher told us they were getting a call every 20 seconds, which was not sustainable.

"No doubt it's been a very challenging winter," Health Minister Simeon Brown told Morning Report on Wednesday. "In fact, it's been, I think, one of the worst influenza seasons in a very long time with very high levels entering our hospital system, and so it has put the system under significant pressure this winter and our frontline staff have been working incredibly hard to respond to that."

Brown said the coalition reintroduced targets scrapped by the previous government so it could be held accountable, claiming "year-on-year improvement as we work towards our 2030 health targets after years of decline".

Labour ditched the targets in 2018, saying they created perverse incentives.

The proportion of people being admitted, discharged or transferred from EDs within six hours was at 68 percent at the end of 2023, and had improved slightly - but about a quarter of people were still waiting longer than that, some several times longer than the six-hour target. The proportion was virtually unchanged from 12 months ago, the data showed, and as low as 57 percent in some regions.

The government's target is 95 percent nationwide by 2030.

"What I expect as minister of health is we want to see year-on-year improvement against all of our health targets, which is what we are seeing. We acknowledge there's too many people waiting too long."

Asked about short-staffing in EDs, Brown said recruitment was "happening up and down the country all of the time", saying the previous government's changes to the health system slowed decision-making processes down.

"We're now devolving that decision-making back down to districts and regions, so that those decisions can be made much faster. Now, that change is in process that is happening, but ultimately that context is important because it tells us where we were and where we're going."

Data showed only 54 new FTE nurses were employed by Health NZ in the two years from March 2024 to March 2026.

Asked if the lack of recruitment was down to orders to Health NZ to save money, Brown said he "never made that instruction".

"We put record funding into healthcare in every single Budget. We put more funding into our healthcare system and we continue to do so because ultimately we want to meet those health targets and we want to see people being seen faster and we want to see wait times reduced."

In 2025 Brown instructed hospitals and public health services across the country to find more than half-a-billion dollars in "efficiencies" to re-invest in patient care.

And in August, documents released under the Official Infomation Act showed strict recruitment rules had been in place throughout 2024/25, which a union described as showing "the health minister was aware that our health system was not filling hospital vacancies as part of a deliberate savings plan and that patient care has suffered as a result".

And recent data showed fewer than a quarter of adults have received the flu vaccine this year, similar to recent years - and targets for over-65s were not being met, dropping over the last few years, experts citing cost and post-Covid hesitancy.

The government did not extend the free flu vaccine to under-fives until 1 September, after the August peak in cases. Brown said that was a decision for Pharmac and Health NZ to make.

World.title: Woman falls through glass shower after fainting with flu
World.content:
This story contains a graphic image of an injury.

A woman who fainted through a glass shower door while sick with Influenza A is urging others to take the flu seriously, as a doctor warns hot showers can trigger fainting.

Kat Murray was 26 at the time of the incident two years ago, where she suffered multiple deep cuts in ther back, with the glass narrowly missing a critical nerve that could have left her paralysed.

Hospitalisations from flu and flu-like illnesses have been in the "very high" category for weeks, according to data from PHF Science. In Auckland they were at 10-year highs.

When Murray first woke up feeling unwell she assumed it was a cold and took the day off work, but the next day she felt even worse.

"I felt really cold so I took a hot shower to warm up, while I was in the shower I was hit by overwhelming nausea and instinctively tried to make it out to avoid being sick in the shower."

Murray remembered leaning towards the window before passing out.

"I fell backwards into the shower glass and went through it... there was blood everywhere, glass everywhere. I didn't know my name, the day of the week, anything."

Murray said her partner helped get her to a local A&E, where she sat in a blood-soaked jersey for four hours.

"It was scary - I had a big gash from my shoulder blade leading towards my neck and all the way down my back. I had eight stitches in one gash and the majority taped up so they couldn't split."

While there, Murray did a swab test to rule out Covid-19 and was told she had Influenza A.

"It took three weeks for all the stitches and the scabbing to heal and another three weeks to kind of normalise all the scar tissue. I've got a good handful of scars on my back still."

Murray said it was important for people to take having the flu seriously and to be more aware that it wasn't just a standard bug.

"We treat the flu like a minor inconvenience rather than the aggressive systematic threat it is," she said.

"Young people often feel invincible, pressuring themselves to keep working, moving and functioning when they need rest and proper medical care.

"Stay home, get checked by a doctor and take your health seriously."

Some of the injuries on Kat Murray's back. KAT MURRAY / SUPPLIED

Medical director at Tū Ora Compass Health, Dr Louise Poynton, said anyone could still get really unwell with the flu and it could be serious and needed to be treated a such.

Poynton said anyone who was unwell with a fever or dehydration had a higher chance of falling as it could lead to a drop in blood pressure.

"Hot water can cause blood vessels to relax which can also cause a drop in blood pressure."

For anyone with the flu it was important to stay hydrated and take care when moving from sitting to standing, as well as giving the body time to adjust before moving around after standing, Poynton said.

Jumping into a hot shower when feeling dizzy or light-headed could increase the risk of fainting.

She said even someone who was otherwise fit and healthy, would normally need between seven and 10 days at home to recover - and some effects of the flu could last several weeks.

"Anyone who has had it will take it seriously," she said.

While the number of cases this season seemed to be slowly easing, there were still a lot of cases around and doctors were sill seeing people with complications of the flu.

"Stay home if you're unwell, wear a mask, keep your house well ventilated... more broadly stay healthy - eat nutritious food, sleep well and stay active."

She also urged anyone who hadn't had a flu vaccine this year to get one as there was still time.

World.title: Fashion brand Cue in receivership
World.content:
Cue Clothing Co has gone into receivership along with its sister brand Veronika Maine.

In a statement, FTI Consulting, appointed as receivers and managers for Cue on Tuesday, said increased sales and other improvements across the group were not enough to offset the overhead costs, the ABC reported.

The company, which was founded in 1968, will continue trading while the receivers assess the business and restructuring options.

A sale process seeking offers for the business would "commence immediately" to secure the future of the brands, according to FTI Consulting.

Duncan Clubb and Shaun McKinnon of BDO were appointed as voluntary administrators on the same day.

It is unclear at this stage whether there will be any job losses due to the company's receivership.

Cue has three standalone retail shops and one department store presence in New Zealand.

Retail NZ said on Tuesday that it was still a turbulent time for retail.

Card spending in August was flat, with no change compared to the same month last year, after a 3.5 percent lift in July.

"We experienced a uniquely strong July buoyed by a public holiday and the men's Football World Cup gave a boost to hospitality, while an extra trading weekend and flat petrol prices gave shoppers more opportunity to spend, August represents a return to something more cautious" Retail NZ chief executive Carolyn Young said.

"Actual monthly spending on durables, which had performed strongly in July, was completely flat, while hospitality was down 1.8 percent. Consumables only saw a 1.4 percent increase on August 2025, well below the rate of inflation."

World.title: 'It's hell': Queenstown workers, mayor, firefighter fed up with traffic congestion
World.content:
Katie Todd reports fron Queenstown’s traffic jams Morning Report Download MP3 4m

Queenstown commuters say chronic traffic congestion is ruining their quality of life, with three-hour school bus rides and missed volunteer firefighter call-outs.

The regional tourism organisation warned in August that the town was struggling to cope with a big influx of tourists and Queenstown Lakes District mayor John Glover announced that he was setting up an anti-traffic congestion taskforce.

Fernhill's Ornella Proni said traffic jams were not confined to peak periods and seemed to strike at any time.

"It doesn't matter when you go, for example, to the supermarket. It could be midday and it's going to be hell. It's random," she said.

"There must be something they can do. This is not normal. You can try to stay at home or go out early in the morning or late but it's just a bit frustrating."

When Jono Brown first moved to Lake Hayes, he enjoyed a 15-minute commute to central Queenstown, but that quickly changed.

"The commute now can take anywhere from on a good day, around 30 minutes, to on a bad day around an hour," he said.

"When we moved down here from Auckland 12 years ago we didn't buy into Queenstown, with a 50,000-odd population, [being] stuck in traffic for 45 minutes to an hour. So yeah, it's frustrating."

Tanya Stone from Arthur's Point said traffic congestion was affecting her role as a volunteer firefighter.

"There are a fair few of us on that side of town that have not been able to make the truck in time, making turn-out times incredibly long and delaying an emergency response," she said.

Stone said she also worried about traffic delays working as the artist transfers co-ordinator for the Snow Machine festival.

"I briefed the whole entire driving team and I had to let everyone know, all the artists, that this is what we're experiencing in Queenstown at the moment, so be prepared for possible delays," she said.

Driving instructor Rachael Gerard said her business could not take on more clients, despite demand for afternoon lessons.

"I wouldn't take money off anybody to sit in a queue of traffic," she said.

"When you're teaching somebody to drive you have to be moving, you have to do manoeuvres. Now it's even becoming difficult even in between peak times like lunchtimes as well. You can often sit in a gridlock for 45 minutes to an hour-and-a-half trying to get somewhere."

Queenstown mayor John Glover said he decided to set up the traffic taskforce after hearing stories of three-hour school bus rides, people turning up late to school and missing appointments.

"When it's bad, it is really bad, and you don't know what's going to cause it. That's really challenging," he said.

Glover said the taskforce group of about 20 - comprising district and regional councillors, business leaders, transport representatives and mana whenua - had been working on practical traffic solutions.

Early ideas on the table included passenger ferries and traffic forecasting.

"I think we need to work out what is the most important thing to fund soon, and straight away? Where do we get that money from? If the normal sources just aren't going to work, we've got to be quite creative. Who else can pay? How else can we fund some of these?" he said.

Brown said he wanted the brakes put on major housing projects, particularly fast-tracked developments.

"Get the infrastructure in place before we build more residential houses. We've got 7000-odd residents in Lake Hayes Estate alone. The southern corridor's full," he said.

"The cart is so far ahead of the horse. It needs to slow down and we need to focus on the public transport solutions. There are some really good solutions out there, i.e. gondola."

Glover said the mayoral taskforce was aware of concerns about infrastructure and many more houses planned for Queenstown.

"We're getting thousands and thousands of houses being built, potentially through the fast-track and we know the state highway is already full," he said.

"We know NZTA's annual spend is going to decrease in real terms over the next three to five years. So everyone's looking around and saying, well, we're going to get busier and busier, the networks are already stretched at times and there's going to be no money coming in to address that, so that's a real concern."

Stone said the situation should never have been allowed to get so bad.

World.title: Pieces still missing from Tom Phillips inquiry - academic
World.content:
Lillian Hanly reports on reaction to Tom Phillips inquiry Morning Report Download MP3 3m

An expert on family violence says it is indefensible Family Court proceedings were excluded from the government's inquiry into the Tom Phillips case.

She says the government should be looking at reinstating protective mechanisms that were stripped out of the Care of Children Act in 2014, and she is "a little sympathetic" to police, with a caveat that she doesn't usually say that.

"It's just really hard for me to know whether we should be stringing them up by their toenails or not when we just don't know what came out of the Family Court."

Phillips was shot dead by police a year ago, after nearly four years on the run with his children.

Government ministers apologised on Tuesday after the damning inquiry found multiple failings by authorities including information sharing and following up certain leads.

Oranga Tamariki and police have admitted errors, although police dispute the inquiry's finding that agencies working together could have prevented the children's disappearance or brought them back sooner.

University of Auckland associate law professor Carrie Leonetti told RNZ the principal judge of the Family Court court could have opened its files to the inquiry, and although such files would be sensitive they could have been redacted from public view.

Lillian Hanly reports on reaction to Tom Phillips inquiry Morning Report Download MP3 3m

"The inquiry starts four years too late," she said.

"Tom Phillips had court ordered care of the children from 2019 at least, and was given court ordered care of the children back, it appears, in October 2021 after the first abduction.

"The inquiry makes very clear that Oranga Tamariki had... very limited involvement with Tom Phillips and the children before 2021... we're starting the movie half-way through."

Leonetti said the children's mother's concerns were not taken seriously partly because of her Family Court dispute with Phillips.

"It's pretty clear that these agencies brushed her concerns off ... It's well established in the social science literature that there's just this pervasive societal myth that women fabricate claims of domestic violence for some kind of tactical purpose in custody proceedings.

"And I think it's even worse for the Phillips kids' mother because she's Māori... a Māori woman trying to get the police and Oranga Tamariki to take her Pākehā ex-husband's threat to their children seriously.

"He made threats to her at the time of their separation in 2017 that he was going to take the kids and not let her see them again, and he he made those threats to third parties that he was going to take off with the kids and go bush."

She said there was a "weird sort of hot potato problem", where police, Oranga Tamariki and the Family Court would defer responsibility for a case to whichever of the three was approached first.

"If people go first to the Family Court and they award care to the person, then I think Oranga Tamariki and the police say to themselves, 'well, how dangerous can he be?'"

She said the report seemed to indicate police and Oranga Tamariki had made errors in the investigation or passing on information, but without the details from the Family Court "it's like we're looking at this mosaic with half of it blacked out".

Phillips may never have had unsupervised care of the children in 2019 and 2021 had the "Bristol clauses" that required courts to ensure a child's safety before granting custody in domestic violence-related cases not been scrapped under the John Key government in 2014.

"You go to Family Court, you lose custody of your kids to the perpetrator. You go to the police, they seem to write a lot of reports but not take a lot of action. You go to Oranga Tamariki and they roll your eyes and think you're a disgrunted ex-wife."

However, she said police may be right to say the situation may not have ended differently "if they had done everything right, but the Family Court and Oranga Tamariki still failed".

World.title: Renshaw scores first ODI century as Aussies defeat Zimbabwe
World.content:
Matt Renshaw has scored his first ODI century, while Nathan Ellis took five wickets to guide Australia to a ​59-run win over hosts Zimbabwe in the first clash of their three-match series.

Australia chose to bat first, and the surprise decision from captain Mitchell Marsh was vindicated as ​the tourists scored 8-294 from ‌their 50 overs, setting Zimbabwe an imposing target at Harare Sports Club.

In reply, Zimbabwe was dismissed for 235 in 45.1 overs, showing good fight but always behind ‌the required run rate.

Renshaw, who last scored an international ton in ⁠a Test against Pakistan in 2017, made 109.

He featured ‌in some key partnerships, while Cooper ​Connolly made 51.

Renshaw put on 72 runs with Alex Carey for the fifth wicket and 75 with Ollie Peake for the sixth wicket, leaving Zimbabwe with a ​required ‌run rate of 5.90.

The 20-year-old left-arm quick Newman Nyamhuri finished with 5-62, only the second Zimbabwe bowler to take five wickets in ⁠an ODI against Australia.

Zimbabwe lost four ‌wickets quickly before Craig Ervine ‌and Sikandar steadied the innings with a 98-run partnership that offered the hosts hope ‌of victory on a surface that traditionally gets better for batting as the day wears on.

Ellis had taken two ‌wickets ​in his first spell and when he was reintroduced, took three balls to clean bowl Ervine for 59 and put the brakes on Zimbabwe.

Sikandar was dispensed by Spencer Johnson for 57 to leave Zimbabwe ⁠still significantly adrift.

Ellis finished with 5-31 in 9.1 overs, also cleaning up the tail.

The second ODI ‌will be played on ‌Friday in Harare, ​after which Australia moves to South Africa.

Reuters

World.title: SA school charged after student hurt in hammer-throw incident
World.content:
Criminal proceedings have been lodged against an Adelaide school after a student was seriously injured during an athletics training incident.

A Christian Brothers College student was struck in the head with a hammer-throw ball at St Albans Reserve at Clearview on September 5, 2024.

In a statement, SafeWork SA said a worker was also allegedly "exposed to the risk of being struck".

It said it had lodged the proceedings against Edmund Rice Education Australia Colleges Ltd, trading as Christian Brothers College (CBC), in South Australia's Employment Court earlier this month.

The safety watchdog said it had charged the school with a category two offence under the Work Health and Safety Act.

"It is alleged that workers and students participating in athletics training at St Albans Reserve, Clearview, were exposed to risks to their health and safety while undertaking javelin and hammer throw activities, in close proximity to each other, on 5 September 2024," SafeWork SA said in the statement.

"SafeWork SA alleges the school failed to provide adequate instruction or training to workers responsible for organising and supervising the athletics training and failed to ensure its safety policies and procedures were followed."

SafeWork SA says it lodged the proceedings against Christian Brothers College earlier this month. (YouTube: SafeWork SA)

The safety watchdog said it would be further alleged that the school "failed to perform an adequate hazard identification and risk assessment for the athletics training".

According to the statement, the school allegedly "failed to maintain a safe work environment" by failing to ensure the hammer throwing was not carried out in close proximity to students participating in javelin and by not using a safety cage that complied with the relevant industry safety standards.

"SafeWork SA alleges these failures exposed workers and students to a risk of death or serious injury from being struck by a hammer throw ball," SafeWork SA said.

The matter is expected to appear in the SA Employment Court at a later date.

World.title: Cowan warns BBL privatisation could 'spiral out of control'
World.content:
Former Australian Test opener Ed Cowan believes that the Big Bash League doesn't need to rush privatisation to compete with other T20 leagues around the world.

A Cricket NSW board member, Cowan told the ABC Cricket Podcast fears of a player exodus to rival leagues was premature, and a move toward privatisation could "spiral out of control".

Cricket Australia (CA) confirmed earlier this month that they would go ahead with an opt-in model that allows states to take their BBL teams to market with the option of selling stakes or entire franchises to private investors.

"[In previous seasons] they've been able to reshape scheduling, to reshape international stars and the salary cap around that. We've seen already there's no friction to attracting some of the world's best players," Cowan said.

Former England captain Ben Stokes will join the Adelaide Strikers for BBL16. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde-ICC)

"Ben Stokes is going to Adelaide, Finn Allen has just signed a mega deal. So the argument that is put forward is we're gonna lose players to the South African League. We haven't lost one yet.

"There's a view that the business could be run more effectively, which would enable some time to work out whether you actually do need to sell your star assets or not.

"Because when you start burning the furniture to warm the house, it can spiral quickly out of control from there."

The BBL has, in recent seasons, reshaped the fixture of the competition to make it shorter and in turn has increased viewership and attracted some of the games biggest names.

In the 2025/26 BBL season fans were treated to the likes of Colin Munro, Chris Jordan, Muhammed Rizwan and Sam Billings tearing up the competition. Coupled with Australian Test stars like Steve Smith, Alex Carey and Mitchell Starc who joined the tournament after their international duties finished.

Steve Smith has played 40 matches for the Sydney Sixers, including 6 in BBL15. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

Compare that with recent seasons of The Hundred where Mitchell Marsh, Adam Zampa, Jos Buttler and Trent Boult were some of the biggest name players in that competition, all of whom have played in the tournament or are set to play in the upcoming BBL16 season.

Can't get enough cricket from Grandstand? Tune in for the latest cricket news, interviews and analysis from the ABC team in the Grandstand Cricket Podcast.

Cricket Australia believes that privatisation would allow the BBL to keep up with other T20 leagues around the world, like The Hundred in the UK and the SA20 in South Africa.

"There are opportunities now for our best Australian players to play in other leagues at the same time potentially with bigger salary caps. So when we talk about should we wait for two years or four years? No, we can't wait," CA chief executive Todd Greenberg said.

"Those challenges are on our doorstep today. So we've got to make some decisions about how we compete.

"We're a relatively small country in a big global sport. So it's incumbent on us to make decisions that we can compete with elsewhere and that's exactly what we're doing."

Cricket NSW has been the most vocally opposed to the current model, while Queensland Cricket has also said it will likely have further questions but intends to hold on to its BBL franchise for the time being.

Mitch March playing for the Leeds Sunrisers in The Hundred in the UK. (Getty Images: Annabel Lee-Ellis)

"We will closely monitor the sales process and at this stage, intend to retain 100 percent ownership of the Brisbane Heat, but of course remain open to private investment at the appropriate time," Qld Cricket Chair Kirsten Pike and CEO Terry Svenson said in a statement.

Meanwhile, Cricket Victoria is in support of the move, and will be the first to sell a license with the Melbourne Renegades set to be put to market to be sold in full.

"Private investment will unlock value for reinvestment across Victorian cricket, from the grassroots through to the elite game," Cricket Victoria Director Shaun Richardson said in a statement.

CA and the state's cricketing associations will continue negotiations ahead of the BBL16 and WBBL12 seasons starting, which are likely to be the last seasons involving the original eight franchises.

World.title: Dockers will not be 'ambushed' by 'galvanised' Swans, Longmuir vows
World.content:
Many see it as a golden opportunity for Fremantle to reach just their second AFL grand final, but Justin Longmuir insists there is no chance the Dockers will underestimate a Sydney side missing a host of star players in Friday night's preliminary final at the SCG.

Fremantle is set to enter the game as warm favourite, despite being away from home against a team which thrashed reigning premier Brisbane by 53 points in their qualifying final, with the Swans hard hit by suspension and injury.

When Sydney stood down Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice in the wake of the off-field scandal at a Melbourne hotel, Swans chairman Andrew Pridham said they had "effectively torpedoed" their season.

Remarkably since then, they have defied expectations, beating North Melbourne just days later before the stunning upset of the Lions.

Swans show what 'Bloods' culture is supposed to look like Many questions were asked about Sydney's famed culture in the wake of the Pullman Hotel scandal. As the finals got underway, the players showed exactly what it is supposed to look like on the field.

That was despite losing Callum Mills during the game, with the captain joining the long list of absentees, ruled out for the season with a knee injury.

Longmuir has urged his side to put its full focus on the Sydney players who are taking the field, rather than those ruled out.

"Already done that. They dropped 141 points on Brisbane who were the flag favourites, it's a wake-up call," he said.

Errol Gulden and the Swans are undermanned but coming off a dominant qualifying final win. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"They didn't seem to miss those guys, so we just play what's in front of us.

"Clearly they haven't lost any of their scoring power, and all I can go on is what I see from the last two games, and playing like a really galvanised team, playing with great spirit, great physicality.

"It looks like whatever has happened has galvanised them, and they're playing a really tough brand of footy.

"We're definitely not going up there and getting ambushed by what they're trying to do. We've seen [it] in the last couple of weeks and we've seen it work really well.

"We've got to make sure that we don't just think it's going to happen for us, we've got to make sure we impose our footy."

Longmuir calls for no fear

The Dockers rebounded from their qualifying final loss to Hawthorn with a 14-point semifinal victory over Geelong, with Longmuir pleased with how his players took the contest on against the Cats.

Luke Jackson was instrumental in Fremantle's semifinal win and shapes as a big factor against Sydney. (Getty Images: James Wiltshire/AFL Photos)

He urged his side to not to be afraid of making mistakes on the big stage, and to always be prepared to move on to the next contest.

"If we're going to make mistakes, let's make sure we make mistakes playing our way and playing with the right mindset, because usually those mistakes you can move on from a little bit quicker," he said.

Dockers show they have the steel to be AFL's best Fremantle booked a spot in the AFL preliminary finals with a stirring win over Geelong, breathing life into the club's premiership dream.

"At times we didn't make those mistakes the right way against Hawthorn and we stood still after, because we didn't move on from them.

"It's been a message for a long time because we play such an imperfect game, players who have played their best games would've been full of mistakes. It's just the nature and the scrappiness of our game, so let's make them with the right mindset."

The Dockers are set to fly to Sydney on Wednesday, with the two clubs naming their teams on Thursday ahead of the clash.

World.title: The moment this Knights finals rookie will hold on to forever
World.content:
Last Friday's semifinal win over South Sydney was one of the great nights in Newcastle's recent history, and nobody enjoyed it more than Jermaine McEwen.

In his first finals match, the 21-year-old had the game of his young life, inspiring the 20-10 upset victory that has the whole Hunter dreaming big ahead of Sunday's sudden-death clash with the Warriors.

McEwen scored the first double of his NRL career and ran for 187 metres, the best mark of his 37 first-grade matches, and set the tone for the Knights' right-edge defence with a physical brutality that would make a mafia kingpin proud.

Knights win is proof the future has come Stars were born under the finals lights as Newcastle knockout finals win over South Sydney announced the dawn of a new tomorrow.

On a night of many highlights, McEwen's personal favourite was his second try that helped Newcastle kick clear in the second half, as he backed up winger Dom Young to score right in front of the Knights faithful.

McEwen crawled the last few metres before slamming the ball down so hard it's a wonder they could dig it out of the turf.

"The only reason I slammed it was because my parents and my family were right in front of me. I just looked at them, and I was like, 'hell yeah,'" said McEwen.

"That was the best moment I have ever had in my footy career. That moment right there, that's something I will hold forever. So I am just super grateful and so happy."

McEwen's first try of the evening helped get things started as he again trailed Young after the Englishman claimed a bomb inside the first five minutes.

It brought Newcastle into the match and gave the team the start they needed en route to their first away finals win since 2013 and just their third since their last premiership 25 years ago.

Repeating the dose in Auckland is a tall order, but even before the win over Souths, McEwen and his teammates did not lack for belief.

"The Knights have given me everything, and I believe in the coach, Justin (Holbrook). He's allowed me to be the greatest version of myself on that field," said McEwen.

"But when I put the ball down and looked up and saw all the fans, I was (thinking) how happy I am to be a Knight. I'm just so grateful.

"We just wanted to go out there and play with energy and lift each other up."

Newcastle's right edge did a fine job shutting down South Sydney's attack. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

McEwen spent much of the week thinking about how the Knights would shut down South Sydney's left edge, which is just about the most dangerous attacking weapon in the NRL.

Between them, Alex Johnston, Latrell Mitchell, Tallis Duncan and Cody Walker scored 63 tries in 2026, two more than Newcastle managed as an entire club last season.

But McEwen, Sandon Smith and Dane Gagai rose to the occasion magnificently, locking onto the superstars and refusing to let go, moving and defending as one.

Souths did end up scoring down the left through Jye Grey, but only after McEwen had left the field late on.

"When you have challenges, you get more prepared for it. You think about it more. When you're at home or training, you get flashbacks of what you have to do," said McEwen.

"When I have Cody Walker and their left edge — they do it the best in the whole comp. Cody Walker, he is just so good at that stuff.

"Us in D, we had a big job to do, and we just went out there and did it."

Jermaine McEwen and the Knights will look to pull off another finals ambush this Sunday against the Warriors. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

The journey through this year to Sunday's knockout final has not always been smooth for McEwen.

He was suspended for one match in June after being charged with low-range drink driving, an incident for which he apologised unreservedly and left him "deeply ashamed".

At the time, McEwen said he let his community down, and he's been trying to make amends ever since.

"Bro, at the end of the day we're all human and just because I play footy doesn't mean I'm special," said McEwen.

"In those circumstances, with the rollercoaster (of this year), that has taught me a lot in life.

"I feel like people can either shy away from it or own up to it. I wanted to show up for the fans and show them what I could do, and repay them in that way."

"Because I know how much the town speaks to this club and the hold this club has on the town. I wanted to repay them with good footy."

A sellout crowd is expected at Eden Park on Sunday, and a win would send Newcastle to just its second preliminary final in the last 25 years.

They'll again be underdogs against a Warriors side that beat them just three weeks ago, and the match marks the biggest game of McEwen's career, as it is for several of his teammates.

But the same was true last Friday, and by leaning on the experience of men like Gagai and prop Tyson Frizell, McEwen was inspired to make a difference, and all he wants is to do it all over again.

"These are experienced boys who have been in the game for a lot of years, and when you have them talk to you, it makes you more comfortable," said McEwen.

"You're not nervous. You're going out there to do a good job."

World.title: HYROX apologises after Aussie athlete soils herself mid-race
World.content:
A founder of HYROX has apologised after an athlete who suffered sudden faecal incontinence mid-competition was allowed to continue, with the incident sparking rule changes after backlash online.

Australian athlete Joanna Wietrzyk experienced the medical episode during the competition that she went on to win in Beijing at the weekend.

The incident went viral on Chinese social media, with videos of her competing while visibly soiled shared widely.

HYROX sees competitors combine running with multiple workout station challenges, including sandbag lunges, burpees, sled pushes and rowing using shared equipment.

Joanna Wietrzyk (middle in black top) holds the HYROX Women's Solo Pro world record. (Instagram: joannawietrzyk)

Following the incident, many online criticised HYROX's health and safety standards, while some also questioned athlete responsibility.

"Blast HYROX. Blast the race director," Chris Hersh posted on a HYROX community Facebook page.

"But please leave the athlete alone or have a tiny bit of empathy for someone that really just was in a horrible situation and got zero assistance from anyone in a high pressure, make a decision on the fly scenario."

HYROX co-founder Moritz Fürste took to Instagram to apologise "to all who were directly or indirectly involved".

"HYROX made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race," Fürste said in a statement on Instagram.

"In the end it is my job to foresee these potential incidents — and I did not."

He said that new event procedures and rules were being drawn up to "prevent situations like this from happening again".

The rules now state that if a "racer's blood, vomit, urine, or faeces poses a welfare or contamination risk to the racer or to other racers, a Race Director may withdraw the racer from the race on medical grounds".

Before the rule change, competitors were penalised for littering, spitting, or clearing their nostrils onto the race course, which some online described as a double standard.

Following the event in Beijing, HYROX World issued a statement saying that "protocols designed for elite competition and mass participation became blurred, creating ambiguity in how they were applied and understood".

HYROX China said the competition area was cleaned after the competition finished and relevant equipment was removed.

It also said it would replace the floor at the venue to protect future athletes.

The incident went viral in China, with many taking aim at HYROX organisers and rules. (Weibo, RedNote and Douyin)

Wietrzyk, an elite HYROX athlete, was invited to compete at the Beijing event.

She has been contacted for comment.

The ABC has also contacted HYROX for comment.

Event's growing popularity

HYROX is held in indoor venues, with a consistent race format that lets athletes compete against each other worldwide.

Organisers say it suits both elite athletes and people trying to improve their general fitness.

Chinese netizens have described HYROX as "paying to do farm work", with an individual entry fee of 799 yuan (about $170), on top of the cost of training and equipment.

The sport has attracted Chinese celebrities, including elite athletes, singers, and actors, helping it reach beyond the traditional fitness crowd.

Hybrid training is a healthy social media trend Thousands of social media followers are trying out the hybrid training model, but it's not something to dive straight into.

Some Chinese media have even dubbed HYROX "the new identity card of the middle class".

HYROX held its first event in mainland China in November 2024, attracting fewer than 1,700 contestants.

By 2025, average registrations had surged to 5,079 per event — more than three times the previous year's figure, according to Grace Yu, research director at Daxue Consulting.

"China's HYROX scene is heavily community-oriented, with doubles and relay formats accounting for roughly 66-72 per cent of Beijing participants across 2024-2026," Ms Yu said.

By April 2026, the #hyrox hashtag on Xiaohongshu, known as RedNote outside China, had surpassed 130 million views and generated more than 780,000 discussions.

World.title: Young Brisbane Lions star Logan Morris re-signs with reigning premiers
World.content:
Young Brisbane Lions star Logan Morris has signed a two-year contract extension, tying him to the club until the end of 2029.

The 21-year-old, who earned his first All-Australian blazer this year, was set to be one of the biggest names on the market at the end of next season.

The signing comes as the Lions prepare to take on the Hawks in a preliminary final on Saturday at the MCG.

"There’s no point dragging [contract negotiations] out if I know what I want to do, and I wanted to stay at Brisbane," Morris said.

"I wanted to just get it done and now I can focus on this week, and hopefully the next few years will be exciting."

Morris kicked 67 goals in the 2026 home-and-away season, finishing second in the Coleman Medal behind Sydney's Charlie Curnow.

It marks the third huge signing coup for the Lions in a week, after Zac Bailey and Dayne Zorko also extended their careers with the club.

When asked about interest from other clubs that may have made higher offers, Morris said he had not given much thought to the money.

"I just thought … more about what I'm happy with and the team that I'm at; I don't want to leave a team where I'm happy where I am mentally and I've got a good group of mates," he said.

"I think playing within a good team that’s got good values and playing with all my mates is more valuable to me than a bit more money, so that's what it ultimately came down to."

World.title: Ella Heads cops big ban for bump that broke star Demon's jaw
World.content:
Port Adelaide defender Ella Heads has been handed a three-match AFLW ban for her bump that fractured the jaw of Melbourne's Eliza McNamara.

McNamara had just fired off a handball in Sunday's 51-point win when Heads ran in and collected the midfielder front-on with her shoulder.

A dazed McNamara had blood coming out from her face as she was assisted from the ground.

The 24-year-old was taken to hospital, with the Demons confirming on Monday she had undergone surgery, with no timeline set for her return.

The incident was classified as careless conduct, severe impact and high contact, drawing a three-match ban.

"That was a really poor challenge," former AFLW star Kate McCarthy said.

"It was probably one of the worst bumps I’ve seen on the AFLW field in regards to being late, being high and just being really careless and not eliciting that duty of care that we now know is placed on you as an AFLW player when you elect to bump."

That equates to a quarter of the 12-round home-and-away season, and Heads will miss games against Sydney, the Western Bulldogs and Adelaide unless Port can downgrade the charge.

In other tribunal news, West Coast's Abbygail Bushby was handed a one-match ban for her clumsy collision with the Brisbane Lions' Sophie Peters.

Peters had her head over the ball when Bushby ran in and tumbled over her opponent.

Richmond's Montana McKinnon was handed a one-match rough conduct ban for her run-in with St Kilda's Jesse Tawhiao-Wardlaw.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

Tech.title: What if social media isn’t hurting kids?
Tech.content:
Two years ago, social psychologist Jonathan Haidt released his New York Times bestseller The Anxious Generation. The book posits that the rise of social media and smartphone use is largely to blame for the prominent decline in teen mental health since 2010. It quickly became a central rallying cry of the social media backlash. Haidt has been credited with helping inspire Australia’s nationwide teen social media ban. He has joined forces with bereaved parents who are fighting tech companies in court. His name comes up unprompted in conversations with people in power who say his book opened their eyes to an online crisis.

Haidt’s theory has received regular critiques from recognized academics. Candice Odgers, a leading adolescent mental health researcher, wrote a scathing review of Haidt’s analysis in Nature that opened by conceding, “this book is going to sell a lot of copies, because Jonathan Haidt is telling a scary story about children’s development that many parents are primed to believe.” Now, in the wake of that highly accurate prediction, a former colleague of Haidt’s seeks to not only take down his theory, but also offer an alternative. The biggest question may not be whether he’s correct — but whether it’s too late to change course if he is.

In his new book Restoring Childhood, psychology researcher Peter Gray argues that teens’ mental health declined thanks to decades of steadily reduced autonomy, and after a brief period of reprieve, fell again in the 2010s not — as Haidt argues — because of phones and social media, but because of rigid schooling methods linked to the Common Core curriculum and government pressure to improve children’s performance. And far from being damaging, Gray also argues the adoption of home internet in the 1990s and 2000s actually drove a rebound in teens’ mental health by restoring freedom and connection lost in earlier decades. He fears social media bans aren’t just — as Odgers has argued — a distraction from real solutions, but a new harm in themselves.

“You take a smartphone away from your kids and that study suggests you’ll make them less happy”

In an interview on The Vergecast, Gray told me that Haidt’s book “completely ignored” dozens of meta-analyses and other research that’s found “not even a meaningful correlation between the amount of time kids are on social media or on smartphones and their mental health.” Where there is some connection, Gray adds, studies suggest that teens may use social media to cope with their depression or anxiety. He references a study in Florida that found 11-to-13-year-olds who owned smartphones were more likely to spend real-world time with friends. “You take a smartphone away from your kids and that study suggests you’ll make them less happy and they’ll have less friends,” he says.

Gray says that in studies through the years, kids consistently identify school pressure, not social media, as their top source of anxiety. “That doesn’t mean it’s the primary source for everybody, but when you’re looking at the population at large, every single study that I’ve been able to find where kids are asked, ‘What’s the primary source of your anxiety or your stress or your depression?’, in every single one of them, school pressure comes out on top,” Gray tells me. “Nothing else comes close.”

Gray and Haidt both believe that since at least the 1980s, increased restrictions on kids’ independence and unstructured play have damaged their resilience. While it used to be common for kids to play together unsupervised, that practice has diminished in part due to the rise of “stranger danger” narratives fostered by rare, but high-profile, crimes. In 2017 the pair helped cofound an organization called Let Grow, which advocates for policies that make it easier for parents to let their children play freely, like ensuring they can’t be considered neglectful for letting kids outside by themselves. But the two have split sharply over the impact of the internet. Gray’s book is intended as a deliberate rebuttal to Haidt’s — after The Anxious Generation’s release, Gray resigned from the board of Let Grow to avoid conflict within the organization.

Haidt did not respond to a request for comment from The Verge, but he told The Atlantic’s Kaitlyn Tiffany in a July article that the 1990s and early 2000s dip in teen suicide rates may be credited to a phase-out of leaded gasoline, since lead exposure has been linked to mental health issues. He also told Tiffany that Gray relied too heavily on a minority dissenting group of researchers. Tiffany writes that many of the more than a dozen tech and child development researchers she spoke to “expressed concern that Haidt overstates the strength of correlational findings and suggests causation where it hasn’t been proved.”

Gray accuses Haidt of stirring a moral panic over technology that isn’t, on the whole, harmful. Looking across research, he says, Common Core is the clearest explanation for the sudden decline in teen mental health. And at the population level, the impact of social media “balances out. Some kids are doing better, some kids are doing worse because they’re on social media.”

“We need to stop treating kids as if they’re idiots”

Gray says he’s not opposed to all guardrails, including school phone bans and the concept of age verification for accessing pornography. But he questions the effectiveness of bans on social media, knowing kids are likely to get around them, and is hesitant to restrict platforms that let kids express themselves — suggesting instead that parents focus on teaching their children to navigate them. “We need to stop treating kids as if they’re idiots,” he told me. “We need to start understanding that kids are pretty good at knowing what’s good for them and not good for them and they can benefit from our help in learning how to do these things.”

But increasingly, parents of younger teens may not have that choice. Haidt’s theory holds undisputed dominance in many circles, including among politicians. Since Australia’s social media ban for teens, the UK and European Union are among those considering their own bans or platform limits. In the US, states like California and New York have enacted limits on certain social media features, and a federal proposal would restrict algorithmic feeds for kids under 17. Even among people who find Gray’s arguments about Common Core convincing, some might still see taking kids offline as a harmless precaution.

With so much momentum behind the backlash against phones and social media, can Gray’s book still make a difference? “I certainly hope it’s not too late,” he says. He points out that some moral panics have petered out. In the 1990s and 2000s, for instance, many people worried that video games like Mortal Kombat and Doom were making kids more violent, connecting their rise to that of school shootings. Eventually, research showed many mass shooters didn’t play video games after all. Attempts at regulation — including a California ban on the sale of violent games to children — were largely overruled. And many kids who did play them grew up to become those in charge. “The science won out eventually,” Gray says. “So it’s not me that’s going to win out. It’s the science that’s going to win out.”

Tech.title: Kia’s electric van lineup is getting more interesting with reveal of PV7
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

You may not know it, but minivans are making a comeback in the US. Look around, and you’ll start to notice an uptick in these breadboxes on wheels. Sales were up 21 percent in 2025, suggesting that the humble minivan is shaking off its “uncool” stigma and finding new fans among an SUV-weary public. I’m here for it.

One of the companies currently carrying the torch for minivans is Kia, which has sold its popular Carnival minivan here since 2021. Kia is also one of the few automakers making all-electric vans. This week, the Korean automaker rolled out its new PV7 at IAA Transportation in Germany. This is the second electric van from Kia’s Platform Beyond Vehicle (PBV) lineup, following the PV5 “people mover,” which went on sale in 2025. The PV7 is longer than the PV5 by about 2 feet and comes in two variants, one for passengers and one for cargo.

All of which is to say that Kia should bring its increasingly interesting electric vans to the US. If they are attractively priced — and this is Kia, so it’s safe to assume that’s possible — I really think these vans would do numbers. The people yearn for a moderately priced electric van!

Previous Next







1 / 5

The PBV vans are technically impressive on several levels. They’re built on Kia’s dedicated PBV architecture (E-GMP.S) that features a flat-floor layout for easy loading and unloading. The PV7 will come with a 71.5kWh nickel-manganese-cobalt battery pack or a 96.2kWh one. Kia claims the Cargo Long-Range version will get 460km (285.8 miles) on the generous WLTP cycle (which tends to be around 10–20 percent more generous than the EPA’s estimates). It’s built on an 800-volt architecture, which enables 10—80 percent charging in under 25 minutes using a 350kW DC fast charger. And it supports vehicle-to-load outlets to power external tools and equipment. The infotainment runs on Kia’s Android Automotive-based Pleos Connect OS, which includes its Gleo AI natural-language voice controls.

Previous Next









1 / 6

This all sounds great! And the design is just forward-looking enough to erase any concerns about the typical clunkiness of van ownership. The front end features a distinctive two-tone design with a dark upper section that wraps around the windshield, giving it a visor-like appearance. The upright look and tall, flat roof suggests a large interior space perfect for vanlife compartmentalization. The low front bumper and plastic body cladding around the base add a rugged, practical border. Both the passenger and cargo versions feature distinctive wheels with a squarish multi-spoke design. It’s not boring, but it’s not so in your face as to challenge your worldview.

While Kia’s not saying whether the PV7 will be making its way to the US anytime soon, a version has been spotted testing in the US, according to Electrek. Officially, the van will be launched in Europe and Korea in the second half of 2027, with “additional markets, derivatives and conversion models to follow.”

PBV was introduced during CES 2024 as a family of EVs built on a flexible vehicle architecture with different swappable body types. The vehicle can be transformed from a minivan to a full-size van to a small truck, depending on the specific need. The driver cab remains fixed, while the rest of the vehicle is interchangeable, like a real-life Duplo set. Of course, that was a concept from a different era. We’ve now veered into a darker timeline, at least for EVs.

I get why Kia would hesitate to name the US as a future market, what with our well-documented history of cutting off our nose to spite our face. The minivan market may not be as red-hot as, say, the one for lifted trucks that roll coal and grind up spandex-wearing cyclists for breakfast. But the times, they are a-changing. Gas prices are going up and up. And an electric van could just be thing that finally heals our broken nation.
